(Title Page) Oṃ.
The Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies.
Volume Number 60:
The *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī*,
composed by the venerable and eminent teacher of the Great Maheśvara, Śrīmad Abhinavagupta.
By the command of His Majesty the illustrious Harisiṃhajī Bahādur, King of Kings, Emperor of Great Kings, Sovereign of Kashmir,
the Superintendent of the Research Institute, Paṇḍita—
After the correction and other refinements by Madhusūdanakaula Śāstrī, assisted by other scholars at the designated office.
Having been completed and printed at the Nirṇayasāgara Press in Mumbai, it has been brought to light.
(First Part)
Samvat 1994, Śrīnagara, Kashmir; the Christian year 1938. (The rights to print and publish this work have been secured by the aforementioned noble Maharaja.)
(Page 1) Now begins the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī*.
Composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, the venerable Abhinavaguptapāda.
*Oṃ*, salutations to the embodiment of auspiciousness!
Bearing that heart which is inseparable from the triad of Śaktis, and making it one with his own self—

May that glorious abode of Bhairava be victorious, which manifests as the universal form through its readiness to accept the collection of hymns offered as gifts by the inner selves of devotees; it is the throbbing of the path of intense joy, firmly established within the physical forms appearing and disappearing [within it]. || 1 ||
Having obtained grace from the Lord, who illuminates the mass of his own splendor,
and having found a firm footing in this body fashioned by Narasiṃhagupta, [Abhinavagupta],
following the path shown by Śrī Lakṣmaṇagupta, [is established] in the procedure of the venerable Pratyabhijñā.
The disciple’s disciple composes this commentary, the *Ṭīkārthapravimarśinī*, for his teacher.
It brings about maturation regarding the means of valid cognition consisting in the functioning of words,
and it repeatedly shatters the anxiety of the fear of death;
such is the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* for one of fresh intellect.
In the very investigation of the words of the commentary, both worldly enjoyment and liberation [are found]. (3)
Compelled by the request of his younger brother, who has proclaimed the true path of his heart's desire, Abhinavagupta— who has established his own self within the state of the "Good Foot"—
reveals this path so that even ordinary people may become transcendent (*unmanāḥ*).
He proceeds to that abode of Śiva, which is not visible on the path to the eyes of bound souls (paśus).

Having purified himself by plunging into the complete grammatical treatises, he worships the deity of his heart with the flowers of discernment from the wish-fulfilling vine of wisdom, which has its roots in right reasoning.

Now I rest, accompanied by the beloved of the narrative of non-dual Īśvara, partaking in the satiation of great literature which is as beautiful as the essence of nectar and wine— an infinite, unsurpassed nectar situated within the wheel of the sixteen powers of Aghora.
I bow to that which serves as the primary prologue for the firm establishment in the state beyond the mind.

In this work, there is but one author of the treatise, the illustrious one named Utpala, who— having had his limitations removed by the grace of the feet of the venerable Somānanda, our supreme preceptor— has sanctified the horizons with the fragrance of the blossoming lotus of his own heart, and has composed the aphorisms, the commentary, and the sub-commentary for the sake of establishing the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.

He composed [this work]. Therein, abiding in the status of the author of the aphorisms (*sūtrakāra*), he reflects upon himself as being somehow prostrate before Maheśvara by means of the words "kathaṃcit" and so forth; perceiving the necessity of the commentary (*vṛtti*) by way of reciting those very words, he then abides in the status of the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) through another mode of activity.

This is so that even the author of the Sūtras— who has reached this very stage— may demonstrate that he does not perceive the constant flow of devotion toward the Supreme Lord within his own self. Furthermore, although this was shown in the Vṛtti through grammatical coreferentiality (*svasāmānādhikaraṇya*) as "I recognize [Him] and may I be satisfied," [it is stated here again].
By [the words] beginning with "ityādinā," otherwise it would have to be stated that the author of the Sūtra himself composed it in this way;

and the purpose of showing that is to dispel the suspicion that the author of the Commentary (Vṛttikṛt) might not have understood the meaning of the Sūtra. Even in pointing that out, his intention is not one free from doubt, but rather for the sake of providing an explanation of the meaning once it has become clear.
It has been stated merely by way of synonym in this manner, as you know from the method of explaining the commentary on poetry: "Some of my activities are not for my own sake" (Kumārasambhava 6.26).

In this context, when the statement of the Blessed One is being explained, even though the commentator explains that "I have no activities of my own," one might still suspect that he is not perceived as non-different from the Blessed One himself;
for this [statement] consists precisely in the performance of a different salutation.

(Page 3) The activity of the Teacher— consisting first in the composition of the Sūtra and immediately thereafter in the composition of the commentary (*vṛtti*) on that Sūtra— indicates his unity; otherwise, it would not be so.

Because it is impossible for the manifestation of the single reality (*bhūta*) to be sustained [otherwise], the author of the treatise, who occupies the position of the commentator (*ṭīkākāra*), must necessarily be joined with another purposeful activity (*pravṛtti*). And in that case, the reading of the root verse (*mūlaśloka*) does not precede it;
for its introductory sequence (*avatāraṇakrama*) must necessarily be stated, and in that other activity—

When that which is inevitable occurs, the contemplation of prostration toward the Supreme Lord must once again be necessarily recollected. For even the mere unfolding of this entire manifold of objects and subjects— which is established within both oneself and others— is but the manifestation of the power of the Lord recognized through *pratyabhijñā*.

It is nothing other than being directed toward the Supreme Lord; what need is there to mention the formal construction of the means of knowledge consisting in the recognition of the power of the Lord? Nevertheless, according to the logic of the festival of a king, the adornments of a woman whose husband is under her control, and the arising of the festival of love, one must necessarily attend to the reflection upon one's own essential nature, which is the complete essence of that [recognition].
That which falls between the two activities must be performed for the sake of conceiving the success of the future activity.

Furthermore, the fact that [this work] was composed by a single author will be stated by the author himself in the passage beginning with "In the threefold speech" (*trayyāṃ vāci*). In this regard, this author, having attained the status of a commentator (*ṭīkākāra*), [will address] the context of the treatise to be explained...
Having disregarded— even though it must necessarily be performed for the sake of instructing others— the preliminary objection (*pūrvapakṣa*) and its refutation,

which are like the husk, the chaff, and the straw [of the grain], he performs a salutation with the words "By his own will," etc., in order to grasp that supreme, stable, and most essential object of attainment.
Salutations to Śiva, whose very nature is the course of all worldly existence manifested according to his own will,
and whose activity is eternally unobstructed, pure, and autonomous.
"From itself" means from the Self; "in itself" means in the Self alone.

And by its own will, all worlds—whether pure, impure, or mixed—which appear as subjects and objects, having been brought forth and manifesting through mutual exclusion in the form of duality, [arise]. And of these...

The "journeys" (*yātrāḥ*) are acquisitions consisting of mutual relations, such as the diversity of cause-and-effect, action-and-agent, and so forth; their "self" (*ātmā*) is the ultimate nature, which is Śiva himself.
And although this term is one, due to the differentiation of its powers (*śakti*), [it assumes various forms].

(On page 4) Through repetition in the tantra or otherwise, it embraces many meanings— just like the meanings of mantras concerning the internal (*adhyātma*), the divine (*adhidaiva*), and the sacrificial (*adhiyajña*)— and is employed in this manner for the sake of achieving simultaneous ascension to a single certainty, as he will state:

Regarding the word "śleṣayā" (by means of union): the word "namaḥ" (salutation) illuminates an act of bowing down directed toward that Blessed One who is of such a nature—that is, it expresses a state of prostration with respect to Him. Now, [one might ask]: does He not, by His own will, manifest the entire expansion of the objects of knowledge and the knowing subject—which exists in its own essential nature—as something external to that very essence?

While contemplating external objects, he causes even those things that have become external to manifest within his own self; and since he alone is the self of those very things as they are thus manifested, all of this appears to be contradictory.
For it is precisely this: the entire course of worldly existence proceeds while resting within the essential nature of the conscious self.

How, then, is this to be understood? If [the object] is manifested externally by its very own will, then how is it that it is now manifested within itself? For manifestation within oneself as non-differentiation is contradictory to manifestation externally; for that which is manifesting cannot at that very same time manifest elsewhere.

It is logical that it is external to that [the body], just as a jar is both inside a house and outside of it. Furthermore, it is utterly contrary to experience to claim that Śiva alone is the self of these [objects] even while they appear in such a way;
for appearing in such a manner is pervaded by the manifestation of duality, whereas being of the nature of Śiva is not.

Since these [entities] are pervaded by their unity, which is the opposite of that [multiplicity], who could believe that these entities are simultaneously both manifold and unitary? Furthermore, for what purpose does his will arise to manifest externally the collection of the objects of knowledge and the knowing subject, which are established within his own self?

Or [it may be] without cause. If one accepts the arising of such a desire, then that state would exist either eternally or never at all; suspecting that all this is largely inconsistent, he says "constantly" (*śaśvat*). As for what was stated—that the entire universe rests within the self of Śiva—how is this so? To that, it is replied: here...
The existence or non-existence of entities cannot be established without resting upon consciousness; for it is only when they rest upon consciousness that [they are established].

Entities become manifest. And this manifestation of theirs is nothing other than non-difference from consciousness (*saṃvit*), for manifestation itself is consciousness. If it were said that they are distinct from that manifestation yet still manifest, then blue would be called "blue" while being distinct from its own nature. Therefore, these [entities] reside within consciousness.

It follows that all entities are at rest, for their activity does not exceed that of consciousness. Furthermore, a division within consciousness itself is not tenable; for if a distinction were established between one consciousness and another based on a difference in essential nature within consciousness—which is of the single form of luminosity—it would imply that one of them lacks the nature of luminosity.

Otherwise, it would follow that consciousness itself would lack the nature of consciousness. Furthermore, if these objects of knowledge—which share an identity with its own essential nature—were to tolerate being differentiated by themselves, they might even differentiate consciousness through their own power.
However, they are not capable of assuming differentiation from their own side. Thus, this [differentiation] of theirs must be produced solely by consciousness.

This distinction is clearly a case of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore, since space and time rest upon the mass of objects of cognition, they too—by virtue of being cognizable—assert their identity with consciousness; how then could they divide that consciousness? For the entire mass of objects of cognition is non-different from the Light (*prakāśa*). Whatever shines forth, that...

It is non-different from light, just like the light of consciousness (*saṃvit*). For it is not logical that something different from light—which is itself non-luminous—should possess luminosity, due to the contradiction involved. Thus, because luminosity is the opposite of being different from light, it excludes here the state of non-luminosity, which is contrary to its own nature.
Having disregarded that which has established its footing [as an external object], it is pervaded by being non-different from manifestation;

thus, in the establishment of this pervasion (*vyāpti*), there is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Furthermore, those who cannot tolerate the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of consciousness should be understood as having been refuted by this very argument. Therefore, just like the difference among objects of cognition, even the difference of space and time does not belong to consciousness.

The differentiator [objects]. Furthermore, limiting adjuncts such as space, time, and so forth, can never divide an entity that is non-different from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). They merely establish a difference in nature that is already occurring; however, in the case of consciousness (*saṃvit*), there is no difference in nature whatsoever under any circumstances.

For it has been stated that [the Lord] is of the singular nature of light (*prakāśa*). Therefore, these entities (*bhāva*) ultimately rest within light itself. And light is never devoid of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Consequently, reflective awareness alone is the eternal will of the Blessed One, consisting of the pleasure and pain of the class of subjects—the Rudras and the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*).
(Page 6) It illuminates the collection of objects of cognition, such as blue, yellow, and so forth; and even while thus appearing,
it rests within the very light that consists of consciousness (*saṃvit*), for otherwise its very existence would be like a mere mental construction, and furthermore—

It does not abandon its nature as pure luminosity, for if it did, there would be the absurd consequence that even a blade of grass distinct from that luminosity would not be manifest. Thus, how could such a thing—which is appearing—be denied?
Therefore, there is no contradiction here whatsoever. For if blue were indeed not abandoning its state of being the manifestation of blue...
If [consciousness] were to manifest as something other than blue, who could proclaim the absence of contradiction between blue and non-blue?

Here, however, blue and the rest, while manifesting without ever abandoning their status as blue and so forth, consist of nothing other than non-difference from manifestation. This very thing is the sovereign freedom (*svācchandyam*) of the Blessed Lord—that which consists of the nature of consciousness.

Thus existing, although not exceeding the nature of consciousness, He shines forth and likewise reflects upon Himself as having a body that appears to exceed the nature of consciousness by way of the manifold subjects and objects;
the appearance of that which is not in excess as if it were in excess is called "transparency," just like that of a mirror. For that [mirror]—

That which, through various worldly transactions— such as walls, houses, elephants, horses, men, jars, and potters, as well as the relations of part and whole, locus and located, cause and effect, and so forth— is, even by the slightest degree, neither additional to nor exceeding its own essential nature, yet appears as if it were something distinct.

It manifests; thus, it is said to be "lucid" (*svaccha*). However, because it lacks such self-reflection (*vimarśa*), its lack of autonomy is its insentience (*jaḍatva*). The Supreme Lord, however, indeed reflects upon Himself as manifesting in that way, because consciousness culminates in reflection (*vimarśa*). And as it has been stated: "Always in that very manner..."

"It might appear. In that regard, if "always" or "sometimes" were some kind of time that was independent of its manifestation and autonomous, then it could indeed be questioned by relying upon it. But it is not so.
For instance, at this time, there is no other meaning for this word "manifestation" (dyotya) than that which appears as such.

[This arises] from the vibration of the sun. This would mean: why does the entire universe, such as blue and so forth, appear only in concomitance with that vibration of the sun and other [factors]? Why, then, is this not also questioned: "Why does yellow not appear as blue? [Objection: But in this way, blue would not be appearing at all. [Response: If that were the case, it would be because it appears otherwise.
(Page 7) That very [light] stirred by the sun would not even appear; for if it were manifested by the merging of the seven oceans,
today’s day would be the very day of universal dissolution (*pralaya*), and in its presence, there would be no such thing as today’s day.

It appears even as having both natures; nor does the Supreme Lord appear with a separate, additional body, so there is nothing here that is contrary to experience. For it is observed—in cases such as dreaming, mental construction, and the composition of treatises—that even when a multitude of objects situated within are projected outward, there is no actual transcendence of consciousness itself; on the contrary, [it remains identical].

That which is excluded from direct experience is an imaginary construction (*parikalpana*) and thus lacks experiential reality (*aprātītika*). By the term "eternal" (*śaśvat*), the impossibility of any temporal limitation is expressed. By "uncovered" (*acchanna*), it is meant that there is no transcendence of its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). By "transparent" (*svaccha*), although there is no actual transcendence, the possibility of the appearance of transcendence is indicated. By "autonomous" (*svacchanda*), the union with the freedom of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-svātantrya*) is signified.

By the word *vṛtti*, the manifestation of these forms as identical with the Lord Śiva, who possesses power, is expressed. The term *śaśvat* means unconditioned by time; *acchannā* means not undergoing even the slightest alteration of its own nature; *svacchā* means as if enduring an excessive luminosity; and *svacchandā* means autonomous.

He whose mode of being— his very existence— is characterized by a vibration of his own essential nature (svarūpa-spandita), which is free from dependence (pāratantrya) defined as the petitioning for another locus of awareness because of the emptiness of any investigation into a final place of rest;
he alone, through the application of casting aside the delusion of transmigratory existence consisting of non-Śiva-nature, is the essence of blissful enjoyment.

Śiva is the Supreme Lord because he is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) consisting of the supreme and inferior bliss (*parāpara-śreyaḥ*) whose form is the group of labials (*pavarga*). "Salutation to him" thus expresses the author of the treatise’s prostration of speech, mind, and body toward Him. And this prostration—of the nature described above—is the state of having one's body dissolved through the power of His will, by means of perceiving the excellence of the Blessed One’s essential nature.

When there is the possibility of residual mental functions consisting of the impressions (*saṃskāra*) from the contemplation of limited subjects constructed through the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth,

one must eliminate the intensification of the conceit of subjectivity residing in the body and other such things that arises at the time of emergence; thereby, one’s own true nature— which is consciousness itself, wherein the conceit of being a limited subject of *māyā* has been surpassed and rendered latent— [is realized].

The immersion (*samāveśa*) consists in being submerged by that [consciousness]. One rests upon such a nature of Śiva as the primary subject (*pradhānapramātṛ*), thereby setting aside the conceit of being a subject under the influence of *māyā*.
Thus, this word "namas" is merely indicative, like other particles (*nipāta*). As for the [view] regarding the word "namas"...

If it is asserted that [the word "namas"] refers to its own form (*svarūpa*), that is not satisfactory. For there is nothing gained by offering the form of the word "namas" to the Blessed One; for, according to the principle of the *gītā*, the word "namas" is heard [only as a sound].

The meaning that "the Blessed One attained complete satisfaction" is to be trusted on the basis of an oath; for even in the case of *svāhā* and other such utterances used in oblations and the like, the meaning to be illuminated is indeed the offering and satiation of the deities who bestow the increase of light, and not a state of resting in their own essential nature (*svarūpa*), as is the case with particles such as *ca*. For if they were intended to refer to their own essential nature, it would be like the recitation of the particle *ca*.

If [the word *namaḥ*] were of a neuter nature (*sattvarūpatā*), it would lack indeclinability (*anavyayatva*) because of the consequence of its connection with gender, number, and so forth. Furthermore, what kind of connection could there be between an object and a word? If such a connection were admitted, the use of the dative case would be undermined.

[The opponent argues: "In the expressions *namaskaroti* and *namasyati*, the meaning culminates in 'one utters the word *namaḥ*'; therefore, [in the phrase *namaḥ parameśvarāya*], [the word *parameśvara*] refers to the Supreme Lord."

The connection with external action is untenable; for in that case, the salutation would have to be either vocal or mental, so how could there be a bodily salutation? Thus, the established threefold division [of action] would be inconsistent. In our view, however, one makes oneself humble and submissive by means of mind, speech, and body.
The meaning of *namasyati* is "to exalt the Blessed One"; thus, everything is logically consistent. As he will state:

"Even by means of expressing victory, salutation, and so forth, the excellence of the Lord is to be made manifest, as well as one's own inclination toward Him. This is also the case in the scriptures regarding terms such as *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, and *vauṣaṭ*.

It is precisely the capacity to illuminate those respective objects that is designated by the term "jāti" (universal), because it is useful for generating various supernatural powers (*siddhi*). Why then insist on relying on an assistance provided by the essential nature (*svarūpa*) while disregarding the possible assistance rendered to the object? Thus, [the universal is that] from which the universe manifests and in which it finds its rest.
That which shines forth, which manifests by its own will, which is the self of the universe as it appears,

which remains entirely unobscured even within the manifestation of the universe, and wherein— by virtue of its absolute freedom— the universe appears as if it were something additional though it is not actually so added; that alone is the supreme reality (paramārthatattva) in its primary sense.

The former is superior, whereas the latter—such as that of ourselves—is merely inclined toward it; this is the primary subject matter of the treatise that has been introduced here into the heart, by means of which there is no rejection of alternative positions such as *vivarta* (illusory manifestation) and *pariṇāma* (transformation). For it has been stated that *vivarta* consists in the appearance of an unreal form; and indeed, the unreal does appear.

And as for how this is so, it has not been considered; however, it has been stated that in transformation (*pariṇāma*), one form disappears and another form appears. But since light (*prakāśa*) lacks any other form, when that [light] is concealed—

There might be blindness; and if that which is non-luminous were to manifest, it would not shine at all—thus, in both cases, the world would remain in a state of sleep, yet this has not been considered. Furthermore, in the theory of reflection (*pratibimbavāda*), consciousness possesses only transparency and not sovereignty; therefore, one must seek another external object to provide that reflection.

To say that ignorance is indefinable yet bestows manifold variety is a contradiction. However, the sequence [of reasoning] that this is indeed the power of the Supreme Lord (pārameśvarī śakti) is what truly wins over the heart. Therefore, the Blessed One, Paramaśiva, whose nature is consciousness and who consists of light and self-reflective awareness (prakāśavimarśa), is undeniable; it is precisely through his absolute freedom (svātantrya) [that all this occurs].

This doctrine of absolute freedom (svātantryavāda) has been revealed: that [Reality] manifests through the majesty of its inherent freedom— which is inseparable from the nature of consciousness— appearing as if distinct, though not actually distinct, both in the form of subjects ranging from Rudra down to stationary beings, and in the form of objects of cognition such as blue or pleasure, without obscuring its own essential nature.

Having thus entered into the nature of the Supreme Lord, the author of the commentary, intending to elucidate the meaning of the aphorisms through the presentation of prima facie and conclusive arguments, addresses the instability [of reasoning] with the words, "Reasoning is unstable," for it may make us non-existent today, or it may turn those who exist into perishable beings.

Since its essence consists merely in displaying one's own power, it is useless for the ultimate goal, being ridiculed by the maxim of the "cow-dung and milk-porridge"; alas, shame on the obsession of commentators who harbor a sense of ownership toward what belongs to others!
"The limit of great reasoning is nowhere to be found even by the wise.

Because of this, due to the occurrence of partial destruction arising from both favoring and hating that [reasoning], the lack of authority in the statement "fire is not water" is merely an incoherent assertion; lest this be imagined, he establishes it through three verses.

By the words "to make a sky-flower real," and so forth: the word *api* ("even") is to be understood as displaced [in order], and so too is *tathā*. Even a sky-flower, which is known to be non-existent everywhere—in space, time, and the subject—is to be brought into existence as real;
likewise, even that which is manifesting before one, by virtue of its being present for everyone and its proximity in space.
Being that very reality which is manifest, and thus possessing the power to bring even that which is non-existent into being,
I cause this world— composed of both existence and non-existence— to be as if startled, as if unstable in its own nature.

"I conceive within myself the capacity for a debate consisting of the adoption of a thesis and its counter-thesis at the time of its commencement, that is, when there is a desire to act. This is the statement of one who says: "Whatever I wish to do, whether as a proponent of a thesis or as an opponent, that shall be accomplished by me accordingly. Thus it is.
By way of intending to manifest his own incapacity, he clearly subjects himself to censure;

for he utters speech that is devoid of purpose, lacking both subject matter and utility, incomplete with its subject matter remaining unestablished, and rendered improbable due to the absence of any stated basis for restriction.

At its highest level, due to my lack of deliberate action (*prekṣāpūrvakāritā*), it flows forth spontaneously and proceeds of its own accord; and in that state, the sole cause is the agitation of the constituent element (*dhātu*) called the internal wind (*vāta*). For whoever would say "this very [thing] is blue" or "yellow," or "it is not blue, it is yellow," or "it is neither blue nor yellow"—he...

Having bestowed upon him the praise of being "the foremost among the insane," there would be no other object worthy of further laudation. The intended meaning is that demonstrating one's own capability by such a path is nothing but the manifestation of madness. And it is not merely madness alone; for even another person, being led along this path, has been carried away [to ruin].

To show that this would result in the acquisition of great sin, he says "of the dull-witted" (*jaḍānām*). For even those who have employed the functions of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and who have exerted themselves through hundreds of efforts such as service to the guru and the study of the scriptures, are nonetheless called "dull-witted" if they act in such a way without prior reflection; it is of such people that the following applies regarding the meaning of the scriptures already studied.

[The term *durucih* refers to] that [intellect] whose taste (*ruci*)— its own radiance characterized by the nature of ultimate reality— is corrupted by those utterances which are like the agitation of wind at the site of belching; these utterances arise from a lack of transformation characterized by the absence of correct modification, are devoid of subject matter and purpose, and proceed impulsively even without logical connection, being mere prattle caused by the disturbance of wind-like breaths.

And in that [consciousness], because of the power of that admixture and intermingling of the unreal form with the real, ultimate form, there arises such a series— consisting of objects, subjects, cognizers,
and the objects of cognition— which, although mutually oriented toward one another, [remains distinct].
The multitude, consisting of pairs, withers on all sides; having abandoned their upturned faces and stiff necks, they seem to bend down as if toward their own deeds.
(Page 11)

She attains a state of indifference. Just as a certain innocent woman, though eager for enjoyment, is overcome by eructations produced by the indigestion of excessive eating on the part of those with weak digestion and gluttonous appetites;

she thus manifests, as it were, a mixture with an unreal and impure form regarding every object of enjoyment, such as betel and the like—and for this very reason, her appetite for food and other things is destroyed.

Desires undergo a state of withering due to the defect of aversion (*arocaka*). This is what is meant: for people of dull intellect who are engaged in a continuous stream of activities regarding various duties—whether worldly or Vedic, and whether for visible or invisible purposes—their taste and relish are destroyed by such false and boastful displays of scholarship; and yet...

It is introduced into the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-tattva*) nowhere because of its non-abiding nature. Therefore, what is the use of such "scholarship" which brings madness to one's own self and does the greatest harm? But this [other kind] is appropriate;
thus he says: "the grasping of things as they truly are. Whatever the thing may be, its excellence, its intensity—

Regarding the point that "these [qualities] are to be imparted to those who possess greatness," the motivating activity (*prayojaka-vyāpāra*)— characterized by the performance of that [imparting] and consisting of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), its refutation, the final conclusion (*siddhānta*), and its support— is the *rasa* (flavor) in this context; that very [activity] is the *rasa* by virtue of its abundance, excellence, and preeminence.

And that series of meanings (*arthāvalī*) belongs to one who possesses it constantly—such a person who is a wise man in reality, who knows thus and not otherwise, who does not see otherwise, nor speak otherwise; and since the wise man acts with foresight (*prekṣāpūrvakārī*), [the series] is situated there and rests there. It is that from which doubt has departed and is stilled, and in which [doubt is stilled].
Consisting of the categories of the knower and the known, it breathes freely because there is no possibility of the loss of what ought to be done;

it maintains steadfastness regarding worldly and transcendental objects—both seen and unseen—as well as regarding the object of the supreme reality that transcends them. For such a wise person possesses discernment (*viveka*), which is the distinctness of everything.
Seeing the very benefit to others as his own fruit, he grants [the gift] while resolving the contradiction by means of their having different objects.

For instance, when one holds the view that "whatever appears in whatever manner, that is the very majesty of manifestation," then why would there not be the state of being atomic (pāramāṇavatva) due to the manifestation of degrees of subtlety? [And why would it not be so] because of its being the producer of pleasure and the like?

Why is there not identity [between the jar and its cognition]? In the absence of cognition, why would the jar and other objects not become like a body that is a mere void, resembling blinding darkness, for the cognizing subject who is the body?
(Page 12)

For indeed, the state of being in another world flashes forth even for the learned, as well as for children, women, and commoners; for he who thinks, "I am that very same person who remains when the body has been reduced to ashes," is one who participates in non-difference from the consciousness of the Supreme Lord.
Thus, both objective entities and subjects are of the nature of the Supreme Lord, and this is the manifestation of their manifold powers.

This is the supreme adornment, not even the slightest fragmentation. Those who dispute, grasping at the apprehension of only such limited portions, are like blind men who, by touching various parts of an elephant's body—such as its trunk or tail—form conceptual constructions of the elephant based on those specific parts. Even that dispute of theirs is merely the unfolding of the power of the Supreme Lord.

It does not bring even a trace of any fault. For example, suppose there is a certain woman of delicate intellect who is driven from that place pervaded by the outpourings of the dull-witted to a state of seclusion and distance by some disagreeable fool who understands her intentions. For the unrefined world would think, "She is fading away because of a loss of appetite."
One sees the other, yet one should not understand that the lack of relish here is produced by a dull-witted outburst; for that [lack of relish] is exactly like this.

But when, regarding whatever object—be it betel, liquor, food, or the like—one's heart is made to grasp it with a firm hold, becoming adept at accepting its excellence, then it recovers itself through the awakening of its own inherent relish.

She casts off her dejection. And a certain young maiden, whose heart was already possessed by the budding sprouts of passion directed toward her lover, was brought to a state of despondency— despite being beautiful, she was defiled by the belching of such vulgar pride, thinking, "Such indeed are men"— until she was freed from her apprehension in a secluded place by a certain clever man.

She is made dependent on the love bound solely to Him; she is rendered one who knows the flavor of enjoyment such as worldly food and the like, yet is also made proficient in tasting the flavor of the supramundane joy. Likewise, by the one who is wise regarding the ultimate truth, she—who consists of both the subject and the object—is made worthy of the bliss arising from the attainment of the higher and lower forms of excellence characterized by *siddhi* and liberation.

The three worlds are brought about. For the purpose of expressing "constant connection" (*nityayoga*) and so forth, although the *bahuvrīhi* compound—which would have been obtained through brevity—was available, it was set aside; instead, the use of a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya*) after a *tatpuruṣa* compound was employed, based on the sense of "this belongs to him" or "he possesses this. Regarding the plural form in the phrase "by the outbursts of the dull-witted" (*jaḍānām udgāraiḥ*), such [a state]...

The two terms [“many” and “not final”] express abundance and lack of completion, respectively. By contrast, the term “learned” (*viduṣi*)—intending singularity—is used for one who is a supreme scholar in the ultimate sense (*paramārthapaṇḍita*).
(Page 13)

And it has been stated that one who is skilled in the ultimate truth is difficult to find. Regarding the phrase "in someone," this refers to a transcendent being. Anticipating the objection—"If such a person exists as only some rare individual, then his existence is indeed improbable"—the author says, "they are indeed fashioned [by Him]. This is what is meant: the very will of the Supreme Lord is the concealment of His own nature.

And while manifesting its own essential nature, it necessarily produces such a person who is a scholar of ultimate truth; however, the mass of *māyā* is vast, whereas the light of knowledge is exceedingly subtle.
For instance, the separation of the two—the heaven and earth—denoted by the word *rodasī* is incomplete.
The knowledge of being strewn [with jewels], as well as specific devotion—which is service characterized by freedom from sin—and fitness for enjoyment:

for these tasks to be performed, seven mountain ranges were fashioned and made capable; even though the world of living beings is filled with hundreds of mountains, there are only these seven and no more, yet they were not created without purpose. [This pertains to] the day and night.
And regarding the honor accorded to that which consists of the nature of darkness and light, only the two—the moon and the sun—are [the agents];

however, there is no power here even for the vast multitude of luminous bodies such as gems and the like. Nor is it the case that those two were not created; for if the sun did not exist, there would be only night, or perhaps even that would not exist. For in the cognition of the nature of light—

The absence of that [light] is known as darkness. Even one born blind, while perceiving the manifestation of forms and so forth ascended within his own mental constructs, knows the lack of such manifestation externally as blinding darkness;
for even upon the very first entry of blinding darkness during sleep or fainting, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of light [remains].

The manifestation occurs due to [the influence of] the *vaśa* (power/condition), but not during the state of being under its sole control. For at that time, the recollection—"nothing at all appeared"—would indicate a consciousness of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnya*). And we shall explain that total darkness is not indeed universal emptiness. For instance, by the followers of Kapila, *chāyā* (shadow) [is defined as...].
It is accepted by the Abhidharmikas that this is a dharma consisting of a resistant substance (*sapratighavastudharma*), and it is merely a specific variety of form (*rūpa*) known as darkness.
For one with eyes closed, there is no cognition of "external blinding darkness"; rather, such a cognition belongs only to one whose eyes are open.
In the absence of light, the consciousness therein is "I do not see anything else," but not "I see darkness."
And if the sun were of a nature that was truly uniform in its essence, then there would be only day; however,
when the moon exists with the full expansion of its orb being filled by the convergence of its own rays—
(page 14).
The solar radiance itself exists in such a state of diversity that, although it is present, it appears as if absent; at that time, what is called "night" shines forth.

By this methodological approach, the moon's nature as the "maker of night" is established; however, one should not understand it here to mean that just as there is day upon the rising of the sun, so too there is night upon the rising of the moon. And just as the principal mountain ranges... [and] just as...

The moon and the sun, as well as the Lord himself— the Creator— because he is the support of the universe, have established a certain fixed rule and logic for the discernment of the existent and non-existent, and the appropriate and inappropriate, as well as being and non-being; it is only some person, and not every wise man, who has been created to perceive and determine this correctly, and not one who has not been so created.

The word *kila* indicates probability (*saṃbhāvanā*). He is radiant by means of that light—characterized by supreme knowledge—which has dispelled (*apoḍha*) and turned away (*vyāvartita*) the darkness characterized by non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), even though it had grown deep through the power of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of beginningless cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*). Being himself of the nature of non-darkness (*atama-rūpa*), he [illuminates] others as well.

By immersing his own nature [in the Absolute], he makes that which was free from darkness full of light; thus, perceiving the lineage of the Guru as the past time, himself as the present manifest form, and the succession of disciples and grand-disciples as the future, the Supreme Lord is one whose manifestation of consciousness is uninterrupted.

It shows: one who sees with distinction is a *vipaśya*, meaning the Supreme Omniscient One; he who acts like that and perceives the reality of existence (*bhāvatattva*) is a *vipaścit*. [Is it not] as in the oath, "like the Sugata, seeing clearly"? For the end of the Sūtra says, "the *vipaścit* perceives," meaning one who is endowed with the nature of consciousness capable of discerning both self and other would indeed be a *vipaścit*.

The venerable Bṛhaspati says: "The supreme [consciousness] reflects," which, with the addition of the causative suffix (*ṇic*) and the elision of the suffix (*kvip*), becomes "the consciousness of this [being] reflects the supreme.

Thus, in this sequence, it remains as the supreme through increasingly subtle stages; what is meant is that this matter is not in any way impossible. In this way, true scholarship consists precisely in resting upon reality (*tattva*). And that—

Having stated that only when it is fully perfected does [a work] culminate in benefiting others, he says the following in order to demonstrate the purpose of the commentary he is about to compose, the fact that the Sūtra, the Vṛtti, and the Ṭīkā were composed by a single author, and the success of composing separate works even though they share a single speaker and a single purpose:

"In the threefold speech" (*trayyāṃ vāci*). That which has three parts—namely *paśyantī*, *madhyamā*, and *vaikharī*—is the "threefold" (*trayī*), whose nature is the supreme reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that embraces [all things].
(Page 15)

The Supreme Goddess, who constitutes the undivided mass of all that is to be reflected upon, is Speech (*vāk*); she is called Speech because she reflects upon her own nature. And within her, this visible world of speech (*vāṅmaya*)—being permeated by the consciousness whose form is the reflective awareness characterized as valid cognition—is a body whose sole essence is verbalization.
Just as the universe has blossomed in due order— being on the verge of blossoming in Paśyantī,

blossoming in Madhyamā, and having attained full expansion in Vaikharī through being perceived as distinct— and just as Gāyatrī is the heart of one skilled in the creation of the impelling forces under consideration;

"Having the form of the splendor and brilliance of the sun of awakening risen in the sky," refers to the cause for bestowing results in the hereafter (*āmuṣmika*); or alternatively, "in that [hereafter]" means within the world-renowned Self of the inner *praṇava* and the *Nigama*, which has gradually blossomed;
"within" (*antar*) means on the ground of intention (*saṃkalpa*)—thinking "I shall act"—it is about to blossom, at the commencement of action.
At that time, she blossoms in the form of assent (*om*) and in the form of the manifestation of the primacy of the mantra;

thereafter, at the time of the accomplishment of the ritual action, she manifests as the *Trayī*— characterized by the *Ṛc*, *Yajus*, and *Sāman*, and their collective totality— in the state where the functions of the *Hautra*, *Ādhvaryava*, *Audgātra*, and *Brahmatva* become clearly manifest.

The term "attained expansion" (*labdhavikāsā*) refers to worldly variety as the result and Vedic [knowledge] as its cause, mentioned here by way of illustration; or else, it means that Gāyatrī has expanded sequentially within the triad beginning with *antar* and within the triad beginning with *paśyantī* in the world beyond. Alternatively, it refers to that which is within the *praṇava*, that is, inside the middle of the *praṇava*.
According to the principle stated in Manu Smṛti 2.74, "The triad consisting of the Vedas, beginning with the Ṛgveda, flows forth without the Oṃkāra;
it perishes both at the beginning and at the end," [the Veda] exists through its identity with the Praṇava.

And according to the principle stated in *Sarve vedā-* (*Ka. Va.* 2.15), therein, just as the Gāyatrī, at the commencement of what is to be performed, takes the form of intuition (*pratibhā*) and gradually unfolds; for that intuition, assuming the nature of sound within the Sāmans in their melodic forms, [manifests] in the Ṛks...

Accepting the indication of the nature of reality as consisting of the praise of ritual action (*karman*), qualities (*guṇa*), and deities (*devatā*), this [work] becomes manifest in the *Yajus* mantras as that which is to be performed. A *nigama* is the Veda because it leads one to certainty regarding the means to dharma and other goals; likewise is the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* in its *sūtras* and *vṛtti*.

That which has its heart throbbing with life attains manifestation here in this commentary; by means of this vision of the recognition of the powers consisting of perception and action, the Lord is gradually and progressively recognized.

By means of the method of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-paddhati*) which establishes the designation of "Lord" (*īśvara*) within one's own self— acting as a means to knowledge directed toward [the goal] in opposition [to ignorance]— that [method] is one in which the heart flashes forth in the *Sūtra*, its essence flashes forth in the *Vṛtti*,
but in the *Vivṛti* it is fully manifest, having entered the sphere of all people. The beginning of the flashing forth is in the *Sūtra*, while the completion of the flashing forth is...

Regarding the phrase "in the [two] modes of being" (*vṛttau*): in the ultimate sense, these two are one because they are produced at the same time; however, it has been shown that through the conceptualization of division, there is difference. This is what is meant: just as the universe exists within the supreme Word-principle (*paravāktattva*) by the abolition of division, it exists in *paśyantī* with its divisions merely indicated, and in *madhyamā* with its divisions fully manifested.
In *vaikharī*, because its form is perceived as differentiated, the appearance of difference becomes manifest;

likewise, it effects distinct purposeful actions for distinct qualified recipients. Similarly, in the place of the supreme *parā-vāk* reality, there is the consciousness of the author of the scripture, who is non-different from Śiva, [arising] through identity (*tādātmya*).

The present ultimate reality (paramārthatattva), being the essence, is denoted by the word "Heart" (hṛdaya). It exists in the *sūtra* as a state of non-manifestation (*asūtraṇā*) characterized by a vibration (*sphuraṇa*) that possesses the fitness for becoming the object of those people who are to be enlightened; however, in the *vṛtti*, that very same [reality] is made manifest, and in the *vivṛti*, it is [further elucidated] by way of posing objections and providing their resolutions.

It becomes manifest as a distinction characterized by fitness for the comprehension of all people; thus, because it bestows various fruits upon each respective qualified practitioner, those who have not grasped the distinctions produced by other systems of philosophy (*darśana*), having been trained by the *sūtra* alone along with its commentary (*vṛtti*), [attain] the meaning of the *sūtra* independently of the commentary.

By way of constant cultivation of the *Mātra*, they become partakers of both higher and lower accomplishments (*siddhi*). However, those whose false views have arisen from the study of other systems (*tīrthāntara*)—once their such delusions have been removed by this commentary (*ṭīkā*) in the form of an exposition—become those whose hearts rest in the meaning of the Sūtra and Vṛtti; and through the gradual resting in the yoga of meditating upon the meaning of the Sūtra, [they attain liberation].
In the same way, these [meanings] are established as being non-different from the reality of the heart of another, which consists of the direct intuition (*saṃvedana*) of the author of the treatise.

And just as within the self of intuitive insight (*pratibhā*), the entire range of things to be done— devoid of differentiation and having reached its culmination in the commencement of action in due order— is the cause for the accomplishment of all worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*).

Thus, this self-awakening, which rests within the heart of the Guru, has become manifest through the sequence of the Sūtras and other scriptures by way of the relationship between the taught and the teacher, free from doubt and dispute.

"It attains clarity. That by which a meaning is strung together is a *sūtra*. The function (*vṛtti*) of a *sūtra* is its operation upon its own subject matter; because it elucidates that [subject matter], a treatise that reveals the meaning of the *sūtra* is also called a *vṛtti*.
It is like the meaning of a treatise that has been covered over—as if concealed—by a heap of dust consisting of suspected rival doctrines.

*Vivaraṇa* (exposition) is the state of being free from obstructions through the removal of the veil of ignorance; the text itself is so called because it brings about that state. It is also called a *ṭīkā* (commentary), for by means of it the meaning—which is fit for the skill of wandering upon the ground of the heart—is made clear and understood. And thus he will say:
And in the *Ṭīkā* it says: "Furthermore, like the progressive accumulation.
But if, indeed, in the case of a woman, there is a conflict [between rules], by way of prohibition (*vipratiṣedha*).
If, however, one does not take this [etymological derivation] into account, then the words *vṛtti* and *vivṛti* should be derived in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*).
But if the word *vṛtti* is used in the sense of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*), then it is only by metaphorical extension (*upacāra*) that the term "commentary" (*vṛtti*) applies to the book.
Thus, by this much, it is correctly stated that even the *ṭīkā* was composed by the author himself; for it is not [composed] by another subject-principle (*pramātṛtattva*).

It is possible that the *paśyantī* and *madhyamā* [levels] rest within another perceiver (*pramātṛ*), and the *vaikharī* likewise; nor is it possible for one person to initiate an action while another brings its execution to completion. Even in cases where both might occur—such as in the composition of a poetic riddle (*kāvyasamasyā*) or the finishing of a covered cloth (*vārakapaṭa*)—there too...
The fulfillment of the single intention that flashes forth from the root occurs in such a way as a unification alone, and not otherwise.

Having thus demonstrated that everyone is benefited by this composition of the triad— the Sūtra, the Vṛtti, and the Vivṛtti— he proceeds, after defining the purpose, by way of stating the intended meaning (*tātparya*).

He introduces the opening statement with the words "At the commencement of the treatise," and so forth. The phrase "commencement of the treatise" refers to that pacification of obstacles which must be diligently acquired when a proper duty is to be performed, as they say:
"Prosperous undertakings are beset by many obstacles..."

Thus [it is said]. Obstacles (*vighna*) are those things which obstruct and destroy what is to be done; they consist of three kinds of impairments, such as internal ones and so forth, including defects like lack of attention, as well as specific deities who preside over them. And these—

Even for the inner self (pratyagātman) whose delusion has been destroyed, there may arise obstacles to its will— obstacles pertaining to the body, vital breath, and so forth, which constitute the state of being a subject that has not yet ceased due to the residual impressions of *māyā*— especially for one who has undertaken the effort to uplift the entire world.

Through the activity of merit and demerit belonging to the world, and by the host of deities who preside over it and seize every moment for the protection of cyclic existence, a gathering of obstacles is inevitably brought about. As it has been said:
Indeed, ten thousand times ten thousand obstacles, joined with the incitement of others,
strike incessantly at a living being who is intent upon a wholesome goal.

"Especially for one who effects the crossing over the ocean of existence," and so forth. Therefore, that host of obstacles can only be destroyed by the Blessed One himself, who employs such extraordinary effort and performs his final personal duty in the form of bestowing grace.

Thus, in the first moment, within the inner self—that is, the body and so forth—by means of the concealment of their [ordinary] nature and through the act of bowing down, there occurs an immersion (*samāveśa*) consisting of the reflective awareness that elevates the essential nature of the Supreme Lord;
for agency, however, this is its primary state. (3.2.12)

That which is characterized by the definitions to be stated hereafter must be accepted. For when that is present, even the entire universe becomes one's own self, having as its ultimate reality nothing but non-dual, independent consciousness; thus, who could obstruct whom, and where?
Immediately thereafter, at the time of composing this work, although the primacy of the inner self alone is to be kept in mind—
Otherwise, the composition of scriptures—which must be carried out through the attainment of the level of *vaikharī* speech—would be impossible;

nevertheless, because the grasp of duality has been cast off by the intensely blazing power of one's own innate energy, ignited by the great force of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of immersion (*samāveśa*) into that [divine state], obstacles have no power over him. Nor is such a state appropriate for those presiding over *māyā*, such as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and others.
"Absorption" (*samāveśa*) is the supreme attainment. The prefix *prati* has the sense of "toward" (*lakṣaṇe*);
by that reason, there is prostration, for otherwise it would not occur toward one who is equal or inferior.
(Page 19)
Or, humility is appropriate for one who possesses authority; or, in this description of a state of being, the prefix *prati-* denotes the relationship between the object and the subject.

[The term] *prahva* means: he calls out (*hvayati*) with intensity (*prakarṣeṇa*), that is, by not disregarding anything else, he makes [the object] resound, he reflects upon its identity as being of that very nature, as if possessing a competitive desire to enter into its qualities—thus he is *prahva*. [The word] *ātmani* refers to the body and so forth.

In the inner self (*pratyagātman*). For it is thus: while the void-consciousness, the vital breath, the organs, and the body exist, the accomplishment of the scripture is to be carried out through the cessation of other [states], through the determination of the ultimate reality, through the construction of words, and through the instruction of others. In that regard, among those things which must necessarily be relied upon as being like petals, the supreme lordly [power]...

He says this by means of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) in the word *parāmṛśan* ("while perceiving"), which indicates that the essential nature (*svarūpa*), acting as the animator (*anuprāṇaka*), is resorted to by way of being the knower. Regarding the word *āsādya* ("having attained"):

although the suffix *ktvā* is prescribed after a verbal root denoting an action occurring at a time prior to another when used in the sense of an abstract state (*bhāve*), nevertheless, it is employed here by virtue of its connection with the verbal root [in the sense of sequence].
The meaning of the suffix -ktvā is perceived as being vitalized by the sense of that sentence; for while in the sentence "He drinks liquor first,

then he sings" only a mere sequence of two actions is perceived, it is not exactly the same in the case of "Having drunk liquor, he sings," because that drinking of liquor functions as a subordinate aid (*upakāra*).
It appears as if it persists by serving as the vitalizing support for the meaning of the principal sentence.
Priority (*paurvakālya*) consists merely in being produced first; it does not mean that having been produced, it must immediately dissolve without a trace.
Thus, if the attainment of the state of servitude to the Supreme Lord has arisen, no delay should be made in informing one's own kin; for if there is delay...

Because, by concealing the conditioned nature of illusion (*māyā-saṃskāra*), there is an absence of the accomplishment of benefiting others through the possibility of liberation consisting in identity with the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) that has arrived unexpectedly; whereas for one who has not attained that essential nature (*tatsvarūpa*),
there would be the state of a deceiver (*pratāraka*) in composing a scripture, [therefore] it must necessarily follow immediately after its attainment.

It is proper to perform service for others, and one must not delay; for that reason, one should attain the state of servitude to the Supreme Lord— who transcends the pure and impure authorities (adhikārin), namely Sadāśiva, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Viriñca, and the rest— through the grace of the Guru of the Supreme Lord, preceded by the acquisition of goodness and motivated by the desire to benefit others.

The term *āsādya* (having attained) is stated through the use of a single syntactical construction (*ekavākyatā*) to indicate that [the work] functions as the means for accomplishing the recognition of the Lord (*īśvarapratyabhijñā*), which is the method for attaining the goal of all perfections; thus,
by the use of the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*), it signifies the absence of interruption (*avicchedābhāva*).
(Page 20) And since the fact that the reflection on humility (*prahvatā*) is the cause has been illuminated, the purpose alone is the primary motivator.
Therefore, he says "for the sake of engagement" (*pravṛttaye*). In that context, the fruit is the meaning of the sentence in its primary sense.

In the view [of the opponent], the very purpose of the perception constitutes the fruit, because the process of establishing the sentence-meaning— which has as its object a recognition that serves as the cause of that fruit— comes to rest in that very [perception].
Even in the theory that the action is the sentence-meaning, since the action exists for the sake of the object, it resides within the denotatum.

Although primacy is immediately perceived from the word regarding an object characterized by recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), nevertheless, because it is qualified as the cause of attainment (*saṃpad*), it is attainment itself that appears as the primary element. This is likewise the case in the theory that the meaning of a sentence consists in action (*kriyā*). For that [action] has the ritual act as its purpose, and that [act] has the fruit as its purpose. But the denotable object (*abhidheya*)...

It is taught [in this way] so that one might not suspect a defect in the means (*upāya*), even though the fruit (*phala*) is already attained. And thus the author of the treatise will indeed say later: "the state of being an incarnation," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the author of the treatise": [it refers to him speaking] concerning Maheśvara, the reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*), which—though established by one's own consciousness and self-luminous—is the means for instructing others and has the result of removing delusion.

"He is reminded by means of the highest [object] through the perception of similarity"—according to this principle, he is one who teaches the means of establishing worldly practice (*vyavahāra-sādhana*) in the form of scripture (*śāstra*).
This is the intended meaning: here, it is not preceded by quarrel, nor even preceded by mere introduction, such as the giving of a gift to a miser (*kīnāśa*).
The instruction for the great ones is intended for the sake of instructing others;
however, one should lead them toward reality by means of [skillful] power.
This is due to their compassion. And in that regard, the listener themselves must first be encouraged even through consolation before being set upon the path.

In this treatise, which by its very nature consists of extensive and detailed inferences for the sake of others, the primary purpose that impels one to engage with it must be stated. For it is precisely through this [purpose] that *nyāya*—when examined from the perspective of the sixteen categories beginning with doubt—is correctly and thoroughly elucidated; thus it was formulated by the Sage Akṣapāda.

One who does not abandon this very view and provides correct exposition is called a "treatise-author" (śāstrakāra). However, those such as the Buddhists (Saugatas) are both practitioners of that [view] and haters of it. This has been explained by me at length in the *Kathāmukhatilaka*; one should seek it there itself. Seeing a certain unprecedented manner of salutation...
Fearing that [the reader] might become confused,
the commentator performs the homage to Jayanātha and so forth; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [he intends to include other such acts].

It is grasped starting from salutation, meditation, and so forth. Here, that form which resides in duality must, when explained through either one of its two aspects, be brought to rest in both. For [in the expressions] "the jar shines" and "the jar sees," it is the jar that is shining which causes [the self] to shine.

It is the comprehension of the meaning. And here, "humility" (*prahvatva*) consists in being established in both [the speaker and the listener], and "superiority" (*utkarṣa*) belongs to the latter on account of the former.

Even when the employment of words such as "conquer," "you conquer," or "victory! proceeds by way of the superiority of the Supreme Lord, one must nevertheless maintain a humility consisting in self-effacement; otherwise, [that] superiority—

Because it cannot be otherwise established. Thus, even in such usages as "namas," "namāmi," and "vande," which proceed by way of a self-reflection that subordinates one's own self, one must ultimately take refuge in the excellence of the Lord.
Therefore, these two—though consisting of two parts—are in fact a single reality, which is here [in this verse] present in its entirety (ā samantāt).
The feeling (*vedita*) has been made manifest through sound, rendered capable of being clearly grasped by all listeners present;

for that which is merely implied by the sense is not within the range of everyone. By the phrase "in some way" (*kathañcit*), it is stated that servitude is extremely difficult to attain, and thus the complete subordination of oneself to the [Lord] is expressed even more emphatically.

"That servitude yields great fruit"—this is the exaltation of the Lord. Since the Lord is attained as the Master precisely through the state of being His servant, the title "Lord" (Īśvara) ultimately culminates in "Māheśvarya" (the state of Maheśvara). By the term "great fruit," the commentator [refers to] the phrase "the cause for the attainment of all perfections."

He shows that even the qualification "recognition" (pratyabhijñā) is a qualification of "servitude" (dāsya). This meaning was also indicated in the commentary by the phrase "the glory of servitude" (dāsyalakṣmīḥ), [meaning] one by whom all glories—i.e., all prosperities—originating from servitude have been obtained through the grace of the Supreme Lord. Otherwise, [it would not be so].
The employment of the word *lakṣmī* would be inconsistent, as it would manifest a multiplicity of referents.

Furthermore, by the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "or even by speech," it should be understood that [this occurs] "even by body. For instance, humility (*prahvatā*) and elevation (*utkarṣaṇa*), as well as the form of reflecting upon the light [of consciousness], exist within mental perception (*mānase saṃvedane*).

And it rests in the reality of speech (*vāktattva*), which is the essence of that [consciousness], and not in the inert body. Therefore, the devotee, by offering that very [reality] which consists of mind and speech and is inseparable from the power of consciousness, [attains liberation].
(page 22)

"The entire universe is offered unto the Blessed One"—thus it is said. "In its arrival, one should offer up one's own self as well. This has been stated. "One should offer" (nivedayet) means one should entrust [it] and, with certainty, render it composed of consciousness (vidyāmaya). Thereafter, however—
Precisely because it is inseparable from that [realization], the offering of even one's body, wealth, wife, and so forth arises therein;

thus, acts such as worship, fire-offerings, bowing the head, and prostration with eight limbs are conventionally designated as "prostration" (praṇāma) by way of metaphorical usage, since they are instrumental causes for that realization, but not in a primary sense. This is true, indeed.

The mere removal of obstacles is accomplished; however, there is a further purpose for that portion of the verse spoken at the beginning which serves as the basis for bowing down to him. "Even now" means that [the teaching] has been transmitted into the hearts of all without interruption by means of its inscription in books. For it is precisely therein that its status as having been communicated is established.

The sense is that there is no application [of this] to the self (*ātman*). The term "commentator" (*vyākhyātṛ*) is placed first because it is more venerable. For, in establishing recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), the presence of the Lord (*īśvara-sāṃmukhya*) is inferred. [The phrase] "preceded by the presence of the Lord" is used. Now, one might object: does this purpose not apply to each individual commentator?

This may be appropriate for the speaker, but how so for the listeners? For a listener does not establish a recognition [of the speaker], nor is it logical for there to be a separate internal reflection such as "servitude," since the reflection on the meaning of the sentence is a single unity.
Even the listener, while first reciting this very sentence, reflects internally in this way: "I, now..."

Precisely because of the grace of the Supreme Lord— grace inferred from his attainment of the status of being a fit vessel for such an instruction on the transcendent secret— it is the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), preceded by the attainment of servitude to Maheśvara,
that is established by this commentator; therein lies [the act of] requesting and the performance of what is conducive thereto.

"I perform the activity of an instigator (prayojaka-vyāpāra), whereby, through my own fitness for the status of a teacher, I lead those people as well to the service of the Supreme Lord, desiring thus to benefit humanity. And so,
even one who is ignorant of the meaning of secret mantras, seed-syllables (bīja), and the like, attains their fruit by contemplating them.

The disciple is likewise. For, although this object has not yet ascended to the cognizer characterized by the intellect (*buddhi*) due to the absence of the application of determinative resolve (*adhyavasāya-yoga*), it nonetheless comes to rest within that true cognizer.

And because, in reality, the nature of such clinging (*parāmarśa*) is one and the same; for indeed, the pursuit of homogeneous force is observed even among the insentient great elements (*mahābhūta*), such as clods of earth, water, and so forth. And thus:

Knowledge (*jñāna*) is of the nature of uncontracted, non-conceptual consciousness (*nirvikalpaka-saṃvit*), which is spiritual (*pauruṣa*); it may also be attained through means such as initiation (*dīkṣā*) even apart from the scriptures. On the other hand, that which has reached the state of conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) is intellectual (*bauddha*), being of the nature of contracted consciousness; it is for the sake of this [intellectual knowledge] that the scriptures and so forth are taught. Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is likewise [of two kinds].

The followers of the Āgamas maintain that [consciousness] is twofold: it has the nature of contracted non-conceptual self-awareness when residing in the *puruṣa*, but when ascended to the plane of contracted conceptual determination, it resides in the *buddhi*; thus one should seek the meaning of this point in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other scriptures.

Even though this is not preceded by conscious intent on the part of the disciples, there arises for them an awareness consisting of such reflection, just as there is an awareness consisting of reflection regarding what is to be done during sleep or intoxication. In the phrase "having attained" (*āsādya*) and "I shall establish the recognition" (*pratyabhijñām upapādayāmi*), there are two causative suffixes (*ṇic*). In the commentary (*vṛtti*) as well, it says "the attainment of solitude" (*ekākisaṃpadā*).

By this statement, it is indicated that for another person as well, the very same transmission of the perfection of servitude—which has solely the grace of the Supreme Lord as its cause—is being conveyed; thus, the meaning of the two *ṇic* suffixes in the word "āsādya" has been explained.
Furthermore, the two *ṇic* suffixes in "pratyabhijñāpayāmi" [are explained] in the commentary, and as far as...

The grace of Maheśvara is to be inferred from the attainment of fitness for receiving secret instruction; [the disciple thinks], "I have indeed become capable of performing benefit for myself and others. This reflection on the part of the disciple is entirely appropriate, just as one might say, "If it has rained, the rice has ripened. And in reality, this is so because of the oneness of the Self.

And since the non-interruption of that manifestation is to be accomplished precisely by the removal of delusion, this is the very effort of the author of the text: "May all [beings] individually become composed of my own self-reflection.
And just as it is with the authors of the scriptures, such an effort is likewise appropriate for commentators toward their disciples.
"A living being who has attained equality with me is liberated"—
this indeed is the intended meaning in the contemplation of the Great Pervasion (*mahāvyāpti*). Thus,
by reflecting upon the reading of the Sūtras and the Vṛtti, even the listeners attain a face-to-face encounter with the Supreme Lord.

He indeed gives. Furthermore, even while the commentator was reciting the Sūtra and Vṛtti texts, desiring to provide this benefit to people by means of securing the service of the Lord who is otherwise difficult to attain,
he established that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*).

Having thus established that such an object— which is like a reflection— has arrived through the process of transition from the state of the Archetype (bimba), which is the supreme human goal, the person [proceeds] by virtue of perceiving his own nature as a qualified candidate (adhikārin).

"Whoever is born is here one who is to be benefited. Thus, from such a conviction ever arisen within myself, I, as a person, am to be benefited; and by means of this reasoning, I establish the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) being presented, which serves as the means for attaining the service of that Lord who is so difficult to obtain.

"I too shall place it in my heart through a logical justification, while attending to that very justification"—this much constitutes the process of realization. Here, by means of skillfulness, the equality of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) has been shown even during the transition; however, it is the same elsewhere as well, because this very [process] is [the case].

The distinction between one who is qualified and one who is unqualified is as follows: having understood the literal meaning of the hearing "I instruct you, 'Go to Him,'" one ascends the second step by reflecting, "He instructs me,
'Go to Him,'" and then reaches the third stage by thinking, "Therefore, I shall go."

One who knows the meaning of a sentence becomes [an authority]; however, one who lacks such qualification rests at the very first step. Thus, "he intends this" and "he impels him"—these other steps are not intended by the speaker;
as for the status of being something to be accomplished (*kāryatva*), he does not rest there. Enough with these intermediate matters. In every respect:
The word *śrotṛ* (listener) has its meaning already established; by the inclusion of the term "and so forth" (*ādi*), it should be understood that "hearing" (*śravaṇa*) is also intended.

Having thus justified this unprecedented manner of salutation and rendered the recitation of those words purposeful, the commentary [proceeds] to explain the sūtra's phrase "in some way" (*kathaṃcit*).

"Only through the grace of the Supreme Lord"—to explain this, he says "And that which... The word "and" (ca) collects another object of knowledge (*prameya*) that is to be explained. Regarding "through devotion" (*bhaktyā*): for it is by the power of immersion into its essential nature that the Lord shines forth as one's own true self in ultimate reality.

Devotion (*bhakti*) is the characteristic of *vidyā*, which consists in the intensity of constant immersion (*samāveśa*) into that very Truth whose nature is full bliss; this arises from the experience of the emptiness of the conceit (*abhimāna*) regarding delusion as being ultimate.
Through that [devotion], there is the full savor (*āsvāda*) characterized by liberation, which, through the desire for infinite fruit, consists of the state of universal form (*viśvarūpatā*).

Vimarśa is the essence of vision and action; it is precisely that which is under discussion here. Therefore, he states that liberation is not the insentient nature described by the followers of Kaṇāda.

And as for the "taste" (*āsvāda*) of liberation (*mokṣa*), it is the reflection on the aspect of how it is exactly like this. For that very light of one's own self (*svātmaprakāśa*), which arises through devotion (*bhakti*)—in the form of an immersion characterized by helplessness toward the Supreme Lord—is itself liberation, because there is no possibility of rising again from that state. This refers to "of dharma."
That is to say, [he causes him] who is otherwise known as *praṇaya* (affection) to move within, to wander in the midst of *māyā*, and to course within *māyā*.

For it will be established that the *māyā*-principle (*māyātattva*) is the locus of *dharma* and the other [qualities], whereas the *buddhi*-principle (*buddhitattva*) is the place of manifestation (*vibhava*). The reason for this is that [the soul] has been raised up by the power of *niyati* (destiny). From the *Aśvamedha*...

The consecration (*adhivāsa*) performed when the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) is contracted is rightly said to be established within that contracted portion consisting of *māyā*, and not within the portion of pure consciousness, because in the latter, where contraction has vanished, such [consecration] is absent. And that very [portion], by virtue of its capacity for determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) within the intellect (*buddhi*), possesses an expanding nature and serves as the fruit. Of that attribute...

The reality of necessity (*niyatitattva*) pertaining to the intellect within *māyā* is the sovereign power of the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarī śakti*), consisting of the expansion of the scriptures such as the *Śrutis*, which serves as the instrumental cause. This is what is meant: the transcendence of *māyā* is the pervasive state of the immersion into the helplessness of devotion to the Supreme Lord, which is of the same nature as the savor of liberation.

And its opposite is the state of existing within *māyā*. How could its cause, *dharma*, function as a reason for one who is bent [toward liberation], being pervaded by that which is contrary to its own effect? Therefore, this is the formal argument: subjection to devotion is not the fruit of *dharma*, because it is perceived to consist of the savor of liberation.

The perception of liberation consisting of the savor of [ultimate] freedom— which is pervaded by transcendence of *māyā*, which is contradictory to being contained within *māyā* that pervades the state of being a fruit of *dharma*— effects the negation of the state of being a fruit of *dharma*, which is itself pervaded by what is contradictory to its own pervader. [This occurs] because [liberation] is unshackled, whereas [the state of being a fruit of *dharma*] consists of *dharma* and so forth as fashioned by its own necessity (*niyati*).

That grace of the Lord which consists of the removal of the turbidity— artificially produced by the concealment of one's own absolute freedom by the veil of *māyā*— and which is composed of the purity that is the manifestation of one's own essential nature;
[by means of this grace] I, who was concealed in the form of these limited subjects, now reflect within the Light by means of my very own true nature.

And thus, its existence is conceivable only through such a nature— that is, by way of a specific modality consisting of that fitness (yogyatā), and not by any other worldly manner. For in every respect, its essence is purity (nairmalya), which is serenity (prasāda) and the very nature of the Lord (bhagavadrūpatā).

Identity (*tādātmya*) is liberation alone. In that state, there is no residual impression of *māyā*; however, here [in this world], even that exists by His will alone, which effects the fulfillment of the task of bestowing grace upon the worlds. This is in the form of being a worthy recipient (*pātratā*).

A qualification that is not commonly known in the world has been employed.
