For the causal relationship pertaining to Māyā—according to the analogy of a potter and a jar within a dream—rests upon the foundation of the causal relationship consisting of ultimate agency, which is grounded in consciousness whose essence is absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) and whose nature is such an appearance; [this occurs] within the world composed of Māyā.

It is well known because it is heart-pleasing. Regarding the explanation that "wherever that [conventional reality] is not applicable, there it is indeed the ultimate reality," the commentator (vṛttikāra) states this very point through this refutation;
such is the style of the author of the Vivṛti throughout. This applies even to things that are the results of merit, demerit, and so forth.
Having raised the objection that the attainment of the grace of the Supreme Lord— which is invariably concomitant with the supervision by an intelligent being who presides over *dharma* and so forth—

is required, the word "only" (*eva*) is used in the commentary (*vṛtti*), and it is explained by the term "unrestrictedly" (*viśṛṅkhala*). Having raised the objection as to how the phrase "in some manner" (*kenacit prakāreṇa*) can be explained by means of the ablative case, [the author] explains it in three ways.

He provides the justification: the suffix *tham* is prescribed after words such as *kim* when they denote an object qualified by a mode (*prakāratva*), in its own sense—as in *kaḥ prakāraḥ* ("what kind?
or *katham* ("how?"). However, with respect to an external correlate, the meaning of an appropriate case-ending is postulated for it;
and here, since the context concerns the nature of a cause (*hetu*), the meaning of the ablative case is intended.

This is appropriate, but not as a third case-meaning (instrumental); rather, it is one way [of explaining] that [the suffix] enters into [the meaning] here by necessity. Now, just as in the rule *bhāvavacanānām*, the meaning "those whose agent is the action" (*bhāvakartṛkāṇām*) is understood because, when the word *vacana* is derived in the sense of an agent (*kartṛsādhana*), the aspect of the base-meaning (*prakṛtyarthāṃśa*) which is merely a means (*upāyamātra*) is not intended to be expressed; so too [is it here].

In the expression *prakāravacana*, the word *vacana* is derived in the sense of an instrument (*karaṇa-sādhana*). Thus, the suffix *thamu* is applied to the base [the word] which is qualified by the meaning of "manner" (*prakāra*) that has attained the nature of an instrument. Consequently, the well-known analysis (*vigraha*) occurs precisely with a word ending in the third case. Even so, in order to demonstrate that it is indeed the cause (*hetu*) that is intended as the causal factor (*kāraṇatva*) in the Sūtra, [it is stated] in the Vṛtti...
The second explanation is that the fifth case (*pañcamī*) is employed to express the cause (*hetutā*) without doubt.
In both of these two explanations, it is specifically a particular cause (*hetuviśeṣa*) that is stated to be a "type of cause" (*hetuprakāra*). Furthermore, it might be argued as follows:
"Type" (*prakāra*) means an excellent cause (*prakṛṣṭaḥ kāraḥ*); it refers to an eminent action, that is, a distinguished variety of action (*viśiṣṭaḥ kriyābhedaḥ*).

And for this very reason, since the word *thamuḥ* is employed merely to distinguish between substance, quality, and so forth— such that when one asks, "Is this a quality, a substance, or an action? there is no usage of the word *kathaṃ* in that sense— it follows accordingly.

The manner of the cause is not expressed by the word "how" (kathaṃ), but rather it is the manner of the action itself. And here, the action is the act of attaining (āsādana); its manner is produced solely by the differentiation of the causes. For the attainment of servitude to the Supreme Lord is one thing, caused by distress, the desire to know, the fruit, eagerness, and so forth; but this [present] is a different kind of attainment altogether.

Thus, the word *kathaṃcit* (somehow) should be explained as being joined with the word *āsādya* (having attained). This specific kind of attainment, which has the grace of Maheśvara as its cause, was explained previously in the *Vṛtti* by means of the word *labdha*, which ends in a *kta*-suffix, because it explains the state of having occurred earlier (*paurvakālikatva*), and because of the compound.
Because it enlivens the meaning of the sentence through the agent, by entering into the body of the agent;

the clarification consists in [showing] the identity of the agent and the connection between the meanings of the verbal roots through the distinction of "having brought" (*āsādya*) and "bringing" (*āsādana*), as the relationship of action and instrument exists in the form of a general and its particular.
Or [it is] the relationship between the perceived and the perceiver. By the word "of that very" (*tasyaiva*), the lack of dependence on anything else is expressed by the particle *eva*.

By the words "by which" (*yayā*) and so forth, the absence of any intention toward a fruit is stated by way of defining the fruit. Regarding "their mind," this refers to the state of devotion (*bhakteḥ*), having reached a state of helplessness through immersion in that [state] by obtaining its savor (*tadāsvāda*).

The essential nature [of faith] has been stated. Furthermore, for one who has not yet experienced its taste, faith is the apprehension of attaining it. As they say: "Devotion is said to be the fruit of faith; without it, one cannot remain.
Now, regarding the portion of the aphorism, "desiring also to benefit people," the commentary is: "I [bestow] the wealth of being alone."

Feeling shame, he begins to explain this [verse] with the words "and by the virtuous person" (*sajjanena ca*). The particle *ca* (and) serves to aggregate another object of knowledge (*prameya*) and indicates the commencement of another explanation, as before.
The state of being a virtuous person (*sajjanabhāva*) consists of fullness precisely through the attainment of servitude to the Lord. For one who is incomplete...
Thinking, "I shall fill myself completely," he harms others and does not benefit them; therefore, he is a wicked person.
For this very reason, the suffix *ṇyat* is used in the sense of "it must necessarily be so" (*bhāvya*), even though it is not mandatory.
(page 28)

"By that self-sustaining one, it certainly does not exist"—this is the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the support of fullness as "I. Since we have obtained the rare service of Him, it should be said: "by my solitary devotion," rather than by the words "prosperity" and "fortune. This refers to the qualification of *pratyabhijñā* (recognition) found in the Sūtra, namely "entirety" (*samasta*).
Fearing that this might be suspected as merely a sycophantic hint intended as a qualification of "servitude" rather than a distinct effort, he says: "Accomplishment" (*saṃpat*).

That which is intended is an eminent devotion consisting of sovereignty, taking the form of immersion into the Great Lord (*maheśvara*), which is distinct from other forms of devotion to Bhavānī’s beloved [Śiva] that partake in the relationship between the fruit and its constituent parts. This is what is meant.

By the word *lakṣmī* and by the term *saṃpat*, it is indicated that these qualify the word "entire" (*samasta*) as a descriptor of "servitude. The term *saṃpat* is placed first due to its proximity to the word to be explained; however, the word *lakṣmī* follows later because of its association with that [term]. Now, one might object: "But supreme devotion is devoid of attachment to fruits."
Anticipating the objection as to how the qualification "entire" (*samasta*) can be compatible [with the state of being unconditioned], he says: "Because" (*yataḥ*).

"Entirety" (*samastatvam*) refers to the lack of limitation (*anavacchinnatvam*) regarding accomplishments (*saṃpadām*). And since that [entirety] occurs precisely through the power of immersion into the Supreme Lord (*parameśvarāveśavaśāt*), there is no contradiction here. Because devotion (*bhakti*), which consists in attaining the Supreme Lord, is thus preeminent, therefore...

The word *lakṣmī* has many meanings; this is the connection at a distance. In the middle, however, there is a corroborating passage, and its application is sung by the Guru to Arjuna: "Four kinds of virtuous people always worship Me... [Gītā 7.16].
"The distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom... (Bhagavad Gītā 3.16).

Thus, by means of that which is denoted by the word "jijñāsā"—whether it be the certainty that [the Lord] is the cause for the removal of suffering, or the certainty that He is the cause for the attainment of happiness, or the doubt regarding the object of both those concerns—[one approaches Him].
Or rather, a state of profound devotion toward the Supreme Lord arises as being inseparable from the knowledge of reality.

Thus he says "me": they worship—that is, they serve and exalt—the Supreme Self who shines forth without interruption; [they do so] with attributes in the former case, and without attributes in the latter. By that—
There are four kinds of devotees. Among them, the last one is "ever-steadfast," as described in Bhagavad Gītā 12.2: "Those who, having fixed their minds on Me, worship Me with constant discipline...

Thus, he is endowed with the yoga of immersion (*samāveśa*) as described, and is constantly joined with devotion; however, his devotion does not waver toward the attainment of results as it might for those belonging to the first three categories. Furthermore, his devotion is directed solely toward the Supreme Lord and not primarily toward the fruit—having thus defined his excellence, he is distinguished as "special" (*viśiṣṭa*).
He confirms his status as the cause of all prosperity by virtue of being an embodiment of the immersion into the Supreme Lord:
"But the man of knowledge is My very Self" (Bhagavad Gītā 7.18).
For Me—whose Self is the Supreme Lord recognized [through such immersion]—the man of knowledge is the Self, that is, my own essential nature.

The meaning "Supreme Lord" has been stated here by way of a figurative turn of phrase, and not as "I am the Self of the Knower. He clarifies this very point with the words, "For the Knower is indeed the devotee. This means that being a Knower (*jñānitva*) itself is what is called devotion (*bhakti*). These [qualities] are appropriate for the Lord and are inseparable from identity with the Lord. [This refers to the word *bahvartha*], which has a function (*vṛtti*) consisting of many meanings; and yet—

There is no need for explicit mention [of the suffix *kap*] because the plurality is already understood from the absence of *ka*. For since the suffix *kap* is established as compulsory after words ending in *lakṣmī-* by the rule *nady-ṛtaś-ca* (Pāṇini 5.4.153), its inclusion among the *uraḥ-prabhṛti* group would otherwise result in the singular forms *naus* and *lakṣmīs* being read there; it is precisely so that the compulsory *kap* may apply to those very singular forms.

But if it ends in the dual number, then there is an option (*vibhāṣā*). By this much, the state of being a servant of Maheśvara has arisen for oneself, a state of devotion animated by the recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) of Maheśvara;
thus, even though it pertains to the *Pratyabhijñā*, the qualification "entirely" (*samasta*) and so forth is somehow explained.

It has been stated that [the state of being a servant] has been forcibly transferred through the gateway of the state of being a knower (*jñānitā*). One who feels shame because of such a singular excellence is, for that very reason, one whose disposition is moist (*ārdrāśaya*), meaning one whose heart is tender and pure;
for that very reason, it is by him that the heart is made fit for immersion into the Supreme Lord who assumes all forms (*viśvarūpa-parameśvara*). This is the remainder [of the argument].
Apart from that person who has recognized his own true nature and attained identity with the Supreme Lord,
there is no other person— whether consisting of a continuum of past, future, or present subjects—
for whom there exists a natural and appropriate Lord, nor for whom there exists a natural subject belonging to that [Lord] who is to cause recognition.
"Indeed, for the knower, the extraction of the deceased must be understood through the continuity [of consciousness];

such is the scripture. This connection of that Lord—characterized by the relationship between the recognizer and the object to be recognized—is of great fruit and the cause for attaining all prosperity; or rather, it is the recognition of Him.
(Page 30) For one whose heart is moist with devotion,

there exists through immersion into the Lord (*īśvara-samāveśa*) a relationship with the All-Powerful One characterized by the recognition of the recognizer and the recognized. Both of these two explanations, moreover—

The statement in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) would result in an improper repetition; for this [statement] is appropriate only in the explanation of the section on the *vṛtti* regarding the phrase "the ultimate goal" (*paramārtha*), and it will also be stated that the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* is of supreme fruit for people. Therefore, it must be explained solely as residing within the moistened disposition (*ārdrāśaya*) of that [person]. Of that...

The relationship characterized by lordship and servitude that exists between the Lord—who possesses a moist (compassionate) disposition and is omnipotent—and [the devotee], is of great fruit and expansive fruit; indeed, just as in the case of one's own self-interest, it culminates even in the interest of others. Therefore, in both the aphorism (*sūtra*) and its commentary (*vṛtti*), the word "alone" (*ekākin*) [is used] in the sense that "all prosperity belongs to him."
This has been indicated: just as a well-known good person, out of consideration for another, reflects, "I am the servant of the Supreme Lord;
I do not enjoy wealth alone, but I also make it known to others so that they too may rejoice in its gain"—so too, by some means, [the devotee acts] through the power of his own disposition.
He reflects on the passage beginning with "the service of the Great Lord" and ending with "I shall establish.

He explains that he reflects in this manner because of his virtuous nature, and thus demonstrates that the formulation of the logical pervasion (*vyāpti*) has also been established by both the aphorism (*sūtra*) and the commentary (*vṛtti*) in the words "for whoever..."— meaning, whoever is a virtuous person who has attained deep intimacy with the Lord, to him everything is given.
He who is denoted by the word "servant" reflects in this manner; and that he is a good person (*sujana*) and the author of the treatise is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*).

For if one does not reflect in this way, there is wickedness (*daurjanya*), which is contrary to goodness; thus, by the perception of what is contrary to the essential nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalambha*), the reason—goodness—is indeed excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), namely, from the state of not reflecting in this manner. Thus...

The establishment of pervasion (*vyāpti*) consists in its being pervaded by the probandum, namely, the state of being an investigator. By the word "acquaintance" (*paricaya*), the condition of servitude devoid of ritual practice is explained as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). It refers to the agent and the object [of the action] for the purpose of making known what is already established; however, it does not refer to the primary object (*mukhyakarma*). This is indicated by the term "the Lord" (*īśvaram*).
The sense is that although it is well-known, it is as if unknown due to the veil of *māyā*. "Toward him" refers to another person.
Now, one might object: in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), God is both the agent and the object, whereas in the case at hand (*prakṛta*), it is the primary object;
thus, there is merely a similarity of words regarding the thing to be proven (*sādhya*). Consequently, it is like saying, "This place possesses cows."

(Page 31) Just as in the example where the usage "possessing a cow" does not establish the usage "possessing a Māheyī" despite the pervasion [of the former] by the usage "possessing brilliance," so it is also in the present case.
Anticipating this objection, he says: "The purpose is twofold. There is no discrepancy here at all.

For the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is as follows: a good person, acting as an assistant, reflects upon making known that which is to be accomplished through a cognition that has two objects. Therefore, by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*), there is a distinction, by which this—

It introduces a certain fault regarding the cause and the probandum. Therefore, it is stated that "this single meaning is clarified in two ways" and thus "the meaning of both. In the present context, the person is the object of the causal action (*prayojyakarman*)—as in "recognize the master"—and the master is seen to be the object of the causal action in the example—as in "he is fit for these duties."

"Let the master recognize his own [self]"—in this way, by turn, there is the status of being the object of the causal agent (*prayojyakarma*). Anticipating the objection that, like the verb *saṃjñāpayati*, the verb *jānāti* preceded by *prati-ā-* does not have cognition as its meaning, he says: "Because it has cognition as its meaning. For even that which is known becomes, through the power of delusion, as if unknown; [the prefix] indicates its becoming present before one's eyes, that is, its reaching the heart.

Knowledge is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). Now, one might object: "The demonstration of the scope of pervasion (*vyāpti*) is not seen in the Sūtra; how then can it be [found] in the Commentary (*vṛtti*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "By that, and of that. In that compound which is formed with the genitive case of residue (*śeṣa-ṣaṣṭhī*), intended to express the general relationship between these two objects of meaning—

The connection (*śleṣa*) which consists in two meanings being expressed by a single word—that relationship is what is included in the Sūtra as well, namely that "both these meanings" [are intended]; this is the connection with the preceding [statement]. Now, an objection:
that which was stated in the Vṛtti regarding recognition—namely, that case where there is a connection with both primary and secondary actions by turns—is not included in the Sūtra.
For in that context, he says "the prompter" (*prayojaka*), because it has been stated that the act of bringing about [an effect] has recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) as its object.
The connection is that this is what is intended by the term in the Sūtra. Now, one might object: in the Sūtra there is the root *upa-pad*, not *prati-abhi-jñā*;
how then can they have the same meaning? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "the means for recognition. [That is to say,] the act of causing recognition (*pratyabhijñāpana*).

For this is the activity of the instigator; it is not here in the form of a command or a request such as "recognize," but rather it is characterized by performing what is conducive to that [recognition]. And regarding recognition, that which constitutes performing what is conducive to it is the determination of its possibility through logical justification (*upapatti*), and nothing else. Therefore, [one establishes] recognition through justification.
"I investigate," "I demonstrate the means regarding that object," "I esteem her as she truly exists," "I establish recognition," and "I cause recognition"— these are all one and the same.

The meaning is as follows: "And thus, by the means that will be stated" is the commentary (*vṛtti*) on the word "I shall establish" (*upapādayāmi*); for the phrase "I shall establish" means "I shall demonstrate the means pertaining to that [subject].
Furthermore, this indicates another forthcoming explanation of the term "this entire perfection" (*samastasaṃpat*). To explain:
Recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is the knowledge that occurs through a renewed confrontation with an object— though it was previously known, forgotten, or obscured—

not by way of mere recollection, but rather with vivid clarity, such as "this is that very same thing," wherein there is a synthesis of the past appearance and the present manifestation, establishing the stability of the object as it persists across the interval between former and present times.

It is indeed the state of being known. Even in the case of [the thought], "This very person was recognized by me today," there has necessarily been some knowledge [of him] previously in a general form. Likewise, although the Self shines constantly, there is again a direct cognition as if it were veiled by delusion (*moha*). And in that regard, the means for the whole [is as follows]:
The attainment (*saṃpat*) of blue, pleasure, and so forth is *siddhi*; its perfect acquisition is the ascent to unwavering reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

Therefore, this is the meaning: I shall establish that [recognition] which has as its cause or means the attainment of all prosperity—that is, I shall provide the proof for such a means to that [recognition]. And the establishment [occurs] within recognition.
The word "rested" (*viśrāntam*), when employed, renders that [subject] which was previously used as qualified by its own [state] effective in terms of its result;

thus, there is no discrepancy whatsoever between the meaning of the Sūtra and the meaning of the Commentary (*vṛtti*). Power (*śakti*) consists of vision and action; that itself is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and the means of recognition (*abhijñāna*). Whatever is independent in respect to knowledge and action, that is Īśvara.

It is as if established by the Purāṇas and Āgamas. And the reality of the subject (*pramātṛtattva*) is thus, and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) is characterized by this alone. Even if a Lord established in the Purāṇas and other texts were not accepted, the definition of sovereignty remains simply the possession of unimpeded instruments of knowledge regarding the domain of a master of a house, a village, or a district. And those...

"In the reality of the subject (pramātṛtattva), [the power] is indeed unimpeded with respect to all objects. The word "api" (even/also) is displaced in its position [to be read after "janasya"]. It is not only my [great fruit], but even that of ordinary people. By this much, the fact that "samasta" (entire/all) functions as an adjective qualifying both [the subject and the fruit] has been made clear; however, it does not mean that all [material] riches [are intended].

(Page 33) They are stated as the fruit in the aphorism (*sūtra*), yet in the commentary (*vṛtti*) only the attainment of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) is explained as the fruit; what does this mean?
To this, he says: "Where... Fullness is indicated by the conjunction with all attainments—namely, royal power, enjoyment, and heaven.
Even when one has attained the enjoyment of the worlds (*bhuvana-bhoga*), since there remains the possibility of desiring something further and further, what room is there for fullness?

But regarding the supreme object of desire, beyond which no other object of desire exists—once that state of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara-bhāva*) has been attained, what further thing could there be to be desired? This is the intended meaning. And by this much... [iti]

By means of the text of the Sūtra and its Commentary (*vṛtti*). [Objection: But how can the attainment of human goals (*puruṣārtha*), which occurs in the world, be the purpose (*prayojana*) brought about by the treatise?
[Response: He says, "by way of being the cause for engagement. For there is no "horn" (i.e., no distinct essence) of a purpose;
rather, that very thing which incites one to action is the purpose. As they say: "That object with reference to which [one acts]... (Nyāya-sūtra 1.1.24).

And regarding the phrase "because it has the desired characteristic": if it is asked, "What is the purpose of the author of the treatise in achieving worldly results?", [the reply is: "What is his purpose even in achieving results for himself? If it is argued that he is satisfied with that [worldly result], [the author] says "But the author of the treatise... with the intention that this is the same here as well. Now, which part of the Sūtra is explained by the commentary [with the words] "I might be satisfied"?

With this intention, he says "by this. Since "freedom from expectancy within oneself" is a negation regarding a specific object, it does not permit anything else; because there is no other possible course for an expectancy consisting of desire, the Supreme alone becomes its object. Nor is it logical that this [expectancy] should have the harming of others as its object, for...

Because he is incomplete due to having desires for his own self, whereas this [Lord] is complete because of his servitude to the Lord, which is the cause for attaining all prosperity; thus, there is nothing whatsoever to be done or desired within his own self. Furthermore, his will—being of the nature of consciousness—is unimpeded; it necessarily results in having only the welfare of others as its object.

For one who is constrained by what can be accomplished for oneself would not desire to benefit another; however, in the absence of anything to be accomplished for oneself, that [desire] necessarily becomes directed toward the service of others. As I have stated myself in the *Śrīṣaḍardhaślokavārtika* and the *Tantrāloka*:
Perceiving some task of his own to be performed, this world exerts its efforts;
it does not direct any activity of its own toward the welfare of others.
"But for him who has abandoned all impurities of worldly existence and attained perfect awakening, his duty is clearly this alone: the mere performance of what is to be done for the world. (2.39).
Thus, since the benefit is accomplished through the attainment of the state of being a servant of Mahādeva—the repository of all perfections for the self—
"Desiring that even for another" means: "I shall be satisfied simply by the unimpeded expansion of my desire," [thinking] "the time has come;
it is appropriate for me to be quickly satisfied in this matter. Here, the *liṅ* suffix indicates the arrival of the proper time (*prāptakāla*).
This is the explanation of the phrase "desiring to benefit": namely, "I would be satisfied. For satisfaction is indeed the non-obstruction of a desire as it expands.

The intended meaning is: "How could one who is capable of benefiting others suppress the expanding desire directed toward that [benefit]—a desire whose flow is unimpeded either by the intensity of accomplishing one's own ends or by the intent to ward off obstacles to one's own ends? Having thus explained the Sūtra and the Vṛtti:
The author of the commentary now determines this with the passage beginning "even for a mere worldly person," etc.,
which he stated at the outset of introducing the Sūtra when he declared that he states the purpose (*prayojana*) for the sake of engaging the audience.
For instance, some believe that because one observes the truth or falsity of human words...
Even when the purpose has been understood from the statement, a doubt may arise regarding that purpose;
because it takes the form of a doubt, the purpose is what prompts action, or because it takes the form of a conviction based on probability.
For, while the author of the treatise is known to possess virtuous character and proper conduct, this [purpose] is not accepted even by a mere worldly practitioner.

By such statements as these: "In this context, desire (*arthitva*) is [the cause]. This means that even when the means to an end are available, how could a person's engagement occur? Thus, desire alone is the primary cause of engagement; the knowledge of the means, however, merely provides a handhold by presenting the object to one who is already engaged. In that regard, concerning habitual worldly activity:

In practical affairs such as the examination of gold and silver, a person regards even the words of goldsmiths, lapidaries, and the like as authoritative— how much more so, then, those of a scriptural author! Furthermore, by the grace of the Supreme Lord, his mind becomes intent upon the goal consisting of the immersion into the very nature of the Supreme Lord.

But one who is ignorant of the means, being terrified and wondering "what shall I do?", immediately hears the opening statement and proceeds without hesitation. Thus he says: "It is seen"—this matter is undeniable. For this very reason:
They accepted that validity is intrinsic (*svataḥ*) regarding a familiar object, [arising] from what is indicated by the scriptures and so forth.
For one proceeds merely upon seeing a leaf, neither questioning the world nor the teacher;
or, having heard the scripture with doubt, one might then perceive its truth. It is for this purpose [that they hold this view].

"Whoever is a seeker"—this means that there is no other restriction regarding the qualified person (*adhikārī*) here. "Let him proceed"—that is, he is entitled to proceed with the hearing of this scripture. For that which has a clearly manifest purpose (*prayojana*), namely the basis for its composition, there is no pointlessness. This is stated in the verse beginning with "In this very [work], somehow."

For the author of the commentary (*vṛttikāra*) would say that the author of the text (*granthakāra*) establishes recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), but not that he himself establishes it. Now, one might object that there is a ground for lack of confidence because of the suspicion that the commentator might state a purpose due to some other reason, such as a lack of understanding; therefore, if the commentator were acting out of a desire to deceive...

It may be suspected: why is this not also suspected—that when it should have been said "I establish," the author of the commentary (vṛttikṛt) instead said "I establish for the sake of leading across"? Anticipating this suspicion, he says: "Because of its being well-known.
For those who lived at the same time as the author of the root text (mūlagranthakāra) were direct witnesses [to his usage] in sequence.

They spread out [their] renown. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that 'renown' (prasiddhi) is not a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) at all? At best, it is an imagined essential reason (svabhāvahetu), and ultimate reality cannot be established through conceptual construction. Anticipating this doubt, he says, "that which will be stated," meaning it will be explained in detail during the investigation of scripture (āgama).

The meaning is "this. For this cannot apply to both the root text (*mūla*) and the commentary (*vṛtti*). Nor is this a statement from the *Ṭīkā* concerning that [passage], but rather it is a sentence from an *Āgama* text. Since its reading is identical here and in what follows, how can it be said that "it will be explained"? For if it were so, one would have to say "this has been stated" even in the subsequent section. Therefore, the meaning is as follows:

The meaning is that this will be explained in the section on the definition of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) in the passage beginning with "this is such-and-such" (2.16). For in that context, [the author] will establish that which produces a firm and unshakeable reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

[It is] a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). And thus it will be stated that well-known tradition (*prasiddhi*), which has its very life in critical inquiry (*vimarśa*), is of the nature of the authority of scripture (*āgamapramāṇa*).

"Possessing reason" (*yuktimat*) means having the support of the hand extended by logic (*nyāya*), as in the case of scriptures such as those of the non-dualists (*advaitin*) regarding God (*īśvara*).

The other [position] is not supported by logical reasoning (*nyāya*). Starting from the enumeration of these many principles (*tattva*) and worlds (*bhuvana*), the scripture (*āgama*) states that through these mantras and these many oblations (*āhuti*), purification characterized by the state of being "no longer subject to bondage" (*apunarbandhakatva*) occurs;
and from that very [purification], there is "union with Śiva" (*śivayojanā*) and so forth. Such is the nature of liberation within the *Vidyā* [tattva].

Regarding the means for attaining one's true nature (*svarūpa*), which is ignorance (*avidyā*)—the ground of *saṃsāra*—and the means for awakening therein, the rational person [holds that] "dharma indeed arises from giving, whereas adharma arises from violence. This is because the mind [is characterized by] the intention to help or harm, resulting in a form that is either stainless or stained; thus, the fruit is of a corresponding kind. This is an inference based on probability (*saṃbhāvanānumāna*). One who lacks such reasoning is irrational.
"From bathing comes merit for one who is initiated; from giving comes demerit"—thus [it is said].

"Without contradiction" is the reason for its authority (*prāmāṇya*). Contradiction (*vigāna*) is the uprooting of that reflection (*vimarśa*); because there is no other reflection [to replace it], there is authority. But when that [contradiction] arises, there is indeed non-authority (*aprāmāṇya*). Now, as for that...

Whence has this scripture (āgama) come? He says: it is divine (aiśvarī), having come from God (Īśvara); it is true speech (satyā vāk). And for this very reason, although it is sought to be obstructed, it cannot be obstructed; for this same reason, it is "uncontradicted" (avigītā), meaning its cognition is not uprooted by conflicting deliberations. By means of that well-known divine speech—by that authoritative word (vāc)—[the scripture is established].

"In whom" refers to a particular qualified person (*adhikāriviśeṣa*) and to a place (*deśa*). "When" refers to time (*kāla*). "That which" refers to the object of knowledge (*prameya*). "Established" means having reached the ground of reflective awareness (*vimarśabhūmi*) and having attained firm, forceful consolidation within the hollow of the heart (*hṛdayakoṭara*). "That" refers to that very form consisting of the specific place, the qualified person, the time, and the object of knowledge. "By those who are free from doubt" means precisely because they are without doubt.
The meaning is that one must rely upon it according to the maxim: "In speech there is one thing, in the throat another; what is graspable is not graspable. By this [it is meant].
“For a person born empty-handed...

37)—this expression is a mere empty phrase. In this world of living beings, which is already full of hundreds of established reputations, the reputation of any single individual is but one thing among many.

According to the maxim: "As if dissolved, as if reflected, as if painted, and as if engraved within" (Mālatīmādhava 5.10), with the intention that it does not depart from the wall of the heart without uprooting that very heart even by hundreds of extractions, he says: "even of the Buddhist. For he...
Likewise, when the two objects [of perception] have been purified, for one who desires to undertake the study of the treatise,
that indeed is the time when there is sublation by the treatise.
Thus he said: "Likewise,
through reflection that is not in conflict with that [teaching], and by means of the desired application established therein,
the acceptance of the scripture is to be justified when transitioning to the third stage."

Thus it is said. And even if one were to go very far in this matter, how could this be ascertained—that by the very same person who correctly described these two objects accessible to perception and inference, that third object, which is not their domain, was also spoken of? For there is no [evidence] here [to establish this].

Probabilistic inference (*saṃbhāvanānumāna*) is also possible according to the logic of the dispassionate omniscient one (*vītarāga-sarvajña*), because the suspicion has not been removed that someone who is a deliverer might also be among them due to such acts as the worship of shrines (*caityavandana*). Furthermore,
the fact that this was spoken by the Buddha is established for both those within our own school and those of other schools, and thus it is beyond doubt.
It may be said: "This is the ascent upon the true path as described by us; enough with groundless suspicion here.

Thus, the ultimate purpose has been stated primarily as the attainment of all prosperity (*samasta-sampat*); I shall now establish that which brings about this attainment. Furthermore, the relationship between these two is one of the means and the end (*sādhya-sādhana-bhāva*). [The subject matter] is...
Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*). The relationship between that [work] and the treatise is that of the object to be explained and the means of explanation.

Because the treatise is the means for that [recognition], it is designated as the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā* (Recognition of the Lord). As for the succession of the lineage of gurus, it has been made manifest... (4.15).

This will be established at the conclusion of the treatise in the context of explaining the meaning of the scriptures; however, what is the use of it at this juncture, which concerns the investigation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establish conventional usage? For the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the logical reason is not established by the mere force of a statement.
Or rather, it is its own nature (*svarūpa*). And in inference for the sake of others (*parārthānumāna*), everything indeed is independent of the form of scripture (*āgama*).

The result here is merely the removal of delusion (*moha*), because even though the subject (*dharmin*), the reason (*hetu*), and the pervasion (*vyāpti*) are already established, they achieve their purpose by dispelling false conceptualizations produced by the obscuration of delusion.

"By the principle that 'the other party is merely reminded of the convention because their similarity has been perceived,' when the locus (*dharmin*) is unestablished, the reason (*hetu*) is unestablished, or the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is unestablished,
the mere statement of the opponent is useless; or else, if there were conviction based on his words, it would be nothing but scripture (*āgama*)."

Regarding inference: here, while the Self is manifesting by itself in its nature as the Lord, the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes conventional usage occurs only upon the removal of delusion. For this very reason, it is said that "reasoning (*tarka*) is unfounded."
Thus, this [argument] does not descend [into validity], because it is constructed from a fundamental consciousness according to the logic: "This is a jar, because it appears as such.

For this is not something fabricated solely by one's own conceptualization—standing outside of true experience like the [fallacious] argument: "This subject is eternal, because it is either the subject or a similar instance (sapakṣa), according to my own admission. Precisely for that reason, even scripture (*āgama*) follows upon this [same foundation].

"Let there be an auxiliary [support]," he says. By the very phrase "in some way," the succession of gurus (*guruparvakrama*) is also indicated; for it has been stated in the venerable *Mataṅga* and other texts that "the connection with a true guru is exceedingly difficult to attain. Thus: "The connection is extremely hard to establish."
Thus, even in the *Vṛtti*, the venerable Guru is designated by the very term "Supreme Lord" (parameśvara),
[as well as] the teacher, the mantra, the scripture, and Śiva.
The Lords of Knowledge (vidyeśas) do not create any diversity whatsoever.

For such is the traditional scripture (*āgama*). Furthermore, the author of the *Ṭīkā* will state: "by those who have directly realized the form of the Supreme Lord. Now, one might object: how could the author of the *Vṛtti* say, "I shall cause [you] to recognize," as if he were established in the sense of "I"?
For by that [statement], it should rather be said: "[He] causes [one] to recognize; [he] should be satisfied."

Anticipating this objection, he says: "In that commentary (*vṛtti*)," meaning in the commentary on this sūtra. This indication is given by way of the reason that follows the sūtra which is to be explained, and not otherwise.

This is according to the intention of its own nature as established within itself. Why follow the Sūtra? He says: because its function consists only in that much—the exposition (*vivṛti*) or analysis (*bhañjana*) of that very meaning which was indicated by the author of the Sūtra as being concealed (*saṃvṛta*), existing just as it is, and not otherwise made. If [the meaning] were [already] according to the Sūtra...

If one were to arrange the exposition otherwise, then there would be the raising of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) and the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) by the proponent and the opponent respectively; and consequently, after the objection made by the opponent, there would be the making of a rebuttal by the proponent at a third stage. In such a case—

It would be a *ṭīkā* (commentary), not a *vṛtti* (gloss). And it was previously stated that [the distinction between] a *sūtra* and a *vṛtti* lies in [the latter's] being gradual. Therefore, for the purpose of not raising objections and so forth, there is no presentation of prima facie arguments (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the like;
and for that reason, there is a concealed exposition of the *sūtra*. For that reason, there is a following of the *sūtra*. For that reason, there is the use of the highest [concise] formulation.

For the Sūtra says, "I shall establish," and following that, the Commentary says, "I shall cause [the object] to be recognized. Even when analyzing the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "desiring," one might employ the expression, "I would be satisfied" due to the unavoidable influence of this shadow [of the original phrasing]. Thus, the primary [function] of the first-person designation is—

Having stated the purpose, the author of the Sūtras says something else as well. The word "ca" (and) is intended to indicate an additional point—that this mention serves as a corroboration for a matter already made known by other means of proof, such as the performance of salutation; and this has indeed been stated previously. || 1 ||
The Opening Statement.
In a reality that is manifested through the power of fundamental and firm means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),

recognition— which consists in the establishment of conventional usage and has the removal of delusion as its fruit— may indeed be examined in isolation, since it is of the nature of the accomplishment of a previously unmanifested appearance. However, where there is no manifestation at all...

It has been stated; therein, first of all, the fundamental means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) must be explained. However, the intention of the word "only" (*mātra*) is that even when that has been ascertained, there may still be delusion (*moha*), and for the sake of dispelling that, let there be the establishment of conventional practice (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, in the phrase "that very [cognition]," the particle "eva" (*evakāra*) indicates priority.

That [non-manifestation] must first be established; thereafter, let recognition be discussed. Manifestation is the pervader of being the object of the means of conventional usage, and it is contrary to that [non-manifestation].

"Non-manifestation is perceived here," thus there is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). God is not an object of any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), because he is in no way manifest.
With the intention that God does not appear to anyone anywhere at any time, he says: "Now, [is it not so]? (*nanu*...).
Regarding the phrases "of that whose existence is established" and "existence itself is not established": here, "established-ness" (*siddhatva*) means being manifest (*prakāśamānatva*).

That very thing—namely, existence—is what is to be proven (*sādhya*). One must state a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) such that knowledge arises therein in the form of the manifestation of something previously unknown. And thus, Uddyotakara and others [state] the proof of God (*īśvara-siddhi*) in this manner.

They engaged in worldly discourse. Now, if the nature of the agent of the body, the world, and so forth—characterized by qualities such as having parts—is manifested in a general form through its sentience and agency, then everything has been manifested in its general essence precisely at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*). In that case, is it not severed?

If it is argued that inference possesses a previously unknown object of cognition (*apūrva-prameya*), what excellence does this confer upon the case of God? If it is replied that here the previously unknown object of cognition consists in the exclusion of non-connection with that time (i.e., His eternal connection), then in the present case as well,
the object of cognition is simply that which follows from the capacity for knowledge and action appropriate for the creation of bodies and so forth.

It might be argued that the mere proof of God (īśvarasiddhi) alone is appropriate, not the recognition of God (īśvarapratyabhijñā). He refutes this with "no. The reason for this is "because [He] is the nature of all selves. For one who seeks to prove anything must necessarily accept that something is already established. Consequently, the manifestation of the prover, the means of proof, and the subject of proof is undeniable.

Otherwise, everything would be a mere magical illusion (*indrajāla*), or perhaps nothing at all would exist. If anything is established as real, then that which is manifest is non-different from manifestation itself. And since manifestation alone is the universal self, the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), as long as this is the ultimate, essential nature of the self for everything, so long does whatever exists remain as such.
Since that which is established is accepted, the very establishment of that [world] is the establishment of the existence of that Lord (Īśvara), the manifestation of His reality;
therefore, what unprecedented or unmanifested thing remains to be manifested? Thus, the expression "Recognition of the Lord" (Īśvarapratyabhijñā) is entirely appropriate.

(Page 41) Thus, that which was stated briefly regarding the anticipated prima facie position— namely, "this is not so," and so forth— is the actual subject matter expressed by the verse. Here, in this commentary (*ṭīkā*), there is a summary of the subject matter that is to be explained in the *sūtra*.

"Introducing the verse" is the style of the commentator. Now, one might raise the objection: "In the Sūtra, the word *svātmani* (in oneself) was used in its pure form, but in the Vṛtti, the related term *sarveṣām* (of all) was stated; from where was that brought? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Sva-". Although the word *ātman*— (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence. The translation reflects the portion given.)

Since "ātman" is used in the sense of "entity" (vastu) and "intrinsic nature" (svabhāva)— as in the view that it is a term denoting an intrinsic nature related [to something else]— there might still be a suspicion, according to the views of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, that the category of "ātman" is an independent entity; however, by the inclusion of the word "sva" (self), its status as a term denoting intrinsic nature is established.
It is understood. Now, if "one's own" (*sva*) means "belonging to oneself," then the meaning of "self" (*ātman*) would be that which is related to the self;
thus, the base (*prakṛti*) expresses the very nature (*svabhāva*). Consequently, saying "the nature of the nature" would amount to saying nothing at all.
True; however, when the word "self" is uttered, the referent of the word "self" is indeed distinct [from the nature].

It is perceived as being situated within a jar. However, in the case of the word *sva*, just as in the expression "one's own cloth" (*svaṃ vastram*), there is the perception of something not attached to anything else—namely, "one's own cloth"—so too [in the case of] "the self is one's own" (*ātmīya ātmā*). The question "Whose is it one's own? arises as a requirement for another [referent], yet since nothing else has been mentioned, it is understood that the self is one's own in relation to everyone. In that regard:

Even regarding that which is for the sake of the "mine" (ātmīya), that which is for the sake of the "self" (ātman) is indeed created separately by virtue of being the means of instruction and the object of instruction;

otherwise, there would be no cognition of a relationship. Thus, even when all [things] are embraced within the bed of the notion "in the self" and so forth, the suspicion of other relationships such as conjunction (saṃyoga) would not cease. But in the case of "belonging to the self" (ātmīyatva)...

It is for this purpose—that [the Self] may be understood as being non-deviating, independent of anything else, and self-abiding—that the Self is indeed manifested through differentiation; for otherwise, the very nature of the teaching, which serves as a means to establish the fundamental reality, would be inexplicable.
For even the statement "the Self of all" involves a manifestation of differentiation, since there is no "all" whatsoever that exists apart from its own inherent nature.
For in all cases, this very same sequence applies to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which follows upon the cognition of words and is devoid of a real object (*vastuśūnya*).
And its being devoid of a real object [is as follows]...
(page 42)

This is stated with reference to conventional usage established at the ultimate level; however, we shall explain that from the perspective of being "being created," it is merely a conceptual object (*vaikalpika-vastu*)— as in [the verse] beginning *svātantryāmukta* (1.47).
Thus, in such passages as these, this word "itself" (sva) is employed solely for the purpose of attracting a related term;

however, that related term which it attracts is not necessarily restricted, because it has not been explicitly mentioned and because it does not belong to the immediate context. Consequently, everything is understood either by the word "because of non-mention" (anupādānāt) or by the context.

The objection is: "Because everything is included within it. The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is: "If that is so... Regarding that objection, first, this is the underlying intention: because the relata are not restricted, the entire category of entities—both insentient (*jaḍa*) and sentient (*ajaḍa*)—is perceived. Among those, that single Self characterized by consciousness (*caitanya*) [belongs] to the non-insentient at some time.
It can be so expressed; however, how could these insentient things—which possess distinct and mutually exclusive natures—be of a single nature?
For there is a contradiction between having distinct intrinsic natures and possessing a single intrinsic nature. But the intention of the latter [response] is this:

here, "its own nature" (*svātman*) refers to that which is not dependent on anything else, such as its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), its causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*), and so forth.

A relative is one's own, independent of others, and free from adventitious conditions (*anaupādhika*). In that regard, as long as those things are considered insentient (*jaḍa*), even existence or non-existence is difficult for them to attain with respect to their own nature; what then to say of being blue, yellow, pleasure, pain, and so forth? For instance, if that which exists in its own self were to become non-existent, [it would follow that it is not truly existent].

If it is argued that what could be defective about this [consciousness], such that it would perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in exactly the same way? If it were the case that it does so, then what of it?

If it is argued that it must manifest in exactly the same way, is this state of being manifested its own inherent power (*svamahimā*)? If you say "yes," then how can it be consistent to say, "it manifests for me" and "it manifests for Caitra"? For that [manifestation] depends upon a subject (*prātipattrī*).

If you say it is "manifestation," then if this [manifestation] belongs to the cognizer, what would it be for him? To say that "it manifests by virtue of that" is an unprecedented argument. For in that case, one might as well say that yellow appears white by virtue of something white.
If it were his own [intrinsic property], then by virtue of that, it would not occur in another thing—just as blueness does not occur in yellow. And so it is said:

Since the nature of luminosity belongs to the cognizer as its own attribute, how could it exist in the blue? For existence therein is pervaded by identity; otherwise, it would [also] exist in the blue.

The thousand-branched inconsistency beginning with "it is yellow," and so forth, would entail a contradiction of the rule that pervades the observed identity [of the object]. Being of another nature (*anyātmatva*) is the opposite of that identity (*tādātmya*), and that very thing is what constitutes belonging to another. Now, how could it be that something else is related to it? Furthermore, this is not the case for blue and the like.

Since there is no existence whatsoever for anything apart from its state of being manifest, by the force of this undeniable manifestation, its identity with the light of the subject must be accepted; thus, even blue and other objects are essentially consciousness itself, and not some other form. Therefore, that very [consciousness] is their own self, the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
This is indeed accepted. What is the purpose of this *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum)? For a *prasaṅga* consists in the occurrence of an undesired consequence.
Thus he says: "Let the clod of earth and so forth be set aside. For regarding that which is clearly manifest, who would dispute its nature as consciousness?
Even that which is considered by someone to be a void non-existence—nothing at all—that too, as long as it is such, [is not distinct from consciousness].

It shines; for as long as that [object] exists, how could it be "other" than Him? If it is being perceived, then Maheśvara alone is its own Self. If, on the other hand, this non-existence is not being perceived, then it is nothing at all; thus, to whom would it then belong as its own Self? The same applies to blue and so forth.
"For one who does not perceive, what is his own self?"—this refers to the state of being perceived. What is meant is this:

when the objection is raised that Maheśvara would also necessarily follow as the "own self" of blue, its absence, and so forth, then the very acceptance of the state of being perceived is the answer; otherwise, the objection would be groundless. But [one might ask]: "However..."

If Maheśvara is thus the self of blue, then he is also the self of yellow; in that case, from where would the distinction arise that "this is blue" and "this is yellow"? He replies: "Everything indeed. Because for the self whose nature is consciousness (*cidrūpa*), whose form is light (*prakāśarūpa*), and whose own-being is such, everything that is to be known (*vedya*) is like a body; just as a body, though it is an object of knowledge, [is not separate from the self].
The universe is likewise permeated by the nature of consciousness due to the non-figurative, firm conviction "I am.

For even among those who consider themselves distinct from the body, the sense of "I" does not appear in the world as being merely figurative on the grounds that the body is an instrument, as is the case with a blanket or other such objects.

(44) And thus, because it is permeated by the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*), just as consciousness itself possesses the form of the universe according to the method to be explained, so too does the series of entities such as blue and yellow; therefore, this [dualistic] division is certainly not accepted by us. This is the point.

He corroborates this with the words of a Vedāntin author: "Even a portion [is not different]. Just as the space within a jar, the space within a cloth, and so forth, are portions of space imagined through its connection with jars and other objects, yet they are neither less nor more than the nature of space—such as its all-pervasiveness (vibhutva)—so too it is with Brahman by virtue of its vastness (bṛhattva).
The pervasive [Light], acting as a nourisher and effecting the sustenance of universal manifestation, is of the nature of Light;

its spatial divisions—such as "the manifestation of blue," "the manifestation of yellow," and so forth—are produced by limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as blue and the like, which are reflected through its own power. These [divisions] constitute the "possession of all forms" within Brahman.

They do not transcend, nor do they exceed even slightly, that state which consists in the undivided operation of all powers, and that non-conceptuality which— being of the nature of pure manifestation— is a consciousness devoid of a counter-correlate because there is nothing to be excluded due to the absence of such a correlate, and thus lacks the nature of conceptualization; [they do not transcend this] individually, nor do they surpass it in the slightest degree.

The duality [of subject and object] indicates a state of mutual causality. Now, one might object: "Granted that this undivided nature is established by reason; however, how do we account for this appearance of division in the objects of cognition—such as 'blue' or 'yellow'—and in the cognizing subjects—such as 'I am Caitra' or 'I am Maitra'? To this he replies: "Merely," meaning the insentient [object].

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is that it appears as insentient (*jaḍa*), having its manifestation dependent on another. "Those which will be mentioned" refers to the three [powers] to be abandoned; this will be stated in the passage: "This agency belongs primarily to the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth, as a subordinate quality" (3.29). It is the very light of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*) that, through His own power of *māyā*...

By means of its sovereignty, which consists in the power to perform the most difficult tasks, it makes its own nature appear as if concealed, even though it is unconcealed. In that state, when the aspect of non-concealment predominates,
there occurs the stage of immersion into the forms of Sadāśiva and Īśvara.

When the predominance is on the manifestation of the portion of the covering (ācchādana-bhāga), the state of transmigratory existence (saṃsāridaśā) takes the form of a magical display (māyāvijṛmbhā). From that arises the differentiation of the objects of knowledge, such as "blue" and so forth; and from that arises the differentiation of the subjects of knowledge, produced by the shadow of consciousness (caitanyacchāyā) colored by the various limiting adjuncts (upādhi)—such as the intellect (buddhi), the vital breath (prāṇa), and the heptad of the city (puryaṣṭaka)—which are characterized by the differentiation of the manifesting body.
Thus, in the manifestation of duality within the state of the subject of *māyā*,
the body is consecrated as the head; and accordingly, from the very moment of its cessation, the conventional usage of "liberation" (*mokṣa*) occurs therein.

In that context, liberation (*mokṣa*) is the state of being free from transformation (*vaikaraṇya*), as in such passages. The phrase "or even the body" (*kāyo 'pi vā*) indicates that this [liberation] is its primary concern.

The word "this" (*ayam*) refers to that which was previously of the nature of light; thus, being essentially consciousness (*cidrūpa*), it has been brought to the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatā*) through its own sovereignty.
Consequently, while it is indeed an object of knowledge just like a clod of earth and so forth, by the very act of casting off the state of non-self (*anātmabhāva*), it emerges as "I."

"Resting in identity with consciousness" means "having immersed itself in the Self. Blue and other objects immerse themselves in the light within their own blue nature, whereby—by virtue of that light—the manifestation "this is blue" becomes limited; by which [immersion], this object, manifest as a property of the cognizable, appears as "seen" or "the object of knowledge" (*prameya*).

Immersed in the body, that limited manifestation— consisting of the notion "I am"— shines forth as differentiated by the distinction of the place of birth, by the reckoning of time such as the past and so forth, by the form of subjects such as Rudra, the Kṣetrajña, and their various sub-types,
and by the differentiation of its own essential nature through its distinctness from other places, times, and natures. The two particles *yadā* and *tadā* [mark this condition].

In the reflection upon the true nature of the meaning of the sentence (*vākyārtha*), that which constitutes a limitation is the delusive activity of *māyā* that gives rise to transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*). With that intention— in other words, with reference to the delusion of transmigratory existence— the venerable teacher Vāsudeva considered Arjuna as an object and spoke to him.
Or rather, the instrumental case in "by that" (*tena*) may signify cause, meaning "by means of reflecting upon that" or "with the intention of expressing that.
And those states of being which are *sāttvika*, as well as those which are *rājasa* and *tāmasa*—know them all here to proceed from Me alone. (7.12)

By this, having declared that all this— which consists of the nature of the object of knowledge (*vedya*) and the nature of the knower (*vedaka*)— is manifold due to being composed of the conjunction of manifestation, its absence, and both, and has issued forth from the pure self-nature of the "I" (*aham*) alone as consciousness; and [having done so] because of the predominance of the appearance of duality in that emanation, and [of the non-duality] of the light of the "I" (*ahaṃprakāśa*).
Because it is characterized by a distinct nature, location, and time, that which is established in the expansion (prasaras) is not established in Me.

For the vital breaths (prāṇās) are merely the portion of the expansion that conceals My own nature; yet, without being established in Me, they would be nothing at all, as they would fall into the state of non-manifestation. However, My autonomous self-luminosity does not depend on them.

There is a certain refutation. And with the intention of [dispelling] delusion regarding saṃsāra (page 46), one must investigate what among all [the statements concerning] Brahman is to be enjoined and what is to be restated. In that regard:

Although Brahman is already established, it is restated as something previously unknown (*apūrva*); everything, however, which consists of the nature of the object of knowledge and the knower, is to be enjoined [as follows]: "Brahman alone becomes all, nothing else whatsoever is all;
indeed, Brahman possesses all powers"—such are the injunction and the restatement. Nevertheless, for the Supreme Brahman who is to be taught...

Something is already established, by virtue of which it may be restated (*anūdyate*). However, since everything here—consisting of the nature of the object of knowledge and the knower—is already established, that [everything] is restated, and its identity with Brahman is then declared. When all this which is perceived is investigated by penetrating into its innermost essential nature, it is found to be nothing other than the reflective awareness of light (*prakāśaparāmarśa*).
Only form remains. Therefore it is said: "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1).
For that very reason, it negates whatever suspicion arises regarding the manifold nature of all these various aspects.

"There is nothing whatsoever here that is manifold" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.14.1). Thus, among all things denoted by the word "all" that are perceived here, there is no form whatsoever that does not exist together with light— that is, which does not subsist in identity with light— for that which is not manifesting cannot exist.

Because it cannot be trusted even through oaths; for even an oath has as its effect the manifestation of that [truth]. Now, if transmigration (*saṃsāra*) is the appearance in which the aspect of difference (*bhedāṃśa*) is predominant, then why is it not so when the aspect of non-difference from Light (*prakāśābheda*), which serves as its foundation, is predominant? He says: "of agency" (*kartṛtāyāḥ*) and "the manifoldness of the universe" (*vaiśvarūpyam*).
From the commencement of the touch of one's own pure nature, there arises the state of Vaiśvarūpa (the universal form) by way of the forms of Sadāśiva and Īśvara;

just as the author of this work has stated here, so too has another stated it, or "another has stated that same manner," or "another has also stated this according to the logical method we have described"— thus, "and so he said."

The corroboration of one statement by another, or the demonstration through numerous statements that another statement possesses vitality— that is, its non-deviation from the true meaning— is shown as follows: the word "mām" (me) refers everywhere to the Light, which is of the nature of the "I," whose manifestation is independent of anything else, which consists of self-reflection, and which is self-luminous awareness.

For when one perceives "this is blue" through total immersion (*sarvopaśleṣa*), such that "blue shines forth," the light itself becomes manifested as "I am manifesting this much. Thus, it is the light alone that is revealed.

He who perceives light everywhere realizes that there is no spatial, temporal, or essential limitation or fragmentation within that light; thus, in "Me"—that is, in the light of self-awareness—everything inseparable from it becomes manifest. In this same way, blue and other such objects are [manifest] within the light of the Self.

For one who sees that "the [Self] shines forth, rooted in the wall," his manifestation as "I" does not perish; it does not undergo fragmentation or modification, nor does it deviate from its nature as light. And I, as his very Self in the form of the Lord of the Universe, do not perish, nor am I concealed. Likewise, he too is such a seer.

The notion "mine" does not perish—that is, it is not obscured—for the Supreme Lord, whose nature is pure luminosity; rather, in that state, the Supreme Lord alone shines forth. By this [notion], even when one's own essential nature is obscured by the individual self Caitra and appears as such, he remains inseparable from the Lord even as the inner self (pratyagātman).

One considers oneself [to be the Self]. And the Supreme Lord shines therein in a concealed manner, whereby it is said that "the Supreme Lord is pleased here. In all beings, which are in their ultimate nature the Self, the Self abides as light, like the universal in particulars; indeed, all beings exist in the Self alone.

"Phenomena abide within the substrate of phenomena"—thus, whether through the universal mouth [of all things] or the mouth of Brahman, there is no difference between an injunction and a restatement according to the logic of "producedness" and "impermanence," which possess equal pervasion.
Even if there were variety, the distinction of the reality itself would be greater than the variety of entry. Therefore, "in me" means that everything is Brahman.

Thus, this teaching of non-duality is to be understood as beginning with "Vāsudeva is all," having "Vāsudeva is everything" as its middle, and ending with "He who dwells in all beings. In this way, it has been demonstrated that the states of being in saṃsāra and not in saṃsāra are determined by the predominance or subordination of qualities, whether in the aspect of all things or in the aspect of light. But when [duality] has dissolved...
As long as even a trace of duality remains, the state of Paramaśiva is not fully unfolded here;

rather, the process begins with the recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of Him by way of His being the nature of all things. Now, is it not the case that the word *ātman* itself denotes the self, the reality, and the essential nature?
Thus, since it will be explained by its established status as a term denoting intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), what is the purpose of using the word "own" (*sva*)?
He replies: "The word 'own'. First of all, according to the treatises, the self (*ātman*) is indeed well-known from the systems of Kaṇāda and others.
It is obtained; even in the world, it is well known that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of blue and other things is precisely their form as blue and so forth.

Blue exists by means of its own nature as that which performs a causal function (*arthakriyākārin*), and not by way of another's form. Therefore, both of these [meanings] are denoted by the word "own" (*sva*);
because they are the locus of establishment, they are non-deviant and beyond reproach when expressing one's own nature.

It is set aside. Now, what indeed is that nature which is such? For instance, the essential nature of all things—whether atoms and so forth, or primordial matter (*pradhāna*), or existence (*sattā*), or emptiness (*śūnya*)—is accepted by other [schools] as being merely insentient (*jaḍa*). Therefore, it must be specified as being "in one's own self, whose nature is consciousness" (*cidrūpa*). He says: "And of that... [referring to the following].

For when it is said "in the knower" (*jñātari*) or "in the agent" (*kartari*), there indeed flashes forth an independence regarding the acts of knowing and acting—of the nature of "I know," "I act," and so on—which does not depend on looking at another. However, if it were stated as "in the form of consciousness" (*cidrūpe*), that would be equivalent to saying "in the form of blue" (*nīlarūpe*).
Consequently, one would have to transfer the states of being a knower and an agent back onto the state of being consciousness itself.

This very [self] must first be protected, because it consists merely of the designation of "this-ness" (*idantā*). Since it is also described there as the "knower" and the "agent," the "this-ness" itself—whose nature is a locus of external repose—would manifest as something to be governed. Even the expressions "he knows" and "he acts" imply a state of detachment, just like "it whitens" or "it turns blue. Even the thought "I know" is a constructed egoity (*ahantā*).

Furthermore, this "thisness" (idantā) cannot be protected in every respect, because that would entail the consequence of its being unteachable; rather, it must be protected as far as its manifestation extends. In that regard, when there is a connection with a case-ending (*bhūtavibhakti*), the subordination of external predominance occurs, which manifests as a touch of the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*) through resting in an internal form; this will be explained in the investigation of the relationship (*saṃbandha*).

This is the meaning of the particle *eva*. The phrase "in the case of the superior" (*śreyasi*) means even when there is an introduction of another [inferior] thing being referred to (*anūdyamāna*). "For this very reason" (*ata eva*):

since consciousness (*cittva*) consists precisely in autonomy (*svātantrya*) with respect to both knowledge and action, therefore, by the word "agent" (*kartṛ*), whether it be unanalyzed (*avyutpanna*) or derived from the root *kṛ* which denotes action in general, [it refers to that which is connected with the limiting conditions (*upādhi*) of specific actions].
By asserting that sovereignty is unblemished by any deficiency, and by employing a pun to show that the sovereignty of knowledge— which rests upon that [sovereignty]—
is inseparable from the state of being a creator, he describes the sovereignty in creation as preceded by that [knowledge], having applied diligent effort to demonstrate this.

"Otherwise" means: if this intention were not to demonstrate pure sovereignty, then that emanation would be seen as preceded by [ordinary] cognition; [it would follow that] the nature of consciousness is the cause.
It will be corrupted; nor would it have been previously designated as "in one who knows that [act] is indeed a creation.

But then, how can there be the status of a locus (*adhikaraṇa*) in the reality that is the nature of consciousness itself—which appears appropriately as "I know thus" and "I act," and which is of a single, independent form? For the very essence of other causal factors (*kāraka*) consists in their being animated by dependence on another.
For even in such [statements] as "from me the universe" and "the universe in me," the referent "I" (asmadartha) is indeed [only] that which has been created;

however, the form of the ultimate *ahaṃtā* consists in the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) within the light [of consciousness] that "the universe is from me and in me. Anticipating the objection as to how there can be a locative case [in "mayi"], he says: "according to the view of others" (*paramatena*). For another [teacher]...

Propounding either a proof or a sublation regarding that object, he endeavors to effect either an affirmation— namely, the manifestation and linguistic usage in the form "it exists"— or a negation— namely, the manifestation and linguistic usage of another entity devoid of it in the form "it does not exist. While acting in this manner, [he relies] upon the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

And he considers the Lord (*īśvara*)—the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) of the proof and refutation established by that [scripture]—to be an object of knowledge (*prameya*) that is itself dependent on another. Thinking thus, he is restated; however, his insentience (*jāḍya*) is here predicated.
By means of the opponent's own view, it is indicated that [the Lord] is the object of proof, for that [status] is not logically tenable [for him].

The literal connection of the words is: "because it has the single nature of the subject" (*pramātrekarūpatvāt*). Now, one might ask: why is the locative case not heard in the commentary (*vṛtti*)? To this he says: "But in the commentary... and "that very [subject] itself. Since the state of being an object is logically untenable, it will be explained by means of the genitive case. Having internalized that very accomplishment as a relation, [he uses] the genitive.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is brought near by the fact that this very state of being an object, through the concealment caused by the intervention of action, is led to a state resembling its own essential nature (*svabhāva*). How is there the state of having become one's own nature? He says:
It is the demonstration of the state of pure subjectivity (*pramātṛmātratā*) by means of the preceding text beginning with "the accomplishment of all objects" (*sarvārthasiddhi*).

It has been done by him. How has the impossibility [of his existence] been explained? He says: by the statement, "The effort of the dull-witted alone [is directed toward this]. This is what is meant: one who asserts that God is the object of proof must be questioned: is he, while being proven, of the nature of manifestation (*prakāśa*), or not? In the latter case, [he cannot be proven] at all.
It would be established. In the first case, what is being proven regarding that which has such an intrinsic nature?
If it was previously thought that it was not so, then upon its establishment, its very essence would, on the contrary, be lost. This applies even to blue and other such [objects].

"None whatsoever exist apart from Light. Thus, this meaning of the locative case is as follows: having caused the "this-ness" (idantā) to disappear within itself and having withdrawn its own [objective] form, it causes [everything] to rest solely within the light of the "I," which is the nature of the knower and the agent.
This is because the sentence from the commentary beginning with "of all [beings], of their own self... was introduced as that which is to be explained.

Therefore, since the future usage [of the genitive] would be inappropriate when this [text] is being explained here—given that other sentences such as "by him" (*tena*) will follow—it is considered improper. Now, one might object: "Even in the sentence as it stands in the commentary, the genitive case is present; so why was it stated in this way [as a future genitive]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "But [it is said] 'of its own self' (*svātmanaḥ*)."
This genitive case is used in the sense of the agent (*kartari*). For knowledge, as well as the instrument (*karaṇa*), has that [Self] as its agent;

it is not a genitive of relation (*saṃbandha-ṣaṣṭhī*). Having thus, in passing, examined the genitive of the future tense (*bhāvi-vākya-ṣaṣṭhī*), he concludes what was previously stated—namely, that "it has the nature of consciousness" (*tasya ca citsvabhāvatvam*) and so forth—with the words "Thus, therefore" (*tadevam*).

The intended subject matter under discussion, which is to be established as pure sovereignty characterized by the states of being the knower and the agent—that reality is indeed "thus" (evam); this has been brought to completion through the methodological sequence of exposition beginning with "this very bed" and ending with "it will be explained. Now, [one might ask], by way of being the subject (*pramātṛtā*)...

The state of being a knower has been stated, but not the state of being an agent; on the contrary, that [agency] has been rejected by the word "one" (*eka*). Anticipating the doubt, "What then is this?", he says: "For action... [verse 2.53]:
"Thus, for one who wishes to remain [in his own nature], the very desire is the cause, the agency, and the action. (2.53)

In this context, it will be stated that the instrument (*karaṇa*) is precisely unimpeded luminous sovereignty (*apratihta-prakāśa-svātantrya*). Now, one might object: "Since agency (*nirmātṛtā*) is also indicated through this same [etymological] compounding, why has it been explained in vain? He thinks as follows: even that agency which shines forth as a distinction—namely, the activity of the potter and so forth—is also [included].

Because it is the manifestation of the power of the Supreme Lord through its vitalizing luminosity, this [subject] is not to be utterly neglected by us. For this very reason, the word "one" (*eka*) here does not negate agency;
rather, a restriction is postulated from its opposite, not from its contradictory.

By this principle, [the text] refers specifically to that state of dependence (*paratantratā*), which consists in being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) and is opposed to the sovereignty (*svātantrya*) that constitutes the nature of the subject (*pramātṛtā*). And so it says: "For this very reason. Because sovereignty is the state of consciousness (*cittattva*).
