The connection is with what precedes. Furthermore, in the absence of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), no means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is applicable or logically tenable there. For agency (*kartṛtva*) is nothing other than the state of being a knower (*pramātṛtva*); therefore, its status as an object of knowledge will be refuted here, but not its status as an effect (*kāryatā*). Otherwise, like its being an object of knowledge, its being an effect would also [be refuted].
The interpretation that "the cause should also be negated, just like the means of valid cognition" (pramāṇa) is not so compelling.

For even according to the opponent's view, the Blessed Lord does not possess the nature of being an effect (kāryatva). Indeed, that whose very nature is the state of being a knower (pramātṛtā) cannot be an object of a means of valid cognition; and that which is thus [not an object] does not fall within the sphere of worldly transaction (vyavahāra), like a ghost (piśāca). Therefore...

It would be more appropriate to say that this [self-awareness] is established through self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*), rather than that it is entirely outside the scope of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). He says "and not" (*na ca*) to address this. Now, one might object: even if it is established prior [to the object], it must have been within the scope of a valid means of knowledge previously, just as smoke is established prior to fire; anticipating this doubt, he says:
This is what is meant: whenever there is an initial commencement (*upakrama*), at that very moment there is the state of being already established (*pūrvasiddhatva*);

this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) here. Therefore, as in the case of the color blue, there is no separate means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) here; nor, even though it is self-luminous (*svayaṃprakāśatva*) like the consciousness of the mind (*cittacaitanya*), is it a form of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) consisting of a newly arisen, unprecedented manifestation.

The manifestation (*prathana*) of that which is blue, pleasure, and so forth—which is governed by the rules of identity (*idantā*), space, time, and essential nature—is the state of being [the subject];

and this state, characterized by the negation of those [objectifications], shines as the cognizer (*pramātā*). It has shone, it shines, and it will shine. Therefore, "ancient" (*purāṇa*) and "pre-established" (*pūrvasiddha*) are not synonyms.

For even though he is "ancient" (*purāṇa*), he is not pre-established like a *piśāca*; and even though he is "pre-established," he is not ancient like smoke—thus both terms are employed. As it is said, "the ancient poet": that supreme light which [makes] those who possess new splendors [appear as such].
And that light, whose nature is the Bhairava of radiance, is withdrawn and projected.

Thus, he corroborates what was stated in the *Itihāsarahasya* and other such works; he speaks of the object that is truly existent, desired, and complete. Alternatively, "antiquity" (*purāṇatā*) in the *Āgamas* refers simply to being established from before, and not [to being old in age].
(page 52)

Like space and so forth, it is devoid of the penetration of light that constitutes mere antiquity; therefore, it "corresponds," meaning it expresses an object in a manner that is equal and identical. And this [correspondence] constitutes the established status of this subject (*pramātṛ*). Consequently, whatever objects other than that subject there may be, their establishment—

The state of being manifest; since he—the subject—is its foundation, its place of rest, and its support by virtue of being the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), the intention is that in the commentary the phrase "in all objects" and so forth should be explained as the reason for its being previously established. Now, establishment (*siddhi*) consists of the nature of consciousness, and of that...

"By what other basis? [The author] says: "Whatever it may be. "In that state" means in the state of manifesting form (*sphuradrūpatva*). "Firmness" means immovability. The establishment of the object is as follows: that which manifests as "blue" is not yellow or the like, nor is it not blue, nor is it not manifesting. "Something" refers to the subject (*pramātṛ*). "Because of having such a nature" means because it has this very character.

For [the experience] is "my blue is flashing" or "Caitra’s blue is flashing"—it is indeed a flashing [belonging to a subject], and not merely "blue is flashing. Therefore, the Buddhists necessarily postulate a single cognizer (pramātṛ) in the form of a mental continuum (*saṃtāna*) or a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), precisely because such a flashing cannot be denied. "Therefore" means: because it is thus.
Its firmness throbs; it will be said [later] regarding that which is like a perfectly even wall for the variegated painting of the universe's manifold diversity.
(30) Thus, in the second chapter. Now, let it be granted that by this much [the status of] the subject (*pramātṛ*) or the intended conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is established.

Or [it may be] imagined by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). To the inquiry, "But how can that which is already established [be so]? he replies: "And those various [things]. For the state of being a "probandum" (*sādhya*) does not apply to the object to be proven when it is devoid of any designation; rather, it applies to the prover who thinks, "This is my probandum. Indeed, the term "prover" implies one who thinks, "I shall negate this self."

Even in the negation of one's own [nature], it is the cognizer alone who falls away; for either the essential nature of the self (*ātmarūpa*) is negated, or that which is conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*), or a superimposed attribute (*kalpitadharma*). That by which the establishment of [the self]—its manifestation—is necessarily implied and accepted, such that one thinks, "I establish or negate myself," or "I [negate] blue."
For in this context, that which is expressed as "I" is not like a state of fainting or deep sleep; rather, it is indeed manifestation itself (*prakāśa*).
Nor does it appear as an "this" (*idantayā*); for if it were so, it would be a separate entity based on independent existence (*pṛthaksiddhi*).

In the search [for the self], how could this very notion of "I" exist? Is it not merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? In that case, it is only the continuum (*saṃtāna*) that is imagined and determined. This is established as residing solely in consciousness (*saṃvedana*), and not in the insentient; it is the establishment of objects of knowledge (*prameya*), and not of effects (*kārya*). Therefore, let there be only consciousness.

"What is the use of a postulated subject? Or, let it exist; nevertheless, let it be merely the substratum of consciousness, like the Vaiśeṣika, or even let it be of the nature of consciousness itself yet devoid of reflective awareness (vimarśa), like the Sāṃkhya.
Thus, in brief, he speaks in order to dispel the delusions of the Buddhists, Vaiśeṣikas, and Sāṃkhyas.
"Because [the establishment] rests upon consciousness.

If the establishment of objects of cognition—that is, of entities—is said to rest upon consciousness, yet that [establishment] does not reside in consciousness; if it were to consist merely in that degree of reality—namely, an entry [into consciousness] by means of the imparting of a form, or by being produced through a single causal complex, which constitutes the attainment of the status of an object—then [it would follow that...].

If one were to say, "I have indeed seen objects, but not their specific particulars such as grass and so forth," there could be no stable distinction [between them]. For there is no such thing as a mere object existing separately from its particularity, which could impart its form, or which could possess a common causal complex, or which could be the producer [of cognition]; this is because only the particular possesses ultimate reality (*paramārthasattva*).

Even though a universal exists, whether it subsists through identity (*tādātmya*) or through inherence (*samavāya*), it does not become capable of appearing as something distinct from its particular instances.
Even in cognitions such as "cow's milk is wholesome" or "a cow must not be touched with the foot," the manifestation of the universal occurs primarily by way of highlighting the perceived particular.

As will be stated by the author of the *Ṭīkā*: "One horn [of the dilemma] is from the perspective of the object," and so forth; that is, the true nature of the object remains unestablished for one who runs along the path [of conceptualization]. Now, what then is the intended establishment grounded in consciousness (*saṃvit*)? He says: that very reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which is "this is grass," and so on, is the subject at hand.

The ultimate reality (*paramārtha-svabhāva*) belongs to that luminosity (*prakāśa*); therein, "perfect binding" means resting and remaining with certainty within consciousness—this is what is called the culmination (*niṣṭhā*). Now, one might object: "In that case, even if it is merely the nature of an object (*padārtha-mātra*), the culmination within consciousness must still be explained. To this he says: "But by being merely an object," and so forth.
For even the reflection "this is an object" (*padārtha*) is indeed a deliberation (*vimarśa*).

Now, one might object: "By this much, there is only the culmination of being established as a certainty (*niścaya*), but not the establishment of the subject (*pramātṛ*. To this he says: "And that very... (*ya eva ca*).
That light which has reflection as its inherent nature and essence,

and in which objects are properly bound together— that alone is the subject (*pramātā*). Precisely because no subject is established apart from mere consciousness, for that very reason, it remains, for the time being, of a transcendent (imperceptible) nature.
The word "ca" (and) adds another argument to the reason, stating that [the position] is untenable, as in the case of the followers of Kaṇāda. Now, one might ask:

"Granted that illumination (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) may exist in the grass to this extent, how can the subject (*pramātṛ*) possess the nature of illumination and reflective awareness? To this he says: "And of him (*tasya*). That which is the light consisting of the reflective awareness "this is grass,"...
If that very [object] were restricted solely to the body of the object of cognition (*prameya*), then the manifestation "this is mine" would certainly not occur;

for in that case, the blade of grass would appear only within one's own self. But this is not so; therefore, the light (*prakāśa*) and the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of "this is this blade of grass" transcend the objective portion of the grass and depend upon the dimension of consciousness (*saṃvit*). And of these two...

In that case, if there were no conjunction of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), or if the process of illumination and awareness did not reach its consummation, nothing at all would exist. Therefore, this reflective awareness that "this is a blade of grass" comes to rest in absolute freedom (*svātantrya*);
that which so rests is called "I" (*aham*). As it has been said:
The fulfillment of this reflective awareness of "this," which is initially fragmented, is that repose in one's own essential nature; that reflective awareness is the realization "I am this."
(A. Pra. Si. 15 Kā.
Thus it is said: consciousness, as long as it is devoid of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), is nothing at all.
When it consists of reflective awareness, it possesses autonomy, subjectivity, and self-luminosity; how [could this be otherwise]?

It would follow that [the self] is established as mere sensation, or as mere substrate, or as consciousness devoid of reflective awareness (nirvimarśa) in the form of the individual soul (puruṣa). For he who consists of infinite light and reflective awareness—being the foundational wall for the manifestation of the object of knowledge as "I"—lacks the state of "thisness" (idantā) which constitutes objectivity; thus, in the absence of distinctions of space and time, there can be no distinction in his own nature.
Furthermore, unity, pervasiveness, and eternity do not depend on any other effort.

The linguistic usage regarding objects of cognition such as blue or pleasure is invariably concomitant with the subject (pramātṛ), who is the basis for the establishment [of those objects] through the nature of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), because it is a linguistic usage regarding an object of cognition. For indeed, that which...
It does not depend on the accomplishment consisting of manifestation (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*);
nor is this conventional usage of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā-vyavahāra*) like that of seeds, sprouts, and so forth, which follow the relation of cause and effect.

This is the state of being (*bhāva*). Therefore, by virtue of its existence in the absence of the aforementioned subject (*pramātṛ*), it is excluded from the counter-example—the empirical usage of the object of cognition (*prameya*)—because that would entail the presence of non-necessity, which is the opposite of the necessity pervading that [usage]. Thus, through the non-existence of the absence of a subject, it is pervaded; this establishes the pervasion (*vyāpti*), and it is therefore a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). "As before" means as follows: [The original Sanskrit text continues: *yathā*... (as previously stated).

Prior to the favor of the light consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśamaya-prakāśa*), this [object] is not established; likewise, even when that favor occurs, it would still remain unestablished because there is no difference [in its nature]. For by that [favor], the form of that entity—which consists of manifestness—would have to arise for everyone at that time, or else for no one at all; such being the consequence. Now, [one might object]:

To this extent, self-awareness (svasaṃvedana) bestows proof as the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) therein. He says, "And not so. For if it were an object of cognition (prameya), its autonomy would be undermined, because at that very moment and in that very place, there is a contradiction between autonomy and dependence. Thus, the object of cognition, being dependent in nature, must rest within a distinct, autonomous cognizer (pramātṛ).

It becomes an object of knowledge (*prameya*). And the subject (*pramātā*), while resting the blue object within his own self—which consists of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—would not rest that very self within another light and reflective awareness, because that would lead to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Nor is there any other light and reflective awareness, because any difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*), location (*deśa*), or time (*kāla*) is impossible. Therefore, this [subject]...

How could the subject (*pramātā*), who consists of natural luminosity and self-reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) that is not dependent on anything else, ever become an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*)? And it is only with respect to an object of knowledge that there is consideration of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Thus, the formal argument is as follows: since the subject is that upon which the object of knowledge is established, he cannot be an object of knowledge. Dependence (*pāratantrya*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*) of the state of being an object of knowledge.

And independence, which is the opposite of that [dependence], is pervaded by being the locus of the object of cognition (*prameya-pratiṣṭhānatva*); for if there were dependence, there would be an infinite regress, and thus it would be impossible for the object of cognition to have its locus in [the subject].

Therefore, this is an "observation of what is pervaded by the contradictory of the pervader" (*vyāpaka-viruddha-vyāpta-upalabdhi*), which negates the status of being an object of cognition in the cognizer.

The reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that is appropriate to self-luminosity is called "I" (*aham*). Now, is it not observed that the status of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) is attributed to the subject (*pramātṛ*) in cases such as instruction? No; this [attribution] does not apply to the subject itself, but rather to another entity that has been projected, which stands in the place of blue and so forth. Furthermore, [the subject] is devoid of space and time because of its connection with uninterrupted manifestation.

Subjectivity (*pramātṛtva*) consists in the state of being manifest all at once (*sakṛdvibhātarūpatā*), which culminates in the negation of the status of objects having life (*artha-prāṇatva*) once again, following their initial appearance as fragmented.
(Page 56)
How could [the object] arise within that which has been created? And how, from this statement, could there be a realization of the Self as the cognizer?

This is true; however, the cognizer is of the nature of self-luminosity and consists of the reflective awareness of "I" (*aham*) that is not dependent on anything else. Whatever object of knowledge (*meyam*) arises through its sovereignty, it takes that very [cognizer] as its fundamental basis.

By the principle of unifying the perceived object with the conceptual construction, it is created through the very unification with its own self-luminous nature by means of a creation consisting of conceptualization. This is what he says: "rather, by the mediation of the 'I-sense' (ahantā)," meaning that it is not the case that it does not shine forth.
From the word *ātman*, it is understood that nothing whatsoever shines forth as distinct from it; rather, it is the Self alone.

However, when there is the intervention of the ladder of self-reflective awareness (*ahaṃparāmarśa*), the objects such as qualities (*guṇa*), actions (*kriyā*), or the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) are produced by words such as "this is a quality" or "this is an action," through which one would conceptualize them. That which is produced—such as "the cloth is white" or "he cooks"—is brought forth by reaching toward the object as it has ascended into conceptualization. For that which is indeed reflective awareness...

That which, by being invariably made into an intermediate step (*sopāna*) through a subsequent reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*), brings about the fulfillment of one's purpose by means of ascending to the object of that awareness, is said to be "intervened" (*vyavahita*) by it. Now, it may be argued that a word expresses its meaning by taking recourse to convention (*samaya*); and that convention is the same everywhere, as is the [meaning] colored by the word.
What could constitute an obstruction for what, on the grounds that consciousness is conceptual? This might be so if the linguistic usage of word and meaning were dependent solely upon convention;

however, insofar as the nature of reflective awareness—which is essentially the nature of verbalization—is, as it were, the very life-breath within the form of pure consciousness, that [nature] is non-conventional.
This will be explained in detail later. That very act of verbalization which is appropriate for an innate, spontaneous awareness (*sahaja-parāmarśa*) independent of linguistic convention—

that alone [constitutes the primary reality] of other words created by convention, of other conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) that depend upon them, and of other appearances (*ābhāsa*) produced as objects to be conceptualized by those very conceptualizations.

That which appears as a conceptual wall (*bhittikalpa*) is called an "obscuring factor" (*vyavadhāyaka*). For instance, when one conceives of the distinction between "self" and "other," the essential nature (*svabhāva*) shines forth as it perceives itself as entering within and exiting outward through specific movements of the eyes, the face, and the fingers. And therein [reside the pronouns]: *ahaṃ*, *haṃ*, *amhe*, *hage*.

Thus, [terms] such as "this one," "here," and "that one" are conventions among siblings; likewise, [terms] such as "self" and "other" are appropriately considered to be mediated by that [convention]. For the determination of word-meaning is sustained solely by the observation of the speaker’s convention.

Even for those who maintain the doctrine of the "string" (hāravādins), conventional designations— which are mostly based on social convention— are manifested only as being mediated by words whose meanings are established through worldly, firmly rooted usage, as well as by the conceptual constructions (vikalpa) associated with them. For instance, in the case of the worldly linguistic usages such as "he cooks" (*pacati*) or "the cloth is white" (*śuklaḥ paṭaḥ*), there are [underlying] notions such as "cooking is the act of cooking," "it is an action," "color is a quality," or "it is a property."

Other words depend upon conventions that primarily relate to specific assemblies (*pārṣada*). Within those as well, there are distinctions based on whether the assembly is restricted or unrestricted, and so forth. And thus:
"having with difficulty passed between the pair of thighs..."
Thus,
while your moon-like face exists—
[iti]

Regarding the verse beginning with "yattvannetra"—in this poetic sentiment (*kāvyarasa*), which is divided into the erotic as longing (*abhilāṣa*), enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*), and separation (*vipralambha*), the general definition consists of the determinants (*vibhāva*), consequents (*anubhāva*), and so forth;
the specific definition consists of its arising from the stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) of love (*rati*), and so forth. By that much—

The term "erotic" (*śṛṅgāra*) refers to the conventional designation of its meaning; thus, when the meaning of a definitional statement depends upon worldly examples, the use of such words as established in common usage is merely for the sake of the assembly.
Consequently, upon hearing a definitional statement accompanied by examples, the word "erotic" and so forth applies to the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) in poetry.
Even though it has been placed [in the text], and even though it seeks to produce a cognition that is as if mediated by a reflection appropriate to such a statement,
it is certainly unable to call to mind any particular worldly sentence; therefore,
according to the logic of manifesting total dependence upon the market, it follows the logic of the state of being an entity that has attained the nature of the primary Brahman.

Nor is it directly non-expressive, because it is incapable of producing the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) that is capable of performing the purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) such as the relish (*āsvāda*) accomplished by the delineation of specific qualities (*viśeṣa*). However, where the very concealment of the qualified nature residing in the object of reflection is the life-force of the propriety of reflective awareness, there [is] that which consists of the plenum of all existents (*samastabhāvanirbharātmaka*).
Or, according to the principle that in the meaning of a sentence— such as the reflective awareness of the Supreme Lord consisting of consciousness—
the expression of a word, the expression of a phoneme, or the expression of a part of a part [of that phoneme] [is involved]. (Page 58)
On the contrary, the primary denotative power resides precisely in the seed-syllables and clusters beginning with the *praṇava*, as well as in their constituent parts. As the Teacher has said:
"The *praṇava* is its denoter" (*Yoga Sūtra* 1.27).

Thus it is said. Enough with this extensive digression. This much remains established: that from words denoting qualities, actions, or universals, the cognition of the object occurs through mediation. Even in the case of memory, there is no new manifestation (*apūrva-prakāśa*) of the object;
rather, it is like the mere opening up of a previous manifestation. And that previous manifestation is experience (*anubhava*).

Even in memory, the object appears through the mediation of a prior experience, not directly. In the same way, that which is referred to as "this-ness" (idantā) is not the subject (pramātṛ) directly; thus, the nature of being an object of knowledge (prameya-rūpatā) is negated with respect to the direct subject.
[The reason] "that which is indicated by 'this-ness' is not the subject because it is an object of knowledge" is a pervader (vyāpaka) of subjecthood.

The property of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*), which is perceived as pervaded by dependence (*pāratantrya*)—the opposite of autonomy (*svātantrya*)—effects the conventional usage of negating the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). This is thus the "perception of what is pervaded by the opposite of the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). Consequently, self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), because it is devoid of an object of cognition (*prameyaśūnyatvāt*), [which is] the pervader of validity (*prāmāṇya*).

The absence of that [object] is contradictory to the state of being an object of cognition; thus, there is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Now, one might object: "The relationship between agent and object is not real. What follows from that? It follows that for consciousness, its very luminosity is its state of being an object of cognition, just like a jar; and its state of being a cognizer is likewise that same luminosity, just as in the case of the cognition of a jar. So what contradiction is there? To this, he replies:
"Even so," it is said. If two forms are not established, then by this much only two words would be established, but no actual entity whatsoever.
For being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) does not consist merely in being manifest; rather, it consists in having its establishment dependent on something else.
How, then, could that which has its own establishment independent [of anything else] be an object of knowledge? It could only be an object of knowledge figuratively.

For it is observed that an object of cognition (*prameya*) is that which is manifest as something previously unknown; thus, because of the similarity between its novelty and its being manifest at that very moment, the status of being an object of cognition would be superimposed [upon it]. And when the status of being an object of cognition is superimposed, the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is likewise merely superimposed, not primary. Even though this mode is figurative, [it is still accepted].
It will be refuted by the absence of the basis for metaphorical designation— the distinction between phenomena consisting of the cause and the purpose—
and also because [consciousness] has luminosity as its nature; nevertheless, this much [is established] for now.

Thinking, "Let another [opponent] understand," he first negates primacy (*mukhyatva*) in order to introduce the discernment (*viveka*). For primacy in the status of being an object of cognition (*prameyatva*) arises either through dependence on a single causal complex (*sāmagrī*), or through being the producer (*janaka*), or through being the bestower of the form (*ākārārpaka*); and in each of these cases, there is necessarily a dependence on something else, expressed respectively as "of this" (*asya*) and "in this" (*asmin*).

Even in the case of the cognition of consciousness, according to the principle that "the object of knowledge is that which appears [in it]," one must take into account the distinction between exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). And that [exclusion]— in the case of the cognition of blue— is the blue portion as an external form.
It is delineated by a conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) that internalizes a portion of awakening (*bodhāṃśa*) directed inwardly.

Even if there were a distinction in exclusion (*vyāvṭtibheda*) due to continuity and non-perception even in the case of pleasant cognition, this path is in no way capable of being established regarding the aspect of pure awareness (*saṃvedanāṃśa*); thus, it is merely figurative (*aupacārika*).

Objectivity (*prameyatva*). Thus, having accepted that cognition is a means of valid knowledge (*pramā*), it has been demonstrated that its objectivity (*prameyatā*) is not primarily tenable. Now, however, it is demonstrated that for this [cognition], validity itself—which is synonymous with establishment (*siddhi*)—is not tenable; for "that" refers to establishment. For blue, pleasure, and so forth, there is either a real exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) or an exclusion as it appears.

Or, in a state of non-attention due to distance, let another form of that very unestablished [object]—namely its "otherwise-established" status (*anyathāsiddhi*)—be called a form of valid cognition (*pramā*). And it is not logical for that [valid cognition] to rest within itself;
for if its own nature were already so [established] previously, there would be no such thing as its establishment only now. And therefore:

Success (*siddhi*)—whether it consists in appearing as something else due to being permeated by latent impressions (*vāsanā*), or in manifesting the form of another because of its clarity and lack of orientation toward anything else (since it is non-inert by virtue of having consciousness as its essence) within the light that is not distinct from its own self—is indeed dependent upon something else, just like the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*). For "that" refers to success; "supreme" (*param*) refers to...

"Distinct from its own self. The term *ābhāsa* (manifestation/appearance) is used by the commentator according to the requirements of each system—namely, the Vaibhāṣika, Vaiśeṣika, Pāramarṣa (Mīmāṃsaka), Sautrāntika, and Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda—as referring respectively to: orientation toward that [object], its illumination, its reflection, and its delineation. "Its own self" (*svātman*)...

Regarding "of that which is unestablished": since even blue and so forth possess a state of being unestablished, one might as well speak of an establishment consisting of the form of blue and so forth; however, for consciousness, [there is no establishment] beyond that very form.

The claim that "nothing whatsoever is established" does not, despite its abundance of fine words, exclude the fact that consciousness is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Then, let it be that consciousness is unmanifest, just like the blue object; this provides an opening for the Vaiśeṣika to awaken, for [the same applies] to him as well.
If that consciousness (*bodha*) in which another consciousness finds rest and achieves its establishment is itself not established, then—

given the absence of the designation "manifestation" for a property resting upon an object of knowledge— that other consciousness would likewise not manifest. In that case, there would be no object, no sense organ, no mind, and no self.

"It is a great delusion regarding the order of the world that consciousness does not shine forth. Alas! And if one were to postulate another consciousness [to perceive it], there would be an infinite regress; this is the very same situation. Now, if it is argued that there exist objects, sense organs, and so forth, then cognition arises within the self; from that, desire; from that, effort; and from that, bodily action; and from that—

Conjunction; from that, pleasure—such is the course of the world. What is broken in this [course] if consciousness lacks the nature of self-luminosity? No, no; let not the one who considers himself a leader of the Naiyāyikas be unenlightened. [Consider: the seed, the sprout, the stalk, the leaf, the flower...

Regarding the sequence of effects known as "fruits" and this [sequence] spoken of by you, how can there be a distinction between them such that one is insentient and the other is non-insentient? If it is argued that consciousness alone is non-insentient, then why could the seed itself not also be non-insentient,
provided it lacks dependence on another and lacks the state of being manifest?
Because any particular [feature] would be equivalent to non-existence. Now, what follows from this?
Let consciousness itself be without any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). What is wrong with an object of cognition existing without another object of cognition?
And what calamity befalls consciousness itself without a means of valid cognition? Here, there is merely a calamity.

The Establishment of the Means of Valid Cognition (*Pramāṇasamarthana*). Since that [consciousness] consists solely of the nature of being manifest, everything desired is obtained by that much alone. Consciousness is not a means of valid cognition (*pramā*), because it is the locus for the conventional usage of the "object of cognition" (*prameya*) due to its independence from anything else. For the status of being the locus for that conventional usage...
If [the effect] were to exist even without depending on another, then it would also exist in a jar situated underground;

yet this is not the case, as determined by the non-perception of the perceptible (*dṛśyānupalambha*). Therefore, this is the "perception of what is incompatible with the cause" (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*). [Objection: But surely entities are established by their own nature (*svātmanā*).

(Page 61) With the word "only" (*kevalam*), he dispels the doubt of others as to how this conventional usage could be possible: just as a seed is established and perfected within itself in its own nature as a seed, so too is the cognizer established within himself by means of his own self-awareness.

It would also follow that the perfected [nature] exists within its own self if it were impermanent; yet it is eternal, because the absence of any distinction in terms of place, time, or essential nature has already been stated and will be further explained. Now, one might object: "In your view, the cognizer is eternal, but for the Buddhist he is not so; therefore, regarding his perceptions..."
The conventional usage of "establishment through non-perception" is not illogical. He says "no," adding "and not in that way. "In that way" means by that mode of arising;

establishment within oneself as having the nature of perception—that is, the establishment through self-perception—is what would have to be called the very essence (*svarūpa*) of that perception. But it is not so.

The linguistic usage "this is the state of being an object of cognition" (*prameyatā*) and "this is the object of cognition" (*prameya*) is established through its connection with a means of valid cognition (*pramā*). For the state of being an object of cognition is not "being an effect" (*kāryatā*), but rather "being made known" (*jñāpyatā*); and that [state] does not exist [in the case of self-awareness]. Consequently, what was asserted by the opponent—that consciousness appears as consciousness through the means of valid cognition consisting in self-awareness—is thereby refuted. Or else, in that manner...

That which is called "accomplishment" (*siddhi*) is not said to be the accomplishment of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) itself, which would be the cause for [the status of] being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*). Now, in the Buddhist view, let there be no status as an object of knowledge within the nature of consciousness itself, and let there likewise be no primary status as a means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*)— which is invariably concomitant with that [object-status]— in the case of another entity that serves as its foundation, since such an entity is impossible.

This is because it is impossible to postulate two exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*)— which serve as the seeds for the conceptualization of the two properties of being a means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) and being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*)— within that which has manifestation alone as its nature. For those who maintain the existence of a Lord (*īśvara*), however, who accept a distinction between the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*) and the ultimate subject (*paramārtha-pramātṛ*), even this consciousness appears within the void (*śūnya*).

He dispels the doubt that something distinct from that [consciousness]— whether it be the vital breath (*prāṇa*) appearing as the subject to those engaged in contemplative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) in the form "I am," or the intellect (*buddhi*) appearing as the grasper in such instances as "I am happy"— might appear as the Self (*ātman) due to its being accepted as such (as indicated by the word "etc."). For instance:

The body, being insentient in nature, should not be suspected as the locus for the establishment of the object of knowledge (*vedya*); likewise, even that which is empty (*śūnya*) and so forth, being an object of knowledge, is not the locus for the establishment of the cognizable (*prameya*). Just as with the body, so it is with emptiness and the rest. For the state of being a locus of establishment— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]

(Page 62) Since the restriction—that the pervasive [entity] is perceived only in certain instances—is not observed among insentient things, it is excluded from the reason that would otherwise entail such a restriction; thus, it is pervaded by non-insentiency. And that which is contradictory to this...

The state of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*) is thus the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Therefore, consciousness alone is the locus of establishment everywhere. That [consciousness], when superimposed upon the void and so forth by the power of *māyā*, is said to be "contracted. As stated in the *Ajadapramātṛsiddhi*:

Although the stability of objects is restricted to the individual soul (jīva), which is constrained by the vital breaths and the subtle body (puryaṣṭaka), even there it remains established in the Supreme Self (paramātman).
"How could there be for him any constriction by means of the vital breath through that very self? (21);
likewise, there is no establishment of objects when the sense of "I" regarding the vital breath and so forth has ceased.

"The state of the Light resting within itself is indeed proclaimed as the sense of 'I' (ahaṃbhāva). (22) [Thus it is said. "Of that very" refers to emptiness and so forth. "That" refers to the Light. "The status of being an object of valid cognition" means both the nature of being a valid cognition (*pramāṇatā*) and the state of being an object (*viṣayatā*). "Because its essence is Light" refers to its figurative nature (*aupacārikatva*).

This is the reason for negating what was previously accepted: for when there is no other property (*dharmāntara*), that which is designated by many intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) arises as a mere verbal赘疣 (*śabdagaḍu*)—a figurative usage (*upacāra*) that is impossible when there is a difference in causes (*nimitta*) or a difference in purposes (*prayojana*). For even in relation to one's own self, [the thoughts] "I am a universal monarch" and "I am a slave" [would be contradictory].
In the case of assuming contradictory forms, there is indeed a distinct cause consisting in the conjunction of two attributes— namely, dependence and being an instrument—

and a distinct purpose consisting in the absence of pride such as non-degradation and fullness, as well as the absence of mutual orientation; however, this is not the case for consciousness, whose sole nature is light.

There exists another property (*dharmāntara*). And according to the aforementioned method, when the metaphorical application (*upacāra*) of the states of knower, means of knowledge, and object of knowledge is intended, ultimately a set of six properties is required. Now, by the logic that "the sky is established in itself," [this is] the establishment through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); thus, in this manner, consciousness is neither useless nor untenable.

It is called a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). This, then, is our view. And thus, [if one follows the claim that] perception is of four kinds, it would be untenable to count self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) as a distinct category of valid cognition.

Regarding the phrase "not being an object of the means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇāviṣayatvam*): when the absence of being an object is concluded, it should be understood that the absence of being a cognizer (*pramātṛtva*) and the absence of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*) are also concluded. For the Buddhist, however, there might indeed be a basis for figurative usage regarding the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatā*), namely, the quality of not having been previously apprehended (*pūrvānadhigatatva*) and the quality of being new (*apūrvatva*) with respect to the consciousness appropriate to that time.

And since the ground for the metaphorical designation of "object of cognition" exists, its status as a "means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is also metaphorically attributed because it consists of luminosity, in order to demonstrate its independence from anything else. However, he shows that this is not possible in our own system in any way whatsoever by stating, "because there is an absence of a previously non-existent form. Or, if the reading is *pramāṇāviṣayatvam*, [the meaning is] likewise.

The connection is with the phrase "being the object of a means of valid cognition" (*pramāṇaviṣayatvam*). How is it that this being the object of a means of valid cognition is even suspected? He says: "Because its nature is luminosity (*prakāśātmatva*), there is a threefoldness even in the one, due to this cause. Being an object would be possible if there were novelty (*apūrvatā*), and if there is being an object, there is the status of being a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇatva*). He elaborates on this [with the words] "unapprehended" (*anadhigata*)—[the rest of the passage begins with] "unapprehended... (*anadhi-*).

The two definitions of Dignāga are as follows: "that which has its object gone" (*gataviṣaya*) is stated by way of the object, while "that which is unknown" (*ajñāta*) is stated by way of its own nature (*svarūpa*), which consists of a manifestation established in the object. Through the notions of "primacy" (*prāthamya*) and "thisness" (*idantā*), the own nature is presented with the object preceding it; [the definitions] also establish the absence of doubt and error, and therein [they indicate] the cause for that.

The intended meaning of the five qualifiers in the Mīmāṃsaka definition is "intrinsic validity" (*svataḥ-prāmāṇya*) in successive order. Now, one might object: although the self lacks novelty (*apūrvatva*) because it is eternal—and thus lacks the primary basis for being designated as an object of knowledge (*prameya*)—nevertheless, it will possess the quality of not having been previously apprehended (*pūrvānadhigatatva*). To this he replies: "And of the self..."
Thus [it is said]. The mention of "one's own" [subject] implies that even if there were a lack of prior cognition regarding another cognizer, no such "duty" (itikartavyatā) need be performed;

for in this philosophical system, the distinction between self and other is not ultimately real (*atāttvika*). Indeed, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*), consciousness is one alone. It is only by virtue of being objects for the illusory cognizers—the imagined void, vital breath, body, and so forth—that [the distinction arises].

For it will be explained later that [the term] "convention regarding self and other" refers to this; therefore, the general statement "from itself" is indeed appropriate. The certainty that "this is a new manifestation" has as its cause the prior certainty that "this jar was not manifested before. Its pervader is the state of being devoid of the manifestation of that jar—

The recollection of a prior time whose nature consists mostly of visible and invisible objects; in the absence of that [prior time], there would be neither the notion "it was before" nor the fact that it was not manifested.

Because there would be no perception of the past time, [the term] "past" (bhūta) would be grammatically untenable. Furthermore, the experience of a time devoid of the manifestation of the jar would be the cause of its recollection; thus, this subsequent section [of the argument] would not be possible.
Even if that [past time] were to exist, how could this experience be a manifestation of something previously unknown? And therefore—
The experience "I am a cognizer of unprecedented manifestation; I manifest now, whereas previously I did not manifest"—

this experience, by implying the recollection of a prior time through the force of consciousness, implies an experience of that [prior] time which subverts both the unprecedented existence and the unprecedented manifestation of the cognizer.
For it must be stated that even at the time of Rāma’s incarnation, he had the experience that "I did not exist.
If it is argued that knowledge of that time comes from scripture (*āgama*), then scripture too implies the experience of a speaker who has himself experienced it;
thus, there must first be an experiencer of that [time]. But surely, by that much, Vālmīki is established as such an experiencer? No.

This is the beginning [of the discussion]. The question is appropriate; however, by this much alone, the eternal existence of the *ahaṃvimarśa* (the reflective awareness of "I") as the nature of consciousness is established. And that is the one and only ultimate subject (*paramārthapramātā*), even if the vital breath, intellect, the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), the physical body, and so forth are distinct, and even if there is differentiation caused by those distinctions.
Regarding the conventional usage of "distinction between cognizers," the reality here is this: that body and so forth which belong to the present time did not exist at that [past] time.

At the time of dissolution (*pralaya*) and at the commencement of creation (*sṛṣṭi*), [one thinks], "We did not exist"; otherwise, there would be no mention of a specific time. Furthermore, even in the cognition "we did not exist," [this temporal specification is implied].
The manifestation of the past time, which is internalized within the *liṭ* suffix, indeed arises. For this is certainly not a non-cognition;

nor is it a cognition consisting of direct experience (*anubhava*), because if it were such, there would follow the consequence of a clear manifestation of the object of a previous time for [the subject] now, as in the case of a yogi. Therefore, this is nothing other than memory (*smṛti*).

It indeed evokes a prior experience. Even when a poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*) occurs, it relies fundamentally upon either memory or direct experience; for a poetic fancy could not possibly arise like an entry into blinding darkness. This is because pure consciousness alone is devoid of temporal coloring.

Furthermore, since the appearance of an object distinct from its own essential nature is impossible, memory—which has as its very form that which is animated by both [the object and the self]—is not possible; thus, it exists only as colored by the body and so forth. And the coloring by the previous body...
(page 65)
Because it is impossible to clearly manifest two distinct types of coloring— namely, "this [consciousness] is differentiated by the coloring of the body"—

the nature of memory is not clearly evident, just as youth is not clearly perceived in one who has become like a mere infant. For it is only where there is a firm conceit of being the experiencer with respect to the body that memory persists due to the non-disruption of the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of identity.

When one is identifying [an object], there is the manifest conceit of being its rememberer; enough with this prolixity. This is established: that the Self does not appear as something previously unknown (*apūrva*). "Previously unknown" means in terms of its existence (*sattayā*);

"the state of appearing as previously unknown" means in terms of its apprehension (*adhigamena*). And here, the particle *ca* (and) should be understood as having a distributive sense. For this very reason, he analyzes it:

Nor is there non-existence prior to the Self, nor is there experience of that which already exists. In reality, even existence rests solely upon the repose in manifestation; thus, the priority of existence finds its ultimate rest only in the priority of manifestation.

With this intention, grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) alone is appropriate. The particle *ca* in the phrase "let [it] be understood" (*pratipadyatām*) is not [to be taken as implying a conjunction].

It is thus applied: the linguistic usage of "newly manifesting" (apūrva-prakāśatva) residing in the cognizer does not occur prior to the existence of the cognizer, because it depends upon the recollection of a preceding time contingent upon the cognizer and the act of cognition. If that [cognizer] were non-existent, its occurrence would lack dependence on a form contingent upon him—just as a cloth cannot exist in the absence of a lump of clay, which is the pervading condition for its production.
And that which is contrary to this is dependence upon another form; thus, there is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).
Well then, let it be that this very existence of the cognizer is the conventional designation of the cognizer as "an unprecedented manifestation.
But how can even this be so? For it is not the case that the same [cognizer] first manifests and now becomes an unprecedented manifestation.
This is untenable due to contradiction. Therefore, this contradiction must be resolved by means of a difference in their respective domains (*viṣaya*).

The body and so forth, which possess a superimposed state of luminosity and constitute a novel manifestation, can only function within conventional discourse while the primordial luminosity—the ultimate subject (*paramārtha-pramātṛ*)—exists. That ultimate subject, however, is the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*).

There is no manifestation of anything previously non-existent, and all subjects are non-different from that [Self]; thus, in reality, there is no such thing as the manifestation of the unprecedented. As it has been sung:
"Indeed, I was never not..."
Having said this:
"These lords of men have not existed, nor indeed shall we not exist. (2.12)
(Page 66) Thus, by this [statement], having declared that the ultimate subject (*paramārthapramātṛ*), which is the Self, possesses a luminosity uninterrupted throughout the three times,
it is likewise declared for others as well due to their non-difference from it. Even though the state of unprecedented luminosity occurs in the subject of *māyā*...

The intended meaning of this text is that [the object] does not embrace the aspect of light (prakāśāṃśa), but rather only the aspect of the cognizable (vedyāṃśa) which partakes in the state of "this-ness" (idaṃbhāva). By the word "that very" (sa eva), he expresses the non-difference from the ultimate subject (paramārthapramātṛ) by means of the particle "eva. He concludes the intermediate point of proof with the words "therefore" (tasmāt). [He says] "of the Self" (ātmanaḥ); according to the Buddhist logic (bauddhanyāya).

However, because cognition possesses an unprecedented manifestation, its status as an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*) may be merely figurative (*aupacārikī*), since self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) is said to be the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); such is the intention. Having thus concluded the intermediate point—that even a figurative status as the object of a means of valid cognition is not tenable—the author returns to the primary subject matter.
He concludes the "Great Object of Knowledge" (*mahāprameya*), characterized by the absence of knowability (*prameyatvābhāva*), with the words "tadevam" ("thus, therefore"). The meaning is:
since such is the case through the collection of arguments, the self's state of being eternally luminous remains established as the very nature of the object of knowledge (*prameyavastu*).

Now, one might raise the objection that in an investigation into the eternity and other attributes residing in the self, the self must necessarily itself be an object of knowledge (*prameya*). Anticipating this:
He says: "It is conceptual. Even in that case, the investigator must already be established; otherwise, investigation would be impossible.
Thus, even while being investigated, the self recedes far away from the domain of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), like the shadow of one's own head. It is merely...
"Having liberated the Self from its state of non-independence... (1.47).

According to this forthcoming principle, that which is to become the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is created there while remaining in identity with the foundational nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*), whose form has not been abandoned; thus, the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) comes to rest within that very subjectivity. It is precisely through that [subjectivity] in such a manner...

Because it becomes fit for transaction through being made heart-felt (*hṛdayaṅgamīkaraṇa*). Whatever contradictory [element] is employed against that which has been manifested in order to make it heart-felt, that contradiction finds no footing there, just as the status of being inferable finds no footing in a jar perceived by direct perception. And thus, the state of being a cognizer (*pramātṛtā*) is made heart-felt—

Thus, the state of being an object of cognition (*prameyatā*) is an optional factor that serves as the cause for obtaining a stable foundation. This consists in its being a manifestation not previously known, just as the state of being inferable from fire exists in a mountain; and its opposite is the state of having been previously manifested. Therefore, this is the "perception of what is incompatible with the cause" (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*). Immediately after the word *tu* (but), and likewise [after] *api* (even).

(Page 67) Although there is indeed a time for deliberation (*vicāra*), he nevertheless indicates that this is the distinction [between the two states]: from pure objectivity (*prameyatva*) and from pure subjectivity (*pramātṛtva*). For pure objectivity belongs only to the jar.

Just as the state of being inferable belongs to fire; whereas pure subjectivity (pramātṛtva) is like the perceptibility of a jar to one who is not deluded regarding the "I-sense" (ahaṃbhāva) when the jar is the object of knowledge (prameya). This [present case], however, is a mixed form consisting of both subject and object. But for one who is deluded, it is subjectivity that predominates, as in the case of a jar [being perceived].

Just as the state of being inferable (*anumeyatva*) is subordinate to the state of being perceptible (*pratyakṣatva*), so too inference—which consists of indirect cognition—is indeed contradictory to direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*); nevertheless, it still brings about practical engagement with that [object], because it is grounded in it. For example, although "this person is fair" (as seen in a mirror) is contradictory to the egoic sense "I am fair," [the former still functions].

This is like ignorance itself. If one were to treat even that [absence of ignorance] as the basis for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), there would be no capacity for transaction whatsoever; yet that [capacity] is desired. Therefore, because it would lead to the undesirable consequence of non-perception, one must necessarily accept that the pervading cause consists of that alone, lest it contradict direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

The state of being restricted to that [subject]—because it is excluded from the counter-example (vipakṣa) due to the absence of linguistic usage—is pervaded by the property to be proven, namely, the state of engaging in linguistic usage; thus, once pervasion is established, this is a reason based on essential nature (svabhāvahetu). Having explained the word *pūrvasiddhasya* as a synonym for the sūtra-word *ādisiddhe*, [the text continues with] the state of having its establishment already encompassed (*kroḍīkṛtasiddhikatva*).

That which was stated in the commentary with the intention of clarifying that [the suffixes] are established from the very beginning has now become clear; thus, he begins to explain it at length, starting with the word "evam" (thus). Since this much of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) stands as established, the words *yāvat* and *tāvat* necessarily indicate its inevitable occurrence; for this very reason, the agent is not mentioned. Of that...
For the attainment of success (*siddhi*) is not what is intended [as the primary goal]. Indeed, something must necessarily be cognized; and by this much, everything is established.

Thus, the "attainment" (*siddhi*) belonging to that cognizer—which is the object of cognition (*prameya*), which has become [realized], which has been reached, and which is appropriate to the object of cognition—is directed toward him—that is, toward the cognizer. "The object of cognition" (*prameyavastu*)...

The term *vastu* (thing) is a synonym for *mātra* (mere). For this very reason—that is, because even a mere blade of grass, when it comes to rest therein, becomes an object of knowledge (*prameya*)—the proof, that is, the manifestation, of the essential nature of one's own self by that knower is embraced by the very proof of the object; it has attained the state of being the heart, as indicated by the word "bosom" (*kroḍa*).
The meaning has been made heart-pleasing (*hṛdayaṅgamīkṛta*).

[This is] stated in the *Vṛtti*: "Indeed, the nature of manifestation (*prakāśarūpatā*), when residing in the subject (*pramātṛ*) and being undivided (*anavacchinna*), constitutes the state of being an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*). (page 68)

How can it endure? For he shows that even though it is uninterrupted, it cannot endure being an object of knowledge (*prameyatā*), by saying "let it be for now. This means that, according to the maxim of the staff and the cake (*daṇḍāpūpīya-nyāya*), this is established without effort. Now, one might object: "The eye and other senses are instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), and they depend upon inference and so forth. To this he replies: "the state of being the most effective means for accomplishing valid knowledge" (*pramitisādhakatamatām*); [it is] not [the case].

The intention is that this [cognition] is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Otherwise, there would be no establishment of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) under discussion—that which has begun to be measured and which consists of what is to be abandoned and what is to be adopted. "For this very reason" means:

because there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) if the means of valid knowledge were insentient and required another means of valid knowledge; therefore, by some [means of knowledge]—that is, by one provided through the coloring (*uparāga*) of the object.
Due to the contraction of space and time: for the manifestation of blue has a function that is even more contracted by its outward orientation toward a limited object;

yet, even though it resides within the vessel of the contraction of the intellect, the vital breath, and so forth—which themselves rest in the ultimate manifestation—it is [distinguished] by the mere contraction of inwardness in comparison to the manifestation of blue that contracts both ways (inward and outward).

Therefore, in the inner self (*pratyagātman*), which is expanded and possesses the capacity to manifest all objects, [consciousness] does not abandon its repose as it manifests with the sense of "mine-ness. It will be stated that the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is the fruit of the self-reflection (*vimarśa*) consisting of the word-sound (*śabda*) that flashes forth spontaneously, directed toward the object of knowledge (*prameya*)— the blue— which appears externally as a manifestation common to all.

Regarding the passage "‘This is such-and-such’" (2.16), one might object: "Surely the eye and other sense organs will be valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) even while they themselves do not manifest;
so how can there be an infinite regress, out of fear of which you claim that an insentient thing cannot be a *pramāṇa*? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For indeed..."

The word "mere" (*mātra*) [in the term] *kāraṇamātram* signifies a specific kind of cause, namely, an instrument (*karaṇa*). By the phrase "by which," it means "for this reason," namely, because it is an instrument as mere cause. Likewise, it is an instrument; however, being an instrument consists in being a superior auxiliary. And that is nothing other than being set into operation by the agent.
[The opponent asks: "What follows from that? [The author] replies: "And the agent... [meaning] "according to the principle to be stated later. Thus:
"In this manner, for one who desires to abide as the world-soul consisting of the manifestations of jars, cloths, and so forth, his very will is the causality, the agency, and the action. (2.53)

(On page 69) this will indeed be stated. What follows from that in the present context? He says: "And that" means the conscious [subject] employs whatever has been perceived as useful for an action, but not that which is unmanifested—this is the connection. [The insentient] does not [employ it].
"The conscious being employs [the body], because it is not manifest"—this is the perception of what is incompatible with the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*).

For manifestation is indeed the cause of employment, since in its absence there is no employment. He demonstrates this very point with the words "otherwise. Therefore, regarding those things that are absolutely imperceptible...

In the view that holds the totality of causes (sāmagrī) to be the means of valid cognition, it is first of all untenable for the mind, the sense organs, space, time, ether, and so forth, to be "employed by an agent" (kartṛprayojyatva). Now, one might object: "Having perceived the eyeball through a particular touch and the like, one opens it; this very act constitutes its being employed by [the agent], and from that arises the perception of blue."

Anticipating the objection that the lack of luminosity in an insentient object (*jaḍa*) is unproven, he says "tasyāpi" (of that too) in order to remind [the opponent] of that very infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Even a specific tactile sensation must be known by means of touch, and that [touch] too must be known by another insentient [sensation]; thus there is no finality. [Objection: But that tactile sensation will be made known by a cognition of touch, and that...
"If it is established by self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), what is this infinite regress? He replies: "By the limit," meaning "characterized by manifestation.
In the case of blue, the manifestation of blue itself is the appropriate instrument, just as the manifestation of touch is in the case of touch. [Objection:
But why this rule that one must resort to the limit from the very beginning? He replies:

Regarding the phrase "the axe and so forth": for instance, in the act of cutting, the sickle is the instrument (*karaṇa*); the hand is the instrument in its impelling; the desire is the instrument in its impelling; and self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is the ultimate instrument in that [desire]. However, it does not follow from this alone that the cutting itself must have desire as its instrument, according to the principle that "one takes up a staff because of the desire to take up a staff. This is true.

In this way, it is established that action culminates in the external; for cutting has as its fruit the result of being split, which resides in the wood, whereas the perception of blue has as its fruit the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of blue, which rests in the subject, just as the desire [to act] resides in the movement of the hand. In that case, there is no external [object].
It is logical that an instrument (*karaṇa*) functions at a distance. Anticipating the objection, "But where does functioning at a distance constitute a fault?", he says:

"Because of its application" (*tadviniyogāt*). Since the act of determining the jar (*ghaṭavimarśakriyā*), which is of the nature of valid cognition (*pramiti*), is already accomplished even before the application of the sense organ, how can the sense organ—which is to be employed at a later time—be the instrument for this [cognition]? Now, [one might object]: [The text continues: ...nanu... (Now, indeed...)

Anticipating the objection that [the reflective awareness] arises immediately after the application of the sense organs, he says: "the cognition of the jar. For one acts having first apprehended [the intention]: "May there be a reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the jar."

One should direct the sense organ [toward its object]; otherwise, how could the sense organ be directed toward a specific object in a specific place and time? Thus, if the intention is the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of a jar, then the jar is clearly manifested; otherwise, why would there not be the intention to cognize a cloth instead? Therefore...

If the reflective awareness of the jar (*ghaṭavimarśa*) has manifested by the power of its intentional focus (*abhisandhāna*), then the jar itself has manifested indirectly through the impossibility of that [awareness] occurring otherwise. The intended meaning is that the manifestation of the jar itself is the cognition of the jar.
That which appears even prior to being employed for a specific purpose is not its effect; just as a seed is not the effect of the sprout.

And because the manifestation of the jar occurs even prior to the application of the sense organs, [the following is established]: posteriority (being subsequent) is indeed pervaded by being an effect of that [manifestation], whereas priority (being prior) is contradictory to it;

thus, there is the perception of what is contradictory to the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). Now, it may be argued that while the mere manifestation of the jar truly exists at the beginning, it is not...
The cognition of the jar intended here is not merely that much; rather, it is the manifestation of the specific particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) as excluded from both similar and dissimilar things.
And that occurs only after the application of the sense organ. This very point is stated in the words "Then, the jar.
The word "and" (*ca*) indicates a reason: because there is the application of the sense organ by the agent, therefore [the cognition] possesses the characteristic of being employed by the agent.

"The status of being an instrument (karaṇatva) is thus established. He refutes this with the word "tat" (that), meaning "being employed by an agent. For it is not logical that something which is remote and unmanifest should be considered "employed by a conscious agent. [Objection: Let it be that "being employed by an agent" is not the definition of an instrument; for that [definition] does not apply in all cases, such as in the case of a pure action (*śubha-karman*).

Anticipating the objection that the definition of the instrument (*karaṇa*) as "that which provides the most excellent assistance toward an action" is appropriate because it is free from the fault of being under-extensive—as seen in such cases as "I eat what is auspicious" (*śubhaṃ bhuñje*) or "the tree stands by its roots" (*mūlaiḥ taruḥ tiṣṭhati*), where [the definition] is impossible—he says: "Nor even... For this much excellence is conceivable: when that [instrument] exists, that very [action] shines forth.

"When that exists, it shines; only when that very thing exists does it shine. Regarding this, he refutes the first type of excellence with the words "nor even... [meaning] "nor even of that sense organ. He refutes this by anticipating the following objection: "But perhaps there will be a primary excellence in relation to properties and categories such as largeness (*mahattva*), being composed of multiple substances (*anekadravyatva*), and possession of color-form (*rūpavattva*). He then proceeds to refute this.

Regarding the term *padārtha* (page 71): by the phrase "of those who seek," [it refers to] the goal of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) which is the object to be accomplished. For even you previously [stated] this very same thing.
The underlying intention here is as follows: [it was asked] "when they were questioned, even with the intention of referring to a jar," and so forth. Now, one might object:

even a mere thing-in-itself (*padārthamātra*) would be useful for those who seek purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such as the prevention of heartbreak, which is to be accomplished merely by its existence. But what indeed is gained by that? [The answer is: when a jar appears, there is the object to be accomplished, which is the qualificandum (*viśeṣya*).

For one who seeks action, that initial excellence of the sense organ might be established; however, the universal status of the sense organ as the instrument (*karaṇa*) in perception must also be established, and that has certainly not been established. This is what he says with the words "But even so" (*athāpi*), etc.; the break in the sentence should be made right after "even so" (*tathāpi*).

The phrase "there is no attainment of the desired goal for those who seek it" is to be connected with what precedes. However, when the word "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) is joined with the subsequent passage, if one provides an answer by refuting the second excellence without first resolving the supplementation required to establish the first excellence, that response lacks proper coherence.

To refute the second [position], namely that it "fills [the senses]," he says "from the luminous" (*prabhāsvarāt*). As for the first [position], let it indeed occur at another time; however, even when the sense organ is active, the discernment of the object does not arise, and thus [the object] simply exists—therefore, the excellence [of the cognition] is not established. This is because excellence, which is of a specific nature, [cannot exist apart from] its general nature.

Or [the particle] *api* is displaced in its position; it refers to "that sense-faculty" (*tasya indriyasya*). Regarding the phrase "here" (*atra*), which refers to the object of cognition when the result is to be produced, the connection is as follows:

even that which was described as having the nature of a second excellence—namely, that there is indeed an unmediated efficacy (*avyavahitopakāritā*)—is absent here. Furthermore, the nature of a third excellence—that "it appears while being in that very state"—has not been considered.

For in this system, this meaning is well-established: that there is a direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*) which is seen even without the operation of the senses, in relation to subjects ranging from the Great Lords of Mantras (*mantramaheśvara*) down to the yogis. Now, one might object:
when a person who has entered a dark room from a bright space, after resting, a cognition of blue arises—does that not involve the sense organ?

When it exists, there is indeed the cognition in the form of the discernment of blue; this is the excellence [of the sense organ]. As for the fact that it does not exist at the first moment, in that case the sense organ has not yet become capable through having reached maturation. We maintain that only a specific sense organ possesses the status of being an instrument (*karaṇa*), not the sense organ in its mere generality. Therefore, [this excellence arises] from the convergence of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*).
(Page 72) Thus,

the specific objection regarding the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatva*) that arises in its absence is not sufficient to refute the instrumentality of the sense organ. Furthermore, it has been stated by someone that the sense organ does not provide an immediate assistance due to an intervening factor.
Anticipating the objection that "it must be cultivated" and that "that very same [cultivated state] would become an insentient instrument," which thus results in a twofold refutation, he says:

"And of the manifestation of consciousness... Here, with respect to the fruit consisting of valid cognition (*pramā*), the excellence of the instrument must be defined. Valid cognition is the determination of an object, and an object is that which is capable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā-yogya*).

For one who desires purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), the cognizer—who is of a single nature despite apparent difference—and who wishes to engage in linguistic and practical intercourse with another such cognizer, the capacity for purposeful action rests upon externality; for even purposeful action is to be sought only as an external form. And this externality consists in being distinct from the cognizer. Nor is that [externality]...

For the ultimate subject, [external objectivity] is established as being of the nature of light, because otherwise the consequence of non-manifestation would follow, and that which does not manifest is incapable of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*). Therefore, both of these must be demonstrated:
manifestation and externality. Of these, the first belongs to the ultimately real Śiva-Sadāśiva...

It is established through non-difference from the nature of the subject whose essence is Śiveśvara. However, externality is consistent when it refers to the state of an imagined subject—that is, the illusory (*māyīya*) body, vital breath, and so forth. Thus, the cognition of blue consists precisely in the determination of the illusory subject as having an external form; for that which is not manifest [cannot be an object of cognition].

Even though external form is not a real entity, it can be determined through conceptual ascertainment (*avasāya*), because without a basis such as a wall, the painting of conceptual constructions (*dharmaparikalpanā*) is impossible. And this [is so] because the ascertainment is an error (*bhrānti*). (1.21)

This will be elaborated upon here through the refutation of the determinative judgment (*adhyavasāya*) of those who falsely imagine [the world] to be without a support (*nirālambana*). Therefore, first of all, the blue must be manifested. And its manifestation occurs thus: in Śiva, the ultimate subject (*paramārtha-pramātṛ*), as "I" (*aham*); on the level of Sadāśiva, as "I-this" (*ahamidam*), due to the lack of clarity regarding the "this" aspect (*idamaṃśa*); and on the level of Īśvara...

This manifestation consists merely of the power of cognition in the form of "I" and "this," differentiated by the portion "this. At this stage, there is no separate existence for the portion "this" apart from the "I-ness," just as blue has no separate existence from a mirror; even when there is a manifestation of separateness from that [I-ness], [it remains so].

(73) And because the body is not separate from consciousness and so forth, this is called the ground of knowledge (*vidyābhūmi*). Furthermore, within this [ground], there is an internal division based on the distinction between the Great Lords of Mantra (*mantramaheśvara*) and the Mantras themselves; this will be elaborated upon in the section concerning the scriptures (*āgama*).

Then, from that contracted subject who is of the nature of emptiness—consisting of the state of being a *vijñānakevalin* characterized by "all this which exists is not I"—there arises a manifestation within the light permeated by that [state]. However, in relation to that which is devoid of identity with it, there is a manifestation as something external; subsequently, this occurs within the form of that cognition.

In the uncontracted light, which is the *savedya-pralayakevala* (the isolation of dissolution accompanied by objects of knowledge), and even further in the *sakala* (the state with parts) which consists of that very body; in this very manner, the light [manifests] through both identity and externality. And regarding the light, that aspect of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which is invariably present within its manifestation as external will be established as "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*). Furthermore, of the light...

Reflection alone is life; and in this context, it assumes the form of conceptualization (*vikalpa*), which bestows an excess over the nature of what is manifest. This is what is conventionally termed "determination" (*adhyavasāya*).
Furthermore, externality is that which exceeds the nature of what is manifest; thus, for externality, there is not mere manifestation.
Rather, it is *adhyavasāya* (determinate conceptualization). However, manifestation through identity (*tādātmyena*) belongs solely to the aspect of light (*prakāśāṃśa*).

Furthermore, there is no difference whatsoever in that [light] among subjects, from Śiva down to the most limited (*sakala*). And since reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) does nothing other than manifest itself within that [light], light is non-conceptual (*nirvikalpaka*), which is to say, it is experience (*anubhava*).

And it is said: such being the case, that state of non-conceptual experience consisting of Śiva, Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidyā—which exists in the interval between the determination of externality (the form of valid cognition) and the operation of the senses—is itself the immediate [cause] of this valid cognition. From the luminous...

Even upon the entry of the excellent [cognition], the determination of blue in another is indeed valid cognition (*pramā*), and it is accepted that this occurs immediately after the experience of blue. Consequently, it is established that the operation of the sense faculty does not provide any immediate assistance in any instance whatsoever. Furthermore, that intervening state is not of an insentient nature; rather, it is—

Thus it is rightly said that [consciousness] consists solely of awareness (*saṃvinmayī*): for it is only that which has the nature of light (*prakāśātman*) that, by bringing about differentiation through some relative perspective, is fit to function as the instrument of cognition (*pramitikaraṇa*), and not an insentient object. This very point he states in the words: "And of the manifestation in consciousness... (*bodhāvabhāsasya ca*).
By the words beginning with "ityādi," the particle *ca* (and), while conjoining what follows, indicates the suspicion of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
And that [suspicion] has already been stated: namely, that because manifestation—which is in its true nature consciousness—is inferior, i.e., by way of deficiency or incompleteness.

When blue is manifesting, there arises a determination (*adhyavasāya*) regarding that which is denoted by words such as "appearance" (*ābhāsa*), which— due to its slight connection with an object in the form of a contraction—

is thought to be "this external [object] from me," and that object is considered to be a real entity (*vastubhūta*).
