This state of the blue being determined in such a manner, which constitutes the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*), is what is here investigated as the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Regarding the worldly [view]: that determination (*adhyavasāya*) of external form which follows immediately upon the operation of the senses—

regarded by the opponent [as the first cognition]— has emerged from the state of Mantreśvara and others, which consists of the manifestation of the power of consciousness (*jñānaśakti*), takes the form of the manifestation of blue (*nīlaprakāśa*), and is rooted in the supreme Sadāśiva and so forth, whose nature is "I" (*aham*).

It consists of knowledge (*vidyāmaya*). For this reason— because it is separated by that which stands in the middle, denoted by the term "experience" (*anubhava*), which is non-conceptual, consists of the reflective awareness of non-duality (*abhedavimarśa*), and whose life is pure luminosity (*prakāśamātra*)— it is logical that that very light, consisting of the reflective awareness of non-duality, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

It is the instrumental cause (*nimitta*) for the valid cognition (*pramā*) which consists in the determination of an external object. He demonstrates its status as an instrumental cause with the words "since it is thus. "Appearing to me" refers to the light (*prakāśa*) residing in the subject (*pramātṛ*), which is the instrument;
for that reason, the determination "this is the external blue" is the valid cognition (*pramā*), and the blue is the object of knowledge (*prameya*). And this...

"This is such-and-such"—this will be demonstrated in [verse] 2.16. Alternatively, this is stated with reference to the operation of the sense faculties (*indriya-vyāpāra*): it is not by the operation of the sense faculty that "this is blue" is determined; for [if it were so], that determination would be its essential nature...

One might suspect the validity of that [cognition] which produces a valid cognition; however, this will be established by means of non-conceptual [perception]. Having thus determined it through reasoning, he concludes what was stated—that even a valid cognition does not, for its part, imply another valid cognition as a cause for its separate establishment—with the words "therefore, of that... (tatastasya).

"Of the manifestation of the object" means of the experience whose nature is the appearance of blue. "Of the instrument of the act of cognition" means of the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Furthermore, a second means of valid knowledge would lead to an infinite regress.

There is no dependence [on anything else] for it. The reason for this is "because its nature is self-luminous" (*svaprakāśātmanaḥ*). Here too, the reason is "because it is non-different from, that is, not separate from, consciousness which is self-luminous. Now, one might object: "How can these states of Śiva, Sadāśiva, and Īśvara belong to a transmigrating soul (*saṃsārin*), such that there could be an interval [between them]? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In that [state]..."

Regarding the word "hi": that which was previously described as preceding the act of determination (*adhyavasāya*), in that [state], it is "pertaining to Īśvara" (*aiśvaraḥ*), meaning it belongs to Īśvara. It is not a lack of awareness (*asaṃvedana*). However, the state of Śiva (*śivadaśā*) consists of the nature of a single-flavored selfhood (*ekarasa-ahaṃbhāva*); and since there is no manifestation of objects (*artha-unmīlana*) here, that [state] does not enter into the consideration of objects.
It is conjoined; therefore, it is said that "the state is divine" (*aiśvaro bhāvaḥ*). For each subsequent stage is inseparable from each preceding one.

Even for a bound soul (*paśu*) who has fallen into the state of *māyā*, there is no separation from the prior states such as those of the *vidyeśvara*s and others; otherwise, the consequence would be a total lack of manifestation. Since he possesses the nature of the Lord (*īśvara*), within that particular phase of time (*kālakalā*)—

In that awareness existing at that time— which is of a single flavor of non-duality and self-luminous— the conventional [distinction] has as its purpose the collective transaction and mutual interaction characterized by difference; namely,
the establishment of a manifold state in the form of differentiation, such as "this is the means of knowledge" and "this is the object of knowledge."

In that state, there is no room for difference, because difference is contradictory to the nature of non-difference. In the state of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*), no other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) exists, because its sole essence is non-difference. For a means of knowledge implies an object of knowledge (*prameya*) and is pervaded by the possibility of difference; whereas being solely characterized by non-difference is the opposite of that, and thus [non-conceptualization] is the pervader (*vyāpaka*).

Through the perception of the contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*), dependence upon another means of knowledge (*pramāṇāntara*) is precluded from the [first] means of knowledge. Now, one might object: "The state consisting of the cognition 'I am this' is of such a nature; how can it be a cause? For the sense of 'I' (*ahambhāva*) is the independent knower (*pramātṛ*), not a means of knowledge. If that were a means of knowledge, then it would be of the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*)."
Anticipating the objection that this must be stated, he says: "But merely by virtue of having the nature of the manifestation of objects.
The word "but" (tu) indicates the distinction of the knower from the means of knowledge, and it points toward the suspicion that there might otherwise be no distinction [between them].
From this manifestation of consciousness, which consists of the state of the Lord, the sense of "I" (ahambhāva) is co-extensive with...
Even from that which has fallen into the state of being an object (*adhikaraṇya*), there may arise a distinction even from the knower (*pramātṛ*) whose nature is "I am this.
How is there a distinction? He says: "the object" (*padārtha*). [This refers to] the manifestation of blue (*nīla*).
(Page 76)

[The object possesses validity] merely by virtue of having that form. For in that case, there is something additional—namely, the blue—and by means of that, it has the status of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). However, the subject (*pramātṛ*) is not of such a nature; therefore, he states a qualification for this [subject] which contains within it the reason [for its difference]: "Since the subject has as its very essence that repose which is the single flavor within the state of 'I' (*ahaṃbhāva*), for that very reason he is full. He is not [full] by way of being a means of knowledge.

There is a certain degree of contraction here [in the limited subject] because the entire mass of objects consists of "I-ness" (aham-mayatva). The word "api" (even/also) indicates the impossibility of any differentiation. For this very reason, the term "mātra" (only) is employed; since the cognizer is thus of the form of "I" alone, and the state of the Lord (īśvara-daśā) is something additional to that, for this reason, it belongs to him alone.

The validity of consciousness that has attained the state of Īśvara is established, wherein there is no infinite regress. But surely, people do not realize the nature of Śiva as the subject (*pramātṛ*) nor the state of Sadāśiva and others as the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Who says this? That they do not realize it? Does even the world not realize, "This is free from conceptual construction" (*nirvikalpaka*)?
If it is argued that experience is established through reasoning (*yukti*), this is not the same here either. Thus he says:

"This very [state]... One who has fallen into the worldly transaction of *saṃsāra* is brought to the state where difference is the sole essence, which consists of *māyā*; for this very reason, even though the state of non-duality (*abheda-daśā*) exists, there is the state of *māyā* conducive to that [transaction].

Disregarding that which is deceptive because it is merely an object of experience, he is called a "bound soul" (*paśu*); yet, its true, ultimate nature has been described—that by which the subject and so forth are established, and which is not assailed by fallacies such as infinite regress.
For without this true nature, the subjectivity of the subject, beginning with the void (*śūnya*), would not exist.

It is logically untenable for [the object] to be exclusively of the nature of the cognizable, because it would consequently be insentient (*jaḍa*), and because in its own establishment it would require another cognizer; furthermore,
the status of being an instrument (*karaṇatā*) is not tenable for the senses and so forth, which are considered to be instruments,

since the state of being an instrument belongs to that which is manifested by being employed by an agent, and for the manifestation of that [agent], there would be a requirement for yet another instrument.

Because of the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). The particle *api* is used either for conjunction, or to indicate the distance of the body from the status of a cognizer (*pramātṛtā*), or to suggest the impropriety of attributing actual subjectivity to it. He indicates this very infinite regress with the words "non-penetration by light" (*prakāśānanupraveśa*) and so forth. By this, it is shown that the establishment of the subject matter at hand is simply not possible.
What was stated has been established; therefore, in the end, there is repose in the state that does not depend on another subject or the like.
(Page 77)
This investigation (*parīkṣā*), consisting of thorough deliberation, serves both to avoid what is to be abandoned and to examine what is to be adopted;

by establishing the possibility of the knower (*pramātṛ*) and the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it also establishes the object of knowledge (*prameya*). However, commoners such as plowmen do not understand this, because they rest solely within the realm of *māyā*, which is essentially characterized by duality.

However, that linguistic convention remains exactly as it is. This is possible because the universal subject exists in the form of Śiva, and the universal means of knowledge exists in the form of Sadāśiva. Thus, when the nature of the means of knowledge is understood, there is no contradiction or connection with sublation (bādhaka) by which its status as a non-valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇatā*) would arise; this has been explained in detail.

Regarding this [verse] "This is such-and-such" (2.16), which defines the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*): what is meant is this—the Māyic subject, being essentially of the nature of differentiation and seeking differentiation, is situated in the midst of thousands of such subjects; therefore, because of his firm and well-established...

Even the state [of worldly existence], by virtue of being exclusively perceptible, utterly surpasses the extreme insentience of the aggregate of the void body, vital breaths, and senses— despite the latter’s slight infusion of the capacity for self-knowledge and the like— by treating the levels of Paramaśiva, Sadāśiva, and so forth with contempt, just as a person who relishes only pleasure disregards the status of suffering inherent in the pursuit of wealth and desire.
Not from the beginning. For this very reason, the instruction on its [the object's] manifestation is itself the means for application of focused attention (*avadhāna*). As it has been said:
"The cognition of the grasped and the grasper is common to all embodied beings;
however, this is the distinction for yogis: vigilance regarding their connection" (Vi.bhai. 106).
"O blessed lady, listen to this tradition; I shall explain it correctly to you:

liberation arises immediately when the eyes are merely fixed [in this manner]" (Viṣṇubhaktikalpalatā 11.3), and so forth. Enough of this digression into other secrets; let us return to the subject at hand, which is submerged in a vast amount of material to be examined.

He concludes with "tadevam" (thus, therefore) in order to bring forth the meaning of the sūtra. Now, one might object: "If there is no dependence upon means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), then what is the purpose of this treatise? Consequently, why was it said, 'I shall establish recognition'?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "to be explained below. For it will indeed be stated immediately thereafter.
"But due to the power of delusion, in this [world]... (1.3),
and so forth.
Beginning with "of the painting of the manifold variety of the universe" (2.30),
and continuing up to "never before set in motion here" (2.32).

And so forth. Now, one might object: "By this much, a self of independent nature is established, but not Īśvara. To this he says: "In mere sovereignty. When sovereignty is thus revealed, knowledge and action are also necessarily revealed.
And that very thing is lordship (*aiśvarya*); what else could remain unrevealed? Whatever constitutes the self, that resides within it.

When [the Self] is manifested, it does not become unmanifest; for if it were unmanifest, there would follow the absurdity of its possessing a nature contrary to its own essence. Furthermore, one's own Self consists of sovereignty characterized by knowledge, action, and power; thus, there is the perception of something incompatible with the pervader [of the Self]. Just as a negation is neither fit to be established nor capable of being established [in this case], so too is the case here.

The same applies to the proof (*siddhi*). By this [verse], he shows that in this sūtra, the positive injunction (*vidhi*) and the negation (*niṣedha*) are to be explained as being mutually related through the relationship of example (*dṛṣ� conscious beings (*sacetasaḥ*), meaning those who possess valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇika*). "Selfless" (*nirātmānaḥ*) means devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

[The examples are] jars and so forth. By the word "insentient" (*jaḍa*), this much has been stated; however, this is what is implied: such an exertion is appropriate for insentient things whose own nature is not yet established. And how could even this be possible? For an insentient thing, which has not itself attained its own establishment, exerts itself to perform the affirmation and negation of another—precisely because of that application of exertion.

If his own self were established, what would be unestablished about God that he would need to establish? Or, in the absence of that [self], what would be established by which he could refute Him? Consequently, both the establishment of God and the refutation of God are entirely sublated by the contradiction of one's own words, by what is commonly recognized, and by perception and inference.
"It is logical that the first sūtra [states] 'it is just like the horn of a donkey'; therefore, I shall establish the recognition of that. || 2 ||
He introduces [the topic] by summarizing the meaning of the verse to be stated with the words "evam api" (even so).
That purpose which was previously mentioned— that it is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)— [applies] even when this jar or other object is perceived.

It is observed in the world that when something extremely worthy of being accepted is not perceived due to the power of delusion, one demonstrates certainty by employing conventional means and manifesting one's own capacity; likewise, although this Self is seen as the Lord, it is not perceived in that way— this is a *svabhāvahetu* (essential reason) regarding that which is extremely worthy of being accepted.

How could there be the apprehension (*upādāna*) of even that which is seen if it has not been reflected upon? For this would entail the non-apprehension of the pervader of apprehension. Thus, the logical reason (*hetu*), being excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*)—which consists in its not being an object for the establishment of conventional usage—is pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*) under discussion; such is the intended meaning of the Sūtra and its Commentary (*vṛtti*).

The word "kim" (what) indicates the fitness for questioning; "tu" (but), however, indicates a distinction. By means of that, the word "kintu" (but rather), indicating that what is to be said is not yet concluded, provides the occasion for stating another object of knowledge (*prameya*). [Objection: But since the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) of the Lord has been established with effort, how can it be said, "even when this Lord is seen"?

He said: "This word 'seen' (dṛṣṭa) [is used here]. That which is a transferred (upacarita) object of action, such as the suffixes *ya* and *ātmanepada*, is merely an illustration there, since we also see examples such as "the granary has opened by itself" (*bhinnaḥ kusūlaḥ svayam*). Alternatively, that which is a transferred object—meaning that which is resorted to figuratively (*gauṇyā vṛttyā*) when the nature of the agent of the verb *dṛś* (to see) is [transferred to the object]—that is the [intended] object.

He who possesses that means of proof is "one who is thus. In this regard, he shows the basis for the sublation of the primary meaning in the metaphorical usage with the words "because of impossibility. For there is no other seer, as it has been stated more than once that [otherwise] there would be an infinite regress, and it will be stated again. Furthermore, the ground [for the metaphor] is the state of being manifest, and the purpose is the clear perception of objects such as jars that are intended to be seen.

By demonstrating their equality, it is proclaimed that [the Self] is not subject to denial. Furthermore, a purpose is to demonstrate the relationship between the example and the exemplified: just as an object perceived without investigation is incapable of performing functions such as providing pleasant rest, so too is the Self. Therefore, although both the aphorism and the commentary...

Even so, in the present context, [the phrase] should be applied as being common to both meanings. For this very reason, the passage in the *Ṭīkā* beginning with "dṛṣṭasyāpi" and ending with "ahīyata" primarily concerns the subject of the illustration. Thus he says:
"vācoyukti. This indeed is the variety of *vācoyukti*: that by means of limited effort, the matter to be established—

The summary: The phrase "of that which is established through self-awareness" (*svasaṃvedanasiddhasya*) in the commentary (*vṛtti*) should be understood as figurative (*gauṇa*), intended to demonstrate that [the object] is as undeniable as pleasure and so forth.

For previously, [the opponent's position] was refuted by such statements as, "Indeed, self-awareness is not established," and "Nor is the self established through self-awareness. In the sūtra, the locative case is used in the sense of cause (*nimitta*). Since this Lord, though perceived, remains uncharacterized, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is demonstrated. By implication, it is understood that this [recognition] belongs to him alone. He...

This meaning, which is obtained through the force of the context (*sāmarthya*), has been explained by means of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) in the commentary (*vṛtti*); however, the meaning of the locative of cause (*nimitta-saptamī*) has been explained by the ablative of reason (*hetu-pañcamī*) because it is not easily understood. What was indicated by the locative in the *sūtra* has likewise been explained by the genitive in the *vṛtti*. "Delusion produced by illusion" (*māyā-vyāmoha*) is [the compound] *māyā-kṛto vyāmohaḥ*.
And *māyā* is indeed the power (*śakti*) of the Supreme Lord. This is also stated in the Sūtra by the words "by the force of delusion" (*mohavaśāt*).
*Moha* is that which causes delusion, namely the Lord; "by the force" (*vaśa*) of Him means by His capacity, which is the power of *māyā*.
Alternatively, *moha* is the power of *māyā* because it is a specific power by which one is deluded; "by the force" of that means by its capacity.
There is no cessation regarding the activity of delusion. As it has been said:
"Māyā is called the deluder" (Vi. Bhai. 95).
Or, *muhir* means delusion (*moha*), which is an obscuration; its power (*śakti*) consists in non-falling away (*avicyuti*) under its influence, and by that [power], through action...

The possessor of power (Śaktimān) is implied; by that, there is the delusion of the bound subjects (paśu-pramātṛs), which consists of non-recognition (akhyāti). And since its cause is the power of the Lord (Īśvara-śakti), it is indeed definable both in terms of its essential nature and its cause. For there is no such thing as a delusion consisting of ignorance (avidyā) whose form is indefinable (anirvācya), because it would be a non-entity.

Because it is impossible for there to be the capacity to manifest such a variety [of phenomena]; or, if such a capacity were possible, it would constitute a full-fledged reality (*vastutva*) rather than indeterminacy (*anirvācyatā*). Nor is delusion (*moha*) a function of *rajas* and *tamas* as in the Sāṅkhya view, because, being insentient (*jaḍa*), it could not account for the variety of activity and cessation. Therefore, it is nothing other than the absolute freedom (*svātantrya*) of the Supreme Lord.

With the intention that it is called "māyā" because it deludes, he says, "but not otherwise. Anticipating the objection, "How can it be both seen and unperceived?", he says, "even of that which is seen. The heart is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); until its attainment, there is seeing, which constitutes being perceived. When that [attainment] exists—

It is for application to conventional usage as it has been established, and not otherwise, just as one does not act toward grass and such things once the path has been seen; with that very intention...
(page 81)

"Sātmatā" means the state of being the self (ātmarūpatā), or the determination of the state of being the self through its totality. Regarding the term "sātmā," it refers to an avyayībhāva compound such as "sākalyāt" followed by the suffix *nin*. He explains "firmness" (*dārḍhya*) by saying "due to the immersion of the knower. To the question, "What indeed is this so-called 'resting in the heart' (*hṛdayaviśrānti*) and 'heart-winning' (*hṛdayaṅgamatva*)? he says:

"Of those that have ascended to manifestation," meaning those appearing by the power of the subject's light, and not by themselves. It is for this very reason that it was said, "through absorption into the subject. Now, one might ask: if something "goes to" or "reaches" the heart (*hṛdaya*), it is called "heart-reaching" (*hṛdayaṅgama*); but how can reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) be the heart? To this he replies:

Regarding the phrase "for it has the characteristic of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*)," [the author] begins with: "Supreme Speech, whose nature is the reflective awareness of consciousness, arises spontaneously" (1.45).

"This very [consciousness]... (1.14), thus it was said. He explains this with its intended meaning by the words "blue, etc. Just as [the qualities] "sattva is light and illuminating," "cognition is momentary," "it is an effect," "it is a cause," and so forth, [are attributes] of one and the same partless [entity].

By the power of mutual exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), the distinction between the subject (*dharmin*) and its attributes (*dharmas*), as well as among the attributes themselves, is postulated in order to pacify misconceptions regarding their respective specific aspects. Likewise, in the case of cognition whose nature is luminosity (*prakāśa*), during the time of instruction by another, [it is established that] whatever appears in this system in whatever manner— such as manifestation (*avabhāsa*), reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), and so forth— that very thing exists in that manner.

This created distinction between the attribute (*dharma*) and the substratum (*dharmin*) is indeed ultimately real (*pāramārthika*). And just as it is created, so too is it ultimately real—because such creation consists precisely in resting within non-difference; otherwise, like a jar and a cloth, what relationship of attribute and substratum could there be? With this in mind, he says: "even though not separate."

And it is said: "Having separated [it], it is made to settle. By the term "made to settle" (*avasāyyate*), he states that this activity is of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and belongs to *māyā*. Even the state of instruction (*upadeśāvasthā*) is indeed *māyā* alone;
however, because it facilitates the easy attainment of the path of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), it will be described as "pure knowledge" (*śuddhavidyā*). This...

That which is considered "pure" and external to consciousness, such as when it is said "blue appears," manifests as an appearance through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with that [consciousness]. For in the expression "this blue appears to me," the blue— though swallowed as it were— is connected to the light within the aspect of "mine" (*mama*), which rests upon the sense of "I" (*ahambhāva*).

(82) It is not very far [from the truth] to say that one is touched by the phenomenon characterized as illumination (*avabhāsa*). However, when purity lies outside of awakening, that which shines forth as illumination does so through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), because for some it has reached the level of objects.

This is considered "manifestness" (*prakaṭatā*). Therefore, consciousness suspects that manifestation—like a servant prone to shifting allegiance due to its contradictory nature and being paid by both sides—to be unfaithful. However, this ground of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), expressed as "I reflect," is like a place not seen by the sun; it does not touch upon extroversion. For this very reason, [it is distinct] from the blue.

In that state, it is precisely the act of deliberation (*karmatā*) that is being reflected upon; for in the awareness "this is being deliberated by me," the vision (*dṛś*) manifests as inward-turned. However, in the cognition "this blue appears," even when there is a touch of self-awareness (*mameti saṃvedana*), it is primarily the outward-turning of the vision that flashes forth. Therefore...
Thus, "I-ness" (ahantā) is subordinate, since this [object] is designated by the genitive case as the locus for the expression "mine" (mama).
This is what is meant: here, the autonomy of manifestation is denoted by terms such as "consciousness" (bodha) and "awareness" (saṃvedana).
And autonomy is the absence of obstruction to the expansion of will therein according to one's desire; by that, [the Self] itself—
"It shines forth by means of the supreme self" (*parātmanā*)—this "shining forth" (*prakāśamānatā*) occurs through the principle of non-limitation (*anavacchedanayā*).

That very autonomy (*svātantrya*) is what is meant by "it shines forth by means of the supreme self. This is precisely what is expressed by the phrase "it causes the supreme to shine forth. For this indeed is the king's absolute autonomy in battle: that he both fights himself and causes others to fight. That...

"It manifests itself" and "manifesting, it causes the jar and so forth to manifest"—within this entire aggregate of actions, consciousness (*saṃvit*) and the other factors reside. Thus, when one reflects by accepting all these constituent parts, the result is the present form of the substratum (*dharmī*), whose essence is the manifestation; whereas "it appears" (*ābhāsate*) refers merely to a single part.

The connection is as follows: "dharma" refers to that manifestation which belongs to the subject (*dharmī*), whose nature is luminous and autonomous; from that [manifestation], "vimarśa" (reflective awareness) is distinguished. Now, one might object: reflective awareness is indeed a cognition conjoined with verbalization (*śabdana*). However, there is no verbalization within pure consciousness, because it is non-conceptual (*avikalpanīyatva*).

Because it lacks the status of being an object of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*). And where a convention is applicable to an object, the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) "this" therein maintains an unimpaired coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "blue" alone. As for what was said—that "I reflect" shines forth by way of inwardness—[that is not the case].

Even when that [object] is manifested, it is the same, because the [consciousness] comes to rest within itself [thinking], "I am manifesting. Having raised the doubt, "How then was it said that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) never ascends to the plane of 'this-ness' (*idantā*)?", he says: "Even from its own side... (*svato'pi*).

Regarding the phrase "of the pure" (*viśuddhasya*): the word *api* (also/even) serves as a conjunction with respect to what follows. The connection is as follows: that reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) which occurs even within oneself, and that which occurs toward a distinct blue object such as "this is blue"—both of these rest solely in the subject (*pramātṛ*), the pure cognizer, and not in the object (*prameya*). The genitive case in "of the pure" (*śuddhasya*) is used in the sense of the agent.

By virtue of its purity, the distinction of the cognizer from the light of cognition—which takes the form of a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) colored by blue and so forth—is stated to consist in not being colored by that [object], characterized by resting in an uninterrupted light of "I" (*aham*). For this very reason, for one who is experiencing [an object] through the mind, there is the exertion of the instrument [of thought]: "I am the enjoyer of this blue and so forth. Now, as for this "I"...

How could there be verbal designation—which is conventional—in the absence of convention or when convention is not remembered? To show that this is not merely conventional, he says "the vital breath" (*prāṇabhūta*), meaning it is the very self (*ātmabhūta*) and non-different from it. The reason for this is "insentient" (*jaḍa*).

For the distinction of the conscious from the insentient consists precisely in its nature as reflective awareness (*vimarśa*); otherwise, there would be no difference between light and what is not light.

How is there a distinction? [The following characteristics]—having that form, being produced by that, being drawn forth by that, and belonging to the same causal complex—belong even to insentient things such as a mirror, smoke, or mercury. Nor should it be argued: "Since even reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is not itself a reflection, how can there be a distinction? For reflective awareness is the ultimate place of rest, and thus it cannot be questioned further.
Because it must be joined [to consciousness]. For from where does the blue appear as such? And from where is that [appearance] likewise reflected upon as such?

At this point, the status of the object as an object of knowledge (*prameyatva*) and the status of the subject as a knower (*pramātṛtva*) reach their culmination; nothing further is required. By the word "also" (*api*), he indicates that the occurrence of the object [within consciousness] is merely a possibility.
"Consisting of the reflective awareness of 'I-ness' (*ahantā-vimarśa-maya*). As it has been said:
"Of this [awareness] 'this,' which is a fragmented reflection... (*Āgamaprāmāṇyasiddhi* 15), and so forth.
For one reflects, "This is blue," even while closing one's eyes. And in that regard, this is the ultimate truth:

"I manifest as the manifestation of blue"—by this much [the author] expresses independence from anything further. In the pure subject, which is devoid of the coloring (*uparāga*) of blue and so forth, there is the state of being consciousness (*cit-svarūpatā*), which consists of self-reflexive awareness (*vimarśamayatva*);
therein lies "selfhood" (*sātmatā*), that is, similarity with the Self (*ātmanā sādṛśya*), the nature of the Self.

(Page 84) The perfection of the expansion [of consciousness] is the totality of its own nature, the repose in its own selfhood, and the determination of its own nature. What need is there for more? It is the complete immersion of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) into the very essence of the Self, the unification of the object within it.

When that [pure reflective awareness] exists, he who is the pure subject (*śuddha-pramātā*) becomes my subject (*pramātā*) with respect to the object. And this being so, that which was an object of knowledge (*prameya*), such as blue and so forth, by virtue of its mere capacity, becomes an object of knowledge in reality through its attainment of the status of being the domain of cognition (*pramā-viṣayatā*). Otherwise—that is, if it does not possess the nature of reflective awareness—[it would not be an object].
If that were so, then in the absence of the general category of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), its specific instance consisting of determinate ascertainment (*adhyavasāya*) would not exist,

because the non-existence of the pervading general category entails the non-existence of the pervaded particular. Consequently, an object would be neither existent nor non-existent, neither blue nor non-blue, neither "here" nor "not here," neither "now" nor "then," and [neither] "by me"...

Whether it be seen by this person or not seen, in either case, such a thing could not exist; thus, by virtue of its twofold nature as the essence of a substratum, it possesses no established reality of its own in terms of space, time, or objective domain. Nor does even its "nothingness" remain established.
Even the state of being inconclusive would not be established. Thus he says: "it is merely oscillation.
Oscillation cannot be suspected for pure subjectivity (*pramātṛtva*), because it is an uninterrupted manifestation.

And for the subjectivity of objects (*arthapramātṛtva*), this very [oscillation] is what constitutes its immovability regarding the object of knowledge (*prameya*), and not any other kind; thus, once again...

That [subject] has not been withdrawn separately; rather, the emphasis lies upon the world's performance of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) accomplished through external objects. Therefore, the withdrawal of the object of knowledge (*prameya*) was made. And at the outset, it was stated that the knower alone descends [into manifestation], whereby the knower becomes the knower; and the object of knowledge is present there as a secondary addition (*anvācaya*).

The world’s cognition begins with "I," has "I know the blue" as its middle stage, and concludes with "this blue is that which performs a causal function. Now, one might object: "But when traveling on a road, grass and such things appear yet are not perceived. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And in the case of going along a street, etc."

Regarding the phrase "this too": by the word *api*, he intends this: because, through the movement into the street, even grass and such things, though manifest, are unmanifest—since they have not been reflected upon as having the form of grass and so on—it is precisely for that reason that they become manifest when there is reflection (*vimarśa*), becoming manifest merely as the portion consisting of the "this-ness" (*idantā*). Therefore, there is both exclusion (*vyatireka*) and inclusion (*anvaya*).

(85) It is precisely here that *prakāśa* and *vimarśa* can be demonstrated. Thus, the author of the *Ṭīkā* has primarily provided the application of the meaning of the Sūtra and its Vṛtti based on the illustrations; however, as an incidental consequence of that:
This very point is applied to the case under discussion (*dārṣṭāntika*) by the words "in this way for him.

Thus, the object of knowledge (*prameya*) is reflected upon; and its reflection consists precisely in this: that within the self, which is the nature of the manifestation of blue, there is the reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) of the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*). It is the same for this [subject] as well.

This very reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) constitutes the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*): namely, the reflective awareness of one's own autonomous self-nature, which consists of the Supreme Śiva (*paramaśiva*), whose essence is the sequence of the forms of Viśuddha, Īśvara, and Sadāśiva. And just as for one who desires [to know] mere blue, that state of being a subject—even while being reflected upon—is directed toward the reflective awareness of the blue.

By being made into an instrument (*upakaraṇīkriyamāṇatvena*), it remains unexamined; likewise, although for one who desires [an object] there occurs a reflective awareness of the Supreme Lord’s own free nature through the mere state of being its subject (*tatpramātṛtāmātreṇa*) by means of the blue [object],
it is nonetheless seized by a constant and firm obsession directed toward the external causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) of the object to be desired.

Even by virtue of not being intentionally willed, it becomes like a non-existent thing (*asatkalpa*) because it forcibly brings about the state of being an instrument for the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*) through the power of its own inherent spontaneity (*svarasavaivaśya*). "Full" (*pūrṇa*) refers to that supreme enjoyment (*paramo bhoga*), which is of the nature of bliss (*ānanda*), consisting of the aesthetic wonder (*camatkāra*) within the essential nature of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) called the I-consciousness (*ahaṃbhāva*), which is uncontracted by objects such as blue and the like; of that [wonder],...

*Āpatti* means attainment; or it is the attainment of wonder regarding the full sense of "I" (*pūrṇāhaṃbhāva*), which is the attainment of being primarily contemplated. That Lord who is one's own self-form is characterized by that [attainment]; the characterization consists of all the attributes of the Lord, such as eternity, omnipresence, and universal agency.

Because [these qualities] such as omniscience and omnipotence—which are attributes unique to the Lord—have been made one's own nature, they were not previously the very nature of one's self due to a lack of reflective awareness; for the establishment of reality consists essentially in luminosity (*prakāśa*) and self-awareness (*vimarśa*). Precisely for this reason, there is the *Nareśvaraviveka*.

It is indeed ultimate; however, upon the arising of *vidyā*, [the Self] becomes one with those [powers] which have manifested and attained the state of being its own essential nature (*svabhāva*). To the question "What is that characterized by?", he says:
"That" refers to the perfect immersion (*samyaṅniveśa*) characterized by the Lord Bhairava—that is, the total acceptance (*svīkāra*) performed by Him from all sides.

Its *rasa* is its flow; its *āsvādana* (tasting) and *parāmarśana* (reflective awareness) on all sides— namely, the non-conceptual realization that "I am of such a nature, without a counter-correlate"— and not [the identification] with the body, vital breath, intellect, and so forth.

And because it is contemplated as non-different from the objects of cognition such as blue and so forth, there is a sublation [of duality], which is the attainment of that [state]. This is an illustration: the "winning over of the heart" (hṛdayasyāvarjanam) refers to its being turned toward that [reality], and its "touching the heart" (hṛdayaṅgamatvam) is said to mean that this very form is the truth. Now, how can it be thus?
Anticipating the objection that sovereignty (*aiśvarya*), never experienced before, cannot become an object of experience, he says: "In the heart" (*hṛdaye*).

"It may be" (*bhavet*) means that its coming into being is indeed possible. That which is uncommon to non-lords and considered impossible—namely, omniscience (*jñatva*), agency (*kartṛtva*), and so forth—that very [set of qualities], consisting of a single essential nature, is the recognition (*abhijñāna*).

It is the means for entering into the essential nature of the manifold reality of infinite phenomena by way of form (*rūpa*); that is, it is that by which an object is known through the total appropriation of its entire essential nature from all sides. This is explained by the manifestation or expansion [of consciousness] through the disclosure of its power (*śakti*). The word "this" (*iyam*) refers to it as something firm (*dṛḍha*), and it is called "recognition" (*pratyabhijñā*).

The word "ascertainment" (*niścaya*) functions as a nominal derivation (*bhāvasādhana*). Now, one might raise the objection: "But since those very [cognitions] are self-luminous, what further manifestation could there be for that which is already unobstructedly manifested? Anticipating this doubt, he pacifies it by stating, "Even though... according to the method that will be explained below.
"And this very reality of consciousness (cittattva), which consists of agency and is intensified by *kalā*,
exists as a subordinate quality (*guṇatayā*) [of the subject], distinct from insentient entities such as the void (*śūnya*)," so it will be stated [in verse 3.22].
"It is brought to manifestation"— here too, the connection is with the phrase "according to the method that will be explained."
For it will be stated that the primary agency belongs to consciousness, which is the conscious self;
in the void and other states where that quality is present, knowledge is characterized by absorption into that [consciousness]. (3.23)

Thus, this— namely, the non-instrumentalization of the nature of consciousness elsewhere, such as in the body and so forth, or rather, the intensification of the nature of consciousness through the immersion of the body, vital breath, and so on into the form of the body and so forth— is itself the *prabhāva* (sovereign power). It is that by virtue of which [the state] is intensely cultivated (*bhāvyate*) and must be performed as distinct from anything else.

"He cultivates" means this; and we shall explain that this occurs through the predominance of both higher and lower accomplishments (*siddhi*). "Of the accomplished one" refers to [the state] by way of essential nature and by way of cognition. Now, regarding that which pertains to an established reality...

It is well known that a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) is indeed the instrument for establishing worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Therefore, anticipating the objection that one might argue that according to that very [definition], only recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) is to be established in the commentary, he says "all" (*sarva*).
For even when an insentient object is established, that which is the means of valid cognition is the instrument for establishing worldly transaction.

Therefore, it necessarily brings about a new accomplishment of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) for some part that was previously unestablished, at least in the form of a description or narrative; however, in the case of the Self, which is God, there is nothing unaccomplished to be achieved, since even description and narrative are already established. For if those were unestablished, not even a trace of an object of knowledge (*prameya*) would exist.

It has been stated that there is a certain accomplishment (*siddhi*). Therefore, even its mere conventional usage is not what is being established here; rather, it is shown primarily through the union with the heart—that it exists in a whisper, hidden, and close at hand.
Those two—the manifestation and the narrative—residing within the Self in the form of the Lord, let them not be led elsewhere to the body and so forth, nor to objects such as blue and the like.

They may serve as auxiliary means, yet one should regard them primarily as those very two. Therefore, it is stated that in the commentary (*vṛtti*), [the matter] is demonstrated strictly in accordance with the aphorism (*sūtra*). That which in the world, regarding insentient objects, is merely a means for practical transaction (*vyavahāra*), even when applied here to the non-insentient, is equivalent to a demonstration and is complete in its integrity.

It is equivalent to a mere demonstration, in the form of causing attention by saying "look, look! through the act of pointing out. Thus, in this sūtra, because [the root] *dṛś* is used in the passive sense (*karmaṇi*) with the introduction of an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), it is intransitive; therefore, when explained according to the intended meaning of the illustrated subject (*dārṣṭāntika*), it refers to the agent (*kartari*).
That which is called "established without dispute" is equally perceived in both cases. (3)

He briefly outlines the meaning of the forthcoming sūtra with the words "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*). That which was stated—that the Self alone is the Lord and that He is established—is indeed so; likewise is that power of His which is manifested as the means for the state of being an instrument (*karaṇabhāva-sādhanatva*), and the firm conviction produced by that—this matter is also "thus."
Having provided the justification, he says [the following] to demonstrate the final conclusion:

immediately after the introduction, the subject matter (*artha*)—that is, the thing to be expressed—of the treatise about to be taught is that very recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which consists of the powers of knowledge and action; it is the topic concerning knowledge and action.
(On page 88:

Because the powers of knowledge and action have been described in detail through these two scriptures— which accord with traditional authority and whose purport is determined by the summary of the true meaning— there is firm conviction.

The purpose of the entire treatise is as follows: for insentient things, their support is that which rests upon the living soul; and for those who are living, life consists of nothing other than knowledge and action. Therefore, it is so: the Self alone is eternally established as the Lord. Indeed, the word "hi" (for/indeed) illuminates the relationship between cause and effect. [This establishes] the established nature of the Self.

And regarding that sovereignty which was stated to reside "in the agent and the knower," it is by that means that this accomplishment—which is universally acknowledged by all people as being submerged in the insentient—is logically established, since the essence of life consists in knowledge and action. Now, one might object: has this account not been described only for the categories of the insentient and the sentient? Not so.

[The question is: "Of what other [thing]? [The answer is: "True; however, there is no other," as the author of the *Vṛtti* says with the words "of things" (*vastūnām*). Now, if all entities (*bhāva*) are thus divided into two groups, then [the categories of] action, relation, generality, substance... (2.9)
Regarding such passages as "In this way,
its *rajas* consists of a duality; suffering is associated with *sattva* and *tamas*" (4.6),
and anticipating the question of how that which will be described as arising from a third category [of *rajas*] can exist, the *Ṭīkā* says:

The term "kāra" refers to existence and non-existence. Blue exists externally or internally; the yellow and other colors are inseparable from its exclusion (from being blue). Thus, blue is not those [other colors], nor are they non-blue; rather, all objects have manifestation alone as their ultimate reality. Therefore, in the subject—the locus of manifestation—there is both grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*).

Or rather, they rest for a time in the blue and the non-blue. And the ultimate form of objects is that which rests in the subject (*pramātṛ*). That has been expressed by the term "their underlying unity" (*tatsamanvaya*). When that form exists, that which is determined as external in exactly that way is not created by the subject at that moment; rather—
That which is determined as being behind an object created by the Lord is indeed a real entity (*vastu*), because it performs causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in that very same way.

For we shall explain later that the emanations (*sṛṣṭi*) of the Blessed Śiva’s powers— namely Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Vidyā, and Māyā— as well as the emanation of the subject (*pramātṛ*), exist in the form of the real, the unreal, both, and so forth.
"...having that duality as its object" (2.11),
and so forth. And therefore, when the form of an object (*artharūpa*) such as blue is produced by creation through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), [it is as follows].

If [one claims] that the non-blue effect has as its cause a cooperative factor, an opposing factor, an intervening factor, a substratum, and so forth, then this relation exists externally. Even in the construction of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), when there is a construction based on dependence, the form is manifold: "the color of the cloth" is such that what is blue is itself non-blue; herein—

The relationship is either one of identity (*tādātmya*) or inherence in a single substrate (*ekārthasamavāya*). Furthermore, there is no contradiction with the doctrine of the variegated unity of the one and the many, because that [contradiction] consists essentially in non-manifestation and is produced by the subject; for in the absence of non-manifestation, it does not exist. When created through absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), it is a composite substance (*avayavidravya*); that which is a blue cloth is that very same [composite].

"Non-blue. Although even for an atom a variegated nature is admitted, and even for space and so forth there is conjunction with a jar and disjunction from a cloth—thus possessing simultaneously contradictory states of conjunction and its absence—nevertheless, the investigation concerns an object within the range of all cognizing subjects. And as for that which pertains to atoms, space, and so forth—
The term *patti* (attainment) is worldly, and for yogins as well, it occurs solely through that [worldly means]; thus, the word "composite" (*avayavin*) is a qualifier of "substance" (*dravya*).

Alternatively, the separate mention of "substance" is for the purpose of including that [composite], by virtue of its being well-known; however, the word "composite" is mentioned separately because of its predominance.
Or else, the phrase "composite substance" (*avayavidravya*) is an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*). And here:

Everywhere, it is precisely the state of resting within the subject (*pramātṛ-viśrānti*) that constitutes the vitalizing essence. Furthermore, because it performs causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*) externally in exactly the same way, he states "the thing (*vastu*) may exist" to show that it possesses reality here as well. Now, one might object: if a third category—consisting of both or neither—were possible, then even though [the reason] is excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), [it would not be conclusive].

The reason cannot be pervaded by the probandum because there would be no other alternative state [for it]. No; for that which is excluded from blue is also excluded from both blue and non-blue. Indeed, even "blue" is merely produced by the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) of bound souls (*pāśava*), lacking both [of those forms], and is not external; therefore, one should not entertain such a doubt even in that case. Furthermore:
The validity of inference will be explained as depending upon the necessity established by God, provided there is no creation by yogis— (2.43) (page 90).

In such enumerations as these, *niyati* (the principle of necessity) relies upon what is already established previously; it does not rely primarily on the exclusion of the contrary (*vipakṣavyāvṛtti*). Let that be the third category here. However, the repose of all entities (*bhāvānām*) is in the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*), but the repose of the principle of consciousness is not elsewhere, by which [otherwise] there would be a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between consciousness and the non-conscious.
Or else, a third category [of blue and non-blue] might emerge. But surely, it will be stated that starting from the very *śakti-tattva*, which is the manifestation of the Lord Paramaśiva,
within the stages of Sadāśiva, Īśvara, and Vidya— in the state that is both transcendent and immanent (*parāpara*)—
there exists a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) expressed as "I am this."

And grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is of six kinds—as stated in [verse] 3.3 and so forth. Furthermore, in the sphere of *māyā*, the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*) will be described as being bestowed upon the void, intellect, vital breath, body, and so on, such that they possess both conscious and unconscious natures (*cidacidrūpatā*). And thus says the *Nareśvaraviveka*:
"The individual souls (aṇu) consist of both consciousness and the unconscious...

[as stated]. And it will be demonstrated that within the Great Subject (mahāpramātṛ), there is the simultaneous manifestation of both the subject of illusion (māyāpramātṛ) and the object of cognition (prameya).
"Object and subject appear as non-different within the cognizer" (1.31).

How then can it be said that "there is no penetration of the insentient into the sentient"? To this it is replied: here, first of all, in the supreme abode (*paradhāman*), there is nothing such as the insentient; however, in the realm of *māyā*, blue and other [objects] are projected. And of these...

This very thing is creation: the manifestation, through manifold branches of distinctness, of various forms—both conscious and unconscious—from one another. For this will be described as the "expansion of fullness. However, even in this state, there is no creation whatsoever of the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*), because if that were the case, it would result in insentience. And thus, in the light [of consciousness], there is the manifestation: "I am this."

That which is the "I" aspect (*aham-aṃśa*) is indeed the full Paramaśiva. Therein, the supreme "this" aspect (*idam-aṃśa*) finds its foundation precisely within the "I" aspect. As will be stated here: "The state of otherness... (3.5).
Having begun thus, [it continues]:
"Because of the concealment by the supreme 'I'-consciousness...

Thus, there is no equality in status between that which is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) and that which is of the nature of the non-conscious (*acid-rūpa*). For the consciousness-nature never lacks the diversity of place, time, and essential form, whereas the non-conscious nature never lacks the absence of such diversity. Furthermore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is merely figurative, signifying only the absence of the manifestation of distinctness established through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*); it is not [literal].

There exists some third locus common to both "I" and "this"; nor is it the case that, as with the thought "the blue is itself non-blue" or "the non-blue is itself blue," there is a manifestation of those two distinct forms even while being unified into one—
as if in a manifestation such as "I am that which is blue" or "that which is blue is I"— but rather, this blue is [blue] by itself.
"Essenceless, I am indeed the manifestation of life. For this very reason, [it is said] in the passage: "The atoms are of the nature of both consciousness and non-consciousness...
etc.
Because they possess consciousness, there is one Maheśvara;
those [others] are none at all, because they lack consciousness.

Thus it has been said. Furthermore, that light which belongs to the subject under the influence of *māyā* exists within the supreme light; it does not belong to a consciousness-form (*cidrūpa*) that is separate [from it], but rather only to the form of the object of knowledge (*vedyarūpa*), such as the body, vital breath, and so forth. His status as a subject (*pramātṛtā*), however, is the very light of Paramaśiva himself; it arises from nothing other than the mere conceit (*abhimāna*) produced by *māyā*.
The conceptualization of [the self] as having the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*) is not ultimately real. For it has been established that the subject is non-inert (*ajaḍa*):

"Even though the stability of objects is restricted to the individual soul (*jīva*), which is constrained by the vital breath and the subtle body (*puryaṣṭaka*), it nevertheless rests within the Supreme Self."
"How could there be for him any constraint by means of the vital breath through that very self?

(21), and so forth. All of this has been stated by the phrase "because the essence of consciousness (*cittattva*) is self-luminous. That which shines by itself and does not shine elsewhere—that is, it is not made manifest by another—is precisely that [self-luminous reality].
In reality, it is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). How could that manifest elsewhere? But "elsewhere" is not, in reality, consciousness.
Thus, it is said to be "pertaining to *māyā*" (page 92).
For this conventional usage of differentiation, characterized by the relationship of apprehended object and apprehending subject, is well-known to everyone;

therefore, with reference to that [conventional usage] and by way of restating it, the teaching of reality must be given—thus the twofold division was stated. Now, as for the statement "there are five elements," which asserts that the word *bhūta* (element) is denotative of five things, and so forth—in that case:

"How is it stated in the Sūtra that [the term *bhūta*] refers to those who are living (*jīvatām*)? Anticipating this objection, he says: "And the living being (*jīva*) as well. For a *bhūta* is said to be one who possesses the form of an agent of the action of "being" (*siddha-bhavati-kriyā-kartṛ-rūpa*). Therefore, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), the status of being a *bhūta* is appropriate only for one who is actually living; however, another may possess it by virtue of his favor. But the convention of the attendants (*pārṣada-samaya*) is unrestricted. And that too—
It is indeed so here. And in the *Bhagavadgītā*,

although in passages such as "Among the intelligent, I am the intellect" (*buddhirbuddhimatām asmi*, 7.10), the genitive case is used in the sense of a general relationship (*saṃbandha-ṣaṣṭhī*), nevertheless, it is predominantly used in the sense of selection or specification (*nirdhāraṇa-ṣaṣṭhī*).

"Dhanañjaya among the Pāṇḍavas" (10.37), and so forth, are heard [in the texts]. If it is argued that selection (*nirdhāraṇa*) applies only to things of the same class, and that consciousness (*cetanā*) is likewise of the nature of a material entity (*bhūta*), then the term "substance" (*vastu*) is used in the commentary (*vṛtti*). It is precisely with reference to that [consciousness]—which was previously mentioned—that [the text says]: "by her... (*sā*).

*Āpekṣā* means that which has the form of dependence upon worldly life (*lokayātrā*). Alternatively, it is a genitive compound (*ṣaṣṭhīsamāsa*) meaning that worldly life, though subordinate (*guṇabhūta*), is separately distinguished and reflected upon by the intellect. For in worldly life—that is, in worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*)—no entity appears apart from the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grāhaka*). [This refers to] "of those who transmigrate" (*saṃsāriṇām*).

The meaning is: "by means of the recognition of reality for those who are to be graced. That which appears in direct perception, which is of the nature of experience—that alone is the real; this is what must be entered into with effort within the form of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), by way of firmly establishing its non-difference [from that consciousness]. Now, one might object: does not even an object that is being remembered or conceptualized enter into consciousness?
Having raised the doubt that [the investigation] must indeed be performed, and not merely for that which is being experienced, he says: "not distinct from that.

Since memory depends upon the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of experience, and since conceptual constructions such as daydreams and imaginings do so as well, there is no investigation of them [in this context]. For how can difference, non-difference, and so forth be investigated regarding that which does not manifest? Now, as for those things established by the scriptures...
Anticipating the objection that "whatever shines forth must now be entirely distinct from the nature of consciousness," he says:
"even for those refined by the scriptures" (page 93).

Although twenty-five principles (*tattvas*) manifest for the Sāṃkhya, nevertheless, direct experiential realization (*sākṣātkāra-rūpa-anubhava*) extends only as far as the five elements and consciousness, and no further. For this very reason,
with the intention that the entire universe is thereby described by the mere determination of the six constituents (*dhātu-ṣaṭka*), [the author] proceeds.

The effort of that [realization] consists in its thorough examination. Even in those cognitions produced by probability, inference, or scripture, it is that very [reality] which appears; there is only an additional element of conceptual synthesis (*yojanā*). Just as in the case of the earth itself—which possesses various odors such as fragrant and foul—it is perceived through subtlety, while setting aside its specific qualities.
Regarding the phrase "the nature of the subtle element of smell": this was stated by means of a figurative attribution (*adhyāropeṇa vāda*), as if it were already experienced.

For the equilibrium, pervasiveness, and other qualities of the constituents (*guṇa*)—pleasure, pain, and delusion—have been superimposed [upon them] to postulate the *pradhāna*. And in that regard, everything such as pleasure and so forth is indeed experienced; at least, it is directly perceived.

Furthermore, equality is observed between sweet and bitter flavors, and pervasiveness is observed in the color of a cloth. Therefore, this is the intended meaning: here there are two possible courses regarding "this" as the primary object. If something manifests separately, it consists of form and so forth. Or, if it does not manifest as "this," yet it nevertheless manifests, then it must manifest solely as "I."

Or [it is not separate] because there is no other possible mode of existence. Now, if it does not manifest, then it is nothing at all. But surely it does manifest as "this-ness" (idantā), and it is distinct from form and so forth, precisely because it has been thus conceptualized. True; nevertheless, one knows:
"It manifests within me," and it is precisely this manifestation within the subject that must be taught.

For it will be stated that "interiority" (*āntarya*) consists in identity with the subject (*pramātṛ-ekātmya*). If that [interiority] is already established, what need is there for anything else? For this very reason, he says: "easily accomplished" (*sukara*). That which has "easy accomplishment" means that its non-separation—the internalizing within the subject—is known by all people. Since that [external object] is equal to a non-entity such as a sky-flower, having restated that, if...
If one were to begin proving that these two are non-different from the cognizer by means of that very perspective on the cognizer,
then this [system] would not differ from other treatises whose primary concern is [the establishment of] distinctness.
For instance, if it were said that "a sky-flower is not separate from the cognizer," it would not follow that a pot or any other manifesting object is [non-separate].

Thus, the non-dual nature [of consciousness] is established. And as for that "sky-flower" which has been so established, no one perceives it as a separate cognition. How, then, can its inclusion within the subject be easily accomplished?
(page 94)

He says: "For it is thus. Those for whom conceptualization is the sole purpose, and not any external object; and those entities which exist only within conceptualization because they do not manifest externally—they are conceptual constructs (*vaikalpika*).
Of these, whose own nature consists of the forms of cognition, there is a frequent manifestation.

"According to the views of the Sugatas, Vedāntins, and others, that which is perceived is an illusion consisting of latent impressions (*vāsanā*)," because it has been so stated. Now, [one might object]: "Is it not the case that neither the self, nor cognition, nor its latent impressions, nor its form exists as a reality?"

It shines, moreover, in the form of "this is silver" by way of an external appearance (*bāhyākāra*). Anticipating the objection—"But that [silver] does not exist for them, and what is the inclusion (*antarbhāva*) of that which is non-existent?"—he says: "Even in the theory of the apprehension of the real (*satkhyāti*). Here, there is no need for inclusion; only the Self exists, and nothing else. Thus, by means of this distinction, the avoidance of duality (*dvaita*) is established.
It is to be taught. Furthermore, because it is a non-entity (*avastu*), its exclusion from distinctness is established by itself. Now, one might object:
"Even if that is a non-entity consisting of conceptual construction (*vaikalpika*), it is nevertheless determined (*adhyavasīyate*) as external silver;
and since that [determination] exists, how can it be a non-entity? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And even with respect to the determination (*adhyavasāya*... [and so forth].
Let us first set aside the question of how determination (*adhyavasāna*), which does not touch the actual object, could convey its reality.

However, in the case of the primary conceptualization (*pradhāna-vikalpa*), there is no such determination that "this external object, situated among pots and so forth, is the Pradhāna. For that [determination] is rooted in non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka-darśana*), and that [perception] is not present here.

The word "api" (also/even) is used to illuminate this much of the meaning: that if [the object] were rooted in another conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

The word "ca" (and) indicates a doubt regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) and conjoins it with the object of cognition (*prameya*). "Nothing at all"—that is, the Primal Matter (*pradhāna*) and so forth do not possess any such form which could be determined even with difficulty through strenuous effort.

It is avoided—that is, excluded—by way of its dual nature and its distinctness. And by this very intention, the Sāṃkhyas have demonstrated that although the *pradhāna* and so forth are objects of knowledge through inference, scripture, and the like, they possess the status of being non-manifest (*asaṃvedya*). In [the context of] memory, conceptualization, and so forth, nothing would be difficult to avoid.
By the word "iti" at the end of this passage (p.
95), he indicates its nature as a reason (*hetu*) and states its relevance to the subject at hand: namely, that [the object] is established beyond doubt.

The intention is that it must be established with effort that [the object] is not unestablished for anyone with respect to its being an object of direct realization (*sākṣātkārajñeyatva*). The phrase "it has been stated" implies "by both the Sūtra and the Vṛtti.
Thus far, the construction of firm reasoning has been explained: namely, that whatever is established for people in a certain case is not [unestablished] there.

Just as the blueness of a blue object must be established through effort, so too is non-difference from Pradhāna, Māyā, and so forth something that must be established through effort. Thus, "unestablishedness" (aprasiddhatva) is the pervader (vyāpaka) of that which requires effortful establishment. For even if it were established, if it were to exist [in all cases], then it would occur everywhere; consequently, no person would ever remain silent. Therefore, its pervader—[namely] occasionality (kādācitkatva)—...
Because its being established through effort is pervaded by non-apprehension— which would entail a contradiction with its being conscious and its being universal—
there is the "perception of what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*), since that [effort] is incompatible with being well-known. Now,
for those who cannot tolerate the firm constraints of logic and are not fit to be instructed by a compassionate teacher, [the following is said]:

Adopting an alternative view with some degree of disregard, he explains the Sūtra and the Vṛtti with the words "Or rather" (*athavā*). The meaning is: what is not included by the word *bhūta* in the Sūtra, which is derived from the root *bhū* ("to exist"), and by the word *vastu* in the Vṛtti, which is derived from the root *vas* ("to dwell")? [The answer is: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) consists of earth and so forth, while indirect perception (*parokṣa*) consists of that which resides therein.

The meaning is that [the world] possesses a diversity differentiated by place, time, and state, which is absolutely beyond the senses from our perspective—but not from the perspective of the Mantreśvaras and others—characterized by being an object of cognition; this is indicated by the qualification with the word "insentient" (*jaḍa*). This is how it is specified in the Sūtra: "of those things that have become insentient."

In the commentary [it is stated], "the insentient nature of things. Now, why is it not said that the many objects of knowledge—consisting of bodies, instruments, worlds, and so forth, from Brahmā down to the immobile—and the knowers themselves, are of one essence with the Lord in that very form? Why is there this intermediate division into two classes based on sentience and insentience?

Anticipating the objection that the *Sūtra* mentions "insentient and sentient" (*jaḍajīvat*) for the sake of establishing [the categories], while the *Vṛtti* uses the phrase "the distinction between the insentient and the non-insentient" (*jaḍājaḍabhedapada*), he says: "And by way of two groups" (*dvairāśyena ca*). The word "and" (*ca*), while gathering together the objects of knowledge (*prameya*), indicates the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). This should be applied similarly elsewhere as appropriate. The underlying intention (*bhāva*) is this: [the categories] are beyond numbering.
Moreover, these entities are first deliberated upon and manifested in the form of "insentient" or "sentient";
and because they are dependent upon that very deliberation and manifestation, they abandon their multiplicity and remain as a duality.

Even their unity is difficult to attain because they are non-different [from Him]. The Lord alone, being autonomous and consisting of the forms of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), creates these [entities] as His own self according to His will; they possess no individual essence of their own. Furthermore, how can the heart suddenly accept the oneness of infinite things?

Regarding the classification: [The opponent objects,] "Surely the non-inert category (*ajaḍa-varga*) should have been mentioned first, because of its primacy. [The author] refutes this with the words, "And of the inert alone... For it is the inert, being already established, that must be diligently brought into inclusion within the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*);
however, the inclusion of the nature of consciousness within another nature of consciousness is not something to be accomplished by effort. [If it were done so,] it would be due to delusion.

In that context, one conceives of both lack of sovereignty and multiplicity; that alone must be removed. Therefore, the prior mention of the "insentient" (jaḍa) was intended to include the consciousness that is to be accomplished through effort. Having read the word *tatra* as a term indicating the state [of the subject], he explains it as "of those two, the insentient and the sentient. And thus, here is the introduction to the universe:

To that extent, one must speak of the state of being identical with the Lord (īśvaramayatva). In that context, since the insentient world's identity with the Lord must be explained according to the principle of "the Person alone is all this" (puruṣa evedaṃ sarvam) and so forth, what is the purpose of defining an intermediate state of being attached to individual souls (jīvallagnatā)? To this, he says:

Regarding the phrase "of the insentient self" (*jaḍātmanaḥ*): what could possibly be defined of that which is insentient, uncharacterized, and unmanifest—more lamentable even than the horn of a donkey? Furthermore, manifestation (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) are not its own; for the conventional usage is: "it manifests to me" and "it is reflected upon by me. [Objection: But surely, in the sphere of Īśvara, Sadāśiva, and Śakti, there is the [experience] "I am this"?
Anticipating the objection that "the identity of entities consists precisely in their being one with light (prakāśa) and awareness (vimarśa)," he says: "And there...

The remaining intention here is: "Is it by means of the removal of the delusion of duality, or because of its very non-existence? But now—in the state of Māyā, at the stage where instruction through effort is required—even those who maintain the doctrine of duality have accepted this.

The establishment of objects rests upon consciousness; thus, through such expressions as "dependent on the living," "clinging to the living," and "merged within the living," it ultimately results in their identity with consciousness.
For "resting" means dependence upon that [consciousness], which is itself a state of repose within it, and that, too, is its being absorbed within it—this is what is meant by "the living."
The intention of the word *bhūta* in the final explanatory phrase, "only being-suchness (*evaṃbhūtatva*)— that is, reality (*vastutva*)— remains," is as follows.

"Established as having dependent existence" means that even by others, the dependence of these [objects] upon consciousness (*saṃvit*) is admitted; the sense is that it is by virtue of this [dependence] that they attain identity with consciousness. "According to the method to be explained" refers to [the verse]:
"The object to be manifested has the nature of manifestation; and that which is not manifest is not established" (1.34).

Thus [ends the section]. Furthermore, the proof of the non-inert subject (*ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi*) is as follows: "In this way, these inert things, which are like non-existents within the Self, exist only as manifestations of Light. (15)

Thus, by this— namely, by the determination of the state of abiding as the living soul (jīvan-niṣṭhatā) within the midst of insentient things— he intends this very instruction on the nature of the Lord (īśvarabhāva) for insentient things by means of ascending the ladder of the living soul;
as stated in the section on the Compendium of the Meaning of Reality (Tattvārthasaṃgraha-adhikāra).
"The Self alone is the one Great Lord of all living beings"—this is the inclusion of "living beings. "The Self alone [pervades] among all entities"—[this is the inclusion of "entities"]. (2)

Thus, in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*, he will read [the verse] beginning with "even though there is no difference in being existent" (*bhūtatvāviśeṣe'pi*) in order to explain the meaning of the seventh case that has been accepted with effort. The intention is that there is no other form [of these entities] that produces their distinction from the insentient (*jaḍa*). By the phrase "connection with life" (*jīvana-sambandha*), it is indicated here that the connection with activity (*kriyā-sambandha*) is the ground for the application of the term.
Keeping in mind the principle that "in compounds, primary (kṛt) and secondary (taddhita) derivatives express a relationship," and considering this,
he indicates that the word *jīvat* ending in the present participle suffix (*śatṛ*) denotes one who possesses the activity of living that is currently being accomplished and has not yet ceased.
This is shown by beginning with "of those who live" (*jīvatām*) and then using the singular number in the statement "living consists of knowledge and action" (*jīvanaṃ jñānakriye*).

He states that oneness in consciousness is ultimate. Now, one might object: "If life consists of cognition and action, then how is it consistent to say that their connection is the cause of sovereignty? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For those two alone will be described as sovereignty."
The supreme Speech, whose nature is the reflective awareness of consciousness, arises spontaneously; this is the primary sovereignty, the supreme lordship of the Self. (1.45) (p.

For in this context, it will be determined that sovereignty (*svātantrya*) consists precisely in this: knowledge whose nature is luminosity (*prakāśa*), and action whose nature is reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). Now, one might object: "According to you, knowledge and action constitute sovereignty, but how can life (*jīvana*) be such?
For that is merely the maintenance of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Anticipating this doubt, he says: "For life... The word "for" (*hi*) serves to [establish] this...

Indicating that this work serves as the means for supporting the aforementioned life consisting of knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā*), it suggests the following objection: "It is true that 'life' (*jīvana*) is well-known as the maintenance of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*);
however, the word *prāṇa* here refers to the pentad beginning with *prāṇa*. And the maintenance of that..."

It is the rendering of the eyes and other sense organs (*buddhīndriyas*), as well as speech and other organs of action (*karmendriyas*), into an immovable state according to their respective locations and functions;
and this occurs when they are joined together with the triad of internal organs (*antaḥkaraṇas*)— namely, the mind (*manas*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and intellect (*buddhi*).
Distinct from the thirteen external functions— such as the perception of forms, the utterance of sounds, and the conceptualization of blue and so forth— is that other internal function which,
although it possesses the nature of destroying external functions such as the perception of forms through specific incapacities like blindness, [remains distinct].

Their unimpeded functioning— synonymous with agitation, exertion, effort, and so forth— is such that the wind, brought under their control, abandons its natural transverse movement and assumes the nature of the fivefold group beginning with *prāṇa*, whose names are derived from their functions of pervading the front, back, upward, downward, and lateral directions.

Furthermore, the impulses, exertions, and efforts are of the nature of knowledge and consist of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). In that regard, within "living" (*jīvana*)—that is, in the empirical activity of living—there is an internal absorption of both knowledge and action, because they are designated as non-distinct from one another, just as the *dhava* and other trees are non-distinct from the forest. Now, let it be granted that knowledge and action exist in the waking and dreaming states; however, in the state of deep sleep (*suṣuptatā*), [how can this be so]?
