But how is it for you [the opponent] when [the body] is in the form of deep sleep? And why is there no conventional usage that "he does not live" at that time?
Having raised this doubt, he says: "Even in the state of deep sleep. He states the reason for this here:
because of the effect of the thirteen—the sense organs of cognition and action—when they are combined.
Even in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), there is the impelling of the fivefold group beginning with *prāṇa*; therefore, [the Self] consists of knowledge and action.

For knowledge is the effect of the sense organs of cognition (*buddhīndriya*), and action is the effect of the organs of action (*karmendriya*). But if this were so, [the notions] "I know" and "I act" would manifest even in deep sleep, and one would remember [them upon waking] as "I knew" and "I acted"; yet this is not the case.

Anticipating this objection, he says "internally latent" (*antarlīne*), which means that its specific qualities have not yet emerged. This is what is being stated: regarding the thirteen sense organs...
In the state of existence characterized by the function of vitalization (*prāṇana*), which is as if waking,

because there is no distinction between subordinate and primary qualities due to their being merged together (*samānābhihāra*), none of those specific varieties of knowledge and action— ranging from "I determine" up to "I am the possessor of the activity that generates bliss"— exists.
Because it appears as something predominant, its manifestation is not clear without the delineation of its specific aspects;

however, in their nature as universals, cognition and action certainly do exist. For in the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) of one who is awakened, this form "I" does not appear as something fragmented, nor as something newly arisen and unprecedented. This has been explained at length.

Regarding the phrase "by one who has previously perceived [objects] as distinct from the self": even in the states of waking and dreaming, there certainly exists that same internal activity of the general organs (*sāmānyakaraṇavṛtti*), which consists of the power of life (*jīvanaśakti*) in the form of a general cognitive activity and whose specific details have not yet been delineated; it is only there, by virtue of the relative predominance or subordination of the qualities (*guṇapradhānabhāva*), that it appears as external.

The activity of some particular sense organ arises, and therefore that very [activity] shines forth with clarity; it does not, however, appear as a universal form (*sāmānya-rūpa*), such as "cowness" (*gotva*) in the perception of a *śābaleya* (a brindled cow). Therefore, the phrase "here and there—even in the state of deep sleep (*suṣupta*)" should also be construed in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). That [state of] living is one with the state of deep sleep even during the waking state and so forth.
Although form (*rūpa*) follows the logic already stated, it nevertheless consists solely of the activity of knowledge and action latent within it. Now, one might object:

"O Lord, the infusion of the essence of the 'I' (*ahaṃśara*) into the intellect, vital breath, and so forth, which is fashioned by the power of Your Māyā, constitutes life; and since knowledge and action are precisely this 'I', they must therefore be innate. To this, [the response is: therein...

How can it be said that [the Self] is the product of the organs of cognition and action? True; however, the transmigrating being is taught by means of the apprehension of difference which he has accepted. Since nothing such as the power of the Lord is known to him, how could he be taught in that form? Or, if it were known, what else would remain to be taught? And in all cases, [this applies] regarding the Lord.

Even though absolute sovereignty (*svātantrya*) remains established in the ultimate sense, this intermediate relationship of cause and effect is also accepted as real because it appears as such through the power of its inherent necessity (*niyati-śakti*). In that regard, just as the external activity of the cognitive and active senses consists of such determinations as "I am perceiving a jar," so too—

Since that which has not yet manifested its specific qualities exists even in an intermediate state as the nature of living being, there is nothing problematic. But [it may be objected]: if this is so, then [the self] would exist only within itself...

There would be the manifestation of life, whose nature consists of knowledge and action. What follows from that? It would not have been stated that those other living beings possess sovereignty. What follows from that? In that case, duality appears. O proponents of valid authority, if those other living beings do not appear as being alive, then they are insentient; and yet, it has been stated that their very state of being attached to life [is what constitutes their existence].

How can there be duality by means of those [two]? If they appear, even so, since living consists only of knowledge and action, how can there be duality? Furthermore, the position that "they appear" alone is logical, because in the case of the opposite—[if they did not appear]—there would be a difference in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). Anticipating the objection, "But the internal state consisting of living is not perceivable by another; how then could it be known? he says: "Even externally."

First, internal vitality has been demonstrated; furthermore, even that which consists of specific functions such as speaking and grasping is of the nature of vitality—either because the particular is inseparable from the general or because it is a transformation of the general—and it is not only self-perceived, but is perceived by others as well. In this regard:
In this regard, he writes the scripture recited by the venerable Bhartṛhari, beginning with "at its departure":
"Speech impels all embodied beings toward purposeful actions;
it is this very speech that constitutes the consciousness of transmigrating beings, existing both externally and internally."

"At its departure, this [body] is seen to be unconscious, like a piece of wood or a wall" (Vākyapadīya 1.128). When it departs, this [body] is perceived by direct observation itself as being like a piece of wood or a wall, devoid of consciousness;
and that which appears as "existent" through direct observation appears as if it were lost. Therefore, by means of speech and the other [senses], that...

Even internal life-force, having attained identity [with the self], is apprehended as a direct perception itself; it is not apprehended by observing a deliberate action in one's own body or elsewhere.
If it were to be postulated that this is due to cognition— |||

(101) According to this principle, [the self] is known solely through the domain of inference (*kevalānumāna*). This is what is meant: even in another's body, as long as there exists that which is experienced—such as fairness or darkness of complexion, hunger, thirst, pleasure, pain, and so forth—it is like any other insentient object.
That which is reflected lives and shines; however, life itself consists of knowledge and action, existing through identity with one's own Self.

And such manifestation—which has as its fruit the uprooting of the duality of subjects and which is the nature of Pure Knowledge (śuddhavidyā)—is what is meant here by the term "the world" (*loka*) in the context of protecting the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).
According to the principle that [the former] is preceded by intelligence, he directs his exceptional devotion toward inference alone. (4)

One might object: "Granted that the designation 'Lord' (aiśvarya) can be established for the Self on the grounds of its recognition of the powers consisting of knowledge and action; however, how is that very ground itself established? Anticipating this doubt, the commentator [Vṛttikāra] provides the aphorism *jñānam* (knowledge), which briefly states the intended meaning.
He explains this with the words "and thus":
"In that case, cognition is established by itself; whereas action, being dependent on the body, is perceived even by others. By means of that [action], another's cognition is inferred. (5)

In that regard, between those two, within one's own self, cognition is self-luminous; action as well—being internal, inseparable from pure awareness (*saṃvedana*), and consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—is self-luminous. That very same [action], when it extends to the body, is accessible through external seeing, touching, and so forth; however, in another subject, it extends to the body.

Having the nature of activity and verbal expression, and being accessible through means of knowledge such as perception, it—due to its identity with consciousness, its being an effect thereof, and its culminating therein—produces even the manifestation of internal self-awareness. Thus, life residing in both the self and other subjects, consisting of knowledge and action, is established as the causal form; from that arises the worldly discourse of sovereignty.

This is the intended meaning of the verse beginning with "sādhanaṃ. He states that "it is inferred" (*ūhyate*) does not mean that the cognition of another's mind is merely an object of inference; rather, he explains: "inference (*ūhana*) means reasoning (*tarkaṇa*), that is, conceiving of a possibility (*saṃbhāvana*). In this respect, there is also the operation of the sense faculties, and therefore "inference" (*ūha*) indicates direct perception (*sākṣātkāra*). For that [perception] too—

From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is indeed the cognition of another; however, it has been stated in the introduction (page 102) that "otherness" consists merely of the essence of conceit (*abhimāna*), produced by illusion and delusion (*māyāmoha*).

Even in the case of an operation upon oneself, it is established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*), because of the general statement [to that effect]. Now, it might be argued that at the time of the manifestation of an object, cognition does not manifest exclusively; rather, it is the object that manifests, not the manifestation of that [cognition]. And when that [manifestation] does manifest, it is only by way of being apprehended by another cognition.

Anticipating the objection of the follower of Akṣapāda (the Naiyāyika), he says: "It manifests in the other's position. For if it is said that "the object manifests," and this is a property of the object, then by the rule "it belongs to me," there would be no necessity for its being attached to the subject (*pramātṛ*).
If it is argued that this is so because it is an effect of the subject, [we reply: no, for there is no rule that an effect must necessarily manifest as being attached to its cause.
Because no instrument [of perception] is observed; for if that were the case, the cloth would belong to the weaver alone.

Furthermore, in the absence of its being connected to a cognizer, that manifestation of the object would either be toward everyone or toward no one at all, whereby the world would either be omniscient or in a state of deep sleep. Moreover, "it manifests" is not a property of the object.

If it is asked, "To whom [does it belong]? and one says "to the self" (ātman), it follows that because the object is manifest, form is inherent in the self, and thus the self consists entirely of the manifestation of the object. And if that state does not manifest to the self, then since its nature would not be such, what distinction is there for it? For [the distinction] arises from the connection with the quality of whiteness.
A white cloth, being insentient, lacks autonomy because it does not shine forth by itself;

likewise, the Self might also be so. If it is argued that the very connection with the manifestation of objects, occurring through its real mode of being, protects the Self from insentience, let it be so for now; nevertheless, as for its own self...

There would be no distinction from another self (*parātman*). For even another self, though essentially a conscious knower by virtue of the inherence of the quality of cognition whose nature is the illumination of objects, does not manifest; and one's own self (*svātman*) is likewise [unmanifest].
Thus, that independence which is experienced within one's own self in the form "I know" occurs precisely through the distinction from another self.

How is it possible that the nature of being a knower is apprehended by another cognition within one's own self, but not in another self? In that case, how could there be no distinction between one's own self and another self? Furthermore, if that other cognition requires yet another cognition, there would be an infinite regress; and even so, the distinction between one's own self and another self remains unestablished.
Therefore it has been said:
"By what, my dear, should one know the knower?
(page 103)
Thus it is said. Furthermore, since luminosity is not a property of the object, the object itself does not shine;
nor does cognition, which consists of the illumination of the object, shine;
nor does the imagined series of subsequent cognitions that grasp it appear; nor even its inherent cause...
The self does not manifest; even cognition, which is of the nature of its manifestation, does not shine by itself;

and since the series of further cognitions regarding that [first] cognition would likewise be the case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), and thus nothing at all would manifest, resulting in a blind world.
This is what he expresses with the words: "And if there were manifestation by another, there would be an infinite regress, etc."
By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), [the author] indicates the impossibility of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) and circularity (*cakraka*), as well as contradiction with experience.

For, by means of cognition whose nature is the illumination of an object, there arises the cognition consisting of the inference of the self, such as "I know the jar," as well as the illumination of the object itself. This is because even in the case of the thought "this is a jar," [there is an awareness of the subject].

The thought "it is known by me" implies an internal entry [of the object]. Even if there is no verbal expression due to the absence of such intention, this much—namely, the knowledge of "I" and the knowledge of "this"—is mutually dependent (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore, if the self is inferred through another cognition of sound and so forth, which is itself inferred from the cognition of pleasure and so forth, it results in a circular argument (*cakraka*) due to the introduction of an additional element.

The impossibility [of conceptualization] is that its very manifestation as a cause is not possible. Furthermore, there is a contradiction with experience, for when the self is manifesting, not even a trace of an intervention is perceived. "Elsewhere," or rather, the absence of conceptual construction belongs only to the sensory cognition which is established by perception. Thus, "the dull-witted have won," and so forth.

One who possesses praiseworthy wisdom understands that what is called "knowledge of an object" is a means for cognition, not cognition itself. For one whose apprehension is not perceptual, there is no perception of the object;
for the apprehension of an object does not occur through the mere existence of the object, but rather through the existence of its apprehension. And that [apprehension]...

[The opponent argues: "It is without a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇikā*). One who engages in worldly transaction (*vyavahārin*) halts [the inquiry] based on existence; if that [existence] is not established, the object is not established—thus the entire universe would vanish. [The proponent replies: "If you say, 'He perceives consciousness by means of another,' and so forth, this person does not, for the time being, comprehend any object, because [his cognition] terminates in perception (*upalambha*)."
"Waiting," and "it does not exist," etc., [are stated] in sections such as the *Viniścaya-vārttika*. Now, an objection is raised:
"But there is no mention of 'living' (*jīvat*) in the verse (*kārikā*); so how is it said in the commentary (*vṛtti*) 'of those who are living'?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "insofar as being alive is implied."

(Page 104) "Knowledge and action are the life of living beings"—this is obtained simply by reflecting on the meaning of the preceding sūtra. And that [meaning] has been explained in the Vṛtti for the sake of clarification; such is the sense. The word "that" (tat) [refers to this].
The basis and cause for the conventional usage of "living" is the connection with cognition and action; therefore,
the conventional usage "this one knows" or "this one acts"— which begins with the manifestation that "this one is living"—
also occurs in the form "I know" and "I act," whereby it treats another bodily portion as one's own body, [manifesting] as the sense of "I-ness."
It is indeed the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). But was it not previously stated that living consists of nothing other than knowledge and action?
That [statement] appears to be contradicted by this conventional usage of existence (*bhāva-vyavahāra*) which serves as the basis for the objection, because the latter is rooted in duality. True;
however, in the sense that "one lives" means "one sustains the vital breaths" (*prāṇa*), knowledge and action are contained within it; or else, [it refers to] the state of being alive (*jīvatva*)—

By the word "life" (jīvana), the very activity of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*) is expressed. For when the question "How does this person live? arises regarding the transaction "This person lives," they give the answer: "Because he knows and acts. Likewise, when the inquiry "How does this person know and act? is posed regarding the transaction "This person knows and acts," they reply: "Because he lives. However, because of their mutual inseparability, life was mentioned first.

"Knowledge and action alone [constitute it]. Or rather, even though there is no difference, a distinction is nonetheless constructed by conceptual thought (*vikalpa*); for "he lives" is one conceptual construction, while "he knows" and "he acts" are another. Therefore, it is logical that even within identity (*tādātmya*), a distinction may be based on internal differences imagined through the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of those [concepts], just as in the Buddhist doctrine the association with mental forms (*ākāra*) [is possible despite identity].
The state of being the basis for valid cognition (*pramiti*). As it has been said:
"Because of that, there is the determination of that [object]"—thus.
Now, the *sūtra* states, "Cognition and action," yet why is "action" mentioned in the *vṛtti*, bypassing that?
He says, "And action," because it is explained previously. The word "and" (*ca*) indicates the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Having attained the nature of bodily vibration, it is well-known within the self of that acting subject (*pramātṛ*), as well as for another subject distinct from that [first] subject, who possesses clear visual and tactile perception.

That [the existence of another cognizer] is established through direct perception (*pratyakṣāvaseya*) is a point free from dispute; therefore, in this context of stating a reason (*hetu*) to prove the existence of a Lord (*aiśvarya*), that very [perception] should be employed first, because a reason already established without dispute is fit for employment, whereas otherwise it would be subject to fallacies such as being equivalent to the probandum (*sādhyasama*) or infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Regarding another cognizer...

And when the sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) to be proven resides in a subject (*dharmin*), if that [subject] lacks self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) as "I" with respect to the cognizer who infers the sovereignty inherent in all subjects— just as one does with respect to one's own self— [then the proof fails].

In order to protect the established nature of the dharma, accomplishment must be achieved through action alone. Therefore, by means of these two types of excellence, action was explained first in the commentary (*vṛtti*). Anticipating the objection, "If that is so, why was it not stated thus in the aphorism (*sūtra*) as well? he says: "By way of the activity of the speech of others, etc. For that action exists on the level of the root.

It rests upon consciousness alone, because it is of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). And since reflective awareness rests upon consciousness, the word "speech" (*vāk*) is employed to designate its nature as reflective awareness by way of accepting its form as verbalization. For instance, that which is the repose within itself of the non-distinct Light is "I" (*aham*).

That supreme, full, and most excellent activity in the form of speech (*vāk*)— consisting of the conceptualization of an unmanifested counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*), its superimposition, and its removal—

is the act of reflective awareness (*vimarśakriyā*). Even that which is manifested as the "this" (*idambhāga*) is [subsumed] by being swallowed up within the "I-sense" (*ahambhāva*), such that it does not sprout [into duality].

The *paśyantī* stage, which brings forth the state devoid [of differentiation], perceives "I am this"; the *madhyamā* stage, drawing that very [perception] out from the sense of "I," consists of "I know this" and "I do this"; likewise, the *vaikharī* stage, desiring to make it known to another, becomes manifest in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), while in the body it takes the form of action as vibration. And in all these cases, it extends thus far.

The very nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) is what persists [through all action]. For movement in the body and its limbs—such as "I move" or "I shake my head"—has as its essence precisely such reflective awareness. Even an action that is not of the nature of physical vibration, such as "I remain," has as its ultimate reality the reflective awareness of succession within the agent. Therefore, even the movement found in inert things like water or stones [is essentially of this same nature].

Action, such as moving from one place to another, possesses a form distinct [from the subject]. However, even action residing in an insentient object—since it is impossible for an insentient thing to be established within itself—is established in that which supports it; namely, it is established solely in the consciousness of the cognizer. At its root, which is the power of knowledge, it resides in the "I" (aham) as the Self. Thus, even the state of "this-ness" (idambhāva), as in "the Self moves," [is ultimately grounded there].

"Because it is at rest"—thus, every action is of the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). And in the *Vṛtti*, this meaning was accepted by the use of the suffix *cvi* to indicate the possibility of a prior state, and it was explained by the author of the *Ṭīkā*; furthermore, the sequence [of the Sūtra] has been explained. For this very reason, action is merely the "tail" of knowledge.
And cognition is non-different from the knower;

its difference is merely imagined due to the difference in the objects of experience. For this very reason, this is in reality a *svabhāva-hetu* (essential reason), not a *kārya-hetu* (effect-reason).
For vibration, which consists of activity, is indeed merely a partial aspect of the extended stream [of consciousness].
Furthermore, every essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*) results solely in the exclusion of other non-ultimate forms superimposed through the power of delusion.

The author’s intention here is that it is precisely the establisher of conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) that is being designated, and not something whose nature is to establish what is already unestablished;
thus, the actual self-luminosity of cognition, as well as the fundamental sovereignty of the cognizer and his power, is not undermined.
Now, if the subject—the supreme cognizer—is intended to be acted upon by an action...

It is inferred that the causal aspect is the nature of cognition; at that time, since it would have the form of an object of knowledge, both the subject and the cognition would necessarily result in being insentient (*jaḍatā*) because they would be perceivable as "this-ness" (*idantā*).
Anticipating this objection, he says: "And subjectivity...
Subjectivity is the nature of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpatā*), by which Caitra is a subject and Maitra is a subject.

This is the conventional usage. And that [consciousness], insofar as it is manifested within itself as "I"—possessing a reflective awareness appropriate to a life whose manifestation is independent of anything else, and for that very reason incapable of tolerating the reflective awareness of "this-ness" (*idantā*)—is precisely what ought to be inferred by means of inference. For it is not the case that a pervasion belonging to one thing is used to infer something else; rather, [the pervasion must belong] to that which is self-luminous in nature.
And there is pervasion (*vyāpti*). Now, it may be argued: "This Caitra is the cognizer; this is his cognition; I am this cognizer;

this is my cognition"—thus, the manifestation as "this-ness" (*idantā*) is indeed observed in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), and inference (*anumāna*) has conceptual construction as its form and is rooted in the conceptual construction of pervasion. Therefore, why is there not a manifestation of these two [the cognizer and the cognition] as "this-ness" in that [inference] as well?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "For [it is] not in conceptual construction. This is because that nature which is self-imagined by its own essential form—the nature of the subject consisting of unconditioned light and autonomy (*svātantrya*) expressed as "I," and that of cognition characterized by the freedom of light conditioned by its orientation toward the object (*vedya*)—does not exist at all within conceptual construction.

It does not manifest [in its true nature]; rather, the very nature of cognition appears as if veiled by the objects of knowledge such as blue and the like, while being itself shrouded by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as the body and vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, the state of being the subject (*pramātṛtā*) does not fall into the domain of the knowable (*vedyatā*); this is the logical connection. Now, one might object: "In that case, the state of being the subject is then inferred, since cognition..."

And how is it that [the object] is inferred? For indeed, that which constitutes the individual nature (*prātisvikaṃ vapuḥ*) of these two does not appear at all in the conceptualization of inference; and that which does appear, on the contrary, is of the nature of an obscuration (*tadāvaraṇa-rūpa*) thereof.

[The object] may be the body and so forth, or blue and so forth. And there is no need for inference in that case, because it is established by perception and other means as well. Nor is its causelessness perceived therein. Furthermore, what is relevant here is that the sovereignty of all cognizers is inferred from their connection with knowledge and action; in that regard—

To refute the objection that because there are distinctions among specific actions, the subjects (dharmin) themselves must also be many in nature, and thus even the sovereignty residing in them would be divided—making it impossible to establish a single Lord—the author says:
"And [the Lord] is of such a kind. Neither is the body and so forth inferred as being the nature of the subject, nor is it inferred as being of the nature of cognition.

Not blue and so forth; rather, exactly as the nature of the subject and his cognition is contemplated within itself as "I" through self-luminosity, in that very same way it is made an object by inference, even though that inference grasps the "this-ness" (idantā). But surely, there is a contradiction between "this-ness" and "I-ness," which consist respectively of dependence and independence?

To the question "How is this so?", he says: "I-ness" (*ahantā*). The indeclinable "I" (*aham*) resides in the light that is non-distinct [from itself]; its state is "I-consciousness" (*ahamiti-vimarśa*), which is *ahantā*. This alone is the nature of the light, its own characteristic that distinguishes it from what is not-light. By means of that, there is a separation, and through that [separation], there is this [notion]: "this is consciousness."

Immediately following the cognition of inference, there necessarily arises a cognition resting in the "I" (ahaṃtā). For since this [subject] acts and knows, his cognition is thus suited to the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) in the form: "I act," and "I know. And all of this, he thinks, "I know."

"Resting in my light and consisting solely of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of my light"—even at the final stage, the inferer shines as being composed of the reflective awareness of the "I-light. Thus, that ultimate established form which is reached becomes manifested as self-luminous itself. Now, as for that [form] of perception in the middle...

The state of being perceivable as "this" (idantā) is incompatible with its ultimate repose in "I-ness" (ahantā). Indeed, it is not fitting to say that blue in the interim should repose in yellowness. He resolves this [objection] with the words "even of one's own self.
This very thing is sovereignty (*svātantrya*), which consists in the power to accomplish the most difficult tasks. And that [sovereignty] is difficult to accomplish.

This is because, during the state of *māyā*, there is a contradiction arising precisely from the power of necessity (*niyati-śakti*). Furthermore, although autonomy (*svātantrya*) and dependence (*pāratantrya*) are extremely contradictory, they do not suppress one another.
By means of supreme sovereignty, the Supreme Lord joins [the individual soul] to the creation of conceptual constructs such as "I am the Lord" or "I am the Self.
For in that state, through the connection with the aspect of objectivity (*idantā*), there arises the possibility of being an object of contemplation, worship, and instruction;
and through the connection with the aspect of unobscured subjectivity (*ahantā*), the attainment of its ultimate nature will be explained.

"By means of volitions such as 'I am the Lord' and so forth, the Sovereign, having fashioned through His freedom a self that is liberated from [objective] freedom—though that self is in reality non-dual freedom—engages in worldly transaction. (1.47).
And thus: from what is about to be said and from what has already been said.

Although knowledge and the nature of the cognizer, when being inferred in another's body through the logic characterized by the possibility of the union of autonomy and heteronomy, are initially apprehended as objects of "thisness" (idantā),
nevertheless, in the final analysis, they are established as being self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) alone; it is not possible that they remain something yet to be proven (*sādhya*).

Because it is established from the beginning and cannot be proven by other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); and because, at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*) with action, it is already established prior to the time of inference; and because its primary nature is that very synthetic awareness (*anusandhāna*) which has consciousness as its essence and consists of the form of "I," whose nature is the foundation of insentient objects such as blue.

That [object] has the nature of the cognizer; and this has been shown by the statement in the *Vṛtti* that "it is already established, not something yet to be proven. Furthermore, the phrase "it is established" (*sidhyati*) in the *Vṛtti* was stated for the sake of emphasizing the aspect of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*).

For in this context, inference—according to the analogy of a flash of lightning—illuminates the ultimate "this-ness" (*idantā*) in the interim, while at its root [it reveals the identity with the Self].

Because at the time of grasping the pervasion (*vyāpti*), at the conclusion, and at the time when the realization of the inference is established, [the cognition] comes to rest precisely in "I" (*aham*). For just as even blue and other objects of knowledge (*prameya*) come to rest in the knower (*pramātṛ*) alone, so too does the object of inferential knowledge. In that regard, this portion of "this-ness" (*idantā*) [rests] within the "I-ness" (*ahantā*) residing in the inferrer.
The dissolved state (*līna*)—even the differentiation of the substratum (*dharmibheda*), because it takes the form of "this-ness" (*idantā*), ultimately rests within pure consciousness alone.

As for the aspect of "I-ness" (*ahantā*), it does not differ from another "I-ness," because consciousness cannot be divided by space and time; these are submerged within consciousness itself due to their being of the nature of the object (*vedyarūpatayā*). This is because [space and time] are inseparable from consciousness.
And because, if there were a difference in essential nature from another cognition, it would follow that [the cognition] is not a cognition; the same applies to blue in relation to another blue.

There is no differentiation within the blue manifestation itself, because the blue manifestation is one with respect to both the three times and the three worlds. Differentiation therein occurs only through another manifestation, such as space, time, and so forth; however, in a consciousness that is free from manifestations (*nirābhāsa*), there is no intermingling with other manifestations, for if there were a need to depend on another consciousness for the purpose of mixing them, [it would not be self-evident].

Because the states of being an object of cognition (*saṃvedyatva*) and being the act of cognition (*saṃvedanatva*) are incompatible; even if it were an object of cognition, it would simply rest within consciousness (*saṃvit*).
Thus, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), the nature of consciousness is established as entirely non-dual. This is likewise true for any other cognizer.
For even from smoke, what is established is merely the exclusion of non-fire, [pertaining to] the ultimate mountain or forest...

Granted that [the nature of an object] may differ according to the diversity of its substrates, such as a kitchen and so forth; however, in this case, even the substrate—such as the body and so on—possesses no ultimate form in itself, because it rests solely within consciousness.
It is merely through its own power that this consciousness brings forth the manifestation of various objects of cognition.
He shows that even the conceptualization of "possessing the property" (*dharmin*) and so forth does not appear when it is unreal, just like the creation by another [deity].

Thus, although this practice of inference occupies an intermediate position, it does not contradict non-duality. For all this conventional usage of difference produced by means of valid cognition ultimately rests upon the realization of the ultimate reality.

And just as the Naiyāyikas have established that direction (dik), time (kāla), space (ākāśa), and universals (sāmānya) are one— on the grounds that their specific names, such as "east," "west," "long," "short," and so forth, do not differ from the underlying cognitions and verbal designations—

so too, why should there not be unity among the marks of the self, such as cognition, action, and the like, given their lack of distinction? And how is the [observed] systematic arrangement to be explained?

Since this [nature] is observed even in the case of directions and so forth, and since its being conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhikatā*) is not at all untenable even in the case of the Self, it is established that the Lord is indeed one alone. Even for the Buddhists, the inferred object— which is of the nature of an exclusion (*apoha*), non-substantial, and merely a conceptual determination resting upon the form of a previously perceived particular (*svalakṣaṇa*)— is what must be sought by those who desire causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*).

And it is also the initiator [of activity]. However, for those who maintain that things consist of partless entities possessing their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*), this is impossible to establish; for that which exists on the mountain is not perceived and cannot be determined, while that which exists in the kitchen is something other than that [mountain fire]. For us, however, it is the very appearance of fire that is both the real object and a single entity.

In all cases there is no fault. Likewise, in the present context as well, when the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the self—which is independent and inferred as "I"—is determined precisely in its own form, the other cognizer becomes inferred;
and among the means of knowledge that establish worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), [it is established] by the fundamental means of knowledge.
(Page 110) It falls into precisely such a state. Thus, here too, it is the fundamental self-luminosity itself that unfolds.
Because the oneness of the other is established, there are no other subjects distinct from the subject in the form of the inferer.

It has been stated that, from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), they are of a single nature. Furthermore, in the *Vivṛti*, although both the subject (*pramātṛ*) and cognition (*jñāna*) are introduced at the outset, the mention of only one is intended to demonstrate their actual identity of nature. For "cognition" (*jñāna*) is said to be nothing other than the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtā*). In other contexts, this state of being a knower, when it is being inferred, is precisely what constitutes the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*).

Alternatively, by the phrase "and thus," it is stated that this very nature belongs to cognition itself, using the cognizer as an illustration; thus, there is a statement of both [subject and object] which were introduced, by way of the substratum (*dharmī*) and by way of the attribute (*dharma*), in order to define that very nature. Now, if the Self is the Lord, why is everyone not omniscient? [Because] all...
If this statement is made with the intention that there is a plurality of subjects (*pramātṛ*), that is incorrect, because the plurality of subjects is not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*).

It is solely through the power of absolute freedom (*svātantrya-śakti*) that their differentiation appears; however, the subject is one, extending from Śiva down to the level of immobile beings, and he is indeed omniscient. This is what is meant by the words "of all subjects."
In reality, this is because there is no difference in consciousness (*saṃvid*). As it was stated by the venerable Parameṣṭhin in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
"The jar knows through my self, and I know through the self of the jar;
I know through the self of Sadāśiva, or he knows through my self."
"Having spoken thus, Śiva himself remains, knowing his own self through various states" (5.109).
And for that very reason, on the occasion of establishing primordial perfection (*ādisiddhatā*), it was said: "At the time of the descent as Rāma, I..."

In the phrase "he became," even here, it is the speaker himself who is the experiencer at that time by virtue of being the consciousness of another subject; thus, this is now accomplished without effort. As for what was stated there for the sake of establishing omniscience:
"For indeed, everyone [is omniscient] by the power of the mental volition of the Omniscient One."
Or [it is so] because of the capacity for grasping all entities while remaining in a sequential state.
"Whether by means such as direct perception and the like, or even through the absence of means," (5.103, p.
111)—this applies even in the realm of *māyā*; however, here in the investigation of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there is only the state of being of one essence with Śiva.

That was overlooked by the Guru. A concise statement of the subject matter does not have as its sole fruit the mere nourishment of verbal artistry; rather, it is intended to favor a specific type of qualified disciple—one upon whom the descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is intense, whose veil of delusion is dissolving like the fragments of an autumn cloud, and who requires no prolixity in the form of raising or refuting useless prima facie arguments.

He shows this by the words "by just this much. The demonstration of lordship (*īśvaratva*) is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that serves as the basis for establishing its conventional usage. From that arises the realization, which consists of the reflective awareness of lordship and is of the nature of valid cognition (*pramā*).
Its firmness is its unshakeability—its impossibility of being uprooted by the conceptual constructions of others or by fallacious sublaters (*bādhakābhāsa*). From that...

Since the success resulting from this treatise on the Recognition of God (*Īśvarapratyabhijñā*)—characterized by the attainment of worldly prosperity and the splendors of liberation while living—accrues to the listeners, the author’s intended purpose, which consisted in establishing that recognition, has indeed been fulfilled.
Now, one might object: "If the scripture is thus completed, what is the purpose of the subsequent section? Anticipating this doubt:

He said: "Excessive. For those whose descent of power (*śaktipāta*) is weak, there exists an excessive, firmly rooted impurity (*mala*) produced by *māyā*, characterized by the threefold contraction of one's own self, the differentiation of objects of knowledge, and the manifestation of merit and demerit; therefore, this must be uprooted at every step. Otherwise, that very portion [of impurity]...
If it has not been eradicated by "seizing it by the horns" (i.e., by direct and thorough investigation), then that very [doubt], whether awakened by oneself or through the instruction of another,
will surely vitiate his certainty regarding the Lord. As it was said by the venerable Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa:
"Salutations to him who, having manifested the delusion of those bewildered by worldly existence, shatters it.

(71) Here, the genitive case in *tasya* is used through a pun (*śleṣa*) to signify both the object and the agent. He is one who is capable of appearing to himself and others as nothing but the pure "I-consciousness"; for this very reason, he is reviled by fools whose [true nature] is obscured by the power of *māyā*.

One conceives [the Self] in a form contrary to the nature described above; and that very Lord (Īśvara) becomes the object of misconception, because He alone is the agent everywhere. In both cases, the cause is the manifestation of obscuration produced by the power of Māyā. As stated in the *Śivadṛṣṭi*:
"Why [is there] the state of being a proponent and a respondent? Because that [distinction] exists for him" (3.76).
"In this way" means by way of the form of the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) which is about to be stated. "In brief" means silently.
(Page 112)
That by which a subject matter is introduced at the beginning, struck upon, and established is called an *upoddhāta* (introduction); may there be auspiciousness.
Born into the lineage of Atrigupta and joined with a physical body as his support,
he elucidated the introduction to the *Īśvarapratyabhijñā*.
Thus ends the first introductory reflection in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī*, composed by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara, the venerable teacher Abhinavagupta. || 1 ||

Now begins the second reflection: I bow to Śiva, who is bliss, filled with nectar, beyond the mind in the supreme state, the ultimate truth, and who possesses the most firmly established and unsurpassed realization.

Those who are themselves mistaken regarding the very existence of the self—how indeed could they accept its sovereignty? They alone are the primary adversaries here. Among them, how could the Lokāyatikas, being devoid of any establishment of their own position, even refute the positions of others by entering the boundaries of the system of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth?

Because that [position] is refuted, and because entering into that [position] would result in the loss of one's status as a Cārvāka, it is the Buddhists alone who are the proponents of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādin*) here.

For those who accept a self that is manifold and non-superior, or a single [self] whose sovereignty is concealed, have not yet utterly shattered their positions here. By means of the unique [argument],...
Indeed, when a substratum is accepted through its properties, it is easy to admit properties that were not previously admitted;
however, this is not the case when there is no admission whatsoever. Thus, the prima facie argument belongs solely to the Buddhist:
"Is it not the case that [the cognition] has the appearance of the particular (svalakṣaṇa)..."
By such statements as these,
even the agent is imagined [by that same mind].
He says this with these eleven verses; and as he will state later: "This objection is made precisely with reference to that [higher] vision.
(page 113)
In this regard, the proponent of a directly perceptible self (*pratyakṣātmavādī*) is refuted by two verses through the non-perception of what is observable;
however, the proponent of an inferable self (*anumeyātmavādī*) is refuted by three [verses] by demonstrating that memory, synthesis, and so forth can be established otherwise;

furthermore, the one who asserts that the self is proven as a substratum (*guṇin*) because cognition and other qualities (*guṇa*) exist is refuted by one [verse]. Thus, with this much, regarding the self as the subject (*dharmin*)—

Having refuted [the opponent's position], in order to refute the reason characterized by the relationship between knowledge and action—which serves as the basis for the conventional usage of "lordship"—it is demonstrated through two verses that the nature of knowledge, according to the opponent’s view, is untenable;
furthermore, a connection with action is not possible in any case, due to the absence of supporting evidence and the presence of contradicting arguments. Therefore, it is not so.

The intended meaning of the connection [between the verses] is expressed by the triad beginning with "the sovereignty of the self. By stating the subject (*dharmin*) with the words "of the self," the probans (*hetu*), and the property to be proven (*sādhya*) as "being denotable" (*vyavahāryatva*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) briefly restates the position of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*) for the purpose of refuting it, starting with the words "But the self alone... and so forth.

The proponent (pūrvapakṣin) briefly presents his own position as stated in the half-verse. The word "but" (tu), illuminating the distinction of his own view and suggesting its logical consistency, indicates that the position of the opponent (siddhāntin) is to be refuted. Indeed, the opponent [has asserted] the non-establishment of non-perception (*anupalabdhi*).

Anticipating the objection that [the opponent] might say this, he states the meaning of that half-verse in brief with the words "even by the notion of 'I'," and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), there is the inclusion of the continuum of the senses, the vital breaths, cognition, and so on. "He says thus" means that he expresses this matter in two verses. How? By way of refutation (ākṣipan).

By "implication" (ākṣepeṇa), it means that this verbal action is indicated; by this, the particle *nanu* is explained as indicating implication (*ākṣepadyotakatā*). And through this implication, the opponent—whose heart is overcome by the conceit of being skilled in reasoning—is here in disagreement, and due to his own stubborn attachment, he must be addressed with effort.

Indicating that [the opponent's view] is refuted by the proponent— who is devoted to helping others out of a nature of benevolence— he shows that ignorance and doubt are here explained by the very same logic of the "stick and the cake" (*daṇḍāpūpikayā*):
"Now, one cognition has the appearance of a particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), while another..."
That which is called conceptual construction, accompanied by verbal expression, is manifold; yet it is not those two [subject and object]. || 1 ||
(114) Since no eternal perceiver whatsoever appears here [in this cognition],
even this perception of "I" terminates in the body and so forth. (2)

That which has its own nature (*svarūpa*) or its own characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*)— whether by its essential form, by its limiting adjuncts, or by space and time— is in every respect contracted; it cannot be grasped in any way through forms such as identity or difference.
Because it is impossible for many diverse divisions to exist within that single entity.
That form is distinct from everything—
thus [is] the verse that establishes [this].
Neither scripture nor even conceptual construction [applies] because they function only through generality.
Thus, it has been stated that [the object] is characterized solely by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka-jñāna*) arising from its own capacity.

That in which it appears—that is, manifests—or that cognition in which its appearance is its shadow-like form or aspect, is "one" (*ekam*). The singular number is used in the sense of a class (*jāti*), and the word "one" is also used with reference to a collection (*rāśi*); therefore—

In the view of the proponents of formless cognition (*nirākāravāda*), cognitions have the appearance of particular characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*); in the view of the proponents of cognition with form (*sākāravāda*), cognitions possess the forms of particular characteristics. This is the group of non-conceptual [cognitions]. By the word "one," [the author] excludes any distinction within non-conceptual cognition caused by a difference in objects, and—unlike conceptual cognition—establishes it as residing in its own nature, arising from a subordinate genus.

It is said that there is no difference between them. For in that very same object, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) in the form of memory is of one kind, while that in the form of creative imagination (*utprekṣā*) is of another; thus, even though there is no difference in the object of determination (*adhyavasāya*), the diversity belongs solely to the nature of the conceptual construction itself. As for direct experience (*anubhava*), however, it is nothing other than the blue itself.

Because it has that as its appearance, or because it has that as its form; or the word "one" (*eka*) may mean "other," meaning "some [other thing]. However, the middle position was applied by the author of the *Ṭīkā* to the sūtra. "The other" (*param*) means something else, and it occurs at a time subsequent to experience, because all conceptual constructions depend upon it. It is expressed (*abhilapyate*).

By facing toward [the Self], through the abandonment of subjection to both the subject and the object, and by means of the word, [one attains] the sovereignty of consciousness regarding the object. (Page 115)

That by which [an object] is expressed— that is, is reflected upon— by means of bringing it to identity [with the self], through its manifestation, up to the point of its full realization by the subject, is *saṃjalpa*, characterized as internal speech (*āntaraśabda*).
As the venerable Bhartṛhari said:
"When the form [of the word] is unified with the object through the connection 'this is that,' they call that word *abhijalpa*. (Vākyapadīya 2.130).
"It exists together with that"—by this [phrase], at the time of learning the convention consisting of the connection "this is that,"...
By stating that the object conforms to the time of linguistic usage (*vyavahārakāla*), it is shown that its domain is the universal (*sāmānya*).

Furthermore, the reasoning for its manifold nature, which is produced by the distinctions of intermediate sub-species (*avāntarajātibheda*), has been indicated. [The cognition] "that" is memory (*smṛti*);
the synthesis "that is this" is recognition (*pratyabhijñā*); the conformity "this is like that" is poetic fancy (*utprekṣā*); that...

In the inquiry "this is just so," there is exclusion (*vyavaccheda*); such varieties of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) are rooted precisely in the diversity of verbal expression. Although memory, imagination (*utprekṣā*), and the like possess distinct intermediate sub-classifications, they are nonetheless connected to the great universal characterized as conceptual construction; this too is indicated by the term "accompanied by verbal expression. And this is the third [type].

This position has been clarified by the author of the commentary (*vivṛtikṛt*). The word "also" (*api*) is displaced in its sequence. Neither of those two [the object and the cognition] is logically suitable as a relation belonging to some eternal entity denoted by the term "seer" (*draṣṭṛ*), as accepted by others.
For that eternal entity, while these two are appearing here in this pair of cognitions, [the opponent] would have to regard it as the substratum (*ādhāra*) for this pair.

Because even that which is capable of being a manifesting state—though its self-luminosity is admitted—is not manifested; or else, because those two cognitions do not appear here within this substrate, the Self, those two cognitions shine forth quite independently, and not as something residing in any eternal [substrate]. [Objection: But [I perceive] "I [am perceiving] the jar"...
[The opponent argues: "I know" [is like] "the pot"; just as that knowledge exists, so too the Self, possessing those attributes, shines forth as "I.

Thus, non-perception [of the Self] is unestablished. It is replied: First of all, this conceptual construction does not necessarily reveal the actual state of the object. Or, even if it were a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), even so, if there were here a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with "emaciated" and so forth—
"I am thin" and "I know"— it is that very body which appears in this way, being determined as being dependent upon the same causal complex as the cognition. Nevertheless,
(page 116)

"Beyond the body"—the meaning of the word "also" (*api*) here is that even this [body] is merely a continuum of cognition, just as in the case of "a tree in this forest. The author of the *Ṭīkā* first explains the alternative view (*vikalpa*). Having anticipated the position of others—that the nature of non-conceptual [cognition], such as being a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), depends upon that [conceptualization]—[he states that it is so] because of the production of appropriate conceptualizations regarding the blue aspect.

The opponent maintains that non-conceptual [cognition] is a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), whereas it is not a means of valid cognition when it lacks that [non-conceptuality]; for even though the aspect of momentariness—which is inseparable from the blue—is apprehended, it is not a means of valid cognition regarding the aspect of stability and so forth, because it produces conceptualizations that are unsuitable for that [momentary aspect]. And in the *Grahaṇakavākya*, which has been explained, that which is non-conceptual...

This has been recited; therein, the conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) must necessarily be explained first as that which is to be negated. By using the agentive suffix in the term "the conceptualizer" (*vikalpaka*), one superimposes agency independently upon conceptual cognition itself. Thus, by stating that it is "conceptualization," he dispels the opponent's suspicion that there exists some other cognizing subject who gives rise to the conceptual construction.

Because it is invariably concomitant with that [time], it does not deviate from whatever other spatial property is characterized by time throughout the entire duration; such is that which is of the nature of exclusion (*apoha*), consisting merely of a form of cognition, whether internal or external,
or having the form of blue superimposed upon it, its body being produced merely through mental apprehension.

Thus, since it lacks an intrinsic nature (*niḥsvarūpa*), it cannot be supported; since it lacks both succession and simultaneity, it is all-pervasive due to the absence of spatial limitation; since it is eternal, it lacks temporal limitation; and since it is devoid of any restriction of properties (*dharmasaṃkoca*) caused by the impossibility of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), it is determined as a universal (*sāmānya*) that follows after individual instances (*vyakti*).

That very [object] is "mere" (tanmātra) because it is devoid of the reflective awareness of its own specific characteristic (svalakṣaṇa). That in which that [mere object] appears as the apprehended (grāhya) is "conceptual" (vikalpaka); thus its object has been specified. And since its object is of such a nature, this conceptual cognition [engages in] linguistic usage associated with words, that is, being expressed by words.

It endures [the objection], for that [cognition]—even though it is conceptual in nature—is not subject to being expressed in words with respect to its own self, which is of the nature of a particular (svalakṣaṇa) and is grasped through self-awareness (svasaṃvedana), since such expression is impossible therein. As it has been said:
"The self-awareness of pleasure and the like is non-conceptual."
"For the self of pleasure and the like is incapable of being associated [with words], as it does not partake of anything else" (p.
117); rather, [the convention applies] only to the object; and even there, it does not apply to the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) itself, which is restricted by place, time, and specific qualities.

Because it is impossible to establish a convention [for a positive entity], and because it would be useless as it could not persist until the time of practical usage; therefore, it is the shadow of blue— the exclusion of the non-blue— which, being of the nature of apoha, is capable of conceptualization,
suitable for the establishment of convention, and which persists until the time of practical usage.
That is correct. "Simultaneous" (*tātkālikam*) means existing at that very moment and not persisting into another time.

Therefore, it does not touch upon that time of the acquisition of linguistic convention (*saṃketavyutpatti*), which consists of seeing [an object], conceptualizing it, and thus establishing a verbal convention. That which does not touch upon that very [time]—it [is simultaneous].
What possibility is there that it touches upon the time of linguistic usage?

Thus, while the former has a convention that is logically untenable because it is expressed by words, the latter—being clearly manifest as something to be understood—is one whose convention is not functionally required; it is restricted to a specific place and restricted to specific exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*).
Furthermore, because it is incapable of following after other places or other phenomena, [the cognition] does not employ a convention that is not applicable;

if such is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), then that [cognition] is made to appear as that—whether by having its form, by depending on the same causal complex, by being produced from it, or by being manifested by it—and is thus directly perceived. That by which this occurs is "thus" (*tathā*).

Anticipating the objection, "Why has it not been stated explicitly that [the object] has the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) as its domain?", he says: "Even in conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
For even by that [conceptual construction], the particular characteristic is determined (*adhyavasīyate*), because of the worldly activity consisting of engagement, attainment, and so forth.
However, that which is of the nature of direct experience (*anubhava*) becomes [a cognition] of the particular characteristic only when it actually occurs as such.

It imitates the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), and it exists only by so imitating it; for, according to the principle that "it arises through the power of the object," there is the state of being formless (*nirākāratā*).
In that regard, since cognition is by nature merely an experience,
it must possess that specific character by which it is differentiated according to each respective object.

According to this principle, it is said that in its state of having a form (*sākāratā*), this cognition experiences [the object]. And thus, in the *Viniścaya*, it is stated that experience possesses the quality of being an "imitator" (*anukartṛ*) when it imitates the positive and negative concomitance (*anvayavyatireka*) of the appearance of the object within itself. Yet, this is not a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). For this very reason—

(Page 118) Thus, because it is of the nature of experience, that which was implied by its arising from the power of the object (*arthasāmarthya*)— from that very source, the object appears here clearly,
determined by place, time, and form. But if it is said that "knowledge" is thus [defined], [what follows?]

He dispels the doubt that "there is no distinction whatsoever between cognitions such as blue and yellow, and thus it is the Self alone, whose nature is consciousness, that is being described in the Sūtra and the Vṛtti," by saying "and of that" (*tasya ca*). He explains [the phrase] "in many ways" (*bahudhā*) with the words "but of the conceptual construction" (*vikalpasya tu*), meaning "not, however, by way of a difference in objects," because that [conceptual construction], being devoid of an object, is what is to be determined (*adhyavaseya*).
The intention is that even when the object (*viṣaya*) is not different, there is variety due to the very nature of memory, imagination (*utprekṣā*), and so forth.

Thus, he presents the Pātañjala doctrine as being consistent with [his own view]. The phrase "from conceptual construction" (*vikalpāt*) means "from a specific type of conceptual construction" (*vikalpa-viśeṣāt*). This refers to the conceptualization of non-difference within difference, or of difference within non-difference.

That is said to be *vikalpa* (conceptual construction) in that context. *Smṛti* (memory), however, is a modification of the intellect (*buddhi-vṛtti*) whose form consists of the appearance of what was previously experienced.
Thus, it is stated in the Sūtra:
"Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is that which follows upon verbal knowledge and is devoid of a real object" (Yoga Sūtra 1.9).
"Memory is the non-loss of an experienced object" (Yoga Sūtra 1.11).
Now, one might object: "In that case, why have you stated that memory is indeed conceptualization? Anticipating this doubt, he says:
"By the denoter. That is, by means of an internal verbal expression in the form of a universal (*sāmānya*), and not [by the particular].

The definition of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is precisely this: its manifestation therein [in cognition] of an object which, though not a real entity (*avastu-rūpa*), is determined as an object (*artha*) by way of persistence; wherein there is a connection through a variegated blending (*śabalīkaraṇa*)—an entry into a single cognition—that cannot be designated by way of its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*).

The intended meaning is that the phrase "following upon the cognition of a word" (*śabdajñānānupātī*) is the definition of a specific type of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), which is synonymous with *kalpanā*. The expression "already before" (*prāgeva*) means prior to the indication of the object to be defined. Now, one might ask: if this is the distinction between conceptual construction and direct experience (*anubhava*), then from what source does both share the single nature of being cognition? To this, he says:
"Both are thus" means in this manner [they are] of the nature of consciousness (*bodharūpa*). This point will be stated later by the proponent (*siddhāntin*) while restating my own position:
"Vision is indeed self-luminous... (1.18).

Regarding the term "distinct" (*bhinnam*): in both cases, the definition of a self (*ātman*) as being endowed with properties such as permanence and so forth—which is accepted by others—does not exist. thus, "of the second" refers to the knower, who is distinct from knowledge, by means of the phrase "his own experience."

He states the possibility of its being an object of perception: "of that" (tasya) refers to the non-perception of the self (ātman); or, the interpretation of the commentary is that "of that" (tasya) refers to the non-perception of both [self and world] as being connected with something else. Regarding the word *jñeya* (knowable), it does not here denote that which is of the nature of a single insentient entity, because the stream of cognition (*jñāna-saṃtāna*) lacks insentience. "It has been explained by its own throat" means that this should be understood thus in those respective commentaries (*vṛtti*) and sub-commentaries (*ṭīkā*) on the Sūtras. Now, if you do not ascertain [the self] as distinct [from the body], then a spatially limited non-perception would not lead to the conclusion of its universal absence; therefore, this [non-perception] is merely the cessation of the perception of the self.
One who employs a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) refutes another; yet that [cognition] exists even with respect to remote objects, and one might suspect that they do not exist at all.

Having raised this doubt, the author explains the statement "by people" (*loka*) found in the verse by interpreting it as "by all cognizers" (*sarvapramātṛbhiḥ*), and states the reason for this in the phrase "by those of the same class" (*sajātīyaiḥ*). The reason for that [latter point] is "all worldly transaction" (*sarvavyavahāra*).

For otherwise, even blue might appear as non-blue to someone; consequently, even the conventional usage of the absence of identity would not be established, and the distinction between existence and non-existence would be utterly destroyed—this is the intended meaning. As it has been said: "The very cessation of perception [is the proof]."

Non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) is the means of proving non-existence, for the purpose of showing the impossibility of the existence of this object which possesses all its causal conditions. In that regard, since one who perceives only the immediate range (*arvāgdarśana*) employs the cessation of their own direct perception as a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it is logical to negate only that which is capable of being apprehended by it; however, this does not apply to the self (*ātman*).

The meaning indicated by the Sūtra has been clarified according to its stated characteristics; that is to say, the ultimate reality is the independent agency of the knowing subject, which—because it is beginninglessly established—is incapable of being limited by space, time, or form, and thus does not depend on the operation of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Now, one might object: in the word *ahaṃ-pratyaya* (the notion of "I"), the inclusion of the qualification "expressible" (*sābhilāpa*) [is necessary].

Regarding the question "For what purpose [is this] in the commentary?", he says: "It is accompanied by verbal expression. Just as even in a non-conceptual [cognition], the word "blue" is employed in the phrase "this is the experience of blue" to determine the nature of the object, someone might imagine that the word "I" is likewise employed there; such a person is refuted by the term *avasāyinī* ("determinative") in the Sūtra.

The meaning of that very [term] has been explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by means of a word accompanied by an expression (*sābhilāpa-pada*). Furthermore, by demonstrating the weakness of the proof (*pramāṇa*) that establishes the self as it is defined by the proponent (*siddhāntin*), the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*) has revealed the strength of his own position. The quality of being habitually so (*tācchīlya*) is expressed by the suffixal portion (*pratyaya-bhāga*) [of the term] *avasyati-tacchīla*.

By stating that [the cognition] culminates in the independence from signs (*nimitta*), one defines the absence of the nature of a determination (*adhyavasāya*) that conforms to experience; thus, "I who was yesterday...

It has been stated that the ascertainment of the nature of the stable substratum of qualities—through such cognitions as "I am that very same person this morning, yet [my] knowledge and so forth [are not the same]"—is not merely a mental construction (*kalpanā*). Furthermore, in the commentary (*vṛtti*), by the use of the word "together" (*saha*), the non-deviation of the expression of the cognition of "I" (*ahampratīti*) is demonstrated; thus it should be explained. For this very reason:

He says: "By way of conceptualization. The intention of the author of the *Ṭīkā* is that [the opponent] must be made to understand that "my self indeed appears in experience" solely for the sake of accepting its appearance as common to other worldly cognizers. Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: there is no self here endowed with characteristics such as eternity, because it is not perceived despite meeting the conditions for perception. 1, 2.
All experiences of objects such as jars and the like are indeed perishable upon arising. Furthermore, memory is observed to follow after experience; otherwise, it might occur anywhere at random.
Nor does memory arise merely from the occurrence of an experience, for what was seen by Caitra is not remembered by Maitra.

Therefore, the view of the opponent, the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntin*), is that this experience, although sublated by the outward-turned body, must be understood as unsublated when viewed from the inward-turned perspective. (122) If there were no stable self as the subject of experience, whose nature is inward-turned toward that experience, how could memory— which apprehends a specific object by means of accepting the original experience— come to be once that experience has perished?

It might be so. And since this memory exists, one must conclude that it was produced by that [prior experience]—this is the meaning of the verse, should another person argue thus. The author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) demonstrates that [memory] conforms to that [original experience]. "Even then" means "at the time of memory," that is, while it has the nature of memory. If someone were to say: "The experience of the object itself, having a past object..."

Memory is said to be distinct [from perception]; why is this? Is it because memory accepts its object by its own nature, despite being opposed to direct experience (*anubhava*)? In response to that, he first refutes the notion that memory has the nature of direct experience with the words "upon the destruction of the experience," and he harmonizes the statement of the Sūtra with the word "object" (*artha*). This means that memory arises from a latent impression produced by a prior experience, whereas direct experience does not arise from a latent impression produced by another experience. Therefore, since their causes are different, they are distinct. Furthermore, he shows that memory is not direct experience because it lacks the capacity to produce an effect: "And because it does not produce an effect. This means that memory does not produce an effect such as the attainment of heaven or liberation, which direct experience does. Therefore, it is established that memory is not direct experience. Now, he explains how memory is distinct from direct experience through its specific characteristics: "And because it is preceded by a desire for the object. This means that memory arises preceded by a desire for the object previously experienced, whereas direct experience does not arise preceded by a desire for the object previously experienced. Therefore, since their modes of arising are different, they are distinct. Furthermore, he shows that memory is not direct experience because it lacks the capacity to produce a new cognition: "And because it does not produce a new cognition. This means that memory does not produce a new cognition regarding the object, which direct experience does. Therefore, it is established that memory is not direct experience. Now, he concludes by summarizing the proof of their distinction: "Thus, memory is established as having a different nature from direct experience. This means that through these various reasons, it is proven that memory is distinct from direct experience. Therefore, the distinction between them is firmly established. Now, he anticipates an objection: "But if memory is not direct experience, then how can one say 'I remember'? He answers this: "The expression 'I remember' is based on the similarity of the mental state. This means that although memory is not direct experience, the expression "I remember" is used because the mental state of memory resembles the mental state of direct experience. Therefore, there is no contradiction. Now, he shows that memory is not direct experience because it lacks the capacity to produce a new latent impression: "And because it does not produce a new latent impression. This means that memory does not produce a new latent impression, which direct experience does. Therefore, it is established that memory is not direct experience. Now, he concludes the entire section: "Thus, the distinction between direct experience and memory is proven. This means that through all these arguments, the difference between direct experience and memory is firmly established. Therefore, one should understand that memory is a distinct category of knowledge. (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the proximity of the object. In this context, there is utility [of the object] both when it exists by way of being a generator and when it does not exist by way of being an object. "Present" (*saṃnihita*) means that even though it is concealed—as in the Sāṃkhya system—it has attained the status of an object through its own independence; that is to say, it is present.
"Direct perception" (*sākṣātkāra*) means non-conceptual (*avikalpaka*). For a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), on the other hand, does not [perceive] the object directly.
He accepts [this], yet says "it is stated by way of superimposition" (adhyāropeṇa). He expresses this with the words "or rather" (apivā).

[The phrase] "by way of being experienced" means that this conceptual construction (vikalpa) might either be something currently undergoing experience, or it might itself be of the nature of experience; however, it is not [defined] by its having been previously experienced, nor by the recollection of a prior experience as "that very thing."

This indeed is the specific nature of memory (*smṛti*). Consequently, if there were an experience (*anubhava*) at the moment of time pervaded by memory, then memory would not be its pervader; this is because one perceives the cognition "this [experience] contradicts that [memory]. And there is a contradiction because the appropriation of an object by one's own face and by another's face are mutually exclusive.
And because of this identity between the cognition of "this-ness" and the cognition of "that-ness," the following formal argument follows: at the time of recollection,
[the object] does not exist as something being perceived.

The object [of perception] is that which is the objective referent (*viṣaya*) of the cognition "this" (*iti-pratyaya*). For existence (*astitva*), as it is perceived in an object, is pervaded by being the objective referent of the cognition "this"; this perception is the opposite of that [non-existence]. Now, one might object:
apart from memory whose object is a destroyed thing, elsewhere—[is there not the cognition] "this"?

[Objection: An inference [is invalid] if it contradicts other means of valid cognition, such as direct perception. [Reply: Not so. For everything that is being remembered is precisely what was previously experienced. And since that [experience] has perished due to momentariness, what use is there for the existence of another moment? Or, let the object—such as a jar—be stable and unperished, as the Sāṃkhyas maintain.

By means of the two particles "satyapi vā" (even though it exists), he shows that this [memory] is not capable of attaining objectivity independently, because it produces the presentation of the momentary destruction of what was previously present. He says "because of the absence of experience" (*anubhavābhāvāt*) to show that this is not the ultimate truth, but rather a provisional argument (*abhyupagamya-vāda*), since memory does not possess the nature of direct experience (*anubhava*).
The meaning is "because of its existence. "By way of being an object of experience" means by way of being an independent object within the cognition of memory.
Regarding the independent objecthood of a past thing existing at another time, there are three possibilities:
either the cognition itself is stable, and it acquires the form of that object or the appearance of that object through the impact of the object upon it.

It does not abandon [its object] even when the object has disappeared or when another object has appeared. Thus, there is the direct perception of past and present objects; furthermore, there is also that capacity for a specific causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) among present entities, which projects a continuous succession of other causal efficiencies.

Because of its absolute purity, it becomes directly realized; thus, even though its object is future, there is first the cognition of the omniscient one—this is one way. Furthermore, even when the blue object has perished, the experience whose object was blue possesses a consciousness that, by virtue of being the immediately preceding condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), does not abandon its status as a direct realization of blue.
However, due to the proximity of yellow, it also initiates a cognition whose object is yellow, though that object is permeated by a fitness for a continuous stream of its own causal efficacy;
this is the case with other cognitions as well—this is the second [view]. Both of these have been stated in the *Ṭīkā*:
"At that time, even when a process is underway, it is indeed the previous experience [that acts as the cause]. And this applies when there is a stable continuity of the stream.

This is the word "prabandha" (continuity). Thus, there are always two ways regarding the Omniscient One: for one who desires to know the Omniscient One, whatever he wishes to see at whatever time, that very thing appears to him at that very time as something previously unknown through inference.

The third [type of cognition] is that which knows by virtue of the purity of its manifestation (*pratibhāna*), like a cognition whose object has passed away.
