In all three of these modes of apprehension, because there is an experience through independent appropriation of the object, that nature of memory (*smṛti*) which produces a distinction [from other cognitions] is described as being "by way of a previous experience."

If there were no non-forgetting, no non-deprivation, and no manifestation as having been experienced of the object already experienced through the acquisition of the sense-object, then that very [memory] would be contradicted. It lacks an object. Therefore, this memory does not consist of the nature of a specific experience (*anubhava*); yet, it strives to depend upon that experience. However, it is not logical to say that only the outward-turned aspect occupied with the object has not perished.

Because it would follow that there is an absence of memory. For it follows that the experience of an experience—which is self-cognizing and inward-turned—is not lost. Indeed, if memory were to arise without any connection whatsoever [to that original experience], then memory would arise for Maitra even regarding what was seen by Caitra, since there would be no cause for such restriction; or else, it would be just like that [unrestricted case].
Even when [the object] has been seen by oneself, [the doubt] would not arise because that which must be relied upon in every respect has been destroyed. It is said:

there is a restriction; it must necessarily exist in some undestroyed form that follows from it. Now, is the cognition of an experience a cognition in the form of an experience, like the cognition of a Naiyāyika?
[The opponent claims that] its nature is another cognition. [The author] says "no," for it is of the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvidrūpa*) and inward-turned (*antarmukha*).
The state of being engaged with an object (*arthavyāpṛtatā*) or being outward-turned (*bahirmukhatva*) consists precisely in the appearance of an object.
"Outward" (*bahiḥ*) refers to that whose primary form—characterized by luminosity—is directed toward an object distinct from its own nature.
It is so. Of the intellect’s cognition of blue, that very [cognition] is the grasper; therefore, it is inward-facing (*antarmukhā*) within the self, which is of the nature of knowledge.

"Inward" (*antar*) means its face—that is, its luminosity—exists in a non-distinct form. The two *ca*s (conjunctions) indicate the simultaneity of these two attributes. Now, let it be granted for now that the inward-facing aspect is the persisting factor.

But what is established for the proponent (siddhāntin)? He says: "And [the Self] is inward-turned. This is because, according to the logic that will be stated later, when there is no immersion in objects, qualities, space, or time, its omnipresence and eternity are established. || 3 ||

(Page 125) Having thus presented the tenable position of the proponent (*siddhāntin*), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) now questions the proponent with the intention that he himself will state the manner of refuting this [position].

by what?

The aspect of the manifestation as blue must be relied upon, and not the aspect of inward-turned self-luminosity;

for if that [self-luminous aspect] were incapable of presenting a specific object, it would follow that there would be no distinction between the recollection of blue and non-blue, nor between different subjects and a single subject. Whether due to lack of proximity, or due to the absence of sensory operation— as indicated by the word "etcetera" (ādi)— or due to the absence of the purity of vision, meditative concentration, and so forth, which are necessary for omniscience as will be explained later, an object appears as if it were already destroyed; for as long as that causal complex (sāmagrī) described above is absent, there occurs [only] that which consists in the experience of blue.

The nature of direct perception (*darśana*) has been lost. And that very [perception], being solitary and disregarding the application of uninterrupted pure consciousness alone, becomes the support, the gateway, and the means for that memory which attains the object of an experienced thing— even though a pure, inward-turned self-awareness devoid of objects is admitted to exist within the Self.

The meaning of the introduction to the two sūtras is as follows: "In what manner?"—there is no such manner by which it could exist; therefore, it simply would not be. With the intention that the proponent of the Self (ātmavādī) remained silent, seeing that consciousness might be established as inward-turned (*antarmukha*) without the need for memory, [the author] addresses him with the words "And therefore" (*tataśca*).

Worldly linguistic usage must necessarily be justified; and how could that be possible without memory? Furthermore, you have begun to establish even the linguistic usage of the self by means of memory—memory which conforms to that [usage].
"How could it be that the self would not be eternal if...

becomes awakened by means of the awakening of those very impressions produced by such a vision; then,

When that internal cause—appropriation (*upādāna*), characterized by self-awareness and inward-turned cognition—is present as the Self, memory arises in the form of an effect; and because it appears as similar to the original experience, its possession of an object consists solely in this much.
From experience—which takes the form of intense practice, interest, and firm conviction—there arises within the Self a latent impression (*vāsanā*).

Having stated the opponent's position—that there is a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), its awakening occurs through the perception of something similar and so forth, and from that arises memory—the author says "And thus" (*evaṃ ca*) in order to refute it. What is meant is this: the objective content (*saviṣayatā*) must be obtained by memory precisely from the external-facing aspect of the cognition; and that [objective content] cannot logically belong to what has perished.

Nor can it be [memory] from the aspect of inwardness that has not perished; nor is it tenable for the aspect of outwardness to be memory as long as it has not perished, for it has been stated that in such a case it would be nothing but experience (*anubhava*). Therefore, one must accept that this aspect of outwardness, although perished, remains as if it were not perished. And how can that which is perished become unperished, if...
There would be no capacity to produce another cognition that imitates it—that is, one similar to it.

That very [capacity] is its non-destruction even though it has perished. For there is the worldly usage: "Droṇācārya lives, for he has Aśvatthāman as his son. What remains is an imitation of his in the form of memory; such is this state of similarity.

Primarily, the nature of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) consists in its being a mental formation; however, figuratively, even the capacity for its production is a latent impression. To that extent, it is "unawakened" (*aprabuddha*); whereas the state of being engaged in producing that [memory] is the "awakened" (*prabuddha*) latent impression. Alternatively, while it is in the process of seeking to awaken, it is still unawakened; but once awakened, the latent impression is nothing other than the memory itself.

"Because it consists in the imitation of experience. Since the continuity of the non-interruption [of consciousness] is established through its subsistence in the identity with the form of the object, for what lack of logical necessity is this non-interruption postulated? This is because from the experience of blue—which is of the nature of the manifestation of blue—and from the immediately preceding cognition (*samanantara-pratyaya*), as well as from yellow...
A moment of cognition arising from an object, although it consists of the manifestation of blue, appears as such because of its similarity [to that object];
however, due to the predominance of a yellow object, it does not appear in that way, owing to ignorance, visual defects, and so forth.

Or [it may be] due to its greatness (*māhātmya*). For even in self-luminous consciousness, that which exists does not necessarily have to appear; for instance, aspects such as momentariness do not manifest. However, upon the cessation of ignorance and the like, knowledge of previous births arises through the purification resulting from the direct realization of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), as stated in *Yogasūtra* 3.18.

Thus, from the cognition of yellow, the cognition of green arises; although it possesses the power to manifest blue, yellow, and green, it is the manifestation of green alone. According to the reasoning already stated, this sequence continues until something related to the blue—whether by way of belonging to its class, being similar to it, or being its opposite—becomes visible.

Then, from such a perception—which is characterized by that [object] and arises as a perception connected [to it]—there arises, acting as an immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*), a cognition that does not depend on any external object whatsoever; this cognition imitates the prior cognition of blue. This awakened latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is called "recollection" (*smaraṇa*).

As it has been said: "A powerful experience deposits a seed for memory; from a subsequent perception of a similar kind, its awakening occurs. And this awakening is indeed memory itself. For it has been stated by the venerable Teacher that a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) is nothing more than a residual trace of imitation. Therefore, when they raise the doubt—that [memory] does not arise from such a perception—[it is refuted].
The awakening of this latent impression (*saṃskāra*) occurs nowhere: it cannot reside in the preceding cognition, for that has perished;

nor can it reside in the succeeding cognition, because when a cognition of yellow follows a cognition of blue without an intermediate consciousness being perceived, there is no awakening of the latent impression of blue. Thus they argue.

The claim that the conceptualization of blue (*nīlavikalpa*), produced by the impressions of an unawakened mind, brings about memory through the perception of such a blue object—that is simply false, because it leads to the fallacy of mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) and other logical defects. For the conceptualization of blue arises from the recollection of verbal expression, that [recollection] in turn from the recollection of linguistic convention (*saṃketa*), and that [convention] from the recollection of the object "blue"; thus, there is a headlong plunge into a regressus ad infinitum. This is the second [point].

Even if one were to assume that such a perception occurs where there is the awakening of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), and from that arises the recollection of the object "blue," then since recollection is of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it must be admitted that it is preceded by the recollection of linguistic conventions (*abhilāpa-saṃketa*).
Since the same would apply there as well, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*); let this matter rest for now, for this will be analyzed atom by atom later on.

This will be examined later. For now, it is established that memory is of the nature of imitation; and since it imitates a prior perception up to the point of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), it is not of the nature of illuminating an object, nor is it accompanied by verbal expression (*sābhilāpā*).

"This other [substance] imitates that," is the opinion of the feet of the Supreme Guru. But where has such imitation been observed in something unstable and lacking a continuous flow? For it is observed that sesame seeds, being stable, can emulate the fragrance of the *mālatī* flower. He replies: "Even birch bark," because its constituent parts are delicate.

The intended meaning of the word "api" (also) is that [the birch bark] perishes through the sequence of the splitting of its constituent parts, the separation caused by action, and the destruction of conjunction,
while another [birch bark] arises; yet,
having been rolled up for a long time, when it is subsequently unrolled, it returns again to its former configuration, and it is not immutable (*kūṭastha*).
It is eternal, yet its eternity consists in the continuity of its stream (*saṃtāna-nityatā*). It stands firm like a peak (*kūṭa*) in the form of a mass; nothing of it moves.
It stands firm as a summit (*kūṭa*) that is nowhere transgressible; it cannot be altered by anyone.
It stands firm even amidst a universal conflagration when causes of destruction descend, and even in a deceptive guise (*kūṭa*), which is of the nature of concealment.

Because it remains as it is when an action is performed and does not undergo change, it is called "unchangingly eternal" (*kūṭastha-nitya*) by virtue of its immovable nature. This is what is meant: first of all, no purpose for refinement (*saṃskāra*) is admitted by those who maintain the doctrine of permanent entities regarding sesame seeds; for there is indeed a subtle fragrance of nectar [in them].

In that case, it is perceived through conjunction-inherence (*saṃyuktasamavāya*), just as [fragrance] is perceived in water even though the water itself is odorless. Furthermore, no mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) should be postulated here; for that exists only in the self, whereas velocity (*vega*) and elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*) have active objects as their domain—how then could there be any impression (*saṃskāra*) in sesame seeds? Thus, the claim that "a lasting impression arises in sesame and the like" is simply false.

Furthermore, momentum (*vega*) is indeed observed in a turbulent river and in arrows and the like; it is invariably concomitant with the destruction of the constituent parts—which is brought about by the action of the speed of the wind—and it consists of a distinct substance.
Likewise, elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*) is observed in birch bark. In the same way, [momentum] exists as a positive entity within the continuum of cognition (*jñāna-santāna*).

It will come to pass; for in reality, *saṃskāra* is indeed an imitation (*anukaraṇa*). Even in the case of an arrow, it is an imitation of activity produced by effort. Therefore, the ultimate nature of *saṃskāra* is precisely its quality as a "restorer of the original state" (*sthitasthāpaka*), because it establishes the previously existing form.

However, velocity (*vega*) is mentioned separately because of its specific quality of establishing that same form in another location; whereas mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) does not consist in the imitation of activity, and elasticity (*sthitasthāpaka*) likewise [does not].

The phrase "conforming to the arrangement" (saṃniveśānukāra) means, in reality, that imitation itself is for the purpose of mental impression (saṃskāra). And in that regard, even a trace of eternity has no utility. Whatever is established by just as much [evidence] does not postulate anything more than that, just as a sprout [is produced] by a seed and so forth; and thus says the Smṛti: "by means of mental impression. For there is [no basis for] postulating something additional.

The reason [for this] is that the fallacy of being unestablished (*asiddhatva*) would persist by that much alone; otherwise, the postulation of further [causes] would not cease. And the cessation of such postulation is observed to be pervaded [by the absence of unestablished reasons], whereas here, something contrary to that is perceived. || 5 ||

Now, since *saṃskāra* is a quality (*guṇa*) consisting of a property (*dharma*), it cannot be independent; therefore, it must have a substratum (*dharmin*). If it is argued that the continuum of cognition (*jñānasaṃtāna*) itself is its substratum, we reply: no, for the continuum is not something other than the individual cognitions. Thus, if it is said that the *saṃskāra* resides in the cognitions themselves, that is incorrect.
For it is not logical that the nature of experience should reside in one place, the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in another, and the memory (*sm�ti*) in yet another;

for such a state of affairs is never observed in the case of well-known distinctions between subjects such as Caitra and Maitra. Therefore, the non-difference between experience and the latent impression must be established. And since that [non-difference] is not perceived in its own form, therefore...
Because they possess distinct characteristics, that [recognition] is established precisely through the non-difference of the substratum, characterized by inherence in a single object.

And since the non-difference between experience and its latent impression (saṃskāra) is established by way of their common substratum, the recognition of pleasure and so forth is likewise established; for in every instance of recognition, it is the very same "I" who was happy through the experience of pleasure.

"I existed," "that very same [self] I desire," "being in pain I hate," and "possessed by desire and hatred, I strive to grasp or to abandon"— since such [notions] have memory as their essence, for this very reason, in the *Avatāriṇī*, which is a concise commentary, the nature of mental formations (*saṃskāra*) as a phenomenon (*dharmatva*) [is established].

It has been explained that [the self] is not distinct from pleasure and so forth. Therefore, anticipating the view of the proponent of the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣavādin*)— that the substratum (*āśraya*) of the formations (*saṃskāra*) is one, and because it is one, it is stable, and that very thing is the self— he briefly explains the verse while relying upon the meaning of the preceding verse itself, beginning with "In this way" (*tadevam*).

Since the self is eternal, therefore, just as it does not function in memory even when its latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) have not arisen, so too it would not function even when its latent impressions have arisen. (Page 131)

Because its essential nature is not different even in the slightest degree. Indeed, distinction consists only in the impression (*saṃskāra*), or if there were an absence of difference [between the soul and the impression] caused by that [impression], the soul would be impermanent due to the loss of its prior nature. But if [the impression] were distinct, it would have no effect whatsoever on the soul. Therefore, what is the use of a substratum for the impression, which is of no utility in producing memory?

The word "only" (*mātra*) [is used]. Here, both are indeed of the nature of conceptual construction (*kalpanā*); however, with the intention that one is designated as the "standard of comparison" (*upamāna*) in the Sūtra simply because it was previously established, he says: "This is the seer and the rememberer.
Therefore, even though the properties (*dharma*) are distinct, there is no difference in their essential nature (*svarūpa*).
If memory were established through mental impressions (saṃskāra), then the rememberer would be merely a conceptual construct, like the seer [of a dream]. || 6 ||

Therefore, even though conditioned factors (*saṃskāra*) and other qualities exist as distinct from the self, and even though inherence (*samavāya*) exists as something distinct, there is no difference in that self from its own nature—that is, from its prior form—due to the fact that qualities such as conditioning have not arisen therein. For if there were a difference, there would be impermanence. Consequently, [the change] arises solely from the conditioning factors and so forth.

Memory is established by the reasoning previously stated. The conventional distinction between the non-difference and difference of the cognizer is based on the presence or absence of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*); those two, moreover, are produced by the presence or absence of the relationship between material cause and effect. As for that which appears as "I am the rememberer," therein [the following applies]:

It is merely the cognition of "I"; the self does not exist, because it is momentary and unstable. If the object to be cognized by that [cognition]—namely, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)—appears when brought within the range of experience, then it too is indeed unstable. Or, if it is the conceptualizable [object], whether it be the body or the continuum (*saṃtāna*), even so, there is no cognizer whatsoever distinct from the cognized and the cognition.

It shines forth in the form of the knower and the seer. Therefore, the phrase "in [the case of] distinct [entities]" is a sūtra that indicates the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) while also serving the purpose of the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). Regarding this, the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) first explains it according to the former aspect, beginning with "pleasure, pain," and so on. For indeed, attributes such as pleasure and the like are observed to be connected [to a single subject].
And since they are distinct, one must state that their basis is one;

for that very reason, the author of the *Ṭīkā* explains: "there would be no mutual concomitance. Then, explaining it for the sake of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), he says: "of that which is not divided by distinct attributes," which means "that which has not yet acquired entry into them. This...
In the commentary, this is explained by means of the plural form "by these [factors]";
for if there were identity with one among distinct things, how could there be plurality? Or, if there were identity with many, how could that which is non-distinct [be so]?

The intention is: "How can there be oneness? That specific benefit of pleasure and so forth, produced by that [oneness], which arises from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and is characterized by rebirth (*pratisandhi*), is not utilized by this self (*ātman*); the meaning is that it is not employed therein.
Or, because it is produced by the qualities (*guṇa*), it is utilized—that is, accepted. Thus...

In the reconnection [of consciousness] following pleasure and so forth, this [self] has no utility whatsoever. Not only is it not distinguished by pleasure and the like, nor even by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) which performs that reconnection, but it is also not made distinct by that which is the root of the impression—namely, its nature as experience (*anubhava*). Thus, nothing specific has been effected for it.

He explains how this [self] could produce memory by saying, "And of that which is without distinction. By this, he interprets the passage from the *Vṛtti*—namely, "because it is not active in memory"—as having the genitive ending (*ātmanaḥ*) functioning as an adjective for the self, containing within it a conjunction of reasons. Because it is undifferentiated, meaning because no distinctions have arisen, the self [is not active] in the act of recollection.
And because application (*prayoga*) is not occupied with memory...
[the mind] is that which rests upon the body and so forth (2.2).

With the intention that the meaning here is precisely that found in this [sūtra], the commentary (*vṛtti*) beginning with "like the seer" (*draṣṭṛvat*) is not [included] in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*).

This has been explained. Thus, this is the summary: that which, even if imagined, is not possible for the sake of establishing something, cannot be postulated for its establishment—just as a sky-flower cannot be postulated for the sake of establishing a sprout. And likewise, there is no eternal self for the sake of establishing memory and recognition. For in this case, the principle governing imagination is as follows:

It is pervasive; otherwise, it would not cease. And if that which is incapable of producing it is postulated for its sake, then its pervasion would be lost; thus, the postulation for its sake is pervaded by the state of being capable of producing it. Since that pervader is not perceived here, this is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Thus he says:
What effect do rain and sun have upon the sky? Their fruit is found in leather.
If the self were like leather, it would be impermanent; if it were like the sky, it would be as non-existent as nothing.
Thus:
"When X exists, Y necessarily occurs; therefore, to postulate anything other than that [X] as the cause is futile. (Page 133)
Because that [infinite regress] would be the cause [of it], there would be an infinite regress of causes in every case.
And so forth. || 6 ||
Having stated that "thus, since the self as a substratum (*dharmin*) does not exist at all, where could sovereignty be established through the presentation of reasons?",
he proceeds to refute the reason previously stated— namely, "because of the conjunction with knowledge and action"—
by showing that for the opponent, knowledge itself is untenable, whether it be characterized by insentience (*jaḍatva*) or non-insentience (*ajaḍatva*).
Two verses are presented in order to establish a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), because from the reversal of that reductio one's own position is obtained.
For instance, by whatever reasoning the self (*ātman*) is eternal, for that same reason cognition (*jñāna*) must also be eternal; why then is it not?
If it were eternal, how could it be "that" [i.e., momentary]? Therefore, there is a mutual contradiction between the nature of the subject (*dharmin*) and the nature of the reason (*hetu*).

And its establishment is through the contradiction of the relationship between substratum and superstratum. Regarding that, the author briefly introduces what is stated in the aphorism—that for the proponent, cognition in the form of a non-inert entity is not tenable—by the words "of the self" (*ātmanaḥ*). In the aphorism, the term "impermanent" (*anityam*) is employed primarily, though other attributes are also implied.
With the intention of pointing out those factors that produce distinctness, he speaks generally of "the conceptualization of duality.

Since both the self (*ātman*) is of the nature of consciousness (*cit*) and knowledge (*jñāna*) is also [of that nature], that conceptualization which has been made by means of duality, otherness, the characteristics of permanence and impermanence, and the relationship between property and its substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*), is [what is meant].
This [position] is untenable because, lacking a foundation in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it does not establish the reality of things. Regarding this matter, he says:
"If cognition is of the nature of consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*), then like the self (*ātman*), why is it not eternal?
Or, if it is insentient (*jaḍa*), how can it have the capacity to illuminate objects? (7)
The word "ca" (and) adds another logical inconsistency against the proponent of the doctrine:
if the nature of consciousness, like that of the self, were innate, then would it be impermanent? It is certainly not impermanent, just like the self;
for being of the nature of consciousness—which is characterized by self-luminosity—is incompatible with being an object of cognition (*vedyarūpatva*).

Because of the contradiction between autonomy and heteronomy, the state of being illuminated by another is incompatible with self-luminosity; furthermore, since spatial and temporal connection is pervaded by the quality of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*), it is through the perception of self-luminosity—which is the opposite of that which pervades [the former]—that this is established in knowledge (p.

There is a negation of a connection with space and time that is pervaded by contradiction. Indeed, being connected with space and time is itself impermanence. For that which occurs invariably—that is, it does not fail to occur under any circumstances—is permanent. And that which occurs in some place and at some time does not occur in other places and at other times; thus, it is not an invariable occurrence.

Even when there is a conjunction with all space and time, in reality, there is no such conjunction. For if its own nature is not pervaded by that space or by that time, then how could it be said to be "there" or "then"? If you argue that it is "covered," then for one who is completely surrounded by that [space], how could it be supported by something else? For that which is surrounded is indeed obstructed; that...

How could it endure the support of others? For that very reason, everything such as "what is the single whole among the many parts? is untenable. Thus, if cognition is of the nature of consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*), then since it too would be eternal and all-pervading, the reason—"because it is the cause of cognition"—is unestablished in its own nature (*svarūpāsiddha*) with respect to another self. If, on the other hand, it is insentient (*jaḍa*), then...

The meaning of the sūtra is: how can that [Self] have the nature of luminosity with respect to an object? Now, "consciousness" (cit) is said to be knowledge; however, for the Vaiśeṣikas and others, that is not the inherent nature of the Self, for it is merely an attribute (dharma) of it.
Therefore, how can it be stated: "Just as there is eternality in the Self's having consciousness as its nature," and so forth?

Anticipating the objection that this might also apply to cognition (*jñāna*), he says: "Because it lacks the property of being illuminated by another. Here, cognition is said to be the manifestation of blue and so forth; it is an occasional attribute produced by the contact of the self with the mind and other factors.
When it does not exist due to the absence of its own causes, then the self is not manifest as the manifestation of blue and so forth.

In states such as deep sleep, fainting, dissolution, and liberation, although it is by its own nature of the essence of light, it is called "insentient" (jaḍa). However, its true form is indeed self-luminous; it is not like the category of insentient forms such as space, time, and direction, for if it were, it would follow—consequentially—that liberation would not be a human goal, just as in the case of the Śūnyavādin.
For this very reason, the Naiyāyikas beginning with the teacher Bhāsarvajña accepted exactly this;

the possession of eternal knowledge and bliss by the self is established in the *Nyāyabhūṣaṇa*. Therefore, just as the self is luminous by nature, it is not impermanent but rather eternal, and so it is in that same manner.

Even the cognition of blue, which has the nature of the manifestation of blue, is it impermanent? No, it is not impermanent; it is indeed eternal. Thus, the example is established. Or rather, let this be the case for the Vaiśeṣikas, who [assert] the insentience—
Intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is the self (*ātman*); what is the use of this misplaced attachment? For it is the proponents of the self (*ātmavādin*) who must be questioned by me;
others here, who maintain that the self is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), will be refuted by means of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*).
Regarding the "example" (*dṛṣṭānta*), the mention of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*) is not employed here, as this applies to every example.

Because its life-breath is similarity (*sādharmya*). Even when applied by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*)—as in "if it were of the nature of consciousness like the self"—equality is stated with respect to the property to be negated, namely permanence, by the statement "sound is non-eternal, like space, etc. And thus, since the property to be negated has become subordinate (*guṇībhūta*), there is no employment of this [dissimilar instance] in the commentary (*vṛtti*).
[The reason] is established. For it is not the case that "sound is impermanent because it is produced, like space";

rather, [the intended meaning is] "space is eternal and unproduced, like [the nature of sound]," or else, "whatever is not impermanent is also not produced, like space," or else, "because it is unproduced, sound is eternal, like space. Precisely for that reason...
This example, occurring in the context of the negative concomitance (*vyatireka*), functions precisely through similarity (*sādharmya*).

For in all cases, the ultimate reality of the meanings of "like" (*iva*) and "equal to" (*tulya*) is indeed similarity alone. Therefore, it is not employed in the context of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*);
rather, it is used specifically to express that the similarity itself culminates in the negative concomitance.

This is designated as a counter-example (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*). Therefore, the interpretation of this sūtra is as follows: by means of the interrogative particle *kim* used with a rhetorical intonation (*kāku*), a negation is expressed; that is to say, "Is it non-eternal like the self? meaning "It is not non-eternal like the self. Alternatively, by the word *kim*, there is the quality of being subject to questioning regarding the influence of its logical inconsistency (*anupapatti-prabhāva-paryanuyojya-dharmatvam*).
It is explained as follows: just as one might ask whether the self is impermanent, so too one might ask whether cognition is impermanent;

since the property of impermanence is untenable in both cases, this is merely a formal objection (*paryanuyoga*). Alternatively, the negative particle *a-* may have its full force even in a simple negation (*prasajya-pratiṣedha*), as in the rule *akartari*.

This is an *asamartha-samāsa* (irregular compound) supported by the gender [of the word] derived from the inclusion of the term *kāraka*. Consequently, there is equality with that which is to be negated:

"Why does it not exist eternally like the Self (*ātman*)? Furthermore, its nature as consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*) is evident. One should pay attention to this application in various instances. And thus the commentary (*vṛtti*) says: "like the Self."

Regarding the consequence of [the self's] being eternal and so forth: the followers of Jaimini (Jaiminīyas) consider the person to be of the very nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*), though distinct from states such as pleasure; whereas the Sāṃkhyas, however...

It is of the nature of pure self-awareness and is unchanging. Since it is devoid of the entry of any other attributes of a non-conscious nature within its conscious aspect, it is not logical for it to be entered even by an attribute consisting of space or time. Therefore, he says: "For them... For the followers of Kapila, at least, this [consciousness] is indeed eternal.

"Let it be that for the Jaiminīyas as well, [the self] is eternal by virtue of its conscious aspect (*cidrūpāṃśa*), but non-eternal by virtue of its state-aspect (*avasthāṃśa*). Having thus explained half a verse in brief, he now explains it at length, containing within it the premise of alternative possibilities, with the words "by means of consciousness and unconsciousness" (*cidacittvābhyām*). Even though the self is accepted, regarding the cognition that has been admitted—

There is a duality of positions regarding whether that [consciousness] is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) or not; "duality" (*dvaita*) is simply the state of being two. In this regard, *tatra* means "between these two positions. It is not as in the Sāṃkhya system, where there is luminosity through the coloring of consciousness by the reflection of the *puruṣa*; rather, here it is by itself, without that [reflection]. This, then, is the first position.
In that case, pervasiveness is non-limitation by space, eternity is [non-limitation] by time, and by the inclusion of "etcetera," oneness is [non-limitation] by its own nature;
such qualities as these belonging to the self, which is the *puruṣa*, would also follow for cognition (*jñāna*), for the word "and" (*ca*) functions as a reason.
This is because pervasiveness consists in the non-connection with specific locations, and eternity consists in the non-connection with specific times.

And because it is impossible for the specific nature [of consciousness] to be characterized by space and time, there is non-difference; this is indicated by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*).

Alternatively, the word "specific" (*viśeṣa*) may stand separately, denoting the "specificity of the essential nature" (*svarūpaviśeṣa*). Now, one might object: space and time must first be objects of cognition and manifest themselves to the nature of consciousness; they will thus become the factors that cause limitation (*saṃkoca*), and from that limitation [arises the appearance of diversity].

Anticipating the objection that there might also be a contraction of its own nature (*svarūpa-saṃkoca*), he says: "And not by way of the nature of consciousness. By this, he demonstrates that just as in the case of the knower, a contraction is not possible even in the attribute of knowledge, because the underlying logic is the same;
thus, he explains the commentary beginning with "the property of being an object" (*cetya-dharma*) as referring to the possessor of the attribute and the attribute itself. This is what is meant:
If, first of all, manifestation rests within consciousness and shines forth like [an image] in a mirror,

then what contraction could there be for that which is of the nature of consciousness? Even if, moreover, it is said that the cognition of an object is a mere witnessing consciousness— unembraced by and excluded from the state of being an object— nevertheless, what [contraction is there]?
Contraction.
(Page 137) For when there is a merging of mutual natures, they cannot tolerate any mutual alteration— just as [the color] white...
The quality [of blackness] does not belong to the cloth's state of being black, nor does the cloth belong to the whiteness of another locus;

these two are mutually restrictive. The first is a difference of form (*rūpa-bheda*), the other is a difference of location (*deśa-bheda*). Even there, when established, it is a difference of quality as "white," and when to-be-accomplished, it is a difference of action as "it moves. When established...
Regarding the cloth in threads as being neither different nor non-different: if this is the probandum, then it follows that difference and non-difference are themselves subject to transition.

As for its non-restrictiveness, the commonality consists in not being restrictive. And whether that [commonality] is this very entity, or is constructed through exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), or exists by way of inherence (*samavāya*) or identity (*tādātmya*)—what does it matter here in these internal details? In that regard also:

That which was described as appearing in an inseparable manner, consisting of both the established and the to-be-established, is precisely that which appears through immersion (*āveśa*) as being absolutely distinct. External space and time are exemplified by "Caitra is in the house" and "He offers the oblation when the sun has risen.
Therefore, contraction is produced by immersion. For immersion (*āveśa*) is indeed an entry (*praveśa*) on all sides (*ā*).

Even possession (*āveśa*) occurs only between things of equal rank; for that which stands on the same level as another is possessed by it. Indeed, that which is of a different rank is not possessed, because there would otherwise follow the absurdity of a lack of restriction—contrary to the restrictive rule governing the pervader and the pervaded—since possession does not occur between disparate levels. For example, the sky is not contracted by the depths of the underworld (*pātāla*).
And there is a distinct level (*kakṣyā*) of difference between space and time as objects of cognition. For a "level" is a locus of manifestation.

Space and time manifest externally—as "this is the place of the jar" or "this is its time"—through the reflective awareness of externality within the manifestation as "this-ness" (*idantā*), characterized by dependence on an external manifestation.

Because form (*rūpa*) appears as something distinct [from consciousness], whereas light (*prakāśa*), being non-different from itself, shines forth as "I" with absolute freedom (*svātantrya*). That which belongs to a different order of existence than another cannot be its limiting factor (*saṃkocaka*), just as the netherworld (*pātāla*) cannot limit the heavens. Thus, there is a perception of what is incompatible with the pervading property of being a limiter—namely, that space, time, and so forth are not of the same order as cognition.

The categories of space and time are distinct from consciousness because they manifest as "this-ness" (idantā), whereas consciousness manifests as "I-ness" (ahantā). If their categories were non-different from consciousness, they would have to manifest as "I-ness," which is contradictory to their manifestation as "this-ness"; thus, the pervasion (vyāpti) is established.

This is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). This is what is expressed by the words "and not" (*na ca*). Regarding the phrase "that which is not external to consciousness" (*bodhasya yadabahiḥ*):
it refers to a form characterized primarily by bliss, which is defined as self-reflexive awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and is non-distinct from the nature of consciousness itself.

In that regard, there is no manifestation of space and time apart from consciousness, because they are manifested externally by means of an outward-turned cognition. [Objection: But if this is so, of what do space and time become the limiting factors for you?

[The author] replies: "Here is a jar. The word "for" (*ca*) indicates the reason. Because, through the grammatical relation of non-co-referentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*), there is a limitation of space in the form "here"; and as for "that" (*sa*):

When a previously experienced object is being remembered, there occurs an entry into the body of the objective entity (*bhāvaśarīra*), resulting in a fusion of place and time. The phrase "at that time" (*tadā*) signifies a connection with a specific time through grammatical coordination (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*). This is the case everywhere in this context.
In that regard, space and time are determined by means of an "this-ness" (*idantā*) consisting of "this-ness," as they are perceived as distinct objects of reflection.

Since the mere determination of "this is a jar" is sufficient to differentiate [the object] from its equal-level counterpart and to effect the contraction of its own nature (*svarūpa-saṃkocana*), therefore those two do not manifest within self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Consequently, it follows that for consciousness, those two are not of equal status. *Svābhāvya* is simply the very nature (*svabhāva*) itself; or else, even of the nature...

Someone might have the doubt that the occurrence of the limitation of space and time regarding external objects of form, when there is extroversion, is produced by the adjunct (*upādhi*) of the object; as will be stated:
"Merely in accordance with the space and time of distinct cognizable objects..."
"Knowledge, recollection, determination, and so forth appear as sequential" (1.52).

In order to remove that [notion], the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) is employed in the expression "the being of the self-nature" (*svabhāvasya bhāvaḥ*) in order to state the inability [of the self-nature] to tolerate any other form.
Now, is there any figurative nature of consciousness by virtue of which...?

Anticipating the objection that, in order to dispel such doubt, the term "consciousness" (*cit*) is used as a synonym for knowledge— well-known from passages such as "In the Puruṣa, whose nature is consciousness and who is not subject to modification, there is the power of consciousness" (YD 1.2 Bhāṣya)— the author says:

Regarding the phrase "for the Sāṃkhyas": that which is the first transformation of the *pradhāna*, namely the "Great One" (*mahat*), has another constituent called the "instrument" (*karaṇa*)—distinct from its causal constituent (*kāraṇaskandha*)—which is designated by the term "intellect" (*buddhi*).
Although this is insentient because it is a transformation of the *pradhāna*, it appears to possess consciousness due to its connection with the reflection of the conscious Self (*puruṣa*).
In the system of the Great Sage, that which appears possesses the very nature of metaphorical consciousness;
for this reason, it is indeed necessary to dispel any suspicion regarding its metaphorical status. Now, as for the nature of metaphorical consciousness—

Anticipating the objection that "there might then be some cognition in which permanence exists, and thus the fault of the consequence regarding *dharma* would not arise," he says [in the immediately following sūtra], "And such...
[is the case]. Now, one might object: even for the Self, whose nature is consciousness (*cittattva*), connection with space and so forth certainly appears; how then can it be used as an illustration?

Because that [non-conjunction] would follow, it would entail that the quality of knowledge is eternal and so forth. For instance, just as there is the cognition "the jar is here" or "the jar is now," likewise there is the cognition "I know here" or "I know now.
In that case, there is the realization: "There was ignorance [previously], but now I am the knower. True, but that [realization] resides in the body and so forth.
Due to the determination of a connection with cognition— based on factors such as the dependence upon a single causal complex (sāmagrī) regarding the body and so forth—
the Self appears under the influence of those limiting adjuncts (upādhi). Therefore, that which is the non-figurative reality of the principle of consciousness (cittattva)—
consisting of the light of self-awareness and oriented inward— is not [conditioned] by direction in the form of space, nor by time.

Limitation is possible in reality according to its true nature, by means of the reasoning previously stated. He states yet another reason with the words "of that whose essence is consciousness alone. For space and time become qualifiers only when they perform some function through the designation of non-distinct particulars; they do not become qualifiers if they are ineffective, for that would lead to over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*). To illustrate: by virtue of location...
The distinction between iron, cloth, and so forth, as well as that of snake venom and the like, is indeed observed to depend upon time.

But in the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), there is only one form, which is luminosity (*prakāśa*); how could anything additional to that coalesce with the nature of consciousness, given that it would consist of non-luminosity? For such [non-luminosity] touches only the state of being an object of knowledge (*vedyatva*), and thus remains entirely external to it.

[The opponent] objects: "But even in the case of blue, since there is a particularity consisting of the excess of blueness, how could a non-blue form be included? It is said in reply: According to the established doctrine (siddhānta), an infinite variety of manifestations (ābhāsa-varga), having become intermingled through the power of necessity (niyati-śakti), constitutes the functional efficiency (arthakriyākārin) of an object; it is designated according to whichever portion [of that manifestation] is intended.

It occurs as follows: even in the Buddhist doctrine, the nature of an entity—though its essence is partless—is differentiated from this and that [other thing], and thus it indeed accommodates a diversity of forms produced by a causal complex, which is determined through various exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*). Knowledge, however, is self-luminous and constitutes the very manifestation of the object. Therefore, its exclusion—
Even by the conceptualizing thought (*vikalpa*) that performs the act of appropriation, whatever specific quality— such as its particular location or time— is determined,
that [quality] attains a state of exclusion from consciousness itself, because it is situated within the "this" (*idam*) portion, which is non-luminous in nature.

[Objection: But surely, just as there are distinct blue objects—such as "dusty blue," "shining blue," "blue here," or "blue now"—which are qualified by space and time, so too will cognitions be [distinct]; and since there is no cognizer other than them, how can it be said in the commentary, "as in the case of the Self"? [Response: No.
This is equal [to the previous argument], because that which is called "blue" in the form described above has not been stated as anything at all apart from its specific characteristics;

therefore, it is logical that those very things are what are called "blue. Consequently, he says: "because they can sustain a multiplicity of diversities due to being objects of cognition. Furthermore, cognition [persists] even in states such as sleep and meditative absorption.

Freed indeed from the objects of cognition such as blue, pleasure, and so forth, as well as from the space and time that color them, that which is the ultimate reality of pure luminosity alone shines with an inward-turned nature; that alone is its ultimate form, while everything else is merely external to it. For whatever is a thing's own inherent form, that remains eternally as that very thing.

It shines like a tree through its specific nature consisting of branches and so forth; yet consciousness does not always shine through such specificities of space, time, and the like. If it were its own true nature even when it does not always appear in that way, then—just as a jar sometimes appears in conjunction with a cloth—the cloth too would become its nature, and thus the principle of non-restriction (aniyama) would be undermined.
Since a rule (*niyama*) is observed to be pervading (*vyāpaka*), there follows the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving that which is contradictory to the pervader.
Thus, having abandoned the counter-example (*vipakṣa*), it is pervaded by its own nature as it exists, appearing through continuity;
this is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Whatever has a specific form cannot be devoid of one or another of those [specifics].

Just as a tree is devoid of [specific species such as] *dhava* and so forth, consciousness is not devoid of its specific qualities in states such as meditative absorption (*samādhi*), deep sleep, or fainting; therefore, the claim that it does not possess the specific form of the cognition of blue and so forth is likewise a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). However, in the formal argument: "And consciousness is indeed devoid of specific qualities..."

This is the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). For indeed, the distinction among these [reasons] is created solely by the difference in their formal application (*prayoga*); in reality, however, it is established that there is only one [reason], namely, "there is no contact with a specific cognition" (*bodhaviśeṣasparśa*). This very point has been stated regarding that which is of the nature of a single cognition (*bodhaikātman*) [on page 141].
The meaning is: "as it appears as mere pure consciousness, uncolored by particularities. And so it is said in the *Nareśvaraviveka*:
"For just as 'cowness' (*gotva*) is not itself of the nature of particular forms such as the brindled cow (*śāvaleyādi*), so too..."

"It consists precisely of the distinctions such as blue, yellow, and so forth. He further adds another supporting argument here with the words "and because its essence is manifestation" (*ābhāsasāratvena*). Manifestation (*ābhāsanam*) is a slight shining-forth or appearing with a degree of contraction; this is the essence, the reality, and the ultimate truth of spatial succession.
And regarding the sequence of time: this is what is meant—space and time act as differentiators by way of their sequential form.

Indeed, a spatial difference becomes manifest in the mover through the act of going; for while the connection with a single location is designated as "one place," even when one remains there, that spatial difference exists only insofar as it has its ultimate reality in the delineation of sequence. As for the difference of time, however—

It is sequence itself that shines forth, for this [world] has sequence as its essential nature. For instance: "This old man is superior to this youth," or "This youth is inferior to this old man"—thus, the sequential nature of birth is perceived, and by virtue of that, the modifications of being (bhāvavikāra), beginning with existence, manifest. Even in the case of simultaneity, sequence alone is the ultimate reality.

For others hold that the cognition "these two have arisen simultaneously" occurs because the sequence, which exists in relation to something else, appears as if it were identical; thus, the notion of simultaneity is a perception of time based on the capacity for a future sequence, and not an actual difference in time between the two. Furthermore, the cognitions of "slow" and "quick" likewise pertain to a greater or lesser degree of sequence.

Space and time are, by virtue of their underlying connection (*anusandhi*), the ultimate reality of sequence (*krama*). Sequence takes such forms as "it is here," "it is not here," "it did not exist then," and "it exists now. Furthermore, regarding the conventional usage of existence and non-existence, this [sequence] serves as the cause for [the cognition]:
"this appears" or "this does not appear at all. This appearance [of one thing] occurs through the non-appearance [of another].

That which exists with intervals and interstices is the arouser of succession in the manifold [world]. However, in the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), whose sole ultimate reality is manifestation, since there is no portion consisting of non-manifestation even for the slightest object, how could there be a connection of succession in that which is "without manifestation"—that is, having emerged from manifestation and being of the singular form of light? For this very reason, even by the followers of Kaṇāda, [it is held] regarding the cause...
By those who state, "It is called time" (Vaiśeṣika Sūtra 2.2.9), it is shown that the differentiation of time exists only with respect to effects.
As for atoms, however...
(page 142)

By the power of the thing itself, there is merely a conjunction with time, not a temporal distinction [inherent in the thing]. Furthermore, even when there is no conjunction with time, the temporal distinction that exists in the conventional usage "the ancient poet" (referring to Śiva) in relation to a jar and so forth belongs, in reality, only to the effect such as the jar; thus, it does not apply to that which is without appearance and is non-effectual in nature.

To begin with, there is no distinction of space or time within the Self. Consequently, there is no succession of space or time in that which has the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), because its nature is solely consciousness; this is an "observation of what is incompatible with the cause" (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*). The cause of spatial and temporal succession is the state of being manifest or unmanifest, whereas its opposite is the state of having the single nature of pure manifestation.
Thus, the permanence and omnipresence of the Self have been established because it is not subject to the limitations of time and space.

Even the distinction of place and time belongs to objects (*bhāva*) in relation to the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*); for there is no absence of the manifestation of consciousness in the appearance of objects. Indeed, the non-manifestation of that [consciousness] constitutes the distinction of place and time, as in the case of a jar and a cloth.

A pervasive entity is not perceived here. And if there were a difference [of the object] from the nature of consciousness by its own form, then even in relation to that [consciousness], such [pervasiveness] would not belong to it, just as it does not belong to a jar in relation to itself. For this very reason, if there were a difference, there would be mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*); thus, relying on the aforementioned reasoning, he states "for this very reason" (*ata eva*) with respect to the non-difference of the essential nature (*svarūpa*). This is because the non-difference of space and time has already been stated.

Because it does not touch upon distinctions imposed by space, time, or other limiting conditions, and because it is devoid of objective appearance—precisely for this reason, how could the multiplicity of selves, such as Caitra, Maitra, and others, and their differentiation in terms of individual nature, be intrinsic?
For if there were a difference in their inherent nature (*svabhāva*), then that multiplicity would be intrinsic; but where consciousness alone is the form, what else could there be?

There exists no part of its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that could be differentiated. Therefore, there is no differentiation of the Self whatsoever in terms of space, time, or essential form. And here, in all cases, the cause is the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatva*).
Since that [nature] is present in its entirety even in the attribute of knowledge (*jñānaguṇa*), it is logical that [the Self] must be eternal, all-pervading, and one.

In this regard, since the opponent has accepted the eternality and omnipresence of the self, and since its unity is also accepted everywhere by those learned in the Upaniṣads—even by one such as the Sāṃkhya who has not admitted it—he too must be led to accept it through logical reasoning. And all of this applies equally to cognition as well; thus, this is indeed a *prasaṅga* (reductio ad absurdum).
The author has established a firm logical proof for what must be demonstrated through the very mouth of the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin);
for a quality consisting of a separate cognition will certainly not be accepted in the final system (siddhānta),
so why this [absurd] consequence?

[This is said] with the intention that [the opponent] will do so. For this consequence (*prasaṅga*) of his may indeed refute the Sāṃkhya and other schools, but nothing in our own established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is thereby refuted. And the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) has gone as far as this.
He has ascended with the intention of obtaining the reversal of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga-viparyaya*). For instance, this reversal of the undesirable consequence is as follows:

"Even if cognition, though consisting of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*), were accepted by you as being eternal, all-pervasive, and non-dual, how could its self (*ātman*)—which is also of the nature of consciousness—be such [as you claim]? Thus, since there is no distinction in their being of the nature of consciousness...

Just as there is a distinction of place and time, how could there also be a distinction of intrinsic nature among the selves, by which their plurality might be established? If it is argued that plurality is admitted even though they are of the nature of consciousness due to various arrangements—
namely, because of the specific determination of birth, death, and the instruments (Sāṅkhyakārikā 18)— [then...]
If this is so, then there would also be a distinction of place and time. Thus the first half-verse has been explained;

he now explains the second half with the words "Now, this... (*athaitat*). That very consequence which has necessarily arisen from these [attributes]—eternality, omnipresence, and non-duality—is itself the defect, because it destroys one's own position; therefore, one who is afraid of that [consequence]...

If the proponent of the Self (ātmavādin) accepts that cognition is of a single, insentient nature, then cognition would likewise not exist, just as blue is not of the nature of manifesting yellow. Anticipating the objection that even insentient things such as the sun or fire are manifestations, he says: "And manifestation is consciousness. But [one might ask]: "Is it not so..."
Anticipating the objection that consciousness might become something consisting almost entirely of light, having the form of the radiance of pure *sattva*, he says: "If that were so.

This means that even if there were light and the like—such as the radiance of lamps, the sun, or jewels—the object would not appear if the subject (*pramātṛ*) were absent; however, when the subject is present...

In the case of the knower, who is like a lamp, the object must indeed appear through that cognition. If an object does not appear even when a hundred lamps are lit, why would it appear in the same way within the cognition? Whatever does not exist in a certain manner when something of a particular kind is present, its existing in that way [only] indicates the presence of something of a different kind from it.

It illustrates this: just as a jar, though perceived as non-red even in the presence of cool water and cold winds, becomes red upon contact with hot fire; so too, an entity in proximity to that which is insentient (jaḍa) fails to attain the specific qualities consisting of being perceived, being determined, and being fit for linguistic usage.
(144) Whenever [a cognition] is being apprehended, it illuminates the presence of that which is of a non-insentient nature;

for otherwise, by the opposing argument (*bādhaka*), there would follow the consequence of its being causeless. Thus, when the pervasion (*vyāpti*) is established, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) regarding consciousness.

How could an insentient object— consisting primarily of things such as blue— bring about those established states of objects like blue and so forth, which are determinations existing in a manifold and unmixed manner, and which constitute a resting place that is independent of anything else and consists of the nature of experiential certainty?
"Should establish the established states"—this means that he should bring about the established states of the primary [nature].
Alternatively, the designation is made by way of the relationship between the general and the particular, as in "he makes those who have already fallen asleep sleep," or "the intoxication of wine.
Or else, it refers to the various states such as blue, yellow, and so forth, which he establishes.

It determines: "This is indeed blue," or "This very thing is blue. How could such determination be possible for that which is insentient and lacks the nature of manifestation? For that alone is the very essence of manifestation. As it will be stated in the subsequent kārikā:
"In the state of insentience, there is no manifestation of objects."

Thus, regarding what will be said even against the Sāṃkhya who maintains that the intellect (*buddhi*) consists of both conscious and unconscious aspects: according to the principle that two things which are utterly contradictory cannot both be the ultimate nature of a single entity,
if its real form were insentient (*jaḍa*), how could it be of the nature of the manifestation of an object?

The phrase "asau" (this) refers to the established position. The fault regarding non-existence (*abhāva*) that was stated here in order to refute other proponents who accept the nature of cognition as being insentient (*jaḍa*), should also be applied there. With the word "tat" (therefore), the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣavādī*) concludes all that has been previously stated. Thus, because of what has been said:

From the collection of causes; in both ways—whether as having the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) or as having the nature of non-consciousness (*acidrūpa*)—it is not tenable for a distinct attribute called "knowledge" to belong to a self that is itself distinct [from those causes]. If it were of the nature of consciousness, then since its essence is eternal and all-pervading, no conjunction with such [an attribute] has been accepted by the opponent; how much less so [could there be a conjunction] otherwise?

Regarding the relationship between the property and the possessor of the property (*dharmadharmibhāva*): since the very nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) alone serves as the locus for the determination of objects, what is the use of postulating any other property—whether conscious or unconscious? This is the reason given in the phrase "due to the connection with knowledge and action."

(Page 145) This part [of the argument], "due to the sun of the yoga of knowledge," is contradictory (*viruddha*) both because the nature of knowledge is impossible [in that context] and because its connection [to the subject] is utterly unestablished;
furthermore, it proves the opposite of the intended nature [of the subject]. And by way of that [connection], it is also contradictory.
It is "unestablished in its locus" (āśrayāsiddha) because it subverts the very nature of the subject (dharmin). || 7 ||

Anticipating the objection that knowledge might be neither purely conscious nor purely unconscious— lest the aforementioned faults ensue— but rather both conscious and unconscious in nature, the proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣavādī) states the following in the Sūtra in order to refute this position of the self-theorist (ātmavādin):
Just as the intellect assumes the form of the object, so too does it assume the consciousness of the self;
for that very intellect is non-inert. If it were inert, there would be no manifestation of the object.

The commentator explains the meaning of this in brief: "This too is Sāṃkhya. *Sāṃkhya* refers to correct knowledge (*saṃyak-khyāti*) through the discrimination between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, as well as *saṃkhyāna*, which is the enumeration (*parigaṇana*) of the various categories (*tattva-bheda*). A treatise composed concerning that is called *Sāṃkhya*. In that regard:
The function (*vṛtti*) of the principle of intellect (*buddhi-tattva*) is said to be knowledge. Functioning (*vartana*) is "function" (*vṛtti*), which is a specific modification (*pariṇāma-viśeṣa*).

For a certain modification that conceals its prior form, like wood turning into ash, is called a "modification of effect" (*kārya-pariṇāma*); whereas that which does not conceal [its prior form], being established in its manifest form, is a "modification of attribute" (*dharma-pariṇāma*).

It shines like the state of being an earring made of gold. That which, not obscuring [the object], proceeds as the form of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and is thus understood—as for example, "it is understood"—is the transformation of the mental mode (*vṛtti-pariṇāma*). For it is called a "mode" (*vṛtti*) because its functioning (*vartana*) is exactly like that [of the object].
Just as before, the refutation regarding permanence and so forth applies by way of the conscious part (*cid-bhāga*), while [the opposite] applies by way of the insentient part (*jaḍa-bhāga*).

"The impossibility of the determination of objects. Now, the word "atha" (then/now) indicates the opponent's supposition. Consciousness (*buddhi*) is the agent; it assumes—that is, it maintains—in whatever manner its own nature as a reflection, which is related to an object such as blue, by way of its clarity produced by an excellence of *sattva*, in that very same manner of clarity...

The Sāṃkhya statement that the consciousness belonging to the self (puruṣa) assumes the form of a reflection both internally and externally on all sides due to its transparency is plausible; however, he states the refutation of this as well: by means of the reflection of consciousness, [the intellect] becomes of the nature of cognition (*saṃvit*), just as water [becomes of the nature of light] by means of the reflection of light.

It is of the nature of light. Likewise, the modification of the intellect (*buddhivṛtti*) consists of knowledge whose essence is consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Consequently, the previously mentioned defects, such as [the impossibility of] permanence and omnipresence, [do not apply].
(Page 146)
The remaining intention behind the composition of another sūtra is that there would be an association with other defects appropriate to the Sāṃkhya system.
Now, even in the case of a reflection, there is no assumption of the form of the original object, for it is not observed that a mirror becomes burning even when a reflection of fire appears in it.
If that is so, then that intellect remains insentient even while grasping both the reflection of the object and the reflection of consciousness; thus, that very same defect persists.

The meaning of the aphorism is: "How, then, is there a determination of objects? That which was stated in the aphorism from the words "of the object" (*arthasya*) up to "consciousness" (*caitanyam*) is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of knowledge. And by means of the context and the force of the subject matter, the author clarifies in the commentary that "knowledge is the intellect" (*jñānaṃ buddhiḥ*). Now, [one might object]: "But do not the Vaiśeṣikas and others also [assert this]?"

They consider that *buddhi*, *upalabdhi*, and *jñāna* are not different in meaning; what, then, is the distinction of this doctrine from the previous one? For if the self (*ātman*) is understood to have the very nature of consciousness (*saṃvit*), what is the use of postulating a separate "knowledge" (*jñāna*); or if knowledge is a property of the intellect (*buddhi*), what purpose is served by a separate self? Anticipating this objection:

He says: "Of the Sāṃkhya. One objection is thus refuted: that in the view of the Vaiśeṣikas and others, that knowledge is an attribute (*dharma*) of the self, whereas here it is not so; and a second [objection]: that consciousness, being pure by nature, cannot be the manifestation of an object; [and a third]: that knowledge is insentient because its nature is the intellect (*buddhi*), which is a modification of the insentient *pradhāna*. It is not [insentient].

The intended meaning is that it is "of the nature of self-luminosity" (svataḥprakāśarūpa) by virtue of the third case ending. The word *tattva* is used for the purpose of excluding the intellect (*buddhi*), which is metaphorically treated as the Self due to the influence of egoism (*ahaṃkāra*). By the inclusion of the suffix *-mātra*, he negates its connection with other attributes; for indeed, attributes arise and pass away, and thus [if it were associated with them], they would affect the substratum as well.

In some way, through identity (*tādātmya*), they undergo transformational impermanence (*pariṇāmānityatā*). Therefore, in the absence of those [transformations], the self (*ātman*) is ultimately eternal, characterized by the power of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana-śakti*). Anticipating the objection that even in the Buddhist view the self is characterized by awareness (*saṃvedana*), he says "inward-turned" (*antarmukham*) to state the distinction of this [our] system from that one as well.

According to the Sāṃkhyas, the reality of the self (*ātmatattva*) consists solely of the nature of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśamātra*). For the Buddhists (*saugata*), however, it is inward-turned by virtue of being self-luminous, yet outward-turned by virtue of manifesting external objects such as blue. But it is not logical for a single entity to possess both inward- and outward-turning aspects, because that would entail the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the identity of self and other. Nor is that [identity]...
It is logical that the external object appears as distinct from its grasper; therefore, the grasper is indeed inward-turned. For this very reason:
Because it is impossible for [the object] to be external or graspable, nothing else shines forth as its equal peer.

And it is the appearance of such equality that gives rise to the linguistic conventions of the subordinate and the principal, the state of attribute and substrate, the qualifier and the qualified, the adjunct and the adjuncted, and so forth.

And thus, in the case of the cognition "this cloth is white," where the appearance of the cloth and the appearance of whiteness both exist on the external plane as objects of grasping through an identical "this-ness" (idantā), it is logical that the appearance of whiteness— colored by the appearance of the cloth— is either a superimposition (viparyaya) or [the cloth] becomes a subordinate qualifier (viśeṣaṇa). Therefore, in this context, the subordinate element is a qualifier because its form is to be established by something else.

That by which the substrate (*upadheya*), which is distinct from its own nature (*svarūpa*) and is to be colored by its own self, is characterized as having a specific form—this refers to the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*). However, that which is the primary object (*pradhāna*) is the qualified (*viśeṣya*), meaning that its form is to be colored by another, namely, the substrate which serves as the qualifier. And thus, there exists the relationship of qualifier and qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣyabhāva*).
The linguistic usage that occurs with respect to a face is not tenable with respect to the self; therefore, this [usage] is not a property of anything, nor is there any property belonging to it.

Although that which is called "knowledge" is of the nature of cognition (*buddhi*), nevertheless, because it is not a property of the self, this constitutes its distinction from the Naiyāyikas and others. Now, if this is so, let the person (*puruṣa*) be that very [cognition]; what is the use of anything else?

Anticipating the objection that this might be due to *jñāna* (cognition), he says: "But cognition... For if that pure light were to manifest objects in its very own form, then—since that form would never be deficient or excessive even by so much as a blade of grass—there would either be the manifestation of everything at all times, or else the manifestation of nothing at any time.

If there were no manifestation, the world would either be omniscient or ignorant. Therefore, "the cognition of a jar" occurs upon the arising of the manifestation of a jar; "the cognition of a cloth" occurs upon the cessation of that [jar's] manifestation and the arising of the manifestation of a cloth. And yet, the nature of pure consciousness does not consist in a mixture of the manifestations of the jar and the cloth.

The Puruṣa experiences [it], yet consciousness is not the intrinsic nature (svarūpa) of the object, because there is a contradiction between the natures of the insentient and the sentient, and because—as in the previous case—it would entail the consequence of either omniscience or ignorance. Thus, that which is the manifestation in the form "this object shines forth" is neither the Puruṣa, nor is it the blue and so forth; this belongs to the Puruṣa.

It follows, then, that this [cognition] is a shadow of that which is of the nature of light. Furthermore, consciousness does not directly cast a shadow upon the object, for if it did, it would follow that there would be no blind people and so forth; nor does it do so instantly within the sense organs.
(Page 148)

Because it would follow that there is a universal certainty [of identity], perception would become impossible; because it would follow that there would be no synthesis such as "I who see am the very same one who hears"; and because it would follow that external sensory activity, dreams, mental constructs, and memory would not arise. Therefore, in some other object, for this person...
The reflection is transferred; for if this [mind] did not grasp the reflection of the object, the object would again fall into a state of non-manifestation.

Therefore, that very other entity which is capable of grasping the reflections of both consciousness and the object—being predominant in *sattva* and denoted by the term "intellect" (*buddhi*)—is what performs the synthesis (*anusandhāna*).

Because it has a single function, that [cognition] is a specific action whose nature consists of a sequence beginning with the desire to grasp— manifested as the effort "I know"— which has the observation of the object as its body and concludes with the determination "I ascertain"; thus, by virtue of the unity of its fruit, which is the ascertainment of the object, it conceals the reflective awareness of its own substratum (dharmin).
The succession of transformations, known as cognition (*jñāna*), is called "functioning" (*vṛtti*) or "subsistence" (*vartana*).

For instance, the ash of wood is not its "functioning," because the perception of the wood has vanished. Nor is a single moment alone the functioning; for in that case, what distinction could there be such that one could say, "this [moment] subsists in this manner"? Therefore, it must be a plurality of moments.

The transformation (*pariṇāma*) whose essence is action (*kriyā*), which conceals the apprehension of the substrate (*dharmin*) by means of its fruit and is imagined as having various boundaries, is the "function" (*vṛtti*).

For example, as in the case of "Caitra goes. And that function, having reached its final form in the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of the object, attains the nature of illumination through the power of the reflection of the Puruṣa, and is called "cognition" (*jñāna*).

This is the summary of the meaning. He states this very point with the words "knowledge, moreover," and so forth. The word "moreover" (*punaḥ*) indicates the distinction [of knowledge] from the person (*puruṣa*).

The term "constantly" (*satatam*) means uninterrupted, in the form of a continuous flow. For teachers such as Patañjali and others maintain that even in sleep and similar states, there is the nature of cognition (*pratyaya*), because of the reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*) upon awakening.

Defining sleep and so forth as specific types of cognition—such as "I slept happily"—[they explain it] by way of being remembered through connection with a previous place, time, and so on; being experienced through connection with the present place, time, and so on;
and being recognized through the connection of both.
Whether by way of a connection with the present or the future— thus being conceived as something that has occurred, is occurring, or will occur—

or else by way of a mere connection with the future, through the process of imaginative projection (*utprekṣyamāṇatayā*), and therein too, according to whether it is clear or obscure, and through the accompaniment of other appearances, such as other subjects (*pramātṛ*) and so forth...

By the phrase "sāhityena ca" and so forth, it refers to those manifestations (*ābhāsāḥ*) which are variegated by the blending of thousands of diversities; for this very reason, they are expressed by the word *tad*— which denotes qualities— in a compound that is either a *dvirukta* (repeated word) or a *karmadhāraya*, due to its connection with the sense of "manner" (*prakāra*).

The various manifestations (ābhāsabheda) or specific reflections belonging to external objects such as jars, cloths, and so forth, which are designated by their respective names, have their constant arising and dissolution— that is, their manifestation and disappearance— within that [consciousness]. For this very reason, it is "other" (anya), meaning it is distinct from the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva) and different from the principle of consciousness (cittattva) insofar as it is external.
