The object is blue and so forth; therein, that inwardness which follows its positive and negative concomitance—that cognition which is dependent upon that [inwardness] belongs neither to consciousness (*cit*) nor to the object, but rather to the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*).
It is that which consists of successive parts, such as "I see," "I know," and "I ascertain."

Activity (*vyāpāra*) is action; by reason of its having that as its essential nature, it is "functioning" or "occurrence. By this terminology, the Sāṃkhya system has shown that "functions are fivefold": valid cognition, error, [Yoga Sūtra 1.6].

Thus, "the specific characteristic (*svālakṣaṇya*) is the function (*vṛtti*) of the triad" (Kārikā 29), and so forth—in these passages. Now, one might object: "In accordance with that [system], there ought to be a commentary (*vṛtti*) on this [text] by him as well."

How is there an indication through grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "intellect (*buddhi*) is knowledge (*jñāna*)"? To this, he says: "merely" (*kevalam*). For [the word *jñāna*] is drawn toward the intellect by proximity—since the function of the intellect is awakening, experiencing, or seeing—and thus, despite its etymological derivation being weak due to the presence of another word, it is understood in this way.

Action would appear as if latent within the word itself; consequently, one might suspect that this cognition consists of non-inert awareness. However, in the case of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the conventional meaning of the whole (*samudāyaprasiddhi*) of the word *buddhi* is stronger than the etymological derivation from its parts (*avayavaprasiddhi*).

Thus, by this uncontradicted reasoning, when the universal is established as having its constituent parts abandoned, the cognition that expresses an object of an insentient nature is said to be insentient through its grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*).

Furthermore, the doubt as to whether the relationship between the occurrence (*vṛtti*) and that which occurs (*vṛttimat*) is *samavāya* (inherence), as held by the followers of Kaṇāda, is also [addressed] by this coreferentiality.
By means of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), which culminates in non-exclusion, [the possibility of a different referent] is refuted. Furthermore, this coreferentiality,
by reinforcing the conventional usage of the aggregate (*samudāyaprasiddhi*), eliminates the suspicion that there might be a separate cognition, as for example:

He says "And for this very reason" (*ata eva ca*) to show that non-distinction (*avyatireka*) is also established. The word "only" (*eva*) indicates that by means of the non-difference (*abheda*) which has been demonstrated, the suspicion regarding [the existence of] a separate consciousness (*bodhatā*) necessarily subsides. And the word "and" (*ca*) indicates that this is established through the conventional usage of the whole (*samudāyaprasiddhi*). By demonstrating the non-difference between the function (*vṛtti*) and that which possesses the function (*tadvat*) through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), [the author shows that the distinction is not real].

The interpretation that "the doubt has been dispelled by awakening" is the view of those with superficial vision. For indeed, having observed a single result produced by moments occurring in a temporal sequence, one postulates a unity of the process (*vṛtti*), just as one observes the unity of the process of "going" through its result, the reaching of a village; but here, in the case of that which is of the nature of cognition...
"What is the fruit of the action? He replies: "And of that... The word "and" (ca) indicates a doubt regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*).
That portion of it which is called *sattva* has attained the state of being the fruit of the action of realization;
it is the fruit itself. Now, it might be argued that it is only appropriate to call *sattva* a "portion" if it were associated with other portions.

It may be so. He says "of the three-fold" (*triguṇāyāḥ*) to indicate that it exists. Now, one might raise the objection: "If its form consists of the three qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—then why is the fruit [of action] attributed to the *sattva* portion alone? The word "api" (even/also) serves to indicate this doubt. To this, he provides the answer: "Because this [consciousness] is of the nature of illumination (*prakāśasvabhāva*) for another, such as a jar or other objects."

"Sattva is light and illuminating"—thus they say. Now, since even blue and other such objects consist of the three guṇas, why does their own portion of *sattva* not likewise [behave in that way]? It is said: "Because of its purity," meaning because it is not overwhelmed by *rajas* and *tamas*.
Because of its transparency. For this very reason, it has been said:
"The *sattva* aspect of the mind is indeed of the nature of luminosity.
Now, if the *sattva* portion is of the nature of being illuminated by another, why does it not manifest the universe simultaneously?

He dispels both doubts—namely, "How could it shine? and "Once the utility of *sattva* alone has been established, what would be the purpose of the other two qualities?"—by means of the word "also" (*api*) itself, with the words "by the portions of *rajas* and *tamas*.
*Sattva*, whose nature is luminosity, resembles the stainless sky; yet, as if by a mass of clouds on all sides, [it is obscured].
It remains enveloped by *tamas*, whose nature is obstruction; and therein resides *rajas*, which has the nature of activity and stands in the place of the wind.
By its very nature as activity (*kriyā*), it gradually dispels and subordinates the darkness of *tamas*. Consequently,

although this portion of *sattva* is essentially the light of another, it rightly arises in succession as the form of illumination for external objects such as blue and so forth, as well as for internal states such as pleasure and so forth.

And the application of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) is indeed appropriate. Now, even this portion of *sattva*, which consists of luminosity and stands in the place of external light, is itself insentient; how then could it become free from desire, such that its status as the ultimate fruit has been stated? Furthermore, that which consists of the luminosity of blue is of the nature of the luminosity of pleasure.

Or rather, that aspect of the sentient being (*sattva*) which is colored by the reflection of blue and pleasure, and whose modification (*vṛtti*) consisting of cognition is an action—how could that itself be the fruit? It is said: because the Self, whose nature is consciousness, is properly deposited within that pure [mirror] and finds rest there through the reflection, it attains the state of being perceived.

[The object] is apprehended. But by what other [means] could it be cognized? There is no other reality apart from the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*), nor is it logical for it to be cognized in dependence upon a person (*puruṣa*). If that were the case, then the same would apply to blue and other objects;
therefore, enough with the laborious postulation of a separate reality of the intellect. He says: "Cognizability is nothing other than the state of being manifest."

Nor is it something else; rather, through the favor of the shadow of consciousness (*saṃvit*), that objective portion (*sattvabhāga*), submerged in light as if its own manifestation, does not require another light. This alone is "knowability" (*saṃvedyatā*). What is meant is this:
within the intellect-substance (*buddhisattva*), which is entirely transparent, the portion consisting of the reflection of the object is the act of cognition (*jñānakriyā*).
The portion consisting of the reflection of consciousness (*saṃvit*), however, is the fruit. As it has been said:
"The fruit is the awareness of the mental modification (*cittavṛtti*) belonging to the Puruṣa, which is undifferentiated [from it].
Now, one might object: let there be manifestation in the object itself by virtue of the reflection of the Self; what is the need for this postulated intermediate state?

By that principle of consciousness (*buddhitattva*). In the world, the common usage is that the object itself is manifest. And thus, the followers of Jaimini consider the very "perceivedness" of the object to be the fruit [of knowledge]. To this, he says: if manifestation were produced in the object alone, then that object would have become such [manifest] by its own nature; how could it then be otherwise for someone else? For it is not so.
Form conditioned by a cause arises in such a way specifically with respect to that very cause; for it is thus specifically with respect to the potter.

A jar may be a jar in relation to some [perceiver], yet it is a non-jar in relation to others. Indeed, just as duality—though produced by the intellect in dependence upon a particular perceiver—does not manifest to all perceivers, but only to that one [specific perceiver];
so too, when manifestness (*prakaṭatā*) arises through the proximity of an action consisting of a mental state (*bhāvanā*) residing within oneself.

Anticipating the objection that [the cognition] will arise with respect to that very [object], he says: "designated as manifestation" (*prakāśasaṃjñaka*). For duality, once it has arisen, does not have the nature of manifestation; rather, it is preceded by a general cognition of it.
From the cognition of the quality of duality, there must arise the cognition "two substances," and therefore, in that case—

Just as in the production of duality, so too in the production of the cognition of its universal (sāmānya), the enumerative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) serves as the instrumental cause. Moreover, that [enumerative cognition] cannot occur in another cognizer, because it inheres in a single object, whereby there exists a causal relationship between two cognitions. But here, if manifestness (*prakaṭatā*) has been produced, nothing else needs to be required therein either.

Because if [manifestness] were a property of the object of knowledge, it would entail the consequence of an infinite regress of further manifestations. Therefore, when it is said that "the object is manifest," this refers only to the merging of the reflection of the object—which has been reflected in the *buddhitattva*—with the reflection of consciousness; it is not some property of the external object itself. Now, let us grant that manifestness does not reside in the object.

"The jar is manifest to me" will be grounded solely in the self (*ātman*), because we observe that manifestation occurs within the self; so what is the need for the principle of the intellect (*buddhi*)? It is said in reply: the self has the nature of pure consciousness (*saṃvid-mātra-svabhāva*) and is merely the direct witness (*sākṣāt draṣṭā*);
how then could its being the cause of the manifestation of objects—which is called the "manifestness of the object"—be anything other than [the activity of] consciousness itself?

[The Self] would be [pure] in its own nature. How then is it the seer and witness in the cognitions of objects? He says: "Only when the intellect exists. [Objection: But let there not be any further result in that conscious Self, the Person, consisting of a manifestation that brings about modification; yet he himself will be [the witness]. He says: "He is indeed devoid of modification."

If this [light] is the manifestation of blue, then it must belong to the blue universe alone; for it follows that what is called "the manifestation of blue" or "the manifestation of yellow" is simply manifestation itself. Therefore—because enjoyment, characterized by manifestness, rests neither in the object nor in the self, yet it does exist...

(Page 153) The meaning is: from that [purity], there occurs the worldly transaction consisting of the conjunction of enjoyment between the object and the self. For the sattva that has the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*), there is purity because it possesses the capacity to exclude *rajas*—that is, the removal of its *tamas* portion—but not in the manner of [the exclusion of color] as in the case of blue and so forth.

Because it cannot be removed, that reflection imitates the form and shadow—namely, the state of being composed of the blue of cognition—belonging to both itself and its object; it appears by assuming their form, like a white cloth situated between a blue and a red garment. Therefore, for that reason, that reflection [is said to be] the reflection of both the self and the object.

Since this is logically consistent, it follows that enjoyment (*bhoga*) is established as having the nature of the cognition of objects. For that [enjoyment] is characterized precisely as the relationship whose essence is the union of the grasped and the grasper; the intention is that it has no other form.
Now, if there is a conjunction of the two reflections within the intellect (*buddhi*), how can there be [a connection] between the self and the object?
Anticipating the objection that this is merely a conventional usage consisting of the forms of "enjoyer" and "object of enjoyment," he says: "And that...

That establishment of experience exists within the state of enjoyer and object of enjoyment. For since the self is the enjoyer and the object is the thing enjoyed—this being the cause for such conventional usage—therefore, within the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*), there exist the self and the object, which are capable of being enjoyer and object of enjoyment respectively.

The relationship, which consists in the mutual blending of forms to the furthest extent possible—like that of two young lovers in a bedchamber—is precisely what constitutes the state of subject and object. Now, since *sattva* is by nature luminous, if the reflection of an object has fallen upon it, the conventional usage of "manifestation of the object" has already occurred; what need is there for anything else?

He dispels the doubt that [the reflection] is a mental construction of a self by stating "as if colored by the object. For it has been said that this luminosity of *sattva* is insentient (*jaḍa*), like external light. The phrase "by the penetration of consciousness" means by contact with consciousness.
Now, just as in the case of rice grains, this very state of being the object (*karmabhāva*) in the process of cooking consists of the specific change characterized by softening;

In the same way, for an object to be cognized, it must possess some specific quality; that very quality will be its "manifestness" (*prakaṭatā*). This might be so if *karman* were restricted solely to the "produced" (*nirvartya*) and the "modified" (*vikārya*);
however, there is also another kind of *karman*, namely the "attained" (*prāpya*), wherein no further quality arises beyond the mere relation between the agent and the object.
It is just as in the expression, "he goes to the village. Thus he says, "not indeed," for this very penetration into consciousness consists in the union with consciousness.
(page 154)
It is said: "The connection of the object with the intellect by the conscious person.

For this very reason, the Sāṃkhya [author], beginning from the words "That which is this... and so forth, relies upon the previously stated relevant objects of knowledge as the grounds for the existence of the principle of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*). This is because the Self (*ātman*) is changeless, and it is not of such a nature.
The manifestation of an object, as well as the manifestness of that object, is not established as being natural,

nor does it arise from proximity to the Self, nor even from mere proximity to the sense organs; therefore, the reality known as *buddhi* (intellect) is an independent entity in the form of a substance, and is neither a quality of the Self as the Vaiśeṣikas maintain, nor is it...

As for the object, it belongs to the Jaiminīyas [the Mīmāṃsakas], and not to the sense organs, as the Bārhaspatyas hold—this much is the primary course of the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) according to the Sāṃkhya. In the commentary (*vṛtti*), the word "form" (*rūpa*) in the aphorism (*sūtra*) was explained by the word "reflection" (*chāyā*) as its synonym. Therefore, [it is called] "therefore" because it supports both reflections. This is the intellect (*buddhi*). Of the object...

The meaning is that realization (*adhigama*) consists of manifestation culminating in its fruit. Now, if the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*) remains eternally stainless and always holds the reflections of both [the Self and the object], then by that much alone, there would be no ultimate bondage for anyone. For [bondage] does not arise from the extreme cold of a great serpent that has become like a frozen, cool breeze.
Furthermore, Caitra reflected in a fragment of a jewel would not experience the pain of cold,
nor would that fragment of ice become bound to him even through such a metaphorical application,

provided that Maitra— who perceives Caitra as being reflected— were someone other than him. And it is not the case that both the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*) are such [that one could be metaphorically applied to the other].

There is a third [category] which is metaphorical (*upacara*). He says it exists as the "principle of ego" (*ahaṃkāratattva*). The root *karoti* denotes action in general; the meaning is that one knows "I do," or "I eat. For instance, in the expression "the self perceives," there is a reference to the object of cognition, whereas in "it eats," there is a worldly usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding the objects that are the means to pleasure and pain.
Recognition and reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*)—such is its nature; its "function" (*vṛtti*), "mode of being" (*vartana*), or "activity" (*vyāpāra*) consists of these. Now, one might ask:
how could the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) act in this way toward one who is not a cognizer, not an enjoyer, and is blameless? He replies:
because the capacity for cognition and the experience of enjoyment reside in the intellect (*buddhi*), the Self superimposes [these qualities] upon itself in that very manner.

It functions [as such]. But how is it an auxiliary factor (*upakāraka*) in that regard? It is said: because, in its proximity, cognition arises as divided into the two natures of knowledge (*jñāna*) and experience (*bhoga*).
It is established in the intellect. Now, one might object: "Granted that action, characterized by the property of transformation, may not be real for the Self;
but why should its state as an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtā*) not be ultimate? To this he says: "Yes, indeed—but not for the Self.
It is pure consciousness alone, not the state of being an enjoyer of objects. And it has already been stated that no form other than that is appropriate for it.

In detail: Now, it might be argued that by means of the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra), the Self, though not actually an enjoyer, may be treated as such; but how can this [Self] experience enjoyment while being so treated? For in a metaphorical designation (upacāra), there is no modification whatsoever within the nature of the object designated; rather, such a state belongs only to the one who employs the designation.

Conventional usage consists in the acquisition of specific cognitions and words; otherwise, due to the distinction of infinite cognizers, even a young boy—whose body is differentiated by contradictory states such as fire and water being simultaneously attributed to it—would attain an infinite variety of contradictory forms even in a single moment. He [the author] refutes this as follows:

"By means of the self as it functions through the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra). By whom was this stated? That there is some enjoyment for the person (puruṣa) that is additional to its nature as consciousness. For that which the ego-sense (ahaṃkāra) deals with as being non-distinct from itself—the cognition within the intellect (buddhi)—is precisely what constitutes this enjoyment, when [the intellect] possesses the reflection of consciousness and the reflection of the object.

Within the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*), the ego-principle (*ahaṃkāratattva*)— which effects the worldly transaction by merging the two reflections of the conscious and the unconscious, namely "I" and "this"— produces a sense of self-identification (*abhimāna*).

That very [identification], once made the object of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) which is a function of the intellect, [arises] together with the principle of consciousness (*cit-tattva*) as the reflection within that intellect.

Conjunction (*saṃyoga*), characterized by having a single substratum, when it pertains to consciousness (*cittattva*)—because the distinction [between the reflection and consciousness] is not determined due to the reflection of consciousness (*citpratibimba*)—is called "experience" (*bhoga*). For even in systems such as that of Kaṇāda, the quality consisting of cognition is distinct from the self (*ātman*). How, then, could there be experience for that [self]? If you say "through inherence" (*samavāya*), then it is merely a relation.
It is thus stated that this is the cause for the state of being an object of enjoyment (*bhoga*). Here too, the connection has been demonstrated:

the reflection of consciousness (*cit-pratibimba*), which—because it is of the nature of consciousness (*cittva*)—has not yet determined its own difference [from the Self], becomes merged with the ego (*ahaṃkāra*) and, once determined by that very intellect (*buddhi*), [becomes an object] together with the reflection of the objective world.
The conjunction characterized by being the substratum of a single cognition— this is the basis for the entire worldly practice of experience, which is brought about solely through association.
(Page 156)

And let conjunction (*saṃyoga*), characterized by contact (*prāpti*), be the connection (*saṃsarga*)— whether it be inherence (*samavāya*) or some other technical term based on mere conceit— or rather, since such a conjunction cannot be determined as having a beginning even in the successive dissolutions and the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), this conjunction, being beginningless, is [identical to] inherence.

It does not differ. And all this is a property (*dharma*) of the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*). As for the relationship between the property and the possessor of the property (*dharmī*), let it be called conjunction (*saṃyoga*), identity (*tādātmya*), or inherence (*samavāya*).
For once the reality has been apprehended, what attachment to names or actions can be the cause for investigating the true nature of things?

Furthermore, in that very locus of the intellect where there is non-distinction from consciousness due to its connection with the reflection of the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*), there is likewise the connection with the reflection of blue; therefore, let it be said that this constitutes inherence (*samavāya*) by virtue of the relationship between substratum and superstratum and their inseparable existence.
What contradiction is there? In every respect, across all philosophical systems, this [inherence] is indeed produced by conjunction.
The conventional usage regarding enjoyment; as it has been said:
"In relation to external adjuncts, all cognition is merely conventional and non-correspondent to reality."
Thus he says, "either through conjunction or through inherence," using the word *vā* (or) to indicate that all these [alternatives] are untenable.
Activity in the form of "I act" or "I know" belongs to the principle of ego (*ahaṃkāra-tattva*);

it is by means of that activity that the self (*ātman*) engages in worldly transaction. It is the self that is fit for the transaction of experience, characterized by cognition and verbal designation.

The nature of that cognition which has been transferred to the intellect (*buddhi*)— consisting of the fusion of the reflection of the object with the reflection of consciousness— is its luminosity (*prakāśatā*), which is the absence of any determination of difference from the *puruṣa* whose nature is consciousness; and by virtue of this power, it is unfit to rest in mere [intellectual] content, which is like a state of swoon.
Experience is said to belong to the person when it culminates in the determination of non-difference [between the self and the intellect];
as for whether that [determination] arises from conjunction (*saṃyoga*) or inherence (*samavāya*), what does it matter? He corroborates this with the words of the Sage Śeṣa: "And thus:
experience is the non-distinction between the cognitions of the *sattva* and the person, which are absolutely unmixed."
"From *saṃyama* upon the distinction between the object of another and one's own self, knowledge of the *puruṣa* arises" (Yoga Sūtra 3.35).
This is the sūtra. Its meaning is as follows: *sattva* is that which is denoted by the term "intellect" (*buddhi*), and the *puruṣa* is that which is distinct from it; [the former is] insentient—

Because they both possess the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpatā*), just as in the case of the expression "a blue lotus," they occupy an identical level of reality and thus cannot tolerate a confusion (*saṃkara*) characterized by mutual coloring; nevertheless,

within the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of cognition, there is a non-distinction (*aviśeṣa*) resulting from the failure to determine their difference, which is the determination of non-difference.

The unity that is expressed when [the intellect] has come to rest is itself enjoyment (*bhoga*). That very same [unity], even while existing as the substrate of the intellect, is appropriate for the *puruṣa*, the enjoyer, because it is of the nature of consciousness; thus it is said to be "for the sake of another" (*parārtha*). Now, one might object: "Such an enjoyment indeed exists, being brought about by the power of this association; however, since this association is beginningless, how can it be severed?"

Anticipating the question of how there might be an opportunity for liberation, he says: "But when... First, *pradhāna* (primordial matter), as the material cause, undergoes transformation into the form of its effects, such as the *mahat* and so forth. In that process, its insentience (*jaḍatva*) and its state of being an object of experience—its fitness for enjoyment (*bhogayogyatā*)—consisting of pleasure and the like, exist.

It is a cooperative cause (*sahakārikāraṇa*). Furthermore, it is not appropriate for the *guṇas* to possess mutual fitness for experience (*bhoga-yogyatva*) because they are insentient (*jaḍatva*), and because the status of being an experiencer (*bhoktṛ*) and the status of being an object of experience (*bhogya*) are contradictory in a single entity. Therefore, a distinct nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpatva*) is what is appropriately suited for fitness for experience. And that nature of consciousness is manifold, as is evident from the perception of the variety of experiences. As it has been said:
"Because of the specific determination of birth, death, and the instruments" (Kārikā 18).
Furthermore, there is no cause for a restriction such that this object of enjoyment belongs to this particular enjoyer alone;
rather, it is an object of enjoyment for all, and their state of being enjoyers [is established] by means of the casting of their own reflections [into it].
The manifestation of the entire phenomenal world, beginning with the intellect (*buddhi*), occurs within the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*) which is characterized by multiplicity;
although [the Self] appears mixed therein due to the power of conjunction, it is in reality not mixed with the principle of consciousness (*cit-tattva*).
As long as that appearance of mixture is manifested through the force of the reflection of consciousness, so long does transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) persist. When, however—
Furthermore, regarding non-confusion: this is the knowledge of discernment (*viveka-jñāna*).
There is no object of perception (*dṛśya*) that exists apart from the forms of the confused and the non-confused. And as for that [non-confusion], with what could it be conjoined?
The word *ca* (and) here has the sense of the particle *api* (even/also). Nevertheless, this is merely a concessive argument (*abhyupagamya-vāda*); it is not supported by logical reasoning.
This is the meaning. Therefore, [the phrase] "or" (*vā*)—which was employed in the Sūtra to indicate a potential objection from another—is intended to show the acceptance of this position.
(Page 158)

Even though this has already been stated, the author of the *Ṭīkā*—intending to show disregard for the view that this reflection theory (*pratibimbavāda*) is untenable by demonstrating its manifold inconsistencies—clarifies the underlying intention (*ākūta*) of the passage from the *Vṛtti* beginning with "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*) by stating "and not" (*na ca*). [He explains: even though it is clear (*svaccha*),...

For that which is less transparent does not receive the reflection of something more transparent, just as a crystal gem does not receive the reflection of a white silk garment. And so it is with the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*) in relation to the *puruṣa*. For even light is less transparent when compared to the illumination of the intellect; likewise, that [light] too is less transparent in relation to the illumination of the *puruṣa*.

Having considered this: for the light of the Person (*puruṣaprakāśa*) is transparent in every respect, and it is precisely because of its independence from anything else that it possesses the nature of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpatva*). For to the extent that there is clarity of being an object of cognition (*vedyatā*), to that same extent there is an absence of transparency. Thus, a reflection is received by that which is more transparent, [and] not by that which is non-transparent.

The cause for the apprehension of a reflection is clarity; here, "lack of clarity" is the opposite of that cause—this is thus the perception of the contradictory of the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*). And this is the intention of the commentator who speaks in this way:
"Only a Buddhist, while refuting the Sāṃkhya doctrine, will provide an opening for my own position. [This applies] to that which is completely clear.

"The universe is capable of being reflected in the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*). Even for the Buddhist, the object of cognition (*saṃvedya*) imparts its reflection to consciousness (*saṃvit*), and not consciousness to the object of cognition; thus, the establishment of his own position indeed revolves within his own intention.
Now, the opponent might think: "Transparency (*svacchatva*) is not some technical term; rather, whatever..."

"That which is capable of receiving the reflection of another is indeed clear; and the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*) is certainly capable of receiving the reflection of the Puruṣa—so why is it not clear? To this, he replies:
"Only those possessing common characteristics [can reflect]. Here, a restriction is observed regarding the reception of reflections. For instance, in a mirror...

Tangibility, weight, and so forth do not reflect; rather, it is only the configuration (*saṃsthāna*) of form that does. And when its form is perceived as stainless—unclouded by forms of a different kind or by the absence of those of its own kind—and as possessing a dense, compact structure, then there is the possibility of reflection; however, this is not the case with vapors, dust, or other such forms.

We conclude from positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*) that it does not occur when that form is defiled by the absence of its own kind through qualities such as being non-dense or uneven due to heterogeneous elements.
(Page 159)
That which possesses the quality called clarity (*svacchatā*)—in relation to that which projects a reflection—is established as the locus of a specific attribute consisting of that reflection;

it is that very [clarity] which receives the reflection. Thus, although clarity is a common quality, its function is ultimately restricted to the state of being a specific form; he will conclude later that it is indeed not separate [from the substrate]. Thus...

"Only in that which possesses similar qualities. For instance, the quality called form (rūpa) exists in an earthen surface, in a mirror made of diamond-jewels and the like, in a water-body free from waves, and in the visual orb (dṛṣṭimaṇḍala) within the eyeball, which is of the nature of fire; and the quality consisting of configuration (saṃsthāna), which is its arrangement, exists even in those things that are predominantly transparent.

Because they possess form (*rūpavattva*), it is only the reflection of the configuration of form (*rūpasaṃsthāna*) that arises within them, and not other qualities such as weight or touch. As I myself have said: "The hidden lover [is beautiful] when reflected in the beloved."

"Even though she touches the mirror with her jar-like breasts, she does not experience joy. (Tantrāloka 3.6). Furthermore, in the expanse of space, when the solar light is neither too intense nor too faint, or when there is lunar light, and that space possesses a limited, elongated, or circular form, the reflection of the body's configuration is perceived there.

[This occurs] through the cultivation of the instruction on the "shadow-person" (cchāyāpuruṣa). However, it should be understood that the iron mirror and so forth are composed of light (taijasa); yet the Abhidharmikas maintain that even these are merely earthy (pārthiva). And in space, which has sound as its quality, there is a reflected form of the speaker's sound known as an echo (pratiśrutkā). [This occurs] by means of a predominant, stainless taste that perceives other tastes.
The gustatory faculty (rasanendriya) is pervaded, and its locus is the saliva (dantodaka), which is endowed with pure taste; therein, tastes such as pungent, bitter, and sour,
existing in substances like long pepper (pippalī), neem (nimba), and pomegranate (dāḍima), are tasted by another, preceded by the inference of that tasting.

They offer a reflection (*pratibimba*). The mention of "being remembered" (*smaryamāṇa*) indicates merely that, although [the objects] have been experienced, they are not being directly perceived at that moment. Therefore, the touch of rasa (*rasasparśa*) and so forth—whether being remembered, being inferred, or being imaginatively constructed—grasp a reflection. And thus:
Certain parts of the body, such as the *kanda*, the heart, the palate, and the base of the throat, are bases that constitute locations of bliss. Within these,
tactile sensations appropriate for sexual union— whether they are not currently being experienced, or are being inferred, remembered, or imagined— are likewise [sources of bliss].

It migrates to where there may even be the pleasure of the flow of the elements (*dhātu-syanda*). However, some are supports of suffering, such as the *mattagandha*, the belly of the tortoise, the channels (*nāḍī*), the throat, and so forth; in these, [the consciousness] is experienced by others.

Either the touch of spears, blows from clubs, or the like— brought forth by memory, imagination, and so on— produces fainting, pain, and other effects; and the experience of another person merely serves as a cooperative condition for the apprehension of that touch or similar sensation as it is reflected [in one's own mind].

He is awakening [the reader’s] attention. Therefore, this should not be said: "Even if it is not being tasted by anyone, why would the pomegranate juice not be reflected in the saliva? For it is indeed reflected;
however, due to a lack of attention, it might not even be perceived. To illustrate: a delicate woman, when attentive, [perceives] another...
Even when seeing the sharp point of a thorn being touched, one indeed experiences trembling.

Furthermore, due to the sovereign power of karma (*karmādhipatya*), certain supports (*ādhāra*) for some [beings] remain unstained; thus, a diverse reflection (*pratibimba-yoga*) is observed. Even in the case of a field of fragrance (*gandhakṣetra*), the scent of substances such as strong purgatives certainly projects a reflection.

By which [medium], one perceives everything as being filled with that very fragrance. Is it not the case that the rays of the eye, struck by a transparent substance, turn back and grasp one's own face? The notion "the face is in the mirror" is merely an illusion (*bhrānti*); there is no other category apart from reality (*satyatva*) and illusion (*bhrāntatva*).

"There is a third [category] called 'reflection' (pratibimba). Not so. For if that were the case, it would appear even that "this face of mine is tangible"; furthermore, both the original object (bimba) and its reflection are seen in another person’s face, one’s own hand, and so forth. Moreover, when there is a multiplicity of mirrors facing one another, how could there be the perception of many faces?

If it is argued that this is an illusion, let it be just that; what is the point of accepting the perception of a face as real when such a thing is not being experienced? For when there is the appearance of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, no other "real" silver-appearance is admitted. Furthermore, even in the case of an illusion, does it appear that the mirror itself is the face, or rather one's own face?

By virtue of being the face of the city: in the mirror of the previous kalpa, nothing would appear as it truly is, appearing instead as silver, a snake, or a double moon—just like [the appearance of] mother-of-pearl, a rope, or the single moon. And in this case, the face does not exist on the back of the mirror, nor within it, nor on its rear side.
The perception [of the reflection] occurs because the mirror, being free from conceptual construction, manifests [the image]. However, if one's own face were to appear as another's face,
(page 161)

Just as one perceives a mother-of-pearl shell through the cognition of silver, so too, when a mirror is placed near one's own face, one would perceive it through the cognition of another's face; thus, maintaining an attitude of indifference toward that [reflection], one would not attend to the arrangement of ornaments, decorations, and the like. And as for those things reflected...

If the embodied self were the presiding agent for the perception of visual rays that have come face-to-face with its own body, then there would be the cognition "this is I" alone, and not "this is another. For an unlearned person, such as a child, the cognition is of a single flavor, namely "this"; but one who is learned...

Let it be granted, for the sake of argument, that this very body has been transferred here. But surely there is no perception of these rays as distinct from their original source (*bimba*); rather, those rays, presided over by a bodiless self (*ātman*) in the form of a reflection (*pratibimba*), grasp them as something "other. If this is argued, we reply: no, for in that case, the body would not be the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*), since [the experience] would occur even without it.

Because enjoyment arises from the characteristic of external cognition, there would be the same consequence even in the absence of a mirror; furthermore, indifference toward one's own body would follow, and like a yogin, there would be the consequence of perception independent of a body.
Moreover, the reflection of visual rays occurs through their obstruction and rebounding by water and fire, but [this is not the case here].

The phrase "with dense stone surfaces" is a statement made according to one's own whim (*svacchanda*). Furthermore, in cases such as recollection or mental construction (*utprekṣaṇa*), the cognizer perceives the form of the object; yet, in those instances, there is neither any possibility nor any rule for the operation of the rays of the eyes toward that object. Nor is this ultimate form merely non-external while appearing as external.

Otherwise, there would be the consequence of denying external objects altogether due to overestimation (*abhimāna*). Now, if it is possible that even this [reflection] is neither primary nor manifest, then what wrong has been committed by the reflection of the perception? For in that case as well, the apprehension of one's own face is indeed mentioned by the Sage in some Sūtra.

Even though it has not been determined by the followers of Akṣapāda due to its difficulty of grasping, it is established that there is no reflection of the ear and other senses in an echo and the like;
therefore, in that case, the status of being a reflection must necessarily be established. [Objection:
But in that case, it will simply be the primary form of sound and so forth, whereas in the case of a face in a mirror and such, it occurs through obstruction.

The intention of others, such as the Naiyāyikas and so forth, is that the reflection is a negation (an illusion). He clarifies that very point with the words "But some [say]... A *pratiśrutkā* is that which has hearing (*śravaṇa*) by means of reverberation (*pratisaṃkramaṇa*); it is born from sound.
Taste, too, is [born from] the teeth—
(162) That which has become modified through the cause of recollecting the juice of the *nimba* tree and so forth associated with water possesses a very nature of pungent,
bitter, sour, and other such qualities; this specific quality of touch exists precisely within the field of touch.

And [the text says], "the specific fragrance is established in the field of fragrance. Therefore, just as other things such as sound and so forth possess the nature of primary entities (*mukhyavastu*) and are not of the nature of reflections thereof, likewise, in the case of echoes and the like, there is no subverting argument whatsoever against their being real entities. By the term "infusion of taste," [it refers to] saliva in the teeth.

It should be understood here that "the rasa has entered," or else, according to the opponent's view, the term "rasāveśa" (entry of rasa) is employed as a synonym for "pratibimba" (reflection). This opponent considers this "rasāveśa" to be a reflection of rasa;

however, it is more logical that it be considered as an actual entity (*vastubhūta*). Furthermore, it is not tenable to claim that a reflection is something graspable by a cognition that is sublated (*bādhita*).

[Otherwise] there would be the consequence that everything would be of such a nature [as a reflection]. Now, one might object: "In the case of a mirror as well, let it be simply another object, such as a mountain, whose nature consists merely in the configuration of form; why resort to the 'half-old-woman' logic (*ardhajaratīya*) of accepting a reflection even there?
To this he says: "But in the case of the mirror, etc. For, first of all, it is not in that very portion of space occupied by the mirror...
The simultaneous appearance of both the elephant and the mountain is logical, because that single spatial location occupied by one material object, such as a mirror,
cannot be occupied by another material object,
since there is a contradiction in material things occupying the same space; this is evident when a mirror is seen containing the reflections of an entire city.

How could so many material forms occupy a single location in space? This would lead to a hundredfold undesirable consequence of imagining their mutual interpenetration. Nor can they arise on the back of the mirror, because the location of the mirror is limited and it would follow that the mirror itself would no longer be visible. Nor...

That [mountain and so forth] is seen behind [the mirror], yet it is seen within; however, its entry into the unbroken mirror is not logical. Nor is even the slightest fracture observed in it. That mountain and so forth is perceived as if situated in a place much farther away than the mirror, and yet it does not occupy even an atom’s worth of space outside [the mirror].
It is observed that, as it has been said:
"In objects of contradictory dimensions, such as the surface of a diamond or a mirror,
there is no possibility for entities possessing the same form as mountains and the like to exist."

Thus, by the locative case, the substratum is implied. This is the meaning: regarding that which is suspected to be a real entity when reflected in a mirror or the like, this is the sublation (*bādha*). "To that extent" means delimited by the mirror.

Is it the region of space, or a mirror, or its back, its interior, or its rear surface? Furthermore, for as long as that object exists in its primary form, even its perceived connection with a specific location is not tenable; for it cannot exist without its own cause.

The arising of that entity is logical; however, no cause of the same class as those found in well-known entities such as elephants, mountains, and so forth, is perceived here. To that extent, the relation—consisting of conjunction, contiguity, and so on—between the parts that constitute a well-known elephant and their respective dimensions is [not present].

Because it is neither logical nor possible; and in the absence of causes of that same kind—namely, place, time, and material—the effect of that same kind could not exist either. Furthermore, how could there be a sudden, traceless destruction of what has arisen, like one seized by a spirit, while there is no cause such as the disintegration of parts, since [the object] has not yet ascended to such a state?

In the theory of momentariness (*kṣaṇikavāda*), even though that [reflection] is subject to destruction without leaving a trace (*niranvayanāśitā*), there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of seeing it as a separate continuity (*saṃtatyantara*). Furthermore, having arisen as something distinct from the mirror, it would move elsewhere, such as onto the ground;
consequently, for as long as it is seen, it would occupy that very same location delimited by the mirror.

As for the connection, how could it be? While form and configuration may well be devoid of weight, odor, and so forth, they are never seen to be devoid of touch. Furthermore, in this case, there is no sensation of hardness or touch belonging to the reflected mountain;
by the word "etcetera," one includes the coldness or heat of reflections such as water or fire.

It is logical that what is a real entity (vastu) must belong to the same class as other well-known real entities; otherwise, if one were to claim that even a rabbit’s horn possesses the nature of a real entity—such as having form, touch, and so forth—then the necessary pervasion (vyāpaka) of "being a real entity" would be undermined, namely, the restrictive rule that "this is indeed a real entity, this is not," which is observed to accompany it. Without this [restriction], [the definition of reality would fail].

Even "reality" (vastutva) would consist of nothing more than mere words; it would be lost. By the force of the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-perception of the pervader, reality—being excluded from the counter-example (*vipakṣa*) because it lacks the nature of being of the same class as other real things—is pervaded by the probandum, namely, being of the same class as other such real things. Thus, upon the non-perception of that [pervading property], the absence of reality is established.

"Because of the non-perception of the pervader. (Page 164) Thus it is established: that which consists of sounds and so forth produced from echoes and the like is precisely of that nature; there is no state of being a reflection therein.

Let it be so in the case of something like a reflection in a mirror; however, someone has made this distinction: that one's own face alone, being perceived, is mistakenly conceived as being perceived by the mirror. He refutes this distinction with the word "tat" (that). For it has been stated that an echo and the like are indeed real entities, whereas a mirror, an elephant, and so forth, are not real entities.
"Let it be a reflection for now"—this is incorrect when analyzed in detail, because the underlying logic is the same.

He states this very point with the words "here too. By the word "api" (too/also), he indicates the equality of the logic. Here, in the group beginning with the entry into the essence of an echo, as for that which is called an "echo," if it were indeed a real entity (*vastu*) like a sound produced by another sound, then it too—
Just as in the case of elephants and other such objects, that [sound] would indeed belong to the same class as sound; and as for another sound produced from sound,
such as the resonance of a drum (*bherībhāṅkāra*), which is heard in its final stage as being extremely faint, in that place where it is heard,
those perceivers do not hear that initial, most intense sound, nor even—

Therefore, like those who hear the first sound, he [the source] is perceived as the final, faint one. Likewise, as for the echo not being heard by those situated on this side, that would instead be contradicted if it were a real entity consisting of a sound produced from a sound. For us, it is considered to be the original object (*bimba*) by virtue of its being the giver of the reflection (*pratibimba*). Thus...
Thus, this is the primary form of sound. However, according to the opponent’s view, that initial sound is of a generative nature;
the connection is that it is heard as an echo by those living beings dwelling in caves who have not heard that [initial] sound.
The word "api" (even/also) indicates the opposite case: namely, by those situated in the space in front, that initial sound [is heard].

"Is heard" means that it would not be heard by them. Thus, by the phrase "that which is intended as an unperceived reflection" and so forth, the author has primarily stated its dissimilarity to other words that possess real existence (*vastubhūta*). However, this is not a reason for establishing its status as a reflection in the sense that "it is not heard by the primary word which is itself unperceived. For this [reason] does not apply to a reflection.
The rule is that [the reflection] is not perceived without the unseen original form. As I myself have stated in the *Śrītantrāloka*:
"Even without the primary object, the perception of the reflection may occur;
one may see a beloved who has departed behind one's back, yet marked as if carved before one's eyes in a mirror. (3.29)
Thus [it is said on page 165].
Therefore, because it is not perceived as belonging to the same class as a sound produced from a real object (*vastubhūta-śabda*), the echo (*pratiśrutkā*) is also not a real entity.
Furthermore, its similarity to well-known reflections such as those of elephants and so forth is demonstrated in the *Śrītantrāloka*.
Nor is this sound produced from another sound, because it is heard as arriving [from elsewhere] when there is contact with various openings formed by the placement of pots and other such objects.
And because this word is multiform, its reflection appears like that of a face or other objects,
manifesting as "this is the form of another cognizable thing."
"Just as in a mirror, so too shall I listen to whatever is spoken by anyone"—
because of this restriction, the reflection necessarily faces the original object.
But those observers situated in the middle, and not at a distance, hear it;
therefore, that [sound] is reflected in the space within the well, the mountain, and the pot.
The space within the mouth, being accompanied by sound, appears as if it were the speaker of another;
just as one situated behind a mirror does not perceive their own face.
Likewise, one situated behind such a space does not perceive the sound;
and it is certain that an unmanifested sound does not reflect.
In the second moment, there is the manifestation and the hearing of it simultaneously;
and the state of being a reflection and the hearing are simultaneous.

For [it is said]: "At the same time, we have the determination of the form of the shadow of the hand" (3.34), and so forth. Thus, having established the non-substantiality of an echo by demonstrating its difference from a real sound, he establishes the same for the reflection of taste.

Regarding the phrase "pungent, bitter, and so forth": first, substances such as long pepper (*pippalī*), neem (*nimba*), and pomegranate (*dāḍima*) are the inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) of that pungent taste and the rest; and by virtue of their conjunction and inherence, that [taste] is observed primarily in the saliva. But here, when another person is chewing a pomegranate, how could its arising occur in someone else? Now, [if it is argued...]
Even when being savored as a dominant condition (*adhipatipratyaya*) by means of pomegranate juice mixed with saliva,
it is [perceived] as being conjoined with one's own self.
(Page 166)

If, even in the case of water from another's teeth, the primary conceit of it being "juice" due to its belonging to the same genus (*tajjātīyatva*) as juice is established, then— since it is observed that every actual juice is invariably accompanied by touch— it follows that the aforementioned necessity of belonging to that same genus must apply; thus, even when touching a pomegranate, there would be a tactile sensation occurring in proximity to the water from the teeth.
Coldness and so forth would be apprehended; however, this is not the case. Now, it may be argued that the potencies of things are manifold;
thus, by way of its dominant influence (*adhipati-rūpa*), that [taste] is constructed through the conceit of inherence in what is conjoined (*saṃyukta-samavāya*).

Either the production of the mere taste occurs only in the dental fluid, or else its production therein is indeed ultimate; for in that case, regarding another substance endowed with a mere pungent or other taste, it would follow that there is no other taste in the non-dental fluid,
since it is logical that by the application of qualities, there is a fixed rule that the taste in water is only sweet.
If that were the case, then even one who is engaged in the act of chewing the wine from the mouth would experience that [taste] in the saliva of his beloved;
for if it is argued that the taste is concealed there because of its mixing with another portion of saliva transferred into it,
then by that same logic, when a person has withdrawn from such [an experience] and is engaged in tasting a pomegranate, [the previous taste would still persist].

That aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) would be experienced even at a later time, because it is like the water of a well or salt-water in its stability, or because it produces a continuous succession of similar moments. If it is argued that it is not experienced at a later time due to the lack of firmness in the mental impression (*saṃskāra*), then [it must be admitted] that it is experienced only at that very moment.

Even food such as rice with molasses (*guḍaudana*), which when eaten alone has but a single flavor and is therefore not particularly pleasing, becomes delicious when consumed by another after having acquired various other flavors—such as pungent or sour—and having been mixed with water from the mouth, like *śikhariṇī* mixed [with other ingredients]. The particle "iti" indicates the manner [of this]. Not only... [is this so].

In the case of an elephant or similar object appearing in a mirror and so forth, there is sublation (*bādha*). Even for those who have entered into the essence of an echo, you previously maintained that "this is not such-and-such a thing"; since that claim indeed exists, how could there be any reality (*vastubhūtatā*)?
For by means of that [claim], even in the case of a mirror, an elephant, and so forth, another person [the opponent] would deny the status of being a reflection.

The intention is that one might deny the conventional usage of "reflection" merely on account of its resistance [to being touched]. Now, an objection may be raised: "If it is a non-entity because of its difference from a real object, then it must be an illusion, like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; even so, what constitutes its nature as a reflection? Anticipating this doubt, [the author says:]...

(Page 167) He says: "And for this very reason. By this [reason], sublation (*bādha*) is not presupposed. For if the probandum were the absence of erroneousness (*bhrāntitva*), the possibility of sublation would make the logical reason (*hetu*) contradictory (*viruddha*). Therefore, regarding the distinction mentioned in the previously cited passage:
It exists as that which is being traversed, and it is upon this that [the cognition] depends. Therefore, the meaning is this:

just as there is no status as a real entity (*vastutva*) because of the absence of similarity with well-established entities, so too there is no status as an error (*bhrāntitva*) because of the absence of similarity with established errors. He demonstrates this very point with the words beginning "for in that" (*tasyāṃ hi*) and ending with "for this very reason" (*ata eva*).

When the opponent suspects that what is intended to be refuted is erroneous, the previously stated sublation (*bādha*) is relied upon as the reason; thus, the refutation is performed by stating "not so" regarding the erroneous nature that possesses a cause.
And the reason for this refutation is stated by the words beginning with "tasyāṃ hi," etc. The particle *ca* indicates the suspicion.

For this very reason, as for the objection raised by the opponent—that because it is subject to sublation, this must be an illusion consisting of the non-penetration of the mirror, the elephant, and so forth, rather than a reflection—that too is not valid. For in an illusion, only that which is being superposed appears; the name of the actual reality does not even flash forth.

For shape (*saṃsthāna*) is merely a property of form (*rūpa*); when form is concealed, that too is nothing at all. Or, even if shape were a property of the substance, if one were to accept that a substance is complete with all its properties, then even a slight alteration would result in the appearance of an entirely different substance, and not that very same one. But in this case:

The taste of rice and so forth appears even when it is not mixed with even a trace of any modification; rather, it is that very [taste] which appears, and it certainly does appear. If, however, the saliva in the mouth were to appear through delusion as being joined with a bitter taste or the like, then the taste of the rice would also appear as something variegated due to its being mixed with that [saliva]. For when a yellow conch-shell appears [in such a state], it is not [the case that the shell itself has become yellow].

The hand of Vāsudeva appears bearing a white conch. Therefore, just as no elephant exists on the back, inside, behind, outside, or anywhere else of a mirror, yet it appears there through the power of its own clarity, so too the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the rest do not exist in the saliva of the teeth or elsewhere; thus, this [manifestation] is indeed a reflection.
This is logical; and if that were possible, the perception of one's own face and so forth—which would be grasped by the rays of the eye that are not obstructed—would not be unperceived.
(Page 168)
He concludes that it is logical to conceive [the elements] in this way: therefore, sound resides in space; touch in some substratum-wheel (*ādhāracakra*);
form in a mirror and so forth; taste in the saliva of the teeth; and smell in its own field (*tatkṣetra*).
Thus, mounted upon the mind, they manifest as reflections—made evident through recollection, experience, imagination, and so on—according to their respective suitability.

For reflection is indeed nothing other than the essence of manifestation; thus, how could there be a conventional usage regarding the existence of a reflection for one whose mind is not engaged with that object? This is what is meant: if someone were to say, "Indeed, just as a stainless mirror—if it exists—necessarily becomes a reflection of whatever is proximate to it, so too..."
One might argue that reflections of taste and so forth could exist in things such as water used for rinsing the teeth, yet they do not manifest there eternally;
to this it must be said: here, the very essence of manifestation is the principle of reflection (*pratibimba*). As it is stated in the *Śrī Tantrāloka*:
"There is no location, no form, no connection with time, and no measurement..."
"There is no mutual contact, nor is there the loss of that [reflection], nor is there density;
it is neither a non-entity, nor does it possess any inherent essence of its own—thus, certainly, delusion would be stilled. Such is the instruction regarding the nature of the mirror. (3.23)

Thus [it is said]. Furthermore, manifestation depends upon the presiding of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) over the sense organs that grasp their respective objects. For instance, when a mirror is present, if the activity of the eye—which is prompted by the activity of the internal organ—is removed, how can there be the conventional usage of a "reflection of the face"? Indeed, who could perceive a face in pitch darkness?

It has been transferred to the jewel. Likewise, in the field of taste (*rasakṣetra*), which is the locus of the sense organ of taste, how could the reflected taste appear without the impelling of the sense organ of taste situated nearby—an act performed by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)? Nor can it be made an object of the senses by another subject.

It is the locus for the projection of that reflection, like a mirror or like the eyeball, by which its manifestation occurs through the operation of another perceiver's senses, rather than through its own direct apprehension. However, because it exists within the body— as in the case of the saliva and so forth, which are the fields of taste and other sensations— it should not be suspected of being an object for another perceiver.
Nor is it logical for that [object] to appear without the activity of its own sense organ being impelled by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*);
for appearance itself is the very essence [of cognition].
(Page 169)

There is no room for any objection regarding the term "reflection" (*pratibimba*). The phrase "of those not facing it" (*asaṃmukhīnānām*) means "of those whose eyes are not engaged [with it]. This meaning is derived through metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*): that in which something is seen face-to-face is "facing" (*saṃmukhīna*), namely the mirror; and since that [literal sense] is contradicted by tautology and lack of coherence, it refers instead to "clarity" (*nairmalya*).

By defining [the sense organ] as that which possesses the capacity to grasp its own object, it is stated that the sense organ is active (*vyāpṛta*). Others, however, maintain that in the term "vision" (*darśana*), it is also a derivation based on the agent (*kartṛ-sādhana*), and not exclusively a derivation based on the locus (*adhikaraṇa-sādhana*). Having thus concluded his own position, he also concludes the untenability of the opposing position with the word "primary" (*mukhya*): if that...

The word would have to be primary [in its own right]; otherwise, that sound would be heard by perceivers situated in locations other than the space between the place of the utterer and the place where it is grasped—namely, those residing within caves or the interior of mountains. Furthermore, if it were heard from those distant locations as well, like the resonance of a bell, there would be the perception of specific distinctions such as intensity or dullness. And yet, this is not the case.

This is so: even flavor might be perceived by another during the state of kissing; even scent, because it resides in that same location, might be perceived by other subjects; and even touch, such as the touch of another's hand, might become accessible—thus, for as many subjects as there may be regarding an object of a well-known similar kind, [the experience would be shared].

To that extent, it would also apply here; with this intended meaning, all sounds, tastes, smells, and touches would—according to their respective applications—bring about the provocation or pacification of wind, bile, and so forth, as well as their own specific effects. Even a sound existing within one's house, having arisen with its original intensity intact, ranges from the most intense down to the weakest degree.

If it were the originator of the five letters beginning with *ta*, it would be heard as even further beyond the cave (*guhā*). Therefore, there exists a third category characterized by reflection. And since manifestation is observed in something clear that possesses similar qualities, the cause for the acceptance of a reflection is characterized by clarity and similarity of qualities.

Thus it is established that [the reflection] belongs to objects. Furthermore, the fact that the intellect possesses qualities dissimilar to those of the self—namely, its lack of luminosity—is perceived as being contrary to its cause;

this perception negates the intellect's capacity to receive the reflection of the self, which is an effect incompatible with itself. He concludes this point as follows: "In this way, only that which possesses similar qualities..."

It has already been stated that transparency is grounded solely in the qualities (*guṇa*) and that it possesses the same properties as the aforementioned [qualities]; therefore, it is not mentioned separately here. Atidūra—(page 170)

The meaning is this: there is a disparity between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the self (*ātman*), because the intellect consists of the three *guṇas* and is thus an object of enjoyment (*bhogya*), whereas the self is devoid of the *guṇas* and is thus the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*). Therefore, how could there even be a possibility of them possessing identical qualities? Now, it might be argued that the Sautrāntikas maintain that the reflection of blue and so forth exists within consciousness (*saṃvit*), yet that [consciousness] does not possess qualities identical to those [reflected objects].

Anticipating the objection that "due to the connection with those impressions (*vāsanā*) proceeding from beginningless time, a state of having similar qualities will also occur in the intellect (*buddhi*)," he says: "Or even in the case of a reflection. Even while speaking thus, the Sāṃkhya must first be asked this: [How is] the determination of the object [established]?

Regarding that which is said to consist of perception and reflective awareness (*darśana-parāmarśana*), does it depend upon a primary, non-inert power of consciousness (*citi-śakti*) as its enjoyer, such that it cannot exist without it? If you say "yes," then one must instead admit that the *puruṣa* itself possesses the nature of perception and reflective awareness.

Is it by means of the doctrine that the power of consciousness (citi-śakti) is reflected in a cognition that is itself unarisen and not being experienced? Or does it proceed by means of the reflection of consciousness residing within the intellect (buddhi)? If that is so, then since that [reflection] is indeed insentient (jaḍa) and not of the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpa), one should rather postulate the intellect itself as being endowed with such a fourth quality (turya-guṇa), which [perceives] the object.
One will establish [this]; therefore, enough with the postulation of a person (*puruṣa*). As Devalācārya said:
"Having superimposed agency upon the person and consciousness (*cit*) upon the intellect (*buddhi*).
Now, it might be argued that it is the primary consciousness itself, having become a reflection, that acts in such a manner.

That is incorrect, because it is not observed elsewhere in a reflection. For fire reflected in a mirror would not even heat that very mirror, so how could it possibly have the power to burn fuel? And it has been said that what is established as being of a certain kind must necessarily be of that same kind, and not of a different kind.

Thus, the postulation of two entities—the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*)—is entirely useless. He states this with the words "even in the case of a reflection" (*pratibimbe 'pi vā*), and so forth.

By the word *api*, he indicates acceptance; by the word *vā*, he shows that having identical qualities is indeed the cause for a reflection. "We do not respect this" (*etat na ādriyāmahe*)—the word *api* here expresses disregard. In that context, "therein" (*tatra*) means in the intellect (*buddhi*). "Of that" (*tasyāḥ*) refers to [the intellect].

This applies even to a cognition that possesses the reflection of a person. And although this has already been stated previously by the passage beginning with "thus, since cognition is insentient," it is nevertheless stated here again to provide an opportunity for further refutation.
(Page 171)
For this very reason, he states "and of the intellect" (*buddheśca*) as a further point of deviation from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*), adding it by way of conjunction.
It is not possible for a reflection of consciousness (*cit-pratibimba*) or a form of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) to exist individually within its own cause, namely *pradhāna*.

Furthermore, even in that case, if [the world] were created by the Self (*ātma-kṛtatve*), this same fault would apply; moreover, there would be the additional fault of the uselessness of postulating an intellect (*buddhi-parikalpanā-vaiyarthyam*).

Furthermore, since the form existing in the cause is not transferred to the effect, the effect would have to acquire that [cause's] nature, and thus the self would become the cause. — "The Puruṣa is neither the primal nature nor a modification" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 3).

Thus, it would have to be abandoned [as a cause]. In that case, since the first modification of the Self itself is the intellect (*buddhi*), the postulation of a *pradhāna* (primordial matter) would be useless. Now, one might object: "Just as in the case of a jar, the lump of clay alone is the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), while the staff, wheel, place, time, potter, and so forth are merely..."

That which is produced by the material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa) is the mere particularity (viśeṣa-mātra) denoted by the term "residual" (śeṣa), and it is that [particularity] alone which the auxiliary cause (sahakārin) brings about; likewise, the Self would be an auxiliary merely by virtue of performing the assistance of the residual factors, not the material cause. Furthermore, the effect exists in the material cause, but not in the auxiliaries, because otherwise there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of an infinite number of effects arising [simultaneously].

Anticipating the opponent's view, he says: "By the proponent of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause" (*satkāryavādin*). If, first of all, the auxiliary causes do not operate even upon that specific portion which is impossible for the material cause to produce, then these [auxiliaries] are useless;

but if they do produce it, and if that [portion] is non-existent, then why this reproach against the material cause—that it is at fault? For how could there be this censure regarding what is internal...?
The nature of the effect is superimposed upon this [cause],

because the reasoning— beginning with "that which is non-existent cannot be produced" (Sāṃkhyakārikā 9)— is equally applicable. Therefore, the essential nature of the effect resides within the causal complex itself.

This must be accepted by the proponent of the theory that the effect pre-exists in the cause (*satkāryavādin*): that [the capacity] consists of an accumulation of factors (*dharma-saṃcaya*), and not something existing within a single material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), because otherwise it would follow that auxiliary causes (*sahakārin*) are useless. But surely some auxiliaries do indeed enter into the form of the material cause and thereby attain the status of being causes?

For the sap, which is a transformational product of water and earth, enters into the state of existing within the seed itself by means of a forceful heat manifested over time; it is by that much [process] that the variegated sprout [is produced].

Because [the self] attains its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), other factors—such as merit (*dharma*), demerit (*adharma*), and the goals of human life (*puruṣārtha*)—are engaged merely in its manifestation (*abhivyakti*). What consideration can there be regarding their inclusion within the remainder of the task (*kāryaśeṣa*)? If this is so, then since manifestation is not a remainder of the task, these [factors] operating therein are like a lamp, the eye, and so forth.

How could there be a reckoning of causality? If it is argued that the effect is merely a remainder [of the cause], then it is simply non-existent. Just as those [auxiliaries] bring about these [effects], so too would the material cause (upādāna) bring about the primary effect; therefore, enough with this obsession with the doctrine of the pre-existent effect (satkāryavāda). Thus he says:

"Abhyupeyāḥ"—this is the suffix *yat* added to the root *iṇ* in the sense of "deserving. From that [state], how could there be pure consciousness (*cinmātratā*) in the self (*ātman*), given the persistence of the excess of mental afflictions (*ādhi*) resulting from the remainder of one's duties? Now, one might object: "The self will possess such a nature; what is wrong with that, or what does it gain by being pure consciousness? To this, he says: "And in the state of isolation (*kaivalya*..."

Thus: first of all, the abandonment of the accepted [position] that there is pure consciousness (*cinmātratā*) is itself a deviation from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*); and the word "and" (*ca*) indicates that this also brings about another deviation from established tenets.
For instance, in the state of isolation (*kaivalya*), no reflection of consciousness arises in the intellect (*buddhi*);
therefore, at that time, the *puruṣa* is by nature devoid of causal agency. From that—

The two states—being previously joined with the remainder of effects consisting of reflections and subsequently being separated from them—are contradictory by virtue of being existence and non-existence. Consequently, due to this conjunction with contradictory attributes, the unity of the person (puruṣa) could not be immutable. For this very reason, and no other, is the cause for the non-immutability of primordial matter (pradhāna) as well. Now, one might object:

Fearing that even in the state of isolation (kaivalya), its capacity [to produce effects] would not cease, and that this would constitute a remaining task for the Self—just as the primary cause (pradhāna) has a remaining task during the great dissolution (mahāpralaya)—the author introduces another point of proof with a different reason in the middle of the argument, saying "for not... and "never at any time... regarding the phrase "immediately thereafter."

[Objection: Intentionality [is the cause]. Even in a jar, there would be the capacity for a cloth; or even in a person, there would be the capacity for the production of the Great Principle (mahat) and so forth.

Thus, causality, in the form of capacity, is excluded from the counter-example (vipakṣa)—namely, that which lacks the state of existing prior to the effect—by its pervader, namely, being subject to a restriction [of specific effects], and [therefore] it is established by the state of existing prior to the effect.

It is pervaded [by that], and yet it is not perceived here—this is the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). In the state of isolation (*kaivalya*), the self (*puruṣa*) is not the cause of reflection, because of its existence prior to the effect; and the existence prior to the effect is pervaded by its existence subsequent to the effect.

Its opposite, the absence of that [effect], negates the state of being antecedent to the effect. In isolation, the *puruṣa* is never antecedent to an effect, because there is no occurrence of an effect subsequent to it.

This is an instance of the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*). The underlying intention is that if there were even the possibility of the effect occurring at some time subsequent [to the cause], then absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) would not exist. Alternatively, regarding the phrase "the loss of pure consciousness" (*cinmātratāhāni*), this is the remaining intention: that which [arises] from that pure consciousness in the form of an enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*).

If [the self] were greater than the light (prakāśa), how could it be the essential nature of the enjoyer? For, due to the occurrence of contradictory attributes, the nature of the person (puṃs) would not be unmixed; thus, what was said [previously] was intended to exclude the state of being subject to transformation (pariṇāmitva). Now, if it is argued that [the self] is both conscious and unconscious in nature and yet remains one, then the establishment of the distinction [of the self] from the intellect (buddhi) and other [factors] follows.

"Useless," he says. Having thus stated the refutation of the person (*pums*) by including [the soul] within the remainder of the effects, he states another refutation by way of a concessive argument (*abhyupagamya-vāda*), beginning with "And in the state of isolation (*kaivalya*). Even if there were no inclusion therein within the remainder of the effects, nevertheless, there is a contradiction consisting of being both a cause and a non-cause.

The transformation of the dharma into the apūrva is unavoidable. Now, it may be argued that apart from its nature as consciousness (*cidrūpatā*), the self possesses no other form known as causality—[as it is said]:
"The *puruṣa* is neither a primal cause (*prakṛti*) nor a modification (*vikṛti*). (Sāṃkhyakārikā 3)
By the statement "itivacasā," there is the expression of the negation of the sevenfold agency; thus, the purpose of the Puruṣa alone is the cause—(Sāṃkhyakārikā 31).

By this [verse], however, it is shown that because the Pradhāna, which is the material cause (*upādānakāraṇa*) of the entire universe, consists of pleasure and so forth, [it acts for the sake of the Puruṣa].

The nature called "objectivity" (*bhogyatā*) is what is termed "visibility" (*dṛśyatva*); that very thing has been described as the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). However, that [objectivity] is not possible with respect to its own self, because there is a contradiction between the object of enjoyment and the nature of the enjoyer. Therefore, it relates to the conscious, non-inert enjoyer, the *puruṣa*; and since there is no distinction [in this regard], it pertains to all *puruṣas*.

Having restated the opponent’s position—that cognition is established [as the cause], but the person never performs anything at all—he refutes it with the words "even when the intellect exists" (*buddhisadbhāve 'pi*). By saying "not by its proximity" (*na tatsaṃnidhāne*), he negates that proximity is the meaning of the locative case in the sense of being a causal condition (*nimittatva*). This is what is meant:
