That which was stated (on page 174) for the sake of establishing the system of bondage and liberation— "though it has perished for one who has attained his goal, it is not perished because it is common [to all]"— [is now addressed].

Thus, in that context, if the relationship— which is manifested by the case-ending used as a *karmapravacanīya*— expressed as "with reference to that person" (*taṃ puruṣaṃ prati*) is not real, then nothing at all would have been stated. If, however, it is real, then when the proximity [of the person] is declared to be the instrumental cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), how could the person be of a non-causal nature?

If [the soul] were of the nature of a cause, liberation would be impossible because it would be eternal; if it were at some time not of the nature of a cause, its immutable nature (kūṭasthatā) would be lost due to the conjunction with qualities both contrary and non-contrary. Thus, by the commentary (*ṭīkā*) beginning with "And thus, it is not absolutely pure" and ending with "its [impurity] would not arise in its proximity," [this objection is addressed].

The state of being an object of disregard mentioned in the Sūtra has been clarified by the commentary (*vṛtti*) through the phrase "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*), which expresses an admission (*abhyupagamya-vāda*), and further elucidated by the phrase "and thus" (*tathā ca*), which— by demonstrating the untenability of the opposing view through many branches of argumentation— makes the intended meaning explicit. Now...

Even though one desires to avoid the superimposition of contradictory attributes, such a superimposition inevitably occurs because she [the intellect] would possess the nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpatā*).
Thus, he explains this by means of another formulation: "The Self" (*ātmā*). And in this regard, the following alternative must be considered:
"This Self has the nature of consciousness (*citsvabhāva*), and this intellect (*dhī*) is that which bears the reflection of consciousness (*cicchāyādhāriṇī*)."

Is this established by the force of experience, or because some object cannot otherwise be accounted for? He refutes the first alternative with the words "due to the connection with the reflection of the self. "According to experience" means in accordance with experience, that which is suitable to experience; and in experience, there is only one [entity] consisting of pleasure and so forth.

The reality, which is of the nature of consciousness (*caitanya*) due to its self-luminosity, remains as a real entity; it maintains its stability by the force of uncontradicted valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of direct experience. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of "also"; that is, having accepted both the self as the reflector of the reflection of consciousness and the reflection produced therein within the intellect (*buddhi*).

This is what is meant: even though consciousness is produced as a reflection of the Self, the supreme seers—who fear the acceptance of contradictory attributes—have nonetheless accepted a single principle called *buddhi*, which is of the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*) and takes the form of feeling (*sāta*) because it consists of pleasure and the like. And therefore, by the force of its manifestation...

That very thing will be the nature of the grasper. For in this world, the realization "I know" is uncontradicted for everyone. In that context, the "this" aspect appears even externally as a form common to all subjects.

In transactions such as buying and selling, [the Self] is reflected within; yet it is also uncommon [to the body] in mental constructions such as daydreams and in conceptual thought (*vikalpa*). In that regard, it is logical that the reflection of the object of perception is deposited in the intellect (*buddhi*); however, that which shines forth and is determined within the intellect as the very form "I"—that alone [is the Self].

It appears through the permeation of pleasure and so forth; as it has been said: "And this alone is our pleasure, namely, agreeable experience. However, the form "I" (aham) has never been experienced elsewhere [in the objective world] such that it could be projected onto the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*). Nor is that form admitted to belong to the *puruṣa*, because it is a modification (*vṛtti*) of the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*).
Because it is so accepted; for apart from "I" and "this," there is no experience of any other reality whatsoever.

Furthermore, the self does not perceive the principle of the intellect (*buddhi-tattva*) by which it could know: "This is my reflection of consciousness. Nor is there any third observer of these two who could determine it thus.

One may employ such terminology or apply such designations. Furthermore, there is no contradiction between consciousness (*caitanya*) and the nature of pleasure and so forth, because pleasure and the like manifest by virtue of having the nature of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśa*), and self-luminosity itself is the very essence of consciousness.
It is only that [consciousness] which is devoid of the forms of pleasure and so forth, yet consists merely in the apprehension of an object.

"Consciousness is perceived"—by this method, in order to express that [consciousness] is the specific differentiator of the form of the mind (*citta*), the *Abhidharma* and other treatises employ the conventional expression "feeling and so forth," while maintaining that the mind is merely consciousness (*saṃvedana-mātra*).
In that regard, by the force of experience, the "will" (*cicchā*) produced by the Person (*puruṣa*) is established as distinct. Now, [an objection]: [The text continues: "But surely..."
Due to the mutual conjunction of the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*), this delusion arises that pleasure itself is self-luminous.
It has been stated elsewhere:
"If there were non-differentiation due to conjunction, it would be like a fire-ball and fire."
This established distinction between difference and non-difference has been destroyed in all things.

Thus [it is asked]: whose is this delusion? It is not of the intellect (*buddhi*), for it does not perceive the person (*puruṣa*). Nor is there a third [entity], as it has been stated that "there is only one," meaning one that perceives those two as conjoined;
it is neither of the nature of the duality of intellect and person, nor is it of the single form of a delusion produced by their conjunction.

By virtue of entering the sphere of experience; for the object of knowledge is not of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvid-rūpa*)— neither this [subject] nor its object— and precisely because of that difference in objects, it appears in manifold forms such as pleasure, pain, and so forth.
Furthermore, because it exists with a distinction that appears as if excessive, though it is not actually excessive, by way of its mental form (*caittarūpa*),
we perceive it as distinct at every moment, flowing on in the manner of a continuum (*saṃtānavṛtti*).
Since there is no experience of anything beyond this for any cognizers, the doctrine of the illusory transformation of Brahman (*brahmavivartavāda*) is also not [tenable] by means of a single term.

Another [author] suggests that [the self] is established as something else. Thus, he states "only to that extent" (*tāvanmātra eva*) to show that neither the first alternative is logical nor is the second tenable. By the use of the word "only" (*mātra*), [he implies that] whatever form of this [self] appears—be it its self-luminosity, its status as the grasper of objects, its nature as pleasure and so forth—as long as it is a form conceptually constructed through various exclusions (*vyāvṛtti*), by that [form alone], it is not [established].
He shows that there is a certain distinction regarding this [consciousness]. By means of the particle *eva* (only), he negates anything additional.

Since the attainment (*āpti*)—that is, the fulfillment (*saṃpatti*)—of the experience of objects (*arthabhoga*), which consists in the thought "I know this" and which is non-negatable, occurs in its complete form, correctly and without error, therefore [it is] from consciousness (*saṃvitti*) in the form of the experience of objects.

What purpose could be served by postulating that there exists some kind of self (*ātman*) existing through relation, inherence, or other such connections, if it were otherwise impossible for any object? In this way, the word "impossibility" (*anupapatti*) as it occurs in the commentary has been explained. Thus, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that was stated by means of the arguments set forth in the two preceding sūtras—
The meaning is that, by contrast with that, knowledge which is impermanent in nature and not dependent on anything else is established. Thus,

regarding the reason "because of the union of knowledge and action," having examined the aspect of knowledge, the author uses the word *api* (even/also) in the phrase "even though [action] exists" (*sad api*) in order to instruct that action must likewise be analyzed as being inherently connected to that [knowledge], lest the logical reason be undermined.

This is for the purpose of providing an opening for the subsequent verse (*uttarakārikā*). Indeed, the word "also" (*api*) illuminates the *anvavasarga* (granting of permission) regarding *sattva* in the form of acting according to one's own will; furthermore, it reveals that for anything else, even the very existence (*sattva*) cannot be apprehended.
And the commentator (*ṭīkākāra*) will explain this very point with the words "But the action... and so forth, using the word "also."
Thus far [the explanation]. For this very reason, the meaning of the subsequent kārikā has been explained here in brief by the author of the Vṛtti.
"In this way" (*iti*) means by which method of reasoning the Noble One spoke thus; that [method] is [concluded] with this much [on page 177].

This means that it has been determined by the treatise (*grantha*). In that regard, "in perception" (*pratyakṣe*) refers to the apprehension of an object, which consists in the experience of the thing and exists as an undeniable manifestation; [perception] stands as the instrumental cause. "Accomplished" (*samāptaḥ*) means properly attained or established:
characterized by conceptualization corresponding to such a manifestation within one's own self, and likewise [characterized by such a manifestation] with respect to another.

And for this reason, consciousness is [the ground] of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*), which is characterized by the performance of transitions and the presentation [of objects], expressed by the words "renown" (*prakhyā*) and "narration" (*upākhyā*), and preceded by that [consciousness];
and which consists of the purposeful activity of engagement and attainment, taking the form of the manifold mutual acquisition of subjects and objects of knowledge. Therefore, consciousness...

That which is said to be "the mere power of consciousness," characterized as the *puruṣa* and capable of being denoted by an abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) whose primary function is to exclude other attributes— that is useless and purposeless;
for no purpose whatsoever is accomplished without it that could not be established otherwise.

The meaning is that it should be postulated. Thus, the formal argument (*prayoga*) is as follows: "In the midst of the cognition of an object, the self is not to be conceptualized, because neither [the self] nor its cause is perceived, since the experience would otherwise be inexplicable. This is a non-perception of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*).
For fire is indeed something additional to the potsherds and so forth in a kitchen, and to the trees, stones, and so forth on a mountain, as is known through experience.

Or, it is postulated because smoke would otherwise be inexplicable; thus, the postulation that it has that [fire] as its cause arises because a postulation of it being causeless or having another cause is incompatible with the observed necessity.
But, if the determination is made in this way according to experience, then blue is pleasure, yellow is...

One must accept only this much: that "suffering" is what appears; however, the notion of "I" is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), for nothing further shines forth therein. Indeed, it is blue that appears, not some "blue-appearance";
even regarding the cognition of that [blue], what partiality is there, such that one would act as if taking pity on it, even though it exists?
Anticipating the objection that the opponent might accept this [position], he says: "In the case of the non-existence of cognition.

For you yourself have stated that "the blue shines forth. Now, if that part which is expressed as "it shines forth" here were the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the very nature of the blue, then just as the blue exists for all subjects (*pramātṛ*), it would not fail to exist [for them].

Or, he too might be like that. This is what he states with the words "for not," and so forth. "It would be like form" means that its being or non-being should be considered identical [to that of form].
(Page 178)

The particle *tat*, occurring in the sense of "therefore," states that [the following] is the reason—something that must necessarily be admitted because its own opposite, which was indicated by the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*), is actually observed.
For knowability does not belong to all cognizers, nor does it not belong to all cognizers; rather, [it belongs to some].
It is [the state of] cognition alone, and not the essential nature of the object, that exists for a particular cognizer;

this is the meaning of "known-ness" (*jñātatā*). Now, one might object: "Let it be so with respect to cognition, but how can it be *perception* (*pratyakṣa*)? For perception is that which is inferred from the result consisting of 'manifestness' (*prakaṭatā*) residing in the object, and not that which consists of self-luminous consciousness independent [of such a result]."

Or they say that it is to be inferred from its result: for no one perceives cognition when the object is unknown, but once the object is known, one understands [the existence of cognition] through inference. Thus, the existence of the object is not observed to be possible in any other way.
If it is argued that knowledge does not [arise], then a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must be established subsequently for that very reason.

Thus, it is not the mere intrinsic nature (*svarūpamātra*) of the blue that constitutes its "knownness" (*jñātatā*), such that it would be urged [as being known] by all subjects; rather, its "knownness" is its manifestation (*prakaṭatā*) or its cognition (*saṃvitti*). The knowledge that produces this—being of the nature of mental cultivation (*bhāvanā*) and consisting of an activity (*kriyātmaka*)—is what is to be inferred from it, but knowledge itself is not the "knownness. Anticipating this objection, he says:

"From this very [fact]" (*ata eva*). By this, he states that it is an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta* (a conclusion established by the context), according to the definition: "That upon whose establishment the establishment of another topic occurs is [an *adhikaraṇasiddhānta*]" (Nyāya Sūtra 1.1.30).
For here, the reason is indicated by the word *yat*; however, in the phrase *saḥ*, it refers by metaphorical designation to that which has that [reason] as its cause.

The point to be proven (sādhya) has been stated; thus, there is no contradiction with the meaning of the proposition (pratijñā). Furthermore, the reason (hetu) also does not forfeit its status as a tenet (siddhānta), because it consists of an accepted position rooted in valid means of knowledge (pramāṇa). Alternatively, since the reason is implied by the very fact of being "to be proven" in the phrase "for the sake of proving that which is to be proven," it is indeed characterized by a specific reason.

The thesis is thus established: for this very reason—that all cognizers have been shown to be eternal—cognizedness (*jñātatā*) is nothing other than cognition itself, and not "manifestness" (*prakaṭatā*) or "consciousness" (*saṃvitti*). Since this is the case, that cognition must be accepted as being directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*), established through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). The word *yadā* is used here in the sense of *yad*.
The word "tadā" means "therefore"; that is to say, whatever object is established by a specific reason, from that reason [follows] its perceptibility.
(Page 179)
However, if it were explained in the sense of "because" (*yasmāt*), then the fact that "it is thus" (*evam*) would not be stated as the reason for that entity;

rather, when "it is thus" is reflected upon, some other cause would have to be stated as the reason for the probandum under discussion. For [the inference] "he possesses smoke because he possesses fire" is indeed the direct [formulation] of these [reasons].

The reason by which this [mountain] was established as possessing smoke, or rather, that which was known [as such], is the reason for its possessing fire. But this is not what is intended; rather, it is the possession of smoke itself that is intended to be stated as the reason for possessing fire. And that [intended meaning] is not directly perceived from this sentence. Therefore, regarding the intended meaning, it is thus clear:

The verbal formulation is: "Because it possesses smoke, therefore it possesses fire. For at the time of restating [the reason], only its own form (svarūpa) is to be referred to, not its status as a logical reason (*hetubhāva*). That [status] is to be enjoined later when it is to be referred to by the word *tat* (therefore). Therefore, in such instances, it is thus...

The following explanation should be applied: in the case of "possessing smoke" (*dhūmavān*), either the verbal form itself or the cognition [of it] stands as the subject by internalizing the meaning of the word "thus" (*iti*). Since the linguistic usage consisting of the word or the cognition "possessing smoke" arises from the object characterized by the state of possessing smoke, for that reason [one concludes] "it possesses fire" (*agnimān*).

Alternatively, since this [subject] is established as possessing smoke by virtue of the cause consisting in the cognition [of smoke], that cognition of the possession of smoke is the reason for the possession of fire; thus, the ablative case in the explanatory portion (anuvādabhāga), by implying a cognition whose object is the reason, makes it known that a reason which is not cognized cannot function as a reason. This very point is not tenable.
For instance, at the time of being restated (anūdyamānatā), the ablative case is not employed after the word expressing the reason, such as *yasmād dhūmavattvāt* ("because of possessing smoke");

rather, it is only the nominative, as in *yato dhūmavattvam* ("since there is possession of smoke"). Thus, the understanding conveyed by "yasmāt" has been explained. With this intention, the ancient authorities maintained that even when the reason is being restated, the ablative case is used.
For [it is] employed because of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of prior experience— as in [the verse beginning] "from" (2.5)—
whereas those of the present day, relying merely on conventional renown, are like swallowing an unbroken coconut.
Those who do not grasp the true nature of reality engage in conventional discourse. When it is said, "At such a time," or "In this particular moment of time, this object exists;
therefore, that [other] object also exists," there arises an understanding of the relationship between cause and effect.

This is obtained by implication: since that which is being restated (*anūdyamāna*) is already established as prior, it is appropriate for it to function as the cause (*hetu*) in the phrase "when" (*yadā*);

whereas that which is being enjoined (*vidhīyamāna*) in the phrase "then" (*tadā*), being something previously unestablished, possesses the state of being the effect (*sādhyatva*) and thus is the possessor of the cause (*hetumat*). Enough of this prolixity.
The meaning—that cognition itself is the state of being known (*jñātatā*)—is established for all cognizers by this specific reason (*viśiṣṭahetu*).

By means of this [reasoning], for that reason, the perceptibility of cognition is established. However, if we were to establish that "the state of being known" (jñātatā) is indeed cognition itself through some other reason, then in that position, this [other] would not function as its cause;
thus, it is the causality of a cause that possesses a specific cause, and not otherwise.

According to the principle stated in *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā* 2.37, "Even that which is dependent [on another] is itself to be abandoned," when a previously established reason is intended to serve as a further reason for a given point, that prior reason is indeed discarded.
For example: "This [mountain] possesses fire because it possesses smoke; and because it possesses smoke, it possesses fire; therefore... [the initial reason is subsequently subsumed].
In the phrase "producing the affliction of headache," this preceding reason is relied upon; likewise here as well, it is stated in order to express this [point], namely:
"Therefore, when cognition itself is cognizedness...
The intended meaning here is as follows: if "manifestness" (prakaṭatā) is produced here for the object, then what is that [manifestness]?

If the property of an object, like its form (*rūpa*), requires cognition within itself, or does not: in the former case, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), for in that [cognition] as well, another manifestation produced by cognition must be asserted, and in that too yet another; thus, one who perceives the manifestation would never perceive the object as manifested as long as cognitions are not exhausted and do not cease.

It may even take thousands of ages. Now, if that manifestation of the object has occurred, then that object has become manifest; what else remains to be sought? In that case as well, let it be whatever the status of the object may be; however, regarding the relation to a specific subject—such as "it is manifest to me" or "it is manifest to Maitra"—that which faces [the subject]...

Being the basis for the regulation of a multitude of purposeful activities (*arthakriyā*) consisting of a mere succession of conventional practices such as "turning [the wheel]" and so forth, how could that [pot] be the cause of manifestation? If you say it is the cause of the relationship between producer and produced, then when a pot arises from the activity of a potter, it would be so only for that [potter]. For what distinction is there such that—

The jar, however, possesses its own manifestness which generates that [reflection]. Consequently, within the state of being a jar, the purposeful action performed by the reflection would be produced solely by that [manifestness], just as it is in the case of manifestness itself. As it is said:
(page 181)

The form residing in the entity is common to all [entities] for the sake of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*), just as whiteness resides in a cloth; such is its manifestness. For if the form inherent in the entity were not thus [common], its pervading external nature would be lost; therefore, it possesses causal efficiency through its non-commonality with the contrary case.

The reason (*hetu*), having been excluded by the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of the non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*), is pervaded by the probandum (*sādhya*); thus, it is an essential nature (*svabhāva*). Now, one might object: "Duality, which is produced by a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), does not perform a causal function (*arthakriyā*) in common with anything else; therefore, [your reason] is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*). This is not so, for the inconclusiveness is unestablished (*asiddha*).

For the Buddhist, there is no form of duality existing within an entity apart from the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Even for one who holds that view, [duality] does not perform causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) through its own specific uniqueness (*asādhāraṇya*), because the atomicity (*aṇutva*) residing in the dyad arises from duality which is common to all [atoms],
and because duality is not generally productive of causal efficiency.

Moreover, that is knowledge; nor is it an external form residing in an entity. Now, if it is asked why that knowledge should not belong to everyone, it is said in response that this is not denied even here. Just as duality arises here through a relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*), so too does the cognition of its universal (*sāmānya*) arise from that.

There is the cognition of the quality of duality, and from that, the cognition of two substances, namely "two substances. This does not exist for another [type of cognizer], because that very [cognition] is absent in them. If it is asked, "Why is the relative cognition (*apekṣābuddhi*) the cause for the production of the cognition of the universal of duality?", one should counter-question: "In the production of the cognition of color, why is light the cause? For it is according to what is observed [that causes are established].

Let us set aside the established distinction between cause and effect. Now, it might be argued that a jar, being known, performs its causal function (arthakriyā) in a common way, yet there is no cognition within the state of manifestation itself. If that were so, then that manifestation would not serve the causal function for anyone at all. Or, if it is argued that—just as in the case of duality—there will simply be no cognition of it by everyone, then [the following applies]:

It has been stated that if manifestation were itself manifest, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). This objection applies equally even to those who maintain that cognition is inferred from its fruit, which is consciousness (*saṃvit*) not dependent on the nature of a cognizer; for in their view as well, the linguistic usage "this is my consciousness" would remain unestablished. Now, if it is argued that this [usage] occurs even without another consciousness of manifestation, then...

It would apply to all cognizers, because there is no distinction [between them]. If it is argued that the manifestation of those two—consciousness and manifestness—is itself manifestness when it rests within the cognizer, then [we reply] regarding the entity (bhāva):
[page 182]

With the intention of asking "What offense has been committed?", the word *eva* (only) is used to emphasize that it is indeed cognition [that is affected]. In memory, in inference regarding the past and future, and so forth, just as an object—though non-existent—cannot tolerate attributes such as gestures or winking within itself, how could that which is indefinable (*anupākhya*) tolerate even its own manifestation? Thus, it is not [the case that the object is absent].

The meaning of the particle *eva* is also that this [manifestness] is a property (*dharma*) of some object. Thus it is established that manifestness is indeed cognition (*jñāna*), because it is intended as the very cause of "cognizedness" (*jñātatā*), which is of the nature of the cognition sought to be inferred.
It is its adjunct (*upādhi*); for an object is said to be "cognized" precisely because cognizedness is its adjunct. Otherwise, [if it were not so], it would always be [manifest] and to everyone.

How could it not be known? For it has been stated in the *Viniścaya*: "The dull-witted have been conquered," thus mocking [the opponent] who accepts that what is called "knowledge" is an instrument of cognition (*buddhi-sādhana*) but does not accept cognition itself—[the Lord] being one whose progeny are praiseworthy—and [it was asked], "Is this not the cognition of a manifestation? And [it was said]: "Is this not that very knowledge which, by its own nature, is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa-rūpa*)?"

Anticipating the objection that "that very [Self] will be the Self," he says: "And of that... The phrase "having the knowable as its limiting adjunct" (*jñeyopādhi*) means that the spatial distinction produced by the knowable—such as "the jar is here"—which serves as the cause for the suspicion of its being all-pervasive (*vibhutva*), certainly appears; likewise, the temporal distinction—such as "the jar is now"—which is the cause for dispelling the delusion of its being eternal, certainly appears. Furthermore, even that which...

Even in the cognition of pleasure and so forth, a distinction of space and time certainly appears, produced by the limitation of the body which is eternally connected [to it] through dependence on a single causal complex (*ekasāmagryadhīnatā*); thus, in states such as sleep, that very same [cognition] occurs at that very same time. Nor is the distinction of space and time, which is to be engaged with in subsequent waking conceptualization, merely remembered.

Even in a state of stillness, it is characterized by the conventional activity of conceptual memory arising from the emergent mind; thus, cognitions alone—though differentiated by place, time, and intrinsic nature—are pervasive, eternal, and of a single essence, flowing as a continuum and carrying on the course of worldly life. Therefore, he says: "not of another," meaning [it is] related [to itself].
The meaning is "by means of identity, inherence, and so forth. He explains the commentary on the word "of another" according to the reading:

"of that entity called the self," which refers to the continuum (*saṃtāna*). The underlying intention is that it may indeed be designated as being related [to it], because we observe the conventional usage "this is my cognition. As for the commentary, however, there is also a different way of explaining it.
With the intention that it should not be so, and furthermore that there should be no redundancy, the author of the commentary explains in brief.
"By the method to be explained" (iti). || 8 ||

Action, too, is simply the arising of the body and so forth in various locations and so on; it is nothing other than that which is not perceived [as distinct]. Furthermore, such action cannot be unitary, for it is appropriate that it be successive for a single [agent].

He states the meaning of the verse in brief with the words "action" (*kriyā*). He shows that the meaning of "because of non-perception" (*adṛṣṭeḥ*) is "because of its non-apprehension by means of a valid cognition" (*pramāṇenānupalabdheḥ*). [He explains: "perception" (*pratyakṣa*) refers to the operation of a valid cognition culminating in a determinative judgment (*avasāya*); thus, in the sūtra, "perception" should be explained as being one that culminates in a determinative judgment, whereby—

Inference (*anumāna*) will also be included; thus, the word "ascertainable" (*avaseya*)—both in its own nature and as related to something else—should be connected to both [the points] regarding the state of not being ascertainable by means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the state of being sublated by reasoning (*yukti*). The fact of being sublated by reasoning—that is, by the operation of valid cognition—is stated in terms of its own nature; nor is that [sublation] singular or successive.

However, it was stated [in the previous section] that for a single entity, how could there be a succession [of states] if they were related to something else? Furthermore, regarding the two sūtras that express the application of a reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga*), the reversal of that reductio (*prasaṅgaviparyaya*) is obtained by exposing the flaws in the reasons propounded by the opponent— namely, that the sovereignty of the Self arises from its connection with knowledge and action.

Therefore, by implication, knowledge is not tenable; thus, the untenability of knowledge is conjoined with that [untenability] of action here in the sūtra and in the commentary by means of the word "also" (api). With this intention, he explains [the phrase] as "not only [knowledge].
By this, the commentary is explained as meaning that "action also is not tenable. In the commentary on the preceding sūtra, the phrase "even though it exists" (sadapi) [is used].

The meaning of the word *api* has been explained [previously], but now the commentator (*ṭīkākāra*) states that the meaning of this specific *api* occurring in the sūtra is as follows: "In this case too," he says, using the word *api*. By speaking thus, he clarifies that the sūtra and its commentary (*vṛtti*) constitute a single work. Regarding the word *tatra*, although it would have been more appropriate to say "it is not logical," the meaning is "being so"; or alternatively, *tatra* refers to action within the self (*ātman*). That [action] is as follows:

The worldly [activity], which consists of motion, is not accepted by those who know the categories as being the category of action (*karmapadārtha*), because it conforms to form, whereas the self is devoid of form. For they have established that the self's agency consists solely in its connection with knowledge, desire to act, and effort; and these—knowledge and the rest—[are qualities].

(184) Qualities (*guṇa*) and their inherence (*samavāya*) are not action (*kriyā*); therefore, such an action must be stated as that which is possible for the self (*ātman*). Thus he states the definition: "The action of an agent (*kāraka*) which is the cause for the accomplishment of the result..."

The action (*kriyā*) is that which has as its form (*rūpa*), its own characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), an operation (*vyāpāra*) belonging to the agent—that is, inherent in him or identical with him—relative to his own activity.
It is that action whose constituent parts (*bhāga*) are related [to the agent] as being sequential (*pūrvāparībhūta*), meaning they occur in a temporal succession. As the venerable one said:
Whether already accomplished or yet to be accomplished, that which is designated as something to be achieved is understood as "action" (kriyā) because it possesses a sequential nature.
A collection of parts that arise in succession,
whose unity is conceptually constructed by the intellect as they function as subordinate factors, is designated as "action" (kriyā).
Regarding the expression "the white [thing] whitens," once [the object] has been manifested through its whiteness,
the verbal designation proceeds because it possesses a form that depends upon a temporal sequence.
Sound resounds by means of the relationship between cause and effect, thus depending on a temporal sequence;
however, when that sequence has ceased, it is simply called "sound."

Thus it is said. And such an action indeed exists for the self, as is admitted by those who maintain the doctrine of a divine self (īśvarātman), because of the perception of those respective sequential attributes [in the form]: "he desires," "he knows," "he exerts effort. As the venerable Guru, the author of the Śrī-grantha, has said:
"Then will its will be of such extent, its knowledge of such extent, and its action indeed of such extent" (1.3);
thus,
there is never a separation of consciousness from this triadic nature.
"By its power... (1.6),
and "But at the time of perceiving a jar or the like, that action [of consciousness] knows the jar" (1.24).
And so forth. To purify this definition, he explains the two meanings with the words "by its own nature" (*svātmanā*).
Regarding the action of "knowing," those factors which consist of the light of the lamp of intention (*abhisaṃdhāna*)—(page 185)
The acts of presenting, attending, opening the eyes, and so forth, exist merely in their own nature as "present" (neither prior nor posterior),
because posteriority depends upon priority and priority depends upon that [posteriority].
Being neither prior nor posterior, these parts, when arranged in a sequence of prior and posterior through mutual dependence, constitute that [cognition] in which they reside.
That is so. Now, one might object: "What is the use of defining this nature characterized by dependence?

Let it be stated that your action consists of its essential nature alone. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And [it occurs] only for those who are indeed depending," for otherwise, that very life-force of action which consists in its dependence upon a sequence would not exist. As for that...
In this regard, just as the pouring of water and so forth are parts of the act of cooking,
so too should other parts, such as the pouring of water and so forth, be understood [as parts] of those very acts.
And that which is perceived as having reached the limit of diminution—
in that single [moment], a word denoting action is not employed in isolation.

Thus [the text says]. The particle *ca* (and), by collecting another object of knowledge (*prameya*) as being useful for the subject matter at hand, indicates a doubt; therefore, in order to quell that doubt, it illuminates the fact that that object of knowledge functions as a reason (*hetu*) in terms of its result—this is how the meaning of *ca* as a "reason" is proclaimed in this manner. For example: "Food should be given to Caitra..."

And because this [food] is extremely coarse (*audarika*), he established the object of cognition (*prameya*) by questioning why a large meal should be given, as in the passage beginning with "he rejects" (*ākṣipati*). This should be understood similarly in other instances as well. Now, those whose separateness or non-separateness is resolved—that is, those which are analyzed or mixed together within the nature of a single composite whole (*avayavin*)—are those that are analyzed.

That which possesses parts related to it is the "whole" (avayavin). Anticipating the objection that such a whole cannot logically be a property of the self, he says: "because of being successive" (*kramikatvāt*). This reason is intended to reinforce the impossibility [of such a whole]; for the whole is not produced by color, taste, smell, and so forth, simply because those [qualities] are non-successive.
Even though they are simultaneous, because it does not begin [from them], the successive moments here—whether distinguished by time or distinguished by space—are indeed the initiators;

however, even the threads, which possess the observed power to initiate a composite whole (*avayavin*), do not initiate it, let alone the moments of action whose capacity is unobserved. This is the intended meaning. As for the term "part" (*bhāga*): [it refers to the spatial divisions].

(Page 186) It is a subtle part; in that case, the word "constituent" (*avayava*) is used either figuratively or because [the object] lacks separateness (*pṛthaktva*). Now, even for objects such as elephants, horses, and so forth, or dhava and khadira trees, which possess a spatial sequence—

An aggregate is observed to be established by the force of a single cognition, as in the case of an army or a forest; likewise, it might be so for successive moments of action as well. Consequently, one might suspect that "action" (kriyā) is to be defined as an aggregate of parts arranged in a temporal sequence; anticipating this objection, he says: "because of the absence of simultaneity. Now, if the definition were thus...

It is improper to resort to a *bahuvrīhi* compound because neither the whole (*avayavin*) nor the collection (*saṃcaya*) can be obtained as the referent of the other word (*anyapadārtha*). Therefore, this much must be stated: having raised the objection that "the action is merely the parts arranged in a temporal sequence," he says "nor even... For by what has been said here, only the parts are perceived, and thus only their distinctness (*bheda*) is manifested.

It may be so. Furthermore, in the case of difference (*bheda*), resting within one's own self (*svātmaviśrānti*) alone is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Dependent upon another (*parāpekṣā*) is contrary to that, because through it, the state of being established in another (*paraniṣṭhatva*) is manifested. Therefore, since the sequence of priority and posteriority (*pūrvāparībhāva*) is untenable when difference arises, even a touch of non-difference (*abheda*) must be resorted to. But how can there be a touch of non-difference for that which is different by means of something different?

He says "therefore" (*ataḥ*) to indicate that [the sequence] could not exist at another moment. Since dependence upon something else—which would terminate in an external object—is not logical for that which is distinct and self-contained, and since without such dependence there can be no sequence characterized by priority and posteriority, yet this action consisting of such [sequence] appears in the world; therefore, by means of the intellect in its conceptual form, therein—
Unity, characterized by non-differentiation, is also to be determined as belonging to the moments [of consciousness], as it has been said:
"The non-difference is constructed by the intellect.
Now, one might raise the objection: "If the intellect acts independently in this way, what is the restrictive rule? Anticipating this, it is said:

Regarding the term "single factor" (*ekakāraka*): this determination of oneness does not occur through independence; rather, it arises by virtue of the inseparable nature of the factors (*kāraka*) characterized as a single agent (*kartṛ*), and by relying upon the nature of the object-factor (*karmakāraka*) which consists of a single result.
The word *kāraka* is intended here in the sense of both the agent and the object. [Objection: But [what of] the action (*bhāva*) consisting of a sequence of prior and posterior stages?

Anticipating the objection that "just as armies and the like exist through the distinction of location and by virtue of being aggregates and mutual relations, so too will the moments of action be [related]; therefore, what is the use here of a conceptual determination (*buddhyavasāya*)?", he says:
(page 187)

Regarding the phrase "but in the case of an army and so forth": the word "but" (tu) indicates a distinction. "Because of simultaneous existence" means because they exist at the same time. An objection is raised: "Surely the cognition of a collection does not arise merely from simultaneous existence, for there is no such cognition as 'a collection of piśācas'.
To this he replies: "And because of perception"; the meaning is that simultaneity is determined by a means of valid cognition (pramāṇa).

For even in the case of *piśācas*, the cognition of a "collection" is observed when they are understood through scripture (*āgama*) and other means. [The opponent asks: "But what is the object of this perception of unity? [The author] says: "To explain," and so forth. Just as the body possesses the status of a whole (*avayavin*) because of its oneness as an earth-substance (*pārthiva*), despite the difference in the species (*jāti*) of its various constituent parts such as flesh, bone, fat, and marrow; so too...

They consider that this applies even to houses and the like. Even those who do not think thus nevertheless assert either a "conjunction of conjunctions" or a single property characterized as a "collection," based on the view that there exists a distinct category of property,
such as that of elephants and so forth— this is the meaning of the word "even" (api), which implies that it is not only the "whole" (avayavin) [that they deny].

The second [position] is that, in reality, even that collection [is not possible]. Furthermore, regarding the relation: the nature of being a relation is indeed a universal (*sāmānya*) form present everywhere—in conjunction (*saṃyoga*), inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth. And in the absence of a universal, just as there is no particular tree in the absence of "treeness," what possibility could there be for a *śiṃśapā*? This is because [a relation] must reside in two things (*dviṣṭhatva*).

The phrase "even when opposed" means up to this point. First of all, even for two moments, simultaneity is not possible; what then to say of many? Nor can there be the nature of action within a single moment, as it has been said:
"That which is perceived as having reached the limit of diminution..."
In that regard, a word for action is not employed in isolation by itself.

Thus, by resorting to the logic of the meaning of a *bahuvrīhi* compound, the author of the *Vṛtti* states the definition given by the author of the *Bhāṣya*: "that whose external reality consists precisely of its prior and posterior parts, which constitute the totality of the ultimate form. This is because it relies upon the essential nature of a single causal factor (*kāraka*).

It has been stated that there is mutual dependence established by the intellect (*buddhi*). Let that be so; but how can there be unity, such that it was said in the *Vṛtti* that "there is no [such thing]? To this, he replies: "And yet... Even though this action is characterized by the fact that its ultimate reality consists merely of prior and posterior parts, it possesses unity in the sense that "this is one single action."

By means of the intellect (*buddhi*). Thus, because of the determination (*adhyavasāya*) as a unity [on page 188], and because this determination of unity is not without foundation, he says: "having a single causal factor" (*ekakāraka*). But [one might object]: "However..."

Anticipating the objection that no action whatsoever can be accomplished by a single factor (*kāraka*), since the agent (*kartṛ*), the instrument (*karaṇa*), and the locus (*adhāra*) necessarily exist [in every case], he says: "by many factors" (*anekakāraka*). In the school of Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇanikāya*), the distinction between an action residing in the agent (*kartṛstha*) and one residing in the object (*karmastha*) is based on the predominance of the agent and the object respectively, due to their independence and their status as the result (*phala*).
Where a distinction arises from the action (*kriyā*), or where [the distinction] arises from the action, that action is designated as "resident in that" (*tatstha*).

Although every action possesses a distinction residing in the agent, because some [actions] possess a distinction residing in the object (*karman*), they are designated by their unique status of being "object-resident" (*karmastha*); or rather, their status as resident in that is determined by the power of the operation of the word (*śabdavṛtti*).

Thus, since the action resides in one place—either in the agent or in the object—it is singular there. Even in the case of "The sweetmeat is pleasing to Caitra" (*caitrāya rocate modakaḥ*), the sweetmeat is the agent that pleases and causes desire, while Caitra is the object being pleased and possessing desire; therefore, in reality, the state of residing in the object (*karmasthatā*) alone exists, it is merely—

Explaining the meaning that "by the very nature of the power of the word, the internal inclination (ruci) arouses in him a desire for its own object," [the author] sets forth the relationship of subject and object manifested by the denotative function (abhidhā),
and thereby shows that the desire, having that [relationship] as its agent, is primary, as well as his own [desire].
It renders the agent as if subordinate, and thereby subordinates its own causal operation;

thus, when there is such a connection, this designation of "recipient" (saṃpradāna) arises with respect to its object. Furthermore, since Caitra is the agent of the desire even though he is related to that connection, there is also the quality of being "resident in the agent" (kartṛstha). Therefore it is said: "Ruci is a desire whose agent is another."

Now, one might object: "In that case, while cooking and reading, as well as cutting and seeing, would indeed be identical when they reside in the same agent and the same object, the lifting of a load and the felling of a tree would not be identical because they reside in different agents and different objects.
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And [they are identical] by aiming at a single result. However, there is no single result for both cooking and reading.

Or rather, [the unity] is intended with respect to the acts of cutting and seeing; for when that intention is present, there would be unity even for the collection characterized by actions belonging to the entire universe, as it is said: "this world revolves. Likewise, the identity of agent and object is also [intended] with reference to the aggregate, as in cases such as the rising of the sun or the felling of a forest.

That is indeed easy to say. But surely the primary [referent], being sought for its causal efficacy (*arthakriyā*), is perceived as connected with its qualifiers; and the primary referent is the substance (*dravya*).

For the cognition is indeed: "This single white cow moves. In that case, just as there is no mutual connection between whiteness and moving-ness, so too there is none between moving-ness and oneness; thus, how can action possess the number one? As for what is said regarding "two cookings" and so forth, that is due to the power of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

This maturation is indeed substantialized (*dravyībhāvita*), not consisting of action (*kriyātmā*). As it has been said: "An action denoted by a *kṛt* suffix is like a substance" (*kṛdabhihito bhāvo dravyavat*); likewise, one expresses the state of being (*bhāva*) by means of a verbal suffix (*ākhyāta*). However, in a verbal suffix, duality and plurality as numbers appear only as residing in the agent or the object, and not as qualifiers of a specific action determined by its resting in another.

Anticipating the objection, "How was it stated by the author of the *Vṛtti* that [the action] is one?", he says, "And of number," while restating the doubt. By the word "one" (*eka*), number is not what is expressed here; rather, it is the mere absence of difference, characterized by non-distinction. [Objection: If action is of such a nature, then [in the case of] "Caitra moves"...
He asks why that [quality] is not distinct from consciousness (caitramati), and answers: "because they are inseparable" (*ayutā*).

The meaning is that this [quality] is not perceived as separate from the substance, whether by way of inherence (*samavāya*) or identity (*tādātmya*). By the term "inseparability" (*ayutasiddhatva*), the cause for the manifestation of identity is indicated. For indeed, [identity occurs] when two things—or one of them—lack separate establishment (*yutasiddhi*).

It is endowed with the capacity for separate movement; thus, it appears as non-identical [with the self], like a jar and a cloth, or like the space within a jar. Now, one might object: in the expression "the white [cloth] moves," the quality of whiteness also appears to move, because it is no longer perceived in that location once [the cloth] has departed. And likewise, "Caitra cooks," "Maitra..."

Since two actions are indeed manifested in the expression "he cooks" (*pacati*), one might raise the objection: "How then can it be said that number is a property of substance alone? Anticipating this, he says: "Precisely for this reason," because [number] is perceived by virtue of its dependence on the nature of the *kāraka* (the factor of action).
This superimposition is produced by its inherence in a single object (*ekārthasamavāya*). It is precisely due to the firmness of that cause [inherence] that [the superimposition occurs].

It does not depend on a synthesis by a cognizer (*pramātṛ*), as in the case of "the *gaura* [is] a *vāhīka*," but rather occurs spontaneously, like the silver in mother-of-pearl. Therefore, with this intention, the word "one" (*eka*) in the commentary may indeed be taken in its numerical sense—this is the point.
Now, [an objection]: [what of one who possesses such a distinction of characteristics?]

(Page 190) How can the substance that is the agent be one? He replies: "Because of the recognition of identity. For the cognition "This very person is Caitra" is an uncontradicted knowledge for everyone. If that is so, let the substance be one; however, as for the action—
In that regard, how is it that [the action] exists, and that it possesses a sequential nature consisting of prior and posterior stages, being differentiated by cooking, reading, and so forth?

He says: "And of that" (*tasya ca*). The particle *ca* has the sense of "also" (*api*) and is displaced [in the sentence], or it remains in its original position to indicate the aforementioned doubt. Even though there is identity due to the recognition (*pratyabhijñāpana*) of the substance as the causal factor (*kāraka-dravya*), such [a sequential nature] [exists].
The unity established through recognition arises when the causal factors are present;

even though it exists as that alone, it was previously non-existent. Thus, there is a specific result—such as the readiness of the rice-grains and the like—which manifests sequentially in the form of the breaking of hardness and moisture and the resulting softening, up until the point of being brought to the ear.

Since it is perceived in forms such as retention, slight proximity, and endurance, therefore it is possible to conceive that some meaning— residing in a substance, sequential, and distinct in its own nature— is inferred there, attached to a single causal factor (*kāraka*). For if action (*kriyā*) were not present, [this would not be possible].

It would have to be the substance itself [that is the producer]; if that [substance] produces the fruit, the fruit should exist even previously; otherwise, it would not exist even later. And if something else entirely were the producer, then that [substance] would not be required. Therefore, that [substance] alone is the producer. Furthermore, if a property (dharma) associated with another property were not itself successive, [it could not produce the fruit in succession].

That fruit is perceived as if it were suddenly blossomed into an extraordinary state all at once. If there were no distinction between ripening and bursting open, no such transformation of the fruit would be possible. Therefore, it is inferred that there exists a distinct entity—different from the causal factors themselves, dependent upon them, sequential, and possessing a different characteristic—which is precisely what constitutes action (*kriyā*). By the word "also" (*api*), [the author indicates...]

Showing that some have also stated here the argument from presumption (*arthāpatti*), he indicates that the author of the *Vṛtti* has likewise demonstrated the activity called "productive operation" (*bhāvanā*) as accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas: [it is] that which belongs to the person who is the agent (*kāraka*) and the producer (*bhāvaka*),
and which has as its goal heaven and so forth to be produced, and for which the meaning of verbal roots such as "sacrifice" (*yajati*) serves as the instrument (*karaṇa*).

The operation (*vyāpāra*) whose nature is production, expressed by the suffix (*pratyaya*) or the verb (*ākhyāta*), has its number metaphorically attributed to it through its connection with one of the factors (*kāraka*)—either the agent (*kartṛ*) or the object (*karman*)—which is itself expressed by that same suffix; this essence of *bhāvanā* is the meaning of the root *√kṛ*. This alone is the action (*kriyā*) in all cases. Therefore, the meaning...

The view of knowledge accepted by the Mīmāṃsakas— that the activity of the self directed toward that [object], which is otherwise inexplicable given the result consisting of manifestness (*prakaṭatā*),
is the act of knowing (*jñānakriyā*)— is also [a form of] the theory of knowledge.

When the view of the Kaṇādas and Sāṃkhyas has been refuted, the commentator seeks to refute it through the Buddhist perspective. Accordingly, he will state the sūtra that sublates the notion of a relation. For this reason as well, since agency is untenable, the state of being a knower—which consists in being the agent of the act of knowing—is all the more untenable. And this...

We shall explain this very point later. Having stated this supreme view (*paramata*), he refutes it with the word "thus" (*evam*). To clarify the sūtra—"How can that which is one be successive?"—the commentary explains succession (*kramikatva*):
for succession consists in contact with multiple points of time. How could that which is one be both that time and not-that-time?
How could that which is "this" and "not-that" be one at two different times? Thus, from the perspective of its own nature (*svarūpa*), the unity of action is sublated.

Even if there is no difference in location due to the difference in time during its occurrence, since the pervading [agent] expresses a difference in nature throughout all successive stages, both a difference in location and a difference in nature are necessarily admitted.

In the *Ṭīkā*, however, for the sake of clarification, it is shown as a possible corroborative reason (*abhyuccayahetu*) by the word "tāvat. Where a proving means of knowledge (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*) has been stated by the opponent with an assumed degree of firmness, there one first strives to refute that; but here it is not so. Thus, when [the matter] is determined by a means of knowledge...

A discrepancy regarding its own nature is not logical in the case of a thing's own form, just as it is not in the case of blue; however, in this matter, there are many branches among those very proponents [of universals]. For the venerable one who maintains that there is a universal says: "Others speak of an action that resides in multiple individuals."
That which is unattainable in its manifested form is indeed perceived as attainable.
Either that very genus which belongs to the constituent parts of the action is traditionally held to be the action itself,
or it is the existence of the agent and the object as qualified by their own respective operations.
In the various distinctions of activity and operation, either existence (sattā) as inherent (samavāyinī),
or that existence which resides ultimately in the self (ātman), is held by some to be action (kriyā).

Others, however, maintain that it is the intellect (buddhi), while others say it is the genus of intellect; still others assert that it is the very existence of the intellect, which, having its form superimposed upon entities, is designated as "action" (kriyā).
Thus [it is said on page 192]:
"And here there is disagreement regarding this action, which is absolutely imperceptible..."
For this was stated by that very supreme teacher himself:
"Even for those [senses] which are successively real and unreal, it is not the case that they,
as a collective group, enter into a relationship with the eyes and other organs whose objects are real entities."
Thus it is said. Furthermore, even a proving means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must be countered by a subverting one (*bādhaka*).
If the identity of a substance is established through recognition, from where could there be a result?

This is the inference based on action. And since that [recognition] occurs everywhere—even in the case of hair, nails, and so forth—which are distinct, it does not establish the reality [of the object].

Since it is impossible for an object to exist in such a manner [as it appears], the invalidity of recognition depends solely upon a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*); thus, that very [subversion] falls upon the opponent's refutation, as was previously stated regarding the subverting cognition. Furthermore, the locus (*adhiṣṭhāna*) or substratum (*adhyāsa*), which is the superimposition of a property that implies mutual non-existence through its contradictory nature, exists by way of distinction.

The word "pervaded" (*vyāptam*) negates the conventional usage of non-difference. He demonstrates that pervasion with the words "not anywhere. For the conventional usage of difference and non-difference, occurring only in certain instances, is neither causeless nor based on any other cause. Therefore, if the conventional usage of difference does not occur even when contradictory properties reside [in the same locus], then it would follow that it is either causeless or based on some other cause.

In that case, two contradictions with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddha*) would follow. For what are called "parts" (*bhāga*) cannot belong to a single entity, because if it were one, there could be no plurality such that they are called "parts. Furthermore, their sequence of priority and posteriority (*pūrvāparībhāva*) is relative;
and that relativity is not a property (*dharma*) of the parts themselves, but is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpamātra*) of the perceivers. Nor are these conceptual constructions...

They have real entities as their objects, nor does the entity transform in accordance with them; therefore, the notion that "there is a single action" is a mere conceptual construction devoid of an objective referent. [The opponent objects: "Let this cognition exist somewhere in reference to something beyond the parts. To this he replies: "Of that which is beyond the parts," etc. [He means that] what is called "action" is a whole (*avayavin*), a conjunction, or a collection.

You yourself have not accepted that the relation is one, because you have stated that sequentiality— which consists in a difference of time— is the defining characteristic of action. Having thus explained this portion of the Sūtra— "It is not tenable for it to be one and sequential"— which expresses an objection based on its own nature (*svarūpa*), [the author proceeds].

The author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) explains the portion of the sūtra concerning the refutation of the identity of the substratum (*āśrayaikyabādhaka*), stating that "neither is it sequential, nor is it appropriate for a single [entity]," by saying: "nor does it pervade a succession of time."

The two *ca*-particles indicate mutual contradiction. In the sutra, there is only one *ca* indicating contradiction, which expresses a contradiction residing in both. Likewise, there is also a single *ca* residing in the substratum; however, the word *api* serves to conjoin the contradictions. Previously, by means of a single nature (*ātman*) or essence belonging to the substratum...

And other parts are not tenable—this is the meaning. Having raised the doubt as to why they are not tenable, he says "for thus" (*tathā hi*). Since there is a distinction between the prior part and the posterior part both in terms of their intrinsic nature (*svarūpa*) and in terms of time (*kāla*), the connection with the prior part and the connection with the posterior part are distinct both by intrinsic nature and by time.

How could that single substratum tolerate both kinds of difference in its own nature and both kinds of difference in time, which are implied by these two forms? In this context, by the phrase "that single substratum," the difference in time caused by the difference in nature is stated; for [the substratum] consists of a prior part and a posterior part.

How could two things that are distinct by their own nature exist at the same time within a single substratum? For it is not tenable that the very same thing is both that and not that. Therefore, this [objection] brings about a temporal distinction in the substratum. Furthermore, by the phrase "of a single nature," it is shown that there is no difference in essential nature (svarūpa-bheda) caused by a difference in the essential natures residing in prior and posterior parts.

The basis has been shown. Now, he begins to demonstrate the two [types of contradiction] produced by the difference in time with the words "also by the difference in time. The particle *api* ("also") indicates that it is not only by way of a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*) [that there is contradiction], but rather that being connected with the prior part and being connected with the subsequent part are contradictory due to the difference in time.

"Not even at another moment"—if this were so, there would be no difference in time between those two, provided they were to occupy each other's times; yet this is not the case. Having thus stated the difference in time between the preceding and succeeding parts, he now states the difference in the essential nature of the substratum (*āśraya*) by means of that temporal difference inherent in them.
"Nor even at another moment" means that at the time of the subsequent moment—
which consists in the absence of the preceding moment— the nature characterized by connection with the preceding part does not exist; thus, it is the former [nature].

(Page 194) The meaning is that its intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) has perished. Now, he demonstrates that because there is a difference in time between the prior and posterior parts, there is also a difference in the substratum (*āśraya*), by stating "it does not exist. This refers to the state of being connected with the prior part.

Furthermore, connection with the posterior part is contradictory [to connection with the anterior part] due to the difference in time; how could both exist in a single substratum at one and the same time? Thus, for one who maintains a temporal distinction of the substratum: in that case, the connection of the substratum with the anterior part belonging to a prior time cannot possibly exist at a later time. For that [prior connection]...

It is logical that [the two states] belong to different times; since the later time consists in the absence of the earlier time, there would be a temporal distinction of the substratum due to those two properties which are distinct in time.
Thus, this superimposition of contradictory properties is fourfold. In this context, spatial distinction should also be considered; however, that—

It is not shown [in examples] such as "the self knows," because that [distinction of time] is impossible there; for while a difference in time is universal, it ultimately results in a difference in intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Anticipating the objection that "the intrinsic natures of the substratum of existence are distinct," he says: "nor is it distinct from the intrinsic nature. If that is so, then...

He asks, "What might it be? and answers, "Then" (*tadā*). The meaning is: "Because it is so, therefore [this follows]. The particle *eva* (only/just) serves to dispel the doubt that "the nature (*svabhāva*) may perish, but the possessor of the nature (*svabhāvī*) remains," and instead indicates that the possessor of the nature itself has perished. Thus, even for those whose intellects are impaired by conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) born from the study of the scriptures, now—by the force of relying on the subverting [cognition]—because...

This has been obtained; thereafter, he explains the meaning of the Sūtra—namely, that "the body and so forth of an object arise in such-and-such a place"—by means of the commentary (*vṛtti*) beginning with the words "merely going" (*gamana*). However, the prior inclusion [of this point] in the Sūtra was intended for those people whose intellects are simple and unimpaired by the technicalities of the treatise (*śāstra*), because this matter is clear [to them].

Regarding the meaning: [the opponent] suggests, "Let each individual part itself be the cooking," to which [the author] replies, "And not... [The opponent then asks: "If cooking belongs only to the parts, how could the verbal suffix *pacati* (he cooks) apply to many parts as a single unit? Thus, how can this groundless doubt regarding the action belonging solely to the parts have been raised? To this, [the author] says: "The generality of cooking (*pākasāmānyam*)."
Thus, since there is a single universal of "cookedness" (*pākatva-jāti*) as the objective basis for a single cognition across those many parts, this position is indeed well-founded.
If so, why was it said, "and not"? He replies: "as if partless. For if there were actual parts, the very same fault previously mentioned would apply.
This is the intended meaning. "The state of being arranged in a sequence of before and after" means possessing a temporal succession. And as it is said:
"Either individually or collectively, [the parts] possess an induced subsequent capacity."
They are perceived in many forms, appearing as if sequential though they are non-sequential.

Thus, by the word *iva* itself, the unreality of succession is indicated. Furthermore, there is no imparting of any power (*śakti*) by preceding moments to subsequent moments; for if it were so, it would merely amount to saying that the subsequent moment is "distinct" (*viśiṣṭa*), which would be stating nothing more than what is already evident. The phrase "due to deviation" (*vyabhicārāt*) means that [the causal relation] is impossible anywhere at all; it does not, however, mean...

It should be understood that this is because [the definition] is not all-pervasive (*avyāpaka*). Now, one might object: "Let there be no sequential nature as its defining characteristic; rather, whatever additional property (*dharma*) exists, that itself shall be the action (*kriyā*). To this he says: "Nor even... and "The first moment also... Indeed, other moments characterized by conjunction with and disjunction from different locations are accepted even by opponents.

First of all, that by which disjunction—which causes the destruction of the prior conjunction—is produced must be the category of action (*kriyā*). Furthermore, this [action] is not perceived as something distinct from the substance through direct perception. Now, one might argue that this action is to be investigated within the self (*ātman*).
[Objection: That having been stated, what is the connection here between the body, the jar, and so forth, by virtue of which it is said in the Sūtra "of the body and so forth"?

[Reply: True; however, the Sūtra is intended as an illustration. Just as the action of the body and so forth is merely the arising of something new in various locations, so too is the action of going for that which remains in one place.

In the various activities such as sitting and standing at their respective times—as included by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the Sūtra—likewise, within the inner self whose nature is knowledge, there is merely the production of a new cognition whose nature consists of distinct moments of time, expressed as "he desires," "he knows," "he exerts effort," or "he remembers"; it is not, however, any other action. This is what [the author] says:
"And how [is this]? It is said: by means of a conventional word (*sāṃketika-śabda*) established for the purpose of linguistic usage regarding the nature of such objects. As it has been said:
"Denotative words are joined together for the sake of cognizing the distinctions between entities."

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: since this word depends upon an agent who employs it, let "going" (*gamana*) be accepted first, because it is well-known and because it is common to all types of upward throwing and so forth; however, by way of transformation...

Anticipating the objection, "What is the purpose of establishing the view of the Ekīyas?", he says: "Transformation" (*pariṇāma*). Everything that consists of the meaning of verbal roots (*dhātvartha*) and is of the nature of productive activity (*bhāvanā*), being permeated by a temporal sequence undivided by spatial distinctions, is subsumed under transformation. For even though there is a difference in time within the act of going, nevertheless...

Since a spatial distinction (*deśabheda*) that is perceptible to gross vision and unique [to each object] is possible there, a temporal distinction (*kālabheda*) would not be cited in this context; therefore, the word "only" (*kevala*) is used. For this very reason—that the intention regarding transformation is to provide an illustration of the sequence of time alone—there follows the movement.

That which is associated with spatial distinction (*deśabheda*) has been treated separately. Only those specific transformations (*pariṇāmaviśeṣa*) characterized by spatial distinction, such as growth and decay, are grasped [as *sthāna*]; however, those possessing temporal sequence (*kālakrama*), such as standing, sitting, lying down, knowing, remembering, and desiring, are included under "transformation" (*pariṇāma*). Since both terms denote specific types [of change], there is no contradiction.

This objection must be considered: how can there be a *dvandva* compound for words that denote both the general and the particular? For it is not the case that one says "the *dhava* tree and the tree. [The answer is: by the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the rule regarding the formation of the compound, examples such as "the mango ripens" (*āmraṃ paripacyate*) and "the milk transforms" (*dugdhaṃ pariṇamate*)—which possess a clearly manifest difference in their essential natures through qualities such as greenness or yellowness, and sweetness, sourness, liquidity, or hardness—are included.

By means of a distinct essential nature (*svarūpa*) to be described hereafter, [the suffix] includes an action that disregards even the temporal difference (*kālabheda*) that exists; thus, through this, Caitra’s spatial difference is perceived in "he goes," his temporal difference in "he stands for a day," and his difference in essential nature in "he is blue," "he is white," "he shines," or "he blazes."

He concludes with the words "that very thing" (*tattat*), stating that action is precisely the distinctness of place, time, and essential nature. By the mention of the "object" (*vastu*), he indicates its fulfillment of the conditions for perception (*upalabdhilakṣaṇaprāptatā*). It has been stated that direct perception does not operate due to non-perception;
alternatively, results such as reaching a village and so forth are accomplished solely through the continuity of previous births.

For, according to the principle that "in whichever very continuum [the action occurs]," there is the attainment of heaven and so forth; likewise, conjunction (*saṃyoga*) also consists of a moment of Devadatta possessing the same causal complex as that location,
while the cognition of the intention "I am moving" consists of a single causal complex with that [moment].

Furthermore, the inference is as follows: on whose authority is action— whether it be the form of the root-meaning (*dhātvartha*), the nature of *bhāvanā*, or the essence of the object of the verbal suffix (*karmapadārtha*)— accepted as being located in one place [the agent] and then in another place [the object], such that there is a moment of the body in one location and then in another?

There is no [need for] even presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*). In that regard, because the meaning of the Sūtra is primary, with the intention that the meaning submerged in the *vṛtti* and clearly examined in the *ṭīkā* should be established in the intellect precisely according to the sequence of the Sūtra, [the author states] that the fact of being born in such-and-such a place and so forth is nothing other than a portion of the meaning of the Sūtra.
He concludes the preceding [section] with "the action is invalid," and the remainder [of the section] later with "and it is sublated by valid cognition. || 9 ||
It is observed that when this or that [cause] is present, this or that [effect] comes to be;
there is no other relation than that of cause and effect. (10)

Having thus examined both knowledge and action, [the author] states in the verse beginning with "tatra tatra" that, regarding the cause which is sovereignty resulting from their conjunction (*tadyogāt*), there is no valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) to establish the aspect of the relationship denoted by the word "conjunction" (*yoga*); and as an incidental point, he does so regarding action as well.

The remainder is examined as follows: Suppose someone were to say that what has been called "action" (kriyā) is a thing distinct from its respective place, time, and nature, which flows by way of a continuous series (saṃtānavṛtti).
This might be the case in instances such as sitting or walking, where there is either the absence of an object (*akarmakatva*) or the state of reaching an object (*prāpyakarmatā*). And where...

An object such as a jar is that which is to be produced (*nirvartya*); in that case, since the relationship of action and its factors (*kriyā-kāraka-bhāva*) would be absent, how could there be the cognition "the potter makes a jar from clay with a stick and other tools," and likewise, how could the conventional usage established up to the point of the action be accomplished here? Furthermore, how could that [relationship] exist without an action? This too is addressed by this very aphorism.

That [point] is also made clear by the subsequent sūtra through the method of elucidating this very meaning. For this reason, in order to demonstrate both its incidental nature and its already-stated status, the commentator shows the role of action as an illustration by way of a brief introduction with the words "And just as... Furthermore, even the general statement in the sūtra, "and nothing else," [serves this purpose].

It is also brought to its conclusion within the action itself; and by the passage beginning with "it is not [known] through perception," that [action] is employed as an illustration in relation to the connection. He explains the restrictive particle (*evakāra*) from the Sūtra: "it is seen" means merely the final determination of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); this much is the reason.

Since only this much is perceived, there is nothing else; thus, there is no action, nor is there any relation whatsoever [to it]. This is the indication of the probandum to be established by means of the example. And so, he explains it separately in the *Vṛtti*.

And since there is no relation between action and its factors (kriyā-kāraka-saṃbandha) that possesses [the nature of] action, for that very reason, one should not consider there to be a redundancy between the two other words. In the phrase "not another" (*nānyat*), the status of the preceding [word] as a reason was stated in the commentary by the passage:
"because this distinct and separate relation is not perceived, just like an action. Now, in that case—

In that context, having raised the doubt—“What then is that relation which, being distinct from the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadikārtha), is implied by the locative case [in the word *tatra*]?”—the aphorism beginning with “there is nothing else” (*nānyo 'sti*) and so forth is given; its concise explanation is “cause and effect” (*kāryakāraṇa*). By the mention of “arrangement” (*saṃniveśa*), there is the restriction of a specific form preceded by the withdrawal of other forms.
He also states the cause of entry, which is the application of a specific knowledge, desire, and effort belonging to that [agent]:
"The sequence is simply the production of things that have not existed before, and that is what is experienced.
The term "intervening" refers either to the mutual connection of the causal factors with the result, or to that which connects them.

"Place and time" means that one does not rely on such formulations as "here," "now," or "our own experience.
