An objection might be raised: "In the Sūtra, the present tense is used in the word 'is seen' (dṛśyate), and by that, the specific place and the perceiver would be implied. Anticipating this, he says: "And in the Kārikā..."
A *kārikā* is that by which the intellect is made to engage instantaneously with the subject matter to be explained, through the power of its concise form and its quality of being pleasant to hear.
What is meant is this: it is observed that a transcendental desire (*vīpsā*)—consisting of the wish to pervade (*vyāptum icchā*) without restriction of place and so forth—first enters the heart.

On the contrary, because the present tense is connected with a continuity that is eternal—like the flow of a great river—it brings about a state of resting upon an object that is eternally active in form. However, in the case of "citrayājī" (one who has sacrificed with the Citrā), the meaning is past; since it is incapable of assisting the future meaning (*janitā*) in its own form, it conforms to that [future sense].
Granted that this may be accepted; however, this logic does not apply here even in the context of the commencement of the *dhātusaṃbandha* sūtra.

Now, one might object: "In various places, the word 'tatra' in the sūtra has the universal meaning [established] in the commentary (*ṭīkā*) that 'when there is a lump of clay, there is a jar,' and so forth."

(199) Thus it has been explained. Anticipating the objection as to how this could be established through its pervasion of the immediately subsequent space and time, he says: "the nature of existence" (*bhāvasvabhāva*). For existence itself is indeed partless.

To whatever extent it is established at one time by as many dharmas as are conceptually constructed through exclusion, it is inseparable from all of them at all times and in all places. If it were separated from them, it would not be that very thing; consequently, the state of being a jar would be the state of being a stūpa, and the state of being a stūpa would immediately follow the state of being a jar—such would be the nature of cause and effect.

Because the [existence of] those who grasp the pot on the stūpa is established by means of inference (*pramāṇa*) alone. "Of such a kind" refers to the specific nature (*svabhāvaviśeṣa*) of the clay and the potter, consisting respectively in the form of hardness and so forth, and in the form of being intelligent and so forth.
By the inclusion of the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), [it includes] length and thinness for the staff, and so on. Now, what is the cause there, or rather—
[It must be] an effect; if it is argued that the cause is necessarily prior and the effect is necessarily posterior, [the author] asks "What is that?
and says: "And even when... (*yadāpi ca*). The word *yadā* indicates the reason (*hetu*). The particle *ca* suggests the aforementioned doubt. The particle *api* is displaced in its order.
Regarding the smoke which did not come into being in the absence of fire—even for that which has not yet come into being, in relation to that other-natured object (*arthāntara-svabhāve*)...

Since existence occurs when fire exists, that [fire] is designated as "prior" because its existence is the cause (*prayojaka*), while the other is designated as "subsequent" because its existence is the effect (*prayojya*). Thus, priority and posteriority are merely their own essential natures (*svarūpa*) for these two, and not in any other manner, such as through mutual dependence, subordination, or conjunction, as is the case with cause and effect.
There exists a certain time characterized by priority and posteriority. As it has been said:
"Observing one thing and not seeing another, and upon not seeing that [second] thing, a person infers the effect even without the guidance of instructors."
Since the cognition of an effect is not possible apart from perception and non-perception,
even the scriptural mention of "effect" and so forth is employed here for the sake of brevity.

Thus, it is established that the causal relation is universally applicable as nothing other than these two essential natures, which are proven by the non-perception of perception occurring simultaneously. Explaining the word "only" (*eva*) from the Sūtra,
[the author] demonstrates that everything up to the words "is seen" constitutes the reason (*hetu*), while the portion beginning with "not anything else" constitutes the probandum (*sādhya*).

Regarding the phrase "cause and effect": here, at the occasion of perceiving this [statement], namely "in another sense" (*arthāntare*), by means of this [perception], one perceives that which is characterized by the non-deficiency of the essence of other conditions.
He states that [the object] has attained the state of being momentary. Now, what is the meaning of the locative case in the word "tatra" (there)? For that is a kāraka (case) vibhakti.
If so, what is the meaning of the genitive case in "rājñaḥ" (of the king), which is a vibhakti expressing relation (*saṃbandha*)? It is said:
because a relation is characterized by the production of a benefit (*upakāra*), and because that benefit exists only in the absence [of the related object].

Since connection, assistance, and non-terminating regress are untenable when there is no distinction [between cause and effect], the meaning of the genitive case is simply the relation of cause and effect.
Well then, that same meaning must also apply to the case-endings denoting grammatical factors (*kāraka*). Thus he says: "all indeed.
Anticipating the objection that this very relation might be one and the same, he says: "not simultaneous."

If smoke does not exist when fire exists, why should the relationship of cause and effect rest in the fire alone? And it is not so, because [the fire] lacks the nature of being an effect with respect to itself. Likewise, at the time of smoke, the preceding moment of fire has ceased; therefore, why should this [causal relation] reside in the smoke alone? And this is not logical for that [smoke].

Because it is impossible for it to be a cause with respect to its own nature, at what time could that [cause] be one? Therefore, that which is the respective form of the effect and the cause at their own respective times, when designated by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as "one," is called a "relation," but not in reality. As it has been said:
Thus, these entities are inherently unmixed, yet conceptual construction joins them;
and by following that very [construction], there arise words expressing actions and their factors.
"Expressive words are joined together for the purpose of conveying a distinction between states.

[Objection: But even when all other conditions are present, this relation is invisible, like a *piśāca* ghost; to this he says, "Even so" (*athāpi*). "Because of non-perception" (*anupalambhāt*) means, in short, because of its absence from direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). "Granted" (*kāmaṃ*)...

We have proposed that while there should be no certainty regarding non-existence—since this [non-perception] may not be a perception of the perceptible—there is nonetheless an absence of certainty regarding existence. This is because the present occasion is for the investigation of the absence of a proving means of knowledge (*sādhaka-pramāṇa*); hence the inclusion of the word "only" (*tāvat*). By the inclusion of the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "effect, etc.," the essential reason (*svabhāva-hetu*) is also intended. Now, by this much...

Let it be granted that the existence of another [entity], such as a relation (*saṃbandha*) and so forth, is not established; yet, this does not constitute the non-existence of existence itself. To this extent, however, the exclusion of the object of cognition (*prameya*) through the exclusion of the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) is untenable; for causes are not necessarily [determinative].

By this logic, how could it be established that there is no connection to that? For in the *Sūtra* it is said, "there is no other connection," in the *Vṛtti* it is said, "there is no connection whatsoever," and in the *Vivṛti* it is said, "there is no further category of existence"; thus, a negation of existence alone has been stated. Anticipating the question, "How can this be so? he says:

Regarding the phrase "sublating means of valid cognition" (*bādhakapramāṇa*): the intended meaning is that the section beginning with "residing in two" (*dviṣṭhasya*) and ending with "and because of the impossibility of dependence, etc.

(*pāratantryādyayogācca*) is connected by way of repetition (*āvṛttyā*) to the sūtra "there is no other relation" (*nānyo'sti saṃbandhaḥ*). From that very [connection], the commentary (*ṭīkā*) will follow.

From the preceding sūtra: by that connection, the two—namely, the absence of the conventional usage of existence and the conventional usage of non-existence—are stated by the phrase "there is no other"; thus, through the manner of ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*), it is established that "it exists" is not [ultimately] established, while "it does not exist" is established. And this is [conveyed] by a portion of this sūtra.

And when combined with the portion of the immediately following sūtra, [the meaning] is established. For this very reason, the five ablative cases in the subsequent sūtra are indeed employed for the sake of the meaning of this present sūtra. However, regarding that which is established—namely, that there is no [direct] connection due to the necessity of combining those two—the word "tena" (by that) will be used as a reference in order to state its status as a logical reason elsewhere. || 10 ||

Because that which resides in two [places] would possess multiple forms, because what is already established does not depend on anything else, and because dependence on another is impossible, the agent too is merely imagined. (11)

For indeed, he introduces the Sūtra in this very manner with the words "tadevam" (thus, in this way). First, regarding the action, [he says] "evam" (thus); and since the action belongs to the object, it remains as such in each respective case. Because there is no supporting evidence for what is stated in the two Sūtras, and because of the presence of subverting arguments, the non-existence expressed in the two Sūtras—"nānyo'sti" (there is nothing else) and "nānyadasti" (there is nothing other)—is precisely that.
It has been explained that the absence of a relationship— which consists in the absence of certainty regarding its existence and the certainty regarding its non-existence—
is likewise [non-existent] due to the lack of proof mentioned in various places, such as the argument that [the relation] must reside in both [terms].
(Page 202)

When combined with the obstructive [factor], this very quartet of absences is postulated as the agent; thus, in the Sūtra, its status as a cause is conveyed by the word "tena" (by that). That causality, however, is stated concisely in the Ṭīkā by means of the ablative case in the word "abhāvāt" (from the absence). And the word "ca" (and) [serves to] indicate the fifth case.

He connects this with the previous sūtra: "Relation" (*saṃbandhaḥ*)—there is no other relation because that which resides in two things would be manifold, because what is already established does not depend on anything else, and because it would involve dependence and so forth; such is the connection (*saṃgati*). However, the mere term "relation" was pointed out explicitly by his own throat in the Vivṛti.

Although it is stated generally as "of that which resides in two," the meaning "of the relation" may also be obtained from the context. Now, one might object: that object is sublated by the very non-apprehension of the perceptible, which brings about the certainty of its non-existence.
In reality, this alone constitutes its sublation, namely, the communication of its ascertained non-existence; it is not [the mere absence of apprehension].

It is like the shattering of a clay bowl with a mallet; and that [shattering] has indeed been demonstrated here by the non-perception of the visible object through a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
True, however, it is through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*) that one realizes non-existence as delimited by a specific place and time—as in: "There is no jar here now. As it has been said:
"— there is no certainty of non-existence regarding remote things.
Thus, as desired, even in the case of a contradictory effect, there is dependence on place, time, and so forth.
Otherwise, it would be inconclusive, like ashes in a proof for the absence of cold.

Thus, in order to demonstrate the universal non-existence of relation and so forth, one must state a contradiction residing in the object of cognition (*prameya*) which brings about the impossibility of its nature as admitted by the opponent; for that very nature which you yourself have stated is contradicted by another nature stated by you, and it is for this reason alone [that the contradiction is established].

Since the proponent of the subverting argument (bādhaka) achieves his purpose simply by establishing the contradiction between those two forms, there is no occasion for objections such as the "unestablished locus" (dharmyasiddhi) regarding the reason for the refutation; this has been determined in detail in the *Prasaṅga* section and elsewhere, so let it rest for now. In that regard, the door to the general definition (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—
He sets forth an objection: "That which indeed exists simultaneously through the completion of its own nature in two [places] is not one, like two jars situated in two different houses.
(page 203)

For oneness (*ekatva*) is indeed the state of having an undifferentiated form (*abhinnarūpatva*); and that which is opposed to it—namely, the state of having differentiated forms—is pervaded by the simultaneous existence of two things in their entirety as their own essential natures (*svarūpa*). For if everything, such as a jar and so forth, were thus of an undifferentiated form, then even a single thing would be like that; therefore, the state of residing in two [places] occurs only in some instances.

Indeed, such a rule which is all-pervasive would be undermined. By the perception of a pervasion contrary to that [rule], the oneness [of the relation] is negated. Having thus stated the sublation regarding the mere general connection residing in two things, the author, wishing to state it with respect to its specific instance as well, says: "of that which is established. Here, when it is said "the king's,"...

The cognition is not independent, as in the case of the expression "the king"; rather, the king requires something else. That requirement (ākāṅkṣā), appearing in some cases as the very form of a relation, is established as being universal;
thus, it is conventionally designated as "relation" (*apekṣā*). He refutes this by stating that [such a relation] pertains only to things that are mutually beneficial (*upakāraka*).
"It exists. This is its meaning: first of all, dependence is not logical in the case of insentient things. As it has been said:
"Dependence and subordination are not a relation between two insentient entities, because such a thing is impossible" (Saṃsargasiromaṇi, verse 1).

Thus [it is said]. Even where that [auxiliary] exists, it is argued that a definition of relation residing in both (dviṣṭha) as previously stated—which would take the form of a single entity—is not tenable; he says, "defined as a specific excellence of its own nature" (*svarūpātiśayalakṣaṇa*). Since the assistance is non-distinct [from the cause], that which performs it would simply be the cause itself. And the effect, being thus dependent, would have been described in this way. But this is not clear; therefore, he says:
And regarding the phrase "of that which exists": as it has been said, "If dependence is the relation, how can that which is non-existent depend?
This expresses the contradiction of [ascribing] an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) to that which lacks an intrinsic nature. [Objection: In that case, [let us grant that] the cause exists.

Let there be dependence upon an effect; but what dependence can there be upon that which does not exist? And since its form has already been obtained by it, for what purpose would it have dependence? As it is said:
"How can an existent entity, which is free from all expectation, depend [on anything]?"
If it is argued that there must be a dependence on the effect for the sake of attaining the status of being a cause,
[we reply: surely its causality is nothing more than its own nature, and that nature has already been acquired by it.

Reality has been attained, but its conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) has not. This too is true; however, conventional usage—consisting of cognition and verbal designation—is not a property of that [ultimate] cause, but rather belongs to the user (*vyavahartṛ*). Thus, it follows that there is a dependence upon the user. And since it is accepted that this [usage] indeed takes the form of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), this point is established.
"Conceptual construction (kalpanā) mixes those two.

This has been stated by the words "because of the absence of that" (*tadabhāvāt*) and so forth. [The opponent objects: "In that case, there will be a mutual dependence between two existing things, as in the expression 'the king's man' (*rājñaḥ puruṣaḥ*). He refutes this with the words "and not" (*na ca*). The word "of both" (*dvayoḥ*) is a genitive used in the sense of a general relationship (*saṃbandhasāmānye*).
It accepts the sense of the genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) as residing in one [element] and the sense of the locative case (*saptamī*) as residing in the other. For this is the meaning here:
"there is dependence upon a person only when that person exists as a king"; mutual dependence (*anyonyāpekṣā*) is not intended here.

Indeed, that [mutual dependence] will be discussed in the context of dependency (*pāratantrya*). Even the word "mutual dependence" (*anyonyāpekṣā*) results in this same meaning within the commentary (*vṛtti*).

It must be considered as follows: and thus, for the sake of brevity, even in the case of dependence (*pāratantrya*), the application [of the genitive] is intended to convey that very same understanding.

Therefore, in that case as well, one must establish that the relationship between the king and the servant ultimately rests upon a cause-and-effect relation; otherwise, there would be an incompatibility with the actual meaning of the genitive—this is the remaining implication. Now, [one might object]: "But is it not like the sacrifice performed by the wife and the sacrificer?"

Anticipating the objection that—just as in the embrace of a couple in love—their relationship might consist of a mutual dependence characterized by *pāratantrya* (subordination), as in the case of "Let both the *dhava* and the *khadira* trees be cut down," he says:
"mutual orientation" (*parasparonmukhatā*), meaning "reciprocal facing toward one another. This is a single [conceptual] word alone, and not [a relation of subordination].

How could there be a relationship such that "the orientation toward [an object] belonging to one is that of the other"? As for the objection, "Once [the object] is established, what dependence [on another] can there be?", this has been stated repeatedly because the meaning is already clear. Let it be granted, then, that there is some kind of orientation; however, by means of that, the establishment of a relationship does not occur—thus it stands in this case of a position accepted as a hypothesis (*abhyupagamasiddhānta*).
The intended meaning (*tātparya*) is as follows: regarding the statement that "the relation consists in dependence," the construction is this:

even if there were dependence, it would not establish a relation; furthermore, what dependence could there be between two things that are already established? This has also been touched upon in the *Vṛtti* and the *Ṭīkā*. [The King...]

(Page 205) Regarding the term "king": having perceived that specific form in one instance, a proponent of any one of those various forms of relation postulates that very same form to exist everywhere; thus, even in the case of the expectation expressed as "the king's man."

Dependence alone has been demonstrated. Or, with the intention of providing another example—namely, "the king and the man"—as to why it is said that the relationship is simply the mutual acquisition of form, like that of two fingers, he replies to that as well: "even that which consists of the fusion of forms. If there are two forms, how can there be fusion? If there is fusion, it must be due to a single form.
How is there a connection? It has been said:

"When duality exists, how could it [occur]? Now, an objection is raised: the phonetic fusion (*rūpaśleṣa*) was indeed indicated by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the Sūtra; why then was it not explained in the Vṛtti?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "Such things as these have not been explained. This means: what burden is there in revising the text, since it has already been refuted in many ways? By stating, "it was refuted by the new [author] with a zeal for refutation," the author implies that even this prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is accepted in part by the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

He shows that the connection and so forth mentioned in other systems are not accepted; and he will state later that this is true when one adopts the established doctrine (*siddhānta*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), he also indicates what is stated in other tantras.
As the venerable [author] said:
There is no designation by its own property that expresses the relationship;
because it is absolutely dependent, its form is not taught.
Because it provides assistance, that [nature] is followed wherever it exists;
it is the power of powers, and it is the quality of qualities.
"But the designation [of the terms] for those two belongs to their respective properties, namely conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and inherence (*samavāya*)," and so forth.

This, however, is merely a praise of the relationship and not a formal statement of logic; thus, it was not refuted by the author of the text. Furthermore, the relation of cause and effect (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) is not applicable here. For instance, the self (*ātman*) is first of all not—
It must be so. Furthermore, even cognition, when arising from an object, a sense faculty, mental attention, and so forth, would not take itself as its own cause.
(Page 206)
When X exists, Y necessarily occurs; yet if one imagines something other than that [X] to be the cause of Y, there would be an infinite regress of causes in all cases.
According to this principle, since there is no such thing as "action" (kriyā), there is no connection whatsoever here [between action and agent]. Regarding the phrase "based upon that":

by their very nature, the action and the agent must be stated as being connected; yet the sense is that no such connection exists. There exists only the stream of cognitions consisting of experience, conceptualization, recollection, and so forth.

This is because the point that "it is not the knower" has already been established previously. Now, he states its status as an illustration with the word "just as. But how is the commentary [to be understood] regarding the phrase "even agency"? For while knowledge exists in the case of being a knower, nothing other than that [knowledge], nor its relation [to it], is found; however, in the case of being an agent of another, there is neither action, nor anything other than that, nor its relation [to it].

Thus, how is there similarity? Insofar as it is "imagined" (kalpita), this much constitutes the illustrative example; why require complete similarity in every respect? Furthermore, that is not excessively difficult to establish, as he says: "Therefore also," and "all the more so. Even knowledge, for its part, is of the nature of a verbal root-meaning (*dhātvartha*); according to the Grammarians (*vaiyākaraṇa*), it is an action (*kriyā*), and according to the Mīmāṃsakas as well.

However, for certain proponents of cultivation (*bhāvanāvādins*), the distinction is that [the self] is denoted by the suffix of the present participle (*pratyaya*). In that regard, by refuting all action (*kriyā*) in general, even the action of cognition (*jñāna-kriyā*) accepted by others is necessarily refuted. Thus, there is complete parity between the two positions. On the contrary, this firm doctrine holds that even when cognition exists, the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtā*) is not logically established.
Thus, there is a sense of intensification (*prakarṣa*). For that very reason, it is logical for the state of being a knower (*jñātṛtā*) to serve as the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

Furthermore, by means of this reductio ad absurdum (*prasaṅga-dūṣaṇa*), there is an even greater intensification: if the opponent’s position results in the impossibility of knowledge, what then could constitute the state of being a knower?
Now, [the author says]:
Is it not the case that [the objection] beginning with "the appearance of the particular characteristic" (1.2.1) and so forth—
[is answered by the fact that] by that [same reasoning], the agent too is merely imagined?
The author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) states the result useful for the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) regarding this collection of sūtras ending with [the word] "iti":
"How can the Self be the Lord of All? By the word "iti," he indicates the non-establishment of the subject (*dharmyasiddhi*).

He elucidates what was indicated by the words "of knowledge itself, whose nature is awakening," and so forth. He demonstrates the unestablished nature of the reason (hetvasiddhi) indicated [by the opponent] by stating that the definition consisting of mere "action and agent" has been postulated;
thus he declares the absence of the essential reason (svabhāvahetu) for establishing the conventional usage of sovereignty, as stated by the proponent (siddhāntin).
The Buddhist has thus established that the self is merely the continuum of consciousness; may there be auspiciousness! || 11 ||
Thus ends the second chapter, the Examination of the Opposing View, in the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī* composed by the illustrious Great Māheśvara, the venerable Ācārya Abhinavagupta.

Now begins the third reflection: I bow to that Supreme Bliss of Bhairava, which is overflowing with the power of Will, radiant as nectar, capable of generating infinite worlds, and embraced by the surging waves of His own powers.
Now, in response to this prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa), the established conclusion (siddhānta) is set forth by means of two arguments.
Therein,
it is true, however—

By this [verse] beginning with "ityādinā" and ending with "smṛtyapohanaśaktimān," through these seven verses, [the author], while reflecting upon the impossibility of other philosophical systems, refutes them.
Having established the introductory framework with the words, "Now, [the cognition] appearing as the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*)... and so forth, it was stated: [1.2.1].

"If memory is established through mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), then the rememberer must be imagined as being like the seer" (1.2.6). This constitutes the section concerning the investigation of knowledge. The investigation into the relationship with action, however, will occur in the second section. Therein, by means of two verses, it is shown that knowledge is of the nature of self-awareness, [and thus] in memory, there is no [separate] experience.

It has been stated that there is no manifestation [of the object] even when [the cognition] arises from its latent impression (*saṃskāra*). Having refuted the claim that memory is an error by means of two verses while raising an objection, [the author proceeds] with the third [verse] on page 208.

The intended meaning is as follows: having stated that, as a consequence, all determinations (*adhyavasāya*) are thereby refuted—since memory is untenable for one who perceives another even when there is a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), resulting in the collapse of worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)—the author has explained its logical consistency within his own position in the following verse. In that context, regarding the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) which must be entirely pacified, the word "no" (*na*) is employed.

The term "īṣat" (slightly) is used when there is something to be partially accepted, and "satyam kintu" (it is true, but) when there is something to be slightly rejected; this is the style of those who employ speech with foresight. And here, by the word "satyam," much of what was stated by the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is indeed to be accepted in the final conclusion (*siddhānta*). [This applies] in systems such as Sāṃkhya and Kaṇāda.
That which was stated by the Śākya— that knowledge is not possible— is indeed agreed upon. However,
in order to demonstrate another distinction therein, we ask further with the word "but" (*kintu*),
indicating that one should not yet have ceased from the practice of training, so as to remove that delusion.

This has been stated as an effort [to resolve the difficulty]. For indeed, regarding the dilemma you raised with the words, "If knowledge were of the nature of consciousness... (1.2.7), this very point is our established conclusion (*siddhānta*). In that regard, the word "true" (*satyam*) refers to this.

Everything up to the word "in vain" (*vyartham eva*) has been explained; by the word "merely" (*kevalam*), however, [the following is meant]. By this, an introduction to the subsequent portion of the text is made. For instance, [it says] "it does not produce an effect. To this extent, the meaning of this sūtra is introduced, as well as the meaning of the seven verses beginning with "by the Self, the Great Lord" (*ātmanā maheśvareṇa*), by way of knowledge (*jñāna*).

By the phrase "first of all," [the author] refers to the entire scope of the *jñānādhikāra* (the section on knowledge), as opposed to the *kriyādhikāra* (the section on ritual action), because the remainder of the text is established upon that very subject matter. Now, according to the maxim that "a word like *tat* or *kim tu*, when occupied by one [subject], cannot occupy another," this term [*tat*] occupies its own sentence, context, and distinct topic (*adhikārāntara*).

Introducing the entire treatise as being like the primary seed, he says that [the scripture] "speaks of the distinction of knowledge," which is the reality of the Self (*ātmatattva*). One does not achieve the ultimate goal by this alone; rather, it also speaks of "refinement" (*saṃskāra*), as indicated by the word "also" (*api*). Just as the reality of the Self, which is knowledge, is incapable of performing its function without refinement, so too...
In this system, the second *api* (also) implies that even *saṃskāra* [is included] by means of which [the result occurs]; *adhunā* (now) indicates that the time has arrived.
(Page 209)

"Immediately after the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)"—with these words, he introduces the subject matter expressed by the seven verses and begins to explain it. By this, first of all, there is the introduction of the present section (prakaraṇa). "By way of knowledge" means that at the commencement of the section on knowledge, there is an introduction to the entire meaning of the treatise by way of knowledge.

While it would have been sufficient to say "for the purpose of establishing the state of being a knower," the use of the term "agent" (*kartṛtva*) is intended to show that sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) consists precisely in pure autonomy (*svātantrya*), as stated in the *Ādisiddhasūtra*. For indeed, autonomy is characterized by the power to join or separate objects of knowledge according to one's will.

Because its essence consists of the dyad of *prakāśa* (light) and *vimarśa* (reflective awareness), the investigation in the section on knowledge (*jñānādhikāra*) takes the aspect of light alone as primary, whereas in the section on action (*kriyādhikāra*), it is by virtue of the primacy of *vimarśa*. Thus, the term "mouth" (*mukha*) is employed; for "mouth," "door," and "means" (*upāya*) are synonymous, and [the reality] is not [grasped] through the door of only one part within the substrate (*dharmin*).

It has been stated that entry is indeed full (*pūrṇa*). Therefore, agency here must be established as full, consisting of pure sovereignty. In that regard, the investigation of knowledge and action is merely a means. Here, having determined through experience that something is a cause of pleasure, one acquires it through recollection; such is worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*). In that context:

Granted that the manifestation of the object in memory is established through the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) born of experience; yet, by that much alone, nothing is gained, because if the experience itself is unmanifest, there can be no such form [of memory] as "that" [referring to the past]. Furthermore, the manifestation of the experience is not possible even if it is produced from a latent impression—this is the intended meaning of the section. Thus says the Sūtra:

It is true; however, memory-cognition arises from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience, and even though it is established within the self, it does not perceive that original experience. (1)

Regarding the phrase "knowledge consisting of memory" (*smṛtijñānam*): although knowledge in the form of memory arises from the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience, it nevertheless has its firm foundation and repose (*niṣṭhā-viśrānti*) within the Self as its own essential nature (*svarūpa*). It does not, however, serve to make known that original experience; for it does not [unify] itself with that [original experience].

He mixes them together; thus he says, "only mutually distinct. The word "only" (*eva*) indicates that even according to your own system, there is no non-difference—just as in our own system—because even inwardness does not exist for you in any way whatsoever. In that regard, [there is] the relation of knowledge with its object...
(page 210)

Because it is designatable, he establishes its distinction precisely through that [designation], saying "it is clear" (*sphuṭa*). That which is "clear" is the object whose nature is the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*); it appears simultaneously with the cognition, being graspable by imparting its own form to the cognition. In recollection (*smṛti*), however, it is "not clear"; it neither generates the recollective cognition, nor—

It appears simultaneously with that [object]. Whatever kind of object appears in a given cognition, that cognition, at its very own time, is merely the manifestation of such an object as it exists—whether clearly or unclearly—as something whose domain is solely itself; it is not capable of even touching upon an object that appears in another cognition.
Let that manifestation remain for now. But surely, memory manifests an object that existed at the time of its [prior] experience?

True; however, it manifests only its own object as existing precisely at its own time, and only as its own object, not as another's object or through the nature of another's object. "This jar existed," "it exists."

The manifestation of its own object occurs at its own very time through a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that illuminates objects belonging to the three times, [thinking] "it will be. Even when there is a determination (*adhyavasāya*) or a manifestation as belonging to another time, there is no determination of that other time, nor is there a manifestation of an existing real entity (*vastu*) as such— as in the case of [manifesting] silver or a double moon.

For even in the manifestation of a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), there is no such determinative cognition of silver or a double moon. This is what he means by saying "that and that": although the objective reality (*arthavastu*) is apprehended—meaning it is accepted through the medium of determinative cognition—as intermingled or permeated by various temporal distinctions such as past, future, and so forth, nevertheless, it is only to that extent.

It accepts its own object at its own time alone; just as a beloved person seen in a dream is grasped at the very time of the dream and as that specific object, and not at the time of the cognition of the beloved nor as the object of that cognition— because if it were so, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) of perceiving the beloved person [as present]— so too here, according to the *Ṭīkā*, there is a distinction between those respective times.
The mental modification (*vṛtti*) has been explained as being born from the awakening of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a previous experience.

For, by virtue of those impressions, the object in memory appears as if embraced by the time of the previous experience; this is explained by the text [stating] that it does not appear so in other cognitions, because [memory] rests solely upon the self (*ātman*).

This is the statement regarding the function [of the cognition]. By the word "only" (*mātra*), objects of other cognitions are excluded; however, it does not mean that it is restricted to having the self as its object.
(Page 211)

It should be stated in the Sūtra and in the Vṛtti that [consciousness] is indeed the self-cognizer of its own object. Now, one might ask: "Even when cognizing an object, how can consciousness remain established in itself? Who says this? However, if this [self-establishment] were not presented by way of the object, there would be a cessation of worldly transactions such as the grasping of objects through memory and desire.

With that very intention, the commentator has arisen by placing the subject matter at the forefront, through verbal formulations concerning the nature of the self and the objects of meaning and reality whose subjects are clearly manifest. Anticipating the objection, "How then is it said that [consciousness] is merely the self-awareness of the nature established in the Self?", he says: "The Self and the non-Self... and so forth.

The illumination of the self alone is certainly not absent in knowledge during states such as meditative absorption; however, the word "api" (also/even) indicates that here [in this context], knowledge is being examined as it pertains to objects. Regarding the phrase "of that very [self]," in the statement that knowledge is the illumination of the non-self, that which is called "the illumination of the non-self"— [is what is meant].

By the term "manifestation" (*prakāśanam*), it is not meant that the non-self, such as a jar, is being embraced [by consciousness], because manifestation lacks the property of being an object; rather, it is knowledge itself that manifests either as the manifestation of the non-self or by assuming the form of the non-self. Thus, manifestation belongs solely to knowledge as its own inherent state.

Therefore, let it be for now: those who consider themselves well-trained Naiyāyikas have stated that because the inwardness and outwardness of cognition are contradictory in nature, they lead to a distinction [between subject and object], and thus they have entered into the Buddhist view merely to convince those of superficial vision; so let this matter rest. Now, one might object: "In the Vijñānavāda, let there be nothing additional to the essential nature [of consciousness]..."

Anticipating the objection, "In the theory of external objects (*bāhyārthavāda*), however, since it is said that 'the blue manifests,' how can we deny this determination? he says: "Even in the externalist view (*bāhyavāde'pi*).
The particle *api* indicates the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). Manifestation does not embrace the object, because its nature is that of manifestation.

Because an object has the nature of non-luminosity, it possesses the quality of being an object of cognition (*vedyatva*). If consciousness were to enter into that [object], then even luminosity itself would become non-luminous, just as in the false cognition of hair-tufts (*kacaka-cūrca*) in one suffering from ophthalmia. If luminosity were to enter into the hair-tufts, then they would become non-existent. And it is not tenable to say that the luminosity of the hair-tufts is non-existent, because it exists precisely as such, as has been understood for a long time.

This is because it accounts for the practical functioning of medical treatment and the like. Thus, being permeated by those [sensory] qualities is the pervader of form as it adheres to its object; and that [pervasion] does not exist in the manifestation of the hair on the head and beard.

When the proponent of external objects (bāhyavādin) has been made to admit that [the object] lacks the property of being unreal because it is not permeated by the nature of reality, then that external thing possesses the property of being an object of cognition (vedyatva). Its opposite is the state of not being an object of cognition (avedyatva). Being of the nature of light (prakāśarūpatva) is pervaded by that [non-objectivity];

for it has been stated at length that if there were objectivity, there would follow an infinite regress and other such manifold consequences. Thus, [the nature of light] is pervaded by that which is incompatible with the pervader [of objectivity].

[This is] perception. Now, one might object: "If such were the Buddhist position, then they would have shown that self-awareness alone is the single type of direct perception, and not that which is sensory. Anticipating this doubt, he says "merely" (*kevalam*).
This division—consisting of the sensory and so forth—is created by internal differences arising from a difference in causes and a difference in essential natures.

Because it is manifested through its own nature as being illuminated by another, it is designated by that very unique [characteristic] as "sensory" (*aindriyika*) and as "the manifestation of an object" (*arthaprakāśa*). This is just as there is a designation for the cognitions of mental perception, yogic perception, and inference based on their respective unique [causes]. However, where there is another unique cause—

It is not perceived; therefore, the state of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedanatva*) is conventionally designated there as a general rule. Yet, even that, by implication—according to the maxim of "the cow and the bull"—results in being restricted specifically to [the case of] particulars. Consequently, even for one who maintains the fourfold classification of perception, the fact of being aware of its own nature remains established. [Objection: Let it not be so.

The manifestation of the object of another cognition by means of a subsequent cognition—that indeed is the experience; even though it has passed away, it is made manifest by the cognition of memory, just as a torrential downpour is manifested by the flood of a river. He says, "And in the case of the cognition of memory," etc. "Like the object" (*arthavat*) is an example by way of contrast (*vaidharmyeṇa*); for just as an object [is perceived] through its distinction...
"It shines, but not so is there an experience [of it].
Nor is it logical that the object being remembered should appear as distinct from the memory" (1.4.3)—
this is either an illustration by way of similarity based on future observation, or [it refers to] the object such as a deceased father who exists within the memory.

As for the object, there is no possibility of anything external to it [the memory] existing as a distinct entity; thus, the illumination of both memory and direct experience will be established precisely as a non-differentiation of their inward-turned nature. And so, even if the object of experience or the experience itself is not illuminated by the cognition of memory, [the point remains].
Let it be granted, for now, that the impression (*saṃskāra*) merely provides the memory-cognition with an object;
however, as for the determination (*adhyavasāya*) by way of having the object of experience as its own object—
(page 213)
[Otherwise], that [recollection] would not exist. Therefore, if even a third mode is not accepted—namely, that recollection has the very same inward-turned form as experience—then this follows:
the manifestation of recollection itself is indeed the manifestation of the experience, internally, despite the difference in time conditioned by the object.

Because [the object] is unreal in consciousness, that object appears even in memory solely as an object of experience (*anubhava*). Its status as an object might be suspected through three possible ways; however, since two of them are entirely untenable, this is stated as an established fact by way of the third possibility. And thus, "therefore," by virtue of being its object...
Because there would be an absence of illumination, that activity consisting of grasping and so forth, which occurs through memory and desire, would not exist.

This [activity] would be possible if the object of memory were brought into identity with the object of the previous experience. For instance, having seen a wood-apple (*kapittha*) and remembering, "This is a means to pleasure," [one acts].
It grasps [the object]. Furthermore, there is nothing whatsoever in this memory that is a pleasure attached to a previous experience.
As it has been said:
"This alone is our pleasure, namely, a pleasant sensation."

Thus, if the nature of pleasure were derived from the mental impression (*saṃskāra*) alone, this would be a cognition of the experience of pleasure, and not a memory. By this, it is explained that the [opposing] position—that [the impression] serves as the determiner—is untenable. Thus ends the commentary on the first verse.
Now, one might object: "Granted that there may be no appropriation of an external object;
however, why is the appearance of the experience—not accepted—in memory, which was my own internal realization brought about by the power of mental impressions (*saṃskāra*)? Anticipating this doubt:
To refute that [position], the Sūtra states:

"Vision is self-manifesting and is not known by another, just as the vision of color; however, the fact that [the cognition of] taste arises from a mental impression is merely its similarity [to the former case], not the means of knowing it. (2)
Vision is knowledge. That [vision] is the manifestation of itself; "manifestation of itself" means belonging to that very [vision] alone.
And there is no form of it that is not shining forth. Furthermore, its nature is light.
Even if it were dependent upon another's grace, and even though it is always manifest, there would also be a second form that is unmanifest— merely a semblance of the shadow of forms such as blue—
and thus there would be a further restriction of two kinds. Therefore, it is "only its own manifestation," and "only the manifestation of itself."

Thus, by means of both difference in substratum (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) and identity of substratum (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), that whose nature is regulated for everything by manifestation is distinguished from the insentient (*jaḍa*). Therefore, by this definition characterized by regulation, the state of being cognizable by another is refuted; just as the perception of a flavor has the flavor as its object and is not [perceived] by another.
Just as [an object] like form is to be known by a cognition of form and so forth, likewise every act of seeing (*dṛk*) is not to be known by another cognition.
Furthermore, since experience has the nature of seeing, it cannot be known by a memory-cognition. [Objection: What then is accomplished by the mental impression (*saṃskāra*)?
[Reply: He says: because of the absence of a generating object, when objectlessness would otherwise result...

That similarity, which consists in having the same object, is produced by that [object]; however, the designation of cause and effect as non-different is made through metaphorical usage (*upacāra*). The basis for this metaphorical usage is the realization of its exclusive orientation toward that [object] due to the absence of any other effect, and not the state of having that [object] as its form of apprehension, nor the state of manifesting a prior experience, nor being produced by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Its equality with that [the object] is also stated by way of considering the nature of things; however, its apprehension—that is, its comprehension—is not possible.

For what third entity, other than memory and direct experience, could determine similarity? And since those two have not seen each other, they do not perceive similarity; such is the meaning of the Sūtra. Regarding the phrase "there is no apprehension of that," there are two meanings.

By the word "that" (tat), there is a reference to both the experience and its similarity; therein, the first meaning should be understood as the cause for the second. The metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) here in the commentary is made clear by the fact that [the cognition] arises from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). He introduces this briefly with the words "the first," because in the initial experience...

Since experience has the nature of manifesting an object as its very face, memory too would have to consist in the manifestation of an object; yet that is not the case—this is the statement of the intended probandum (sādhya) implied by the Sūtra. By the word "yasmāt" (because), its utility for the implied probandum is demonstrated.
Even though they arise from the same collection [of causes], their equality is also stated briefly by means of the metaphorical attribution of non-difference (*abhedopacāra*).
"It is not cognizable by another cognition"—by this, the phrase "its comprehension is by that" is explained briefly in two ways (p.

The explanation is as follows: memory is neither the apprehension of an experience, nor is it the manifestation of its similarity [to that experience], whether by memory itself, by the original experience, or by a third cognition. The reason stated as common to all cases is that cognition is not cognizable by another cognition; this is because [cognition] has the singular nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*).

This is a concise explanation of the meaning of the passage beginning with "dṛk" (the Seer). By the term "one," the meaning of the particle "eva" (only) is explained: it is that which is one, such as the number one, being alone without any companion, and is indeed that very [Self]; it is never anything else.
Furthermore, its form is that of the non-inert (ajaḍa), not that of the inert (jaḍa). It is that whose single form is self-awareness (svasaṃvedana).

The commentator indicates, by means of the word *hi*, that this aphorism serves as the reason for refuting a suspected opposing view. The definition of the Seer (*dṛk*) is the state of being restricted to its own manifestation, characterized by the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga*) and the exclusion of connection with another (*anyayoga*), expressed as: "the Seer alone is its own manifestation" and "the Seer is indeed its own manifestation. In this regard, it is the Seer alone that is its own manifestation, and not any other object.

Having previously stated the definition of that which is other—namely, the insentient (*jaḍa*)—he now states the definition of the non-insentient vision (*dṛk*), which is preceded by that [definition], beginning with the words "For this...
(*ayaṃ hi*). When it is said that "the insentient is that whose nature is non-luminous" (*aprakāśātman*), one might object that when blue is manifest, it would then not be insentient;
therefore, he includes the term "itself" (*svayam*). For even though there is a manifestation of that [blue] which is being manifested, that [manifestation] is not...

[The object] rests as a related entity within its own nature as blue; rather, it rests within another, namely, the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*). Therefore, this is the analysis of the compound: that whose nature or essence is such that illumination—meaning the act of manifesting—is non-existent insofar as it rests [within itself]. This is what he means by saying, "there is no illumination of itself. Of this very [point]:
The clarification will be as follows: [the blue] does not manifest for itself, but rather manifests for another.

The genitive case is used here in the sense of the locative. Furthermore, that which is called "manifestation" in the statement "the blue manifests" is not the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the blue;
rather, it is something entirely distinct from the blue. For [manifestation belongs to] the cognizers, such as Caitra or Maitra.
That [object] is its own nature (*svabhāva*). The analysis of the compound is: "manifestation is not its self, but rather belongs to it as something other.
Thus he says: "Its manifestation does not occur by means of itself. He will clarify this very point later by stating: "Its manifestation is indeed by means of another.
In this way, just as blue is blue in itself, it is not so in the case of the nature of manifestation.

The intended meaning is that that which has non-manifestation as its nature— such that its manifestation is not of the same nature as the subject (*pramātṛ*), as it is for blue, where manifestation is not its nature— is insentient (*jaḍa*). By the reverse of this, it is non-insentient (*ajaḍa*).

He shows that for whom knowledge is not non-manifestation and whose form is not [material], by the words "but the non-inert" (*ajaḍas tu*). His own self is the manifestation; his own self is its manifestation—thus, for whom manifestation rests within the self. Manifestation is his very self, his essential nature (*svabhāva*), and not something else that is separate from him.

It has been explained through two arguments that [the Self] is of the nature of light (*prakāśātmā*). That very point is clarified in sequence by the passage beginning with "of one's own self" (*svātmana eva*) and so forth. Thus, the definitions of the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*)—namely, being of the nature of non-light and being of the nature of light—are each presented in two ways by way of the application of their essential natures (*svarūpa*).

And by means of excluding other forms (*pararūpavyāvartana*), the author of the commentary has explained [the text], clarifying it step by step. By this very commentary, the rule that "it is indeed its own manifestation" (*svābhāsaiva*) is explained in four ways. To illustrate: it is explained that "that [light] is the manifestation of its own nature alone" (*svarūpasyaiva sā prakāśaḥ*), and as "the manifestation of its own self" (*svātmanaḥ prakāśaḥ*).

It has been explained that its nature is not non-manifest; it has been clarified that since its own self is its manifestation, its manifestation is never derived from another; it has been shown that it shines by its own self alone and not through another; and it has been demonstrated that forms such as blue and so forth are not its true nature.

"The other is not its manifestation" means: for how could that which is "other," such as blue and so forth, possess the nature of manifestation for this [consciousness]? By reversing this, the fourfold definition should also be applied to the insentient (*jaḍa*). In the phrase "for all cognition" (*sarvā hi jñaptiḥ*), the word "all" (*sarva*) refers to the genus, while "vision" (*dṛk*) is in the singular.

This has been explained, but not as being of the nature of non-perception (*adṛgrūpa*); rather, there is the restriction that it is "perception" (*dṛk*). For whatever entity whatsoever manifests its own appearance, all of that becomes of the nature of perception. Indeed, even though a restriction found within another sentence may have fulfilled its purpose once a single aspect has been restricted, [it still applies] here and there.

It is said that the word order is inverted; nevertheless, since that [sentence] becomes complete when all its constituent parts are fulfilled, if there is no sublation regarding the presence of all components, it should be explained in exactly that way. Furthermore, there is no fragmentation of the unity of the sentence; on the contrary, there is the sentence-meaning as a single, compact, and determinate form.
The application [of the rule] becomes clear only through unity;
for that very reason, in cases such as *brahmādi-ghātinaḥ* where *kvip* follows a root ending in a consonant (*hantṛ*), and so forth.
The authors of the *Anupada* and other works have accepted the recourse to four types of restrictive determination (*avadhāraṇā*).

However, for the sake of explanation, the formulation of intermediate sentences does not entail a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*), because such a formulation is necessarily present even within a single restriction or injunction. Thus say Brahmā and others.
Such [entities] must be considered as qualifying adjuncts (*upapada*), for it is impossible to provide an explanation otherwise without resorting to a division of the sentence;

enough of this prolixity. Now, if such a rule is established, it follows that whatever is distinct from the vision (*dṛk*) is insentient (*jaḍa*). Consequently, the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) who is distinct from the acts of knowledge would himself be insentient.

He dispels the doubt—namely, "How can one who maintains the doctrine of the non-insentient subject (ajaḍapramātṛ) triumph by means of the doctrine that cognition is self-manifesting?"—with the words "For this very reason. For this very reason—that is, because of the definition stated regarding the insentient and the non-insentient—the insentient does not manifest itself, nor is it the case that this object acts as its own manifester. Having stated this through negative concomitance (vyatireka), he now states it through positive concomitance (anvaya):

He says: "For it is indeed of the light... Because this positive concomitance (*anvaya*) exists, the word *hi* indicates that this negative concomitance (*vyatireka*) is also ultimately real. [Objection: But if the light were to manifest, there would have to be two lights;
yet this is not the case. For it is only our own self (*asmadartha*) that manifests, and this is either consciousness (*saṃvit*) or the state of being the seer (*draṣṭṛtā*).

Nor is knowledge [considered] so. He says: "For it is indeed manifestation (*prakāśa*). By the word "for" (*hi*), which indicates the reason, he points toward the object that must be refuted as it is being raised as a doubt. In valid cognition (*pramā*), the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is independent, and valid cognition is manifestation. That which does not derive from another, and that by whose grace another [exists], is precisely that [manifestation].

The intended meaning is that [the object] is independent within that [consciousness]. Regarding the phrase "from manifestation" (*prakāśāt*): there is a twofold alternative as to whether the part of one's own self—which is distinct from that aspect of manifestation (the "manifestation" in the sense that "blue manifests")—is of the nature of manifestation or otherwise. If the first position is held, then the manifestation residing in the objective aspect would be something other [than the subject].

What, then, is accepted? For two illuminations do not appear, nor is there a difference in the illumination itself by way of space, time, or essential nature, as has been explained at length previously. Furthermore, it has been stated that manifestness (*prakaṭatā*) is not a property of the object.
Consciousness (*saṃvit*), however, will be examined later. Therefore, according to the first position, the illumination itself is the illuminator.

Thus it is established that [the object] is the knower (*pramātṛ*). As for the second position, however, because it is afflicted by defects, it is to be disregarded; thus he says, "In the state of being of the nature of light" (*prakāśātmatve*). And consequently, blue is nothing but light itself.

Regarding the statement "it shines forth," this is the ultimate truth: within that very form of the Lord which consists of Great Light (*mahāprakāśa*), there shines forth a cognizer (*pramātṛ*) who, by means of his own power, is internally contracted by emptiness, vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth, yet is not entirely contracted with respect to external objects; that same [cognizer] undergoes external contraction.

"It appears as the manifestation of blue. In ultimate reality, this is the unfolding of the power (*śakti*) of the venerable Mahādeva, like a multitude of very subtle mirrors appearing within a great mirror that holds their reflections; thus, it is logical that the Light itself is the non-inert subject (*pramātṛ*). But [one might object]: "Is it not indeed inert?"
Let the cognizer be non-manifest. He asks: "Of what is that non-manifestation? [He replies: "Of 'me'.

For it is only of that which is manifesting—which serves as the foundation (bhitti)—that such expressions as "blue manifests" arise, by virtue of its manifold conceptualization. Furthermore, in that case, "another" refers to a different cognizer who must be expected; "in that state" means in the state of being insentient.
If there were a dependence on another cognizer, there would be an infinite regress. [Objection: Let it be like the seed and the sprout. [Reply:

It might be so, provided it did not destroy its own root; however, it does destroy it. Thus he says: "There would be no apprehension of the object, that is, no manifestation, because there would be nothing whatsoever manifesting that is distinct from its prior form. [Objection: But surely, by this much...
It would be established as mere manifestation restricted to each respective object, but not as the cognizer (*pramātṛ*). He says: "pervasive" (*anugata*).

Although that manifestation is contracted by the differentiation of objects through its outward orientation, and by the differentiation of space and time brought about by the coloring (*uparāga*) of those objects, nevertheless, it also possesses the characteristic of the inward-oriented cognizer.

The undivided and uncontracted form is inherent within that contracted state; without it, no connection—such as the relation of cause and effect or the relation of the sublated and the sublator—among objects, which constitutes the very nature of worldly existence and culminates in the teaching of ultimate reality, would be possible. This will be explained at length later.
In passages such as "deśakālakramajuṣā... (1.7.3),
worldly transactional experience is perceived as being either with impurity or pure (1.7.14).
Thus ends the section. Now, [one might ask]: is it not the case that the nature of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is pervasive throughout all means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) characterized by cognition?
(Page 219)

Anticipating the objection that "the self will be the inherent cause (samavāyikāraṇa), so what is the use of considering whether it is manifest or unmanifest," he says: "Therefore" (tataḥ). Since synthesis (samanvaya) is by nature inward-turned light, and its very nature consists in the reflective awareness of the manifestation of synthetic recollection, it does not [become the self] merely by being a cause of valid cognition (pramākāraṇatva).

Due to its distinction from objects, sense organs, and so forth, it is logical that the insentient self possesses the status of a knower (*pramātṛ*). Now, one might object: according to the Kaṇāda view, let it be granted that insentience is untenable for the knower; however, if the knower is indeed manifest, then—just like a jar or other objects—the knower must possess the characteristic of being produced by a causal complex (*kārakasāmagrī*) consisting in the arising of a consciousness whose object is that [knower].

How so? For the "I-component" (ahaṃśa) does not appear as an object, as in the cognition "I know the jar"; it is for this very reason that it is non-inert and immediate. He equates this Prābhākara view with his own doctrine by means of the statement, "otherwise, however, it is logically established. For just as blue appears to another as "this is blue," it does not [appear]...

"Thus, this is the Self. How could it be insentient (*jaḍa*), given that there is no manifestation of it as "this"? Nor is it [itself] a manifestation. For it is blue, pleasure, and so forth that manifest; thus, a consciousness arises having those as its objects. Now, the Self does not manifest, because there is no arising of a consciousness of the Self (*ātmasaṃvitti*); therefore, it is not perceptible (*pratyakṣa*) like blue.

Regarding the direct perception of blue: it is not the case that the self is entirely devoid of intrinsic nature and yet remains non-manifest; rather, it is precisely its manifestation as "that" which is appropriate, according to our position that the self is self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), and not otherwise. For there are only two possible courses for an existent thing: if it shines forth, it is manifest (*pratyakṣa*); if it does not, it is non-manifest (*parokṣa*).
In that regard, if it were the position of non-manifestation, there would be indirectness (*parokṣatā*); if it were the position of manifestation, there would be directness (*pratyakṣatā*).

Thus, by the mention of "non-indirectness" (*aparokṣatā*), another alternative would present itself, namely non-existence (*asattva*). And that is not tenable; hence he says, "For indeed... [The phrase] "restricted to different persons" means: "It manifests to me, but not to Caitra."

"It shines forth. Having thus demonstrated that, by way of another perspective, immediacy (*apārokṣya*) would ultimately rest only in non-existence, he establishes it through his own doctrine with the words, "But immediacy...
That which is well-known as being cognizable through sensory or mental perception appears to the subject as "this," distinct from himself.

Perception (*pratyakṣa*) arises from the contact with the sense organs; however, the knower (*pramātṛ*) is not like that. Therefore, he is not perceptible, yet because he does manifest, he is not non-perceptual (*parokṣa*). Otherwise—if this were accepted as stated in this figurative expression—[the following would occur].
(Page 220)
The underlying intention is that if its existence consists merely in being beyond perception (*parokṣatā*) regarding the distinction of objects, for the opponent indeed asserts this:
"In such common usages as 'I know the jar' or 'I know the cloth,' the cognitions of objects such as jars appear both as they arise and as they dissolve."

The perceptibility of jars and other objects arises from the grace of the emergence of such consciousness (*saṃvit*). Furthermore, these consciousnesses are not attributes of the object, nor are they attributes of the self (*ātman*), because they manifest with independence. Let this be granted for now; however, as for that which shines as "I," no emergence of consciousness need be postulated there, for if such an emergence were required, the manifestation of that [I-consciousness]...
This would follow from the consequence of [the self] being fragmented, and because it would then be an object (*karman*). But this is not the case, as they say:
"The Self shines forth all at once.
Thus, in this view, only the nature of the Self as light (*prakāśarūpatā*) is admitted, and the same applies to cognitions (*saṃvid*) as well.

Since there is no distinction of essence, place, time, or other factors within the nature of light, how could there be any real difference from that ultimate nature of light? Therefore, one should not—by entering into our own system—accept a limitation caused by the coloring of differences such as "blue" and so forth, which are produced by *māyā*. Rather, such a limitation must be understood as being granted only through the grace of [the Supreme Lord].
The delusion of the Prābhākaras has also been dispelled incidentally. This is what he says with the words "for this very reason.

Since this immediate manifestation (*apārokṣya*), whose essence is the revelation of autonomy, has been accepted, for that very reason this must be accepted as established without effort. Namely, that which will indeed be stated: "existence..."
It is precisely the state of being manifest, and that [manifestation] resides inherently within the nature of Light itself because it is independent of anything else.

As for the insentient object such as "blue" which appears during the state of *māyā* due to the duality imagined by *māyā*, it manifests as residing solely within the subject (*pramātṛ*); thus, this [object] belongs only to the subject and nothing of it belongs to one's own Self (*svātman*). For the Self alone is...
"Of this [Self], there is nothing whatsoever. And thus, the *Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi* states:
"In this way, these insentient things, which are like non-existents to the Self, exist only as manifestations of Light;
for Light alone exists by its own nature through its own and other selves. (13)

Thus [it is said]. But let the Prābhākara, who maintains the doctrine of consciousness (*saṃvidvādī*), be brought down into his own view by this method as much as you wish; however, how about the follower of Kaṇāda? For he says this: "From the conjunction of the mind with the self, acting as the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), and from [that conjunction] acting as the non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*), [cognition arises] through inherence in the same object as the effect."

If cognition arises from proximate causes and instrumental causes— such as the sense organs and light— whose efficacy has been observed, then the object is manifested. And that [manifestation] is dependent upon the manifestation of the object.

Since everyday activities such as desire, effort, bodily action, and the acts of taking up and letting go have come into being, what is the use of postulating a self that is "manifest"? Even when there is the conventional expression "the self is manifest," it is simply the cognition of the self as its object—
produced by inference through the mind alone— that constitutes the manifestation of the self.

What is the loss? To this it is said: Does the arising of cognition cause the object to become manifest, or is that [manifestation] itself [the cognition]? Regarding these two positions, he refutes the first with the words "nor" (*na ca*). For if one accepts that manifestation is an effect, then it would have to be admitted as a property (*dharma*) of the object; and that has been refuted many times.
The second position alone, that [the light] is of the nature of self-existence (*svabhāvatā*), is logical. Thus he says: "Rather, it is cognition itself" (*jñānameva*);

the connection is with "the state of being manifest" (*prakāśamānatā*). Furthermore, the self, the senses, objects, and so forth are not, first of all, characterized by the property of manifestation (*prakāśadharmāḥ*); and if cognition also were not characterized by the property of manifestation, then it would be as before.

Just as nothing at all is manifested when that [cognition] does not arise, so too, let nothing be manifested even when it does arise; what is lost to us? To the objection "What is lost?", he replies: "The object as well. For the very cognition of an object constitutes its perceptibility; if that [cognition] is not manifested, how can there be any practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding it as being perceived?

It is like [the cognition of] whiteness in the manifestation of white. For the cause of its being treated as such is its manifestation in that form; otherwise, how could there be a necessary treatment of it as such? Thus, there is a non-perception of the cause. Now, if it is argued that even perceptuality is manifested by another cognition, then there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

The meaning of the word "as before" (*prāgvat*) is as follows: thus, it is not logically possible for light itself to be illumined by another. By the use of the word "first" (*tāvat*), he intends this: this self-luminosity of light is established; while that exists, being illumined by another is excluded. When that [being illumined by another] is excluded, experience is not illumined by a cognition consisting of memory.
Thus, although this much of the subject matter (*prameya*) has been presented, the knower (*pramātṛ*) is not yet established; nevertheless,
since this inquiry into reality (*tattvacintā*) takes the form of a discussion (*vāda*), it is not inconsistent to reflect upon the true nature of the Light (*prakāśa*) in the commentary (*ṭīkā*).

(Page 222) Precisely for that reason, there is indeed no suspicion regarding this objection. When it was stated by the Buddhist, for the sake of supporting memory, that "experiential cognition should be expressed by means of the cognition of memory," [the author] replied with the verse.

The appropriate response has been stated, and it has also been established through the commentary (*vṛtti*) according to the [author’s] intention. Therefore, there is nothing at all inconsistent between the *sūtra* and the *vṛtti*. However, regarding the distinction between the characteristics of the insentient and the sentient that was stated in order to explain the commentary’s phrase "for every cognition," that is indeed correct: knowledge is cognizable by another knowledge.

"It does not exist"—this is indeed the subject under discussion here. Immediately following that, however, the very text intended to establish the aforementioned object of knowledge (*prameya*)—beginning with "even by virtue of being grounded in a single cognizer" (*ekapramātṛniṣṭhatvena*) and so forth—must be composed.
For by this [text], the cognition belonging to another mental continuum (*saṃtānāntara*) is [addressed] through another cognition, such as inference (*anumāna*), at some time.

Let there be the state of being manifest (*prakāśyatva*); however, it is pointed out that this is not possible in any way within one's own continuum (*svasaṃtati*). As for the passage in the middle beginning with "Therefore, for whom light is not its own nature" and ending with "it is light itself, not an inference of it"—how can that [be explained]?

This is consistent. For by this [verse], no meaning of the commentary on the *kārikā* is established; rather, only an inquiry into whether the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) is insentient or sentient is conducted. And this effort is indeed for the sake of establishing the cognizer through the power of memory (*smṛti*).
To explain: it is not [possible] for cognitions [to establish one another] through mutual contact with their objects.

At the conclusion of this section, it will be demonstrated that a cognizer must necessarily be admitted, because the relationship of the illuminated and the illuminator is mutual, and all worldly transactions such as memory and so forth depend upon it; for [the Self] is not [merely] that which has the infinite forms of the universe internalized within itself. (1.3.7)

Thus, one must investigate "what this is" by examining the matter of manifestation point by point within the inquiry into reality (*tattvacintā*). If the commentator were to disregard what has come up in the course of reflecting upon the nature of self-luminosity (*svaprakāśasvarūpa*), the nature of cognition (*jñaptisvarūpa*) would not have been explained with sufficient clarity by him.

Consequently, one who wishes to refute that [position] has described its true nature and established the doctrine of the self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatā*) of knowledge under discussion. This is the intended meaning: let there be, for the sake of argument, a single manifestation (*prakāśa*), or indeed many in the ultimate sense, or even one whose form is that of the cognizer (*pramātṛ*).

(Page 223) In every respect, it is improper for this [consciousness] to be illuminated by another; and in reality, its oneness alone is proper, because the causes of difference—such as intrinsic nature, location, and time—are inapplicable to it. With this intention, it is called "the Seer" (*dṛk*).

The singular number is used in the Sūtra; however, in the Vṛtti, the plural form "all" (*sarvāḥ*) is employed to indicate a lack of respect [for the specific distinction]. For the sake of corroborating that very point, the corroboration is provided by means of a statement from another Sūtra ending in the plural; thus, there is nothing objectionable here. Furthermore, regarding the introduction of the middle section of the text, we have stated: "if there is understanding..."

If it is accepted that some cognizer exists who is unable to establish memory while asserting that cognition is self-luminous, then, precisely because he is distinct from cognition, he too would necessarily be self-luminous;
thus, a contradiction with the proponent's own tenet (*apasiddhānta*) follows for the proponent. For this is precisely the scope of such an argument where—
When a debate is conducted for the purpose of instructing others or for the determination of truth, a vast amount of material must be established;

in that context, for one who is establishing a certain point, there may arise the connection of another matter yet to be established. For this very reason, this is not the domain of a fallacious reason (*hetvābhāsa*), since the latter pertains exclusively to a single probandum (*sādhya*).

The author of the *Ṭīkā* has thus refuted the suspicion of this being a departure from established tenets (*apasiddhānta*). For that which is called the "knower" (*pramātā*) is not something distinct from cognition; rather, it is precisely that inward-facing aspect of cognitions—which possess outward-directed contractions—that is animated by the absence of distinctions of place and time. Furthermore, [it concerns] self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*).

Thus, the characteristic of consciousness has been stated here; however, if that characteristic were to exist even with respect to an object distinct from the characterized entity (the *lakṣya*), it would be vitiated by the fault of over-extension (*ativyāpti*) and would therefore not be a valid characteristic. Furthermore, this [characteristic] is the cause for [establishing] the definition.
Since, according to your own position, this exists in the cognizer (*pramātṛ*) as well, how can this [be a valid characteristic] for the proponent?

This is the definition of consciousness. Furthermore, the Buddhist might have an opening for the argument that "the establishment of a reality does not occur merely by virtue of its being established for another";
in order to quell even that [objection], there is the middle section of the text—so, enough of this prolixity;
let us speak to the subject at hand. Now, if the knower possesses luminosity, then if he were insentient, there would be an infinite regress.

It has been stated that this [object] is of a non-luminous nature; how then can it be inferred by the activity, speech, and so forth of another cognizer? For even for the Buddhist, cognition alone—whether as a continuum or through conceptualization—is the form of the cognizer. That too, being situated in the continuum of another, is inferred by means of activity and so forth; thus says someone.
