He refutes what was said [on page 224] with the words "yadapi" (even though). Is it not the case that, according to the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), even cognition is non-different from the knower? That...

If that [object] were accepted as being manifest by way of being inferable, then the knower (*pramātṛ*) would likewise necessarily be manifest. He says: "It is imagined. Here, just as in the Buddhist school, even for cognition—which is self-luminous—or for an object such as a jar, which is perceptible, there is a property such as "being an effect" (*kāryatva*).

Even if it is distinct [from consciousness], being conceptualized through the cognition of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti-buddhi*) and even when being inferred, it does not discard its status as established by the direct perception of self-awareness (*svasaṃvid-adhyakṣa*). Likewise, that which is called "orientation toward the object" (*viṣaya-unmukhya*)— which, in the doctrine of formlessness (*nirākāra-vāda*), belongs to the knower through the power of *māyā*, and in the doctrine of having form (*sākāra-vāda*), is the assumption of the form of the object— [is likewise established].

Even that form which is non-excessive appears as if excessive; although it is to be manifested [by cognition], the self-luminosity of the knower is not undermined, because the ultimate reality is not sublated by conceptual construction.
For it is the very form already established in the root [of experience] that is there augmented by conceptual inference.

Because it cannot be established by the aforementioned arguments without its being self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*), knowledge alone is what is inferable, and not the ultimate manifestation (*paramārthaprakāśa*). However, due to the coloring (*uparāga*) of that [manifestation] as an attribute (*dharma*), there arises the conventional notion that "the other," namely the cognizer (*pramātṛ*), is inferred. Now, one might object: the cognizer is also conventionally known to be inferable as something "other"—what is the point here?

There must be a subverting factor (*bādhaka*) by which this conventional usage of "being inferable" (*anumeyatā-vyavahāra*) could occur here, [namely] that light is permeated by a body, vital breath, intellect, or void belonging to another's continuum. Let it be so; nevertheless, even for self-luminous light, its being permeated by a body, vital breath, intellect, or void belonging to another's continuum is inferred there through its activity, speech, and so forth. And therefore—

This is the ultimate meaning: self-luminous consciousness, although pervading all space and time, is now to be established as being directed toward an object and assuming the form of that object within this subject— the body and so forth— as if permeated by identity with this body and so on, because it is joined with the activity and speech of this body and so forth, just like one's own body.
Nor is the self-luminosity of self-awareness lost by this much; likewise,
in the view that "the universal is one and perceptible," it is established by another means of knowledge that "there is a cow in Kānyakubja."
Even though the relation to cowness is what is being inferred, it does not negate the perceptual nature of cowness itself;
for that very same cowness is established as existing there by means of perception, and is thus proven by that inference.

It is reinforced. And that which is reinforced by a particular inference does not become its sublater, just as the means of conventional usage [does not sublate] perception. Likewise, by the inference of another's subjectivity, one's own self-luminosity is indeed strengthened; for in the absence of self-luminosity, subjectivity itself would not exist.

Because [otherwise] it would be untenable. And thus, from the observation of activity in the body, it is determined as follows: here, there is a self-luminous intention (*abhisandhāna*) such as "I am rising," because one observes an intent to swallow with impetuosity;

and "I am eating," because of the impelling of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth during sleep; and "I am impelling," because in all cases the light [of consciousness] rests upon the referent of the word "I" (*asmadartha*).

Regarding the word "of the crow": for the cause of sublation is the uprooting of that [object's] nature; otherwise, everything would be the sublater of everything. And its opposite is its reinforcement;
thus, there is the perception of what is contrary to the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*). The subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) of another body is to be inferred by another. But that...

It is indeed directly perceived; however, since the life-force (*prāṇa*) and so forth of another are always only inferable by their own nature, the mention of the "body" was not made [in that context]. And just as there is no loss of self-luminosity even within one's own continuum, so it is also in the continuum of another. Yet, due to the firmness of the conceit of being a subject (*pramātṛ*) with respect to the body and so forth, this other person is [perceived as such].

The conventional usage is "the cognizer" (*pramātṛ*). However, the ultimate cognizer is indeed self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*). Moreover, that [ultimate cognizer] necessarily appears as self-luminous to this cognizer who exists as an inferential subject (*anumātṛ*), because otherwise the very status of being a cognizer would be impossible. For it has been said:
"Even though the state of the object... (*Āgamaprāmāṇya-siddhi* 20).

However, it does not become the locus of the conceit of being the knower; rather, with the intention that the firmness of the conceit of the body and so forth as the knower [is what must be overcome], the term "entered" (*anupraviṣṭa*) is employed. This is because [the body] serves as the vitalizing principle (*anuprāṇaka*).
"Having entered, it has entered after [the body, etc.]"— in order to determine *where* it has entered, the words "one's own" (*sva*) and so forth are used to denote the inner self (*pratyagātman*),

the body, the vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so on. The meaning is that consciousness, which exists as the subjectivity of one's own body and so forth, has necessarily entered as its animator (*anuprāṇaka*) and is thus capable of manifesting.

Thus, because the ultimate subject of cognition is one, it is not possible for the light of self-awareness to be an object of inference anywhere; therefore, it has been stated that how could it possibly be something that is manifested? Now, however, (page 226):

He said this: "Or let there be many cognizers; nevertheless, for one's own cognizer, there is first of all no state of being manifest. As for other cognizers, that [manifestness] might be brought about through the power of inference. But by inference, the specific individuality (*svalakṣaṇa*) is never touched upon, for its object is always the universal (*sāmānya*)."
Otherwise, it would be impossible to grasp the relationship [between word and object]. Consequently, even if— within another, namely the cognizer—

there exists either a form of exclusion (*apoha*) consisting of the differentiation from non-cognizers, or merely a form of cognition that is not a real entity, or a distinct universal characterized as "selfhood," insofar as these exist, let them be what is manifested.
But for another object, namely the cognizer, what occasion is there for the application of the stain of being manifest?

Furthermore, in the phrase "and even inference," the word *ca* (and) serves to aggregate other objects of cognition (*prameya*). By the word *api* (even), he states that there is no possibility of perception (*pratyakṣa*) being subjected here to the consequence of non-manifestness. By the restrictive particle *eva*, [he implies] even in the case of a jar and so forth.
He states that [the object] cannot be established as being manifest through the direction of inference (*anumāna*).

By the phrase "manifested by perceptual cognition" (*adhyakṣajñānāvabhāsinaḥ*), he has expressed in this manner that the particular (*svalakṣaṇa*) is capable of entering into direct intuition (*sākṣātkāra*); thus, even a jar or the like is not an object of inference, so what need be said of other things?

Regarding the phrase "of the specific characteristic of the cognizer" (*pramātṛ-svalakṣaṇasya*): [An objection is raised: "Even though inference apprehends what is not a real entity (*avastu*), it possesses validity because it determines a real entity (*vastvadhyavasāyitayā*). As it has been said:
'The validity of both [perception and inference] has as its object a real entity...'"

Thus, [the author] dispels the doubt that—because one determines (*adhyavasāya*) the self as a real entity through the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of inference and scripture—it would necessarily follow that the self possesses the quality of being manifest (*prakāśyatva*) due to being thus determined; he does so by stating "the self" (*ātma*).
The connection is with the phrase "by the conceptual construction 'self' and by the conceptual construction 'knower' (*pramātṛ*). By the inclusion of the word "etc. (*ādi*),...

The mention of "scriptures" (*āgama*) and so forth [is made]. The second *ca* indicates a doubt regarding the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*). "It will be stated" refers to the author of the commentary (*ṭīkākṛt*).
Although this was already stated in the *Ādisiddhasūtra* and the *Svataḥsiddhasūtra*, nevertheless, [the objection remains]: "But [the Lord's] independence is not [established]... (1.5.16).

Thus it was stated that [this] will be explained with the intention of a future sūtra. Now, one might object: if another's own self does not manifest directly, how can the knowledge of another's mind appear so vividly?
[It might be argued that] it could be [known] because the other self is not perceptible [to ordinary people], and because its clearly manifest nature is communicated through inference.
To this he says: "in every way. For this is the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of a yogi, and not inference. For instance:
"Therefore, whether it be real or unreal..."
"Thus, through *saṃyama* upon the mental modification [of another], there is knowledge of the mind of another" (Yoga Sūtra 3.20).
According to this principle, when— by the power of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi*— one attains non-difference from the mind of another, [then that knowledge arises].

When one meditates [on another's mind], that meditation follows the actual object; thus, because they are in reality one—since the conceit of difference is produced by illusion—the other's mind appears clearly, and it is not then that the other's mind is merely inferred. [Objection: But surely, let there be no direct manifestation through inference.

By perception, however, only the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) of the self is revealed, and that indeed occurs in relation to another self, since the perception of yogins—such as the knowledge of another's mind—is well-established; thus, the term "intention" (*āśaya*) is used to dispel the doubt that the self might be illuminated by another. This is what has been stated.

In that regard, mental factors such as passion (*rāga*) and so forth are manifested through the direct perception (*yogipratyakṣa*) of the yogin. Because the yogin attains identity with that cognition, the cognition appears as self-luminous (*svaprakāśa*) alone, and not as an object of manifestation (*prakāśya*).
The particle *eva* (alone) is employed immediately after the compound, but here it does not refer to the manifestation of the subject (*mātṛprakāśa*).

By stating that "it is to be accomplished through the cultivation of non-difference because it is eternally manifest," he incorporates his own meaning into the sense of the preceding word (*pūrvapadārtha*), just as in the expression "this is indeed the king's man.
Likewise, even while remaining in his own place, he says this: "This very direct realization (*sākṣātkāra*) belongs to the Supreme Will (*parāśaya*)," and not otherwise.

Inference consists merely of a determinative act (*adhyavasāya*); therefore, that which appears with clarity cannot be an object of inference in any way whatsoever, though it may be so in some limited sense.

Thus, it has been established that even another subject (*parapramātṛ*) cannot be an object of manifestation. As for the Buddhist, however, his proof of another subject is nothing but the refutation of the proof of another mental continuum (*saṃtānāntara*).
The commentator, while composing the *Vāsanāprabodhasūtra*, will investigate this matter in detail; therefore, let us desist here.
Thus, by way of digression, the proponent has examined the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*) within his own philosophical system.
(Page 228)

By this intermediate section, beginning with "ata eva na yasya" and ending with "natu tadanumānam," [the author] now concludes the very subject under discussion—that perception (*dṛk*) is indeed self-luminous—by means of a different approach. To illustrate:
someone might say that cognition is self-luminous within its own continuum, but as for another's continuum...

It may be argued that, in relation to another knower, it will also be illumined by another cognition, since the imposition of contradictory attributes (viruddhadharmādhyāsa) due to a difference in objects is of no consequence— just as that same woman produces pleasure for her lover and pain for her co-wife, yet there is no contradiction whatsoever. To him, the following is said:

"And also by virtue of being grounded in a single cognizer. Two distinct types of memory appear: "This person experienced" and "I experienced. Among these, in the memory grounded in one's own experience, the experience possesses the nature of the Self (*ātmarūpatva*) because it rests within the Self.

This [consciousness], which consists of non-dependence on anything else, must be examined as having "I" as its object; if that does not manifest, what difference would there be from the manifestation of an experience established in another? Now, if this [consciousness]—being established in memory in the form of the cognition and feeling of the experience of "I"—[applies] even to the experience of the object of knowledge...

If it were said that [consciousness] "transfers," then even when there is the experience, recollection, and feeling of another's experience, the cognition would have to be "I experienced. Now, even at the time of the original experience, that which is experienced appears as something capable of resting within the "I-sense" (asmadartha); what kind of statement is it to say that it is "experienced through its recollection"? For the "I-sense" is indeed the very nature of Light.
There is a contradiction: resting in oneself (*ātma-viśrānti*) is independent of anything else, whereas being an object of cognition through memory (*smṛti-vedyatva*) is dependent on another.

Although it is also improper for a cognition existing in another's mental continuum to be illuminated by another, for self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) alone is the unconditioned definition of cognition, and that [self-luminosity] is not [present here].
It becomes otherwise due to the difference in its objective referent (*viṣaya*); for blue earth and the like do not turn into water and the like even in relation to something else.

This is because we observe a reversal only in the case of a contingent nature (*aupādhika-rūpa*), such as its capacity to produce [a certain effect] and so forth; otherwise, everything would undergo reversal, and there would be no fixed nature (*svarūpa-niyama*) for an entity at all. Thus, regarding the process of becoming otherwise...
When being conditioned (*aupādhikatva*) is the pervader (*vyāpaka*),

then, because its contradictory— being unconditioned (*anaupādhikatva*)— is perceived, any other mode of being for self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) as pertaining to cognition is negated. Therefore, it is indeed contradictory to cognition.

(229) "The state of being illuminated by another. For it is with this very intention that he will say: "The nature of cognition is not cognizable by another, because its sole nature is self-luminosity. By the inclusion of the word "sole" (*eka*), [this is meant].

Indeed, identity has been stated as its definition because it is free from adventitious conditions (*anaupādhika*); nevertheless, even the mere manifestation of a difference in objects here would be like throwing dust in the eyes—a futile rejoinder (*jātyuttara*) used to avoid contradiction—but in this case, even that is not present, which is why the word "absolutely" (*atyanta*) is used. It is precisely because they are absolutely contradictory [that they cannot coexist].

"It is not connected by means of a cause. "Cognizable by that" means cognizable by memory. "Even then, indeed" refers to that time which is recognized as being of the nature of memory; at that [time], "situated therein" means situated within one's own continuum, it would not appear as the form of resting in the Self, fit for the rest of "I-ness. "Let it then appear in that way."
He says, "And regarding self-luminosity," for it has been stated that there is a contradiction between self-luminosity (*svaprakāśatva*) and being illuminated by another (*paraprakāśatva*).

By this commentary, the Sūtra and the Vṛtti have been explained in another manner. That vision which is self-manifesting and consists of one's own continuum—that [vision] is capable of resting in the Self; that which is to be contemplated as "I" (*ahaṃvimarśanīya*) is...

Regarding cognition (*jñāna*): in that case, being cognizable by another is not tenable. For whatever manifestation (*jñapti*) there may be—which is of the singular nature of self-awareness and which serves as the locus for the conceit of "self" by virtue of its belonging to one's own continuum—that cannot be known by the consciousness of another. [Objection: But surely, just as blue and so forth are objects of consciousness because they are its causes...

It is said: [the opponent] raises an objection with the intention that "in that case, since experience (*anubhava*) is also the cause of the cognition of memory (*smṛtijñāna*), let it be the object," thus stating: "even so, there would be cognisability by another" (*anyavedyatā*). The meaning is this: if the cognition of experience is called the object of the cognition of memory because it is its cause through a causal chain (*pāraṃparyeṇa*), [then the following applies].

Since the cognition of taste and so forth must necessarily be the cause of the cognition of form— either as its immediate antecedent (*samanantara*) or through a causal chain— the cognition of form would also have to take all cognitions of taste, smell, and so on as its objects.
By the phrase "inhering in a single knower," [the opponent attempts to exclude this] because in the Buddhist view it is distinguished by being a cause, whereas in the Kaṇāda (Vaiśeṣika) view...
It is indicated that while "cognitivity" (*jñānatva*) is undifferentiated, it is differentiated by its inherence in a single object;
therefore, it should be understood as being due to the distinction of cognitivity inherent in one and the same [substratum], and not merely from the non-distinction of cognitivity itself.
For if it were stated in such a way [merely as non-distinct], it would be entirely devoid of meaning.

(Page 230) Furthermore, there would be a great many logical fallacies, such as the fact that even the knowledge of Vāsuki and others would become an object of the knowledge of people like us, whereby everyone would be omniscient; these will be discussed further below. Nor, moreover, is it the case that...

Whether the mutual cognizing of the cognitions of form, taste, and so forth is held to occur simultaneously or sequentially, it follows [by implication]—and thus it should have been pointed out first—that they would necessarily occur together; it is not merely the absence of a restriction regarding the sense organs that is at issue. Therefore, the interpretation of the Sūtra should also be as follows: "Just as the vision whose object is taste is only self-manifesting, it is not [cognized] by the vision of form."
[The object] is to be known, and so too are others; however, later [the author] will apply this without distinction, stating that "the vision of form is itself the vision of taste.

Now, if the cognition of taste is manifest, must it necessarily be manifested by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of cognition? For when a jar is being manifested, there is no cognition of it as qualified by its limiting adjunct.

Since being "produced" (*kṛtatva*) and so forth necessarily entails manifestation, how can it be said in the *Vṛtti* that "if there were mutual cognition, there would also be cognition of each other's objects"—an objection for which this *Ṭīkā* provides the explanation?
[The author] raises the doubt, "the taste, as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), would also manifest," and says: "For it is only the manifestation of the cognition itself... No.

This self, which possesses limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), is like a jar; however, it is rather of the nature of that very illumination. Consequently, since the illumination of taste shines forth within the illumination of form, the manifestation of taste is indeed already admitted.
And because this is so admitted, visual cognition arises from its own cause as having taste and other objects as its domain.

If [cognition] were produced through the connection with the manifestation of taste and so forth, the restriction of the sense organs would be lost; for that [restriction] is established as being threefold. First, there is the restriction of the effect, which is cognition, by virtue of the sense organ: cognition produced by the eye is the manifestation of color-form alone. Second, there is the restriction of the sense organ itself, consisting in its specific capacity (yogyatā), by which the eye [perceives only color-form].

It produces only the cognition of form, and nothing else. Furthermore, the restriction and fixed number of the sense organs—namely that there are six sense organs and so forth—is established. Therein, having first explained the first two modes [of proof], the third is indicated by the phrase "then" (*tataśca*) and the word "firstly" (*tāvat*); he explains that [third mode] with the words "and because of its absence" (*tadabhāvācca*).

By such statements as these: because there is no restriction on the nature of the sense faculties, and because there is no restriction on the objects of their cognitions, and because visual cognition possesses the capacity to manifest all objects, the postulation of multiple sense faculties is redundant. The reason for this is that a single sense faculty possesses such a capacity.
Thus [it is said].
231) Here too, the reason is "of the nature of the effect" and so forth. Here too, the reason is "otherwise" and so forth. It is not.

First, visual cognition is produced by the eye. Even if the taste-cognition is thereby manifested, the faculty of the tongue will still be employed when one wishes to manifest knowledge regarding a pure taste that is not conditioned by anything else; thus, the postulation of multiple sense-faculties is not futile. To this, he says: "And so..."
Thus [it is said]. The word *ca* (and) indicates a reason. For by this very reason being stated, it follows that the eye alone is the illuminator even of a solitary taste;

yet, like a *piśāca*, it would not manifest even though it exists, being merely an unperceived limiting adjunct (*upādhi*). However, space, time, inherence (*samavāya*), and so forth, are always existing as limiting adjuncts.

They exist like the forms and other qualities of the Buddha and so forth. Even under the view that they are directly perceived, there is no consequence of their being perceived in isolation. Therefore, while the manifestation of that which serves as a limiting adjunct (upādhi) is possible, because an isolated manifestation does not exist, it is excluded from isolated manifestation and is instead pervaded by [manifestation] associated with its isolate.

The nature of manifesting the mere [object] is established by means of the nature of manifesting that which has become an adventitious attribute (*upādhi*); thus, this is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*). Now, one might object: visual cognition is not the manifestation of the taste that has become an adventitious attribute; rather, it is the cognition of taste appearing therein that constitutes the manifestation of the adventitious attribute. Therefore, "manifesting that which has become an adventitious attribute" is unestablished (*asiddha*).

Anticipating this objection that it might be the cause, he says: "produced by the eye. There is no cognition of taste for that [cognition of form], because it (the cognition of taste) does not exist in its own nature at that time. For that [cognition of taste] would indeed exist then only if it were produced by the gustatory faculty and were present;
however, like a memory, the cognition of taste—which is past—is non-existent with respect to the cognition of form.

It is manifested; thus, at that time, it is the cognition of form itself that constitutes the manifestation of the erroneous cognition along with its limiting adjunct (upādhi) and its object, the taste. Therefore, the reason [in the argument] is not unestablished. Furthermore, if there were no restriction of the sense faculties, it would follow that blind people and others would not exist, and [there would be the consequence that] an object once perceived...

Even upon the destruction of that object and its experience, there would be the consequence of its manifestation; thus, nothing would ever be lost for anyone. In this way, the fault has been stated regarding the mutual cognition of successive cognitions.
Now, he states the fault regarding the mutual cognition of simultaneous cognitions occurring at the present time.
And regarding the statement "in the theory of *sākāra* (cognition with form)" (p.
232): in such instances as the viewing of actors, wrestlers, or dancers, there arises the cognition, "We see the dancer."
As many spectators as there are, excluding each individual, so many visions are to be experienced by each one.

Although external objects exist, these visions possess forms through the application of their shadows; thus, even when no external object exists, they appear with that very same external form. Consequently, for each individual, there would be the appearance of infinite dancers, as well as the appearance of a single dancer.

It is experienced. Regarding that object, there are other cognitions which are the perceivers of the cognition belonging to each individual [subject], and there are yet other cognitions of which that [original] cognition is the perceiver;
because these [latter] possess forms and consist of mutual perceivers, they are manifold, even when there is the appearance of a single dancer.

The logical connection is that there would be a multiplicity of appearances. Now, it is true that in those cases there is a manifold appearance for each [object] individually; however, whatever the appearance of one is in terms of place, time, and essential nature, such is the appearance of another as well. This is because they consist entirely of such a uniformity, due to their being of a nature that is merged together (*samānābhihāra*).

Due to similarity, multiplicity does not appear. For even when the light of water and flames are merged, there would indeed be an increase [in magnitude]. But here, since there is identity in every respect (*tādrūpyāt*), how could multiplicity appear? He wards off this objection of others with the word "where" (*yatra*). When, for a single spectator, in his eye—

Then, due to that [ocular] defect of jaundice (*kāmalā*), even the orb of the face of a Kerala dancer, which resembles musk, appears as yellow as gold— like the face of a parrot-maiden; for at that time, that appearance is perceived individually, and other appearances are likewise perceived by one suffering from jaundice, and thus [the distinction] belongs to everything.

A combined manifestation would appear as dark-blue, yellow, and white. [An objection: But where has such a mixed manifestation been seen? [The author] replies: "Just as... When one eye is impaired by lines or cataracts (*timira*), while the other eye is clear, there arises the cognition of a jar that is both moving and non-moving. In this same way, within a single continuum, it occurs sequentially.

It was stated that in the case of watching actors and the like, the simultaneous cognition would entail the fault of being cognizable by another cognition. Now, however, he says— beginning with "nacāpi" and ending with "prasajyante tu"— that in this context, within the investigation of direction (*dikparīkṣā*), there is no uncontradicted cognition being perceived by these [opponents].
"I see," [he says]. Furthermore, in that case, each [moment] belongs to a single continuum; nor is there a relationship of cause and effect between things that arise simultaneously.
(page 233)

Nevertheless, since the relationship between the object of cognition (*vedya*) and the cognizer (*vedaka*) is indeed perceived [in experience], there would be a great disorder if all cognitions belonging to every subject were to function as both object and cognizer without restriction. [Objection: But surely, being produced from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) will be the regulating factor here;
thus, all the aforementioned faults will be resolved. With this intention, he says:
Furthermore, "thus" [means]: "due to the restriction of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvaniyamāt*) is because of the absence of being produced by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*);

"due to the diversity of intrinsic nature" (*svabhāvavaicitryāt*) is because of the presence of being produced by mental impressions. Thus, there is no tautology by way of negative and positive concomitance (*vyatirekānvaya*). Alternatively, by the former [statement], the difference in the intrinsic nature of the effect—namely, cognition—was stated.

But by the second [reason], it refers to the *saṃskāra* which is the cause of that [cognition]. Just as an opponent seeks to avoid faults with a single stroke, so the proponent of the established doctrine (*siddhāntavādī*) demonstrates that the very raising of the position that "knowledge is revealed by another" does not even occur at its root; for it has already been stated: "the seeing... (*dṛk*).

Regarding the phrase "it is indeed its own manifestation": the intention is that the intrinsic nature (*nija-lakṣaṇa*) of things, which is unconditioned (*anaupādhika*), undergoes transformation. If one asks, "What is accomplished by its being born from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)?", he says, "Even there...

[meaning] that even while it becomes otherwise through its nature as solely self-luminous (*svaprakāśaikarūpatva*), it does not become something of a different form due to an experience of a distinct nature.

Even for this recollection, there may indeed be a similarity produced by the shadow of the object; for even though it arises from infinite latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), it manifests that previous cognition. This being the case, two possibilities arise: either the manifestation of the objective aspect (*grāhyāṃśa*) residing in the experience, or that of the subjective aspect (*grāhakāṃśa*).

He refutes the previous [objection]: [the object] appears clearly in the conscious experience (*anubhava-saṃcetana*) of the perceivable [object], but not in memory (*smṛti*). By this, it is shown that in the cognition of a yogi, the perception of another—which belongs to the nature of the perceiver—shines forth as something distinct, cast into the category of the perceivable; however, one's own experience does not appear in that same way in a memory-cognition. It is the jar itself [that is perceived].

For here, because it is not clearly manifest, it rests upon the level of the object of apprehension (*grāhyabhūmikā*). By this, he rejects the second alternative. [Objection: What, then, has been undermined by the latent impression (*saṃskāra*)? [Reply: He says, "merely a similarity" (*sādṛśyamātra*).

The inclusion of the word "mere" (*mātra*) is for the purpose of excluding the possibility of its being illuminated by something additional. For that which is indeed destroyed cannot be produced from a latent impression.
Just as a previous configuration enters into a connection with another object through its entry into that new configuration,
so too does memory arise from its own latent impression even though the original experience has perished.

In recollection, it does not enter into a relationship as an object; for proximity is dependent upon the establishment of a relationship. There would be no restriction [in memory] such as "Rāma, though not present, was our king," just as one might say "the entire universe is my king. And its being contrary to that [present state] constitutes its being "destroyed" (naṣṭa).

This is the perception of what is incompatible with the cause (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*). Now, an effort is being made [by the opponent] as to how recollection could have the same object as experience through direct experience. In that regard, even if the experience is not manifested by the recollection, similarity is nonetheless established because [recollection] is born from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*). And since that [similarity] occurs by way of the object, there is also identity of object.

Thinking that "the conventional usage will be established through metaphorical designation based on similarity" because of memory and desire, he says: "by the very nature of the reality of things. Whatever thing is established and firmly rooted—
Therefore, it necessarily deposits a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). For a specific quality characterized by a latent impression arises from germination;
however, for some, the very germination itself—the intensity—is the specific quality known as the latent impression. As Prajñālaṃkāra states:
"The germination of this consciousness, which is its very intensity, must be called the latent impression."

Thus, wherever an impression (*saṃskāra*) is deposited, there is similarity (*sādṛśya*); both of these are observed in cases such as the arrangement of birch bark or the movement of arrows. And here, the prior cognition existed; therefore, it is postulated that this [cognition] must necessarily be produced by both the impression and the similarity, but not by similarity alone.

It is possible to know [this]. For one who perceives two things might, in some cases, perceive two arrangements simultaneously—like a cow and a gavaya—and in other cases, perceive them sequentially in the form of prior and posterior, like birch bark;
such a third person would then understand their similarity. But here, there is no third [observer]. This is true even for one who accepts a stable self.

For the Vaiśeṣika, it is difficult to establish that memory and experience have a single object. Indeed, there exists no third cognition that apprehends both memory and experience, which could perceive their similarity and thereby determine or conclude their identity of object. Furthermore, the similarity between experience and recollection cannot be known, because a third [cognition] is not perceived.

This is the non-perception of a cause. Now, it might be argued that this [cognition] is determined to be produced from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) precisely because of its similarity [to the object]. In that case, if similarity is not perceived, then how can its being produced from a latent impression be determined?
For not every object [is necessarily] a latent impression.
(Page 235) [The opponent argues:

"It acts [upon the self], because [action] is impossible when a light object consisting of grass or the like has been removed from the surface of the earth. The proponent replies: "This is true; however, this is merely a concessionary argument (*abhyupagamya-vāda*)," thereby demonstrating, on the contrary, his disregard for that position.

If it were indeed by means of the word *iti* together with the particle *iti*, then the understanding of that [likeness] would occur; thus, an alternative explanation of the portion of the Sūtra has been made: "the understanding of that" refers to the understanding of similarity. Furthermore, metaphorical usage (*upacāra*) does not establish the actual state of things, since one cognition might have the cow as its object while another has the Vāhīka as its object.

Even if a single object is metaphorically attributed due to similarity, the conventional usage—which depends upon the actual experience of a single object—cannot be established. Consequently, metaphorical attribution is of no avail here, and even such [attribution] is not tenable;
thus, the opponent's position is entirely weak. This is the meaning of the word "api" (even/also) in the context of the Sūtra.

He applies [the reason] to the object of proof by way of a conclusion, saying "thus it is. The word "even" (*api*) in the phrase "even if it is produced from a mental impression" (*saṃskārajatve 'pi*) implies "even if it is somehow admitted [to be so]. || 2 ||

Now, even if memory does not have that [past object] as its object, because it is determined as such, one might claim it has a perceived thing as its basis through error; but this is inconsistent. (3)

Now, if the identity of object between memory and direct experience were ultimately real, one might indeed strive to establish it; but it is not so. For instance, when a father who has passed away appears in memory, how could he—who has by then perished—appear in that memory? He is, as it were, already consumed by fire.

Our father does not laugh, nor does he scratch; likewise, it is certain that he does not even shine. Furthermore, this [silver] cannot be connected with both the present and past times, because that would contradict the nature of the father. And if such a connection were admitted, how could silver—which is excluded from everything else—be manifold elsewhere? Moreover, that [silver] is an illusion, and it is not indistinct.

A conventional (smārta) appearance of an object— such as a father— which is not restricted by place, time, or essential nature, cannot possibly attain identity with a perceptual (ānubhavika) appearance that is the opposite of it. Therefore, while that object remains unmanifested, [the cognition] is called "illuminating that object" because of the ascertainment (adhyavasāya) of it, which consists merely of a conceit (abhimāna).
"Memory is said to have as its object that which has been previously perceived due to the influence of error"— this is the meaning of the three quarters of the verse,
according to a concise commentary (page 236).

[This is] concluded by the words "the delusion has been removed. For instance, Bhaṭṭa Śaṅkaranandana, following the very direction of the Smṛti, denied that manifestness is a property of the object, stating:

"The object does not appear, because [manifestness] is incompatible with error and memory; rather, it belongs to the time of the cognition, nor is there any identity [between the object and the cognition]."
"Or, due to the difference in place and so forth, there is the perception of one's own place and so forth within reality.
He explains that this is inconsistent in brief with the words "ityapi" and so on.

According to the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), memory takes as its object that which is indeed non-existent, or that which is constructed by latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
In the view that the self is the manifestation of the form of cognition (*jñānākāra-ātmākhyāti*), it causes [the object] to appear—that is, it illuminates it;

however, it does not [illuminate] the prior experience or its object, because both are non-existent at the time of recollection. Rather, by relying on the time of that experience, it determines [the object] solely through the essence of conceit (*abhimāna*).

He shows the nature of determinate cognition (*adhyavasāya*) with the words "that which has been experienced. The word "that" (*saḥ*) refers to the contact with the time of experience. "Experienced" (*anubhūta*) refers to the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of both the experience and its object.
Even though the self (*ātman*), while appearing, is non-existent, it is determined by that which was experienced.

Due to the erroneous determination of non-difference—which consists in the failure to determine difference—those who lack discernment do not perceive that the object of memory has a previously experienced substrate. The meaning of the sūtra is this: that whose object is either non-existent (*asan*) or a mental form (*ātmākāra*), and which has neither that experience nor that external object as its actual referent; [this is] "by way of error."

The meaning is "by way of being a bee. The term *asamañjasam* (inconsistent) is explained in the commentary (*vṛtti*) by means of the negation of the entire sense of the sentence with the word *na*. By the particle *ca*, which indicates a doubt, the word *atha* is explained. With the words "immediately thereafter" (*anantaram*), etc., the author of the sub-commentary (*ṭīkākāra*) [indicates] that this matter serves as the reason for the subsequent sūtra.

He shows that [the word] should be joined with what is presented by the function of the sentence (*vākya-vṛtti*). Now, one might object: "This cognition 'this is silver' does not occur in relation to mother-of-pearl in the same way as the cognition 'there is water in the jar'; so how can it be said that [it occurs] 'in mother-of-pearl'? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the location of the mother-of-pearl. For it is because [the person] proceeds toward that [silver] by taking hold of—that is, by making into an objective support—that very location.

Consequently, its status as a substratum has been stated. By means of the statements, "it is contrary [to reality] in relation to the arising of a subverting cognition and the perception by another cognizer," and "it does not exist at all," and "it is a mere mental form" (*ākāra*), [the opponent's position is refuted].
(Page 237)

The three [theories]—namely, non-apprehension (asatkhyāti), self-apprehension (ātmakhyāti), and [anyathākhyāti]—have all been indicated here. To demonstrate the contempt for these, it must first be established that this so-called "memory" is actually an error, because it is not distinct from other types of error.
Furthermore, the theory of misapprehension (viparītakhyāti) alone will be demonstrated as the nature of error according to the Buddhist perspective later on.

Regarding the erroneous nature of the determination (*avasāya*), as stated in the sūtra: "And [the error] consists in the inversion... (1.3.5). This inversion is with respect to the object of activity and attainment;

and the capacity for purposeful action (*arthakriyākāritva*) and the possibility of the thing's existence are with respect to the intended and determined object, as well as from other locations such as mother-of-pearl.

It has been stated, "from silver. By the phrase "the conceptual construction of silver," the author, completing the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) in the commentary (*vṛtti*), equates this with the illustrative case (*dārṣṭāntika*), namely, the conceptual construction of memory. "From that" means because it takes the form of an unreal manifestation (*vitathādi-khyāti*).

How, first of all, can there even be memory? And how can there be the persistence of an object for that which is erroneous? Furthermore, why is dependence upon the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of a prior experience asserted? (4)

This refutes what was stated previously. How? By means of a refutation of every stated point through all possible approaches. For instance, elsewhere something specific is refuted—just as in the case where it is argued that "sound, which consists of phonemes, is perceptible by the ear, eternal, and denotes meaning by depending on convention," it is only its eternality that is refuted, and nothing else.

However, by refuting its constituent parts, this meaning of the sentence would be refuted. Here, however, [the following] is rejected: that memory arises from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), that it establishes objects previously experienced through error, and that both the meaning of each individual word and the meaning of the sentence [are established] by means of that [memory]. That specific nature which serves as the wall for the variegated painting of this inquiry—

The meaning of the word "tāvat" is that what is being relied upon is itself untenable. The author of the *Ṭīkā* restates the meaning of the preceding sūtra in order to introduce a refutation: "If it were indeed non-existent," then the connection is that the primary nature called "memory-ness" would not be logical. By the word "tat" (that), what was stated in the previous verse is referred to here.

The meaning has been restated and examined. The primary nature of memory (*smṛti*) is the non-forgetting (*asaṃpramoṣa*) of an experienced object—that is, an object revealed by experience—for some time; it is not a complete forgetting or deprivation, because [the object] is regained through being manifested again. By this [definition],...
Its distinction from other cognitions is precisely what is being uprooted by the meaning of the preceding sūtra.
(Page 238) If experience itself were not manifest, its object likewise would not be manifest; rather, [it is] perfectly and pre-eminently [manifest].

The meaning of the preceding sūtra is indeed that "this [person] is born as if robbed. By the phrase "due to the non-manifestation of experience," the commentary (*vṛtti*) explains "due to the non-illumination of the prior experience. By the phrase "having that as its object" (*tadviṣaya*), [the commentary] explains "in the confusion regarding that object" (*tadviṣayasaṃpramoṣe*). By the phrase "having the experienced object as its basis" (*anubhūtaviṣaya*), [the commentary] explains "merely through determination" (*adhyavasāyamātrāt*).

By the phrase "designation of a distinction" (*viśeṣavyapadeśa*) and so forth, it is argued that its status as memory (*smṛtitva*) is not tenable; this refers to the word *mukhya* (primary) from the Sūtra. "Otherwise" means by way of having a real entity (*vastu*) as its object. Now, one might object: just as inference, though being an error (*bhrānti*), establishes a real entity, so too memory [establishes it] through its being a means to pleasure (*sukhasādhanatva*) and so forth.

Anticipating the objection that [inference] will establish [the object], he says: "of inference. Let it be, for the sake of argument, that according to your view inference is erroneous, as you have stated: "because of apprehending that in what is not that."
Thus it was said; however, you yourselves have further stated:
"Even error is valid cognition by virtue of its connection [to reality]."

For whatever entity exists in a certain way, that very thing is the cause for a cognition of its mark; therefore, the cognition of the mark arises from that [entity] with respect to the object as it truly is.
Thus, because the cognitions of the mark (liṅga) and the bearer of the mark (liṅgin) are indirectly connected to the real entity,
they are non-deceptive even though they are devoid of the appearance of that [entity].

Thus, if this succession were to exist here in the case of memory— just like the inference of past rain— it would necessarily take the form of a determination of something previously unknown, having as its object either the previous experience or the thing previously experienced.

Because a newborn exhibits joy, fear, and grief due to the continuity of memory from previous practice; because there is a desire for mother’s milk resulting from the habit of feeding in a prior life;
and because no birth is observed for one who is free from passion. (Nyāya Sūtra 3.1.19, 22, 25)

For this reason, as stated above, the cognition "that is the same jar" would be similar to the inference of a previous birth's experience and its object— which is distinct from the memory imagined by a child— and thus it would be a certainty consisting of a prior manifestation.

There would be a loss of the status of memory, which has reawakening as its ultimate reality. Therefore, while indirectness may exist in inference, it is unestablished here [in the case of memory]. Thus, what is the distinction between the error of inference and the error of memory? How could this [memory] establish the object? It is observed...

The capacity of memory to establish an object exists in all worldly transactions, such as the completion of tasks undertaken for the purpose of returning home. Likewise, in this case, even an error will establish [an object] through its connection with the object.
But since that [connection] does not exist in memory, how could it establish the object? It has been said that no error whatsoever [establishes] the object—

[The previous statement] was intended as a definitive rule (*vyavasthāpikā*). As for how memory (*smṛti*) could also be such [an error], that will be explained in the immediately following sūtra; thus, there is no redundancy. Now, one might object: "Memory is conceptual in nature (*vikalparūpā*), and since every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is erroneous (*bhrānta*), memory must necessarily be so as well. To this he says: "And yet not... By using the plural number, he means this: it is not a universal rule (*autsargika*).

If it were the case that all conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is erroneous, then even memory would fall under the principle of the punishment meted out by a wicked king to his own circle of subjects. However, this will be stated in the immediately following sūtra: even in the case of [the perception of] two moons, the determination (*avasāya*) of that [appearance] is not erroneous; rather, it is only the determination of its externality that is so. For that which has a contrary object—

Sensation is precisely that which is erroneous; memory is not so. For memory does not, like inferential cognition, admit within itself the nature of a prior manifestation, by virtue of which it would engage with an object that is not actually present through the determination of an object within its own reflexive appearance—thereby incurring the status of being erroneous. For as for memory...

The previous experience itself is revived and becomes the very life-force [of this cognition]. Nothing new whatsoever is manifested in this [cognition] such that its contrary nature might be suspected. For this very reason, the inclusion of the term "previously experienced" (*pūrvānubhūta*) in the commentary is intended to exclude the manifestation of something new, as is the case with inferential conceptualization and the like.

He shows that [memory] is applied by saying "thus" (*iti*) with these words. Having explained the first half [of the verse] to this extent, he explains the second half of the *kārikā* with the words "of the previous experience" (*pūrvānubhavasya*). However, "otherwise" (*anyathā*) means if it were to have a non-existent thing as its object.
"Of this"—that is, of memory—"the birth from a latent impression" (*saṃskārāt janma*).

(page 240) It is imagined; what purpose, then, does it serve? For through its refinement, there arises a similarity between one configuration and another, as in the case of a previous configuration, or rather, an "infusion" (*āveśa*) of that [configuration] which effects the perception of the non-distinction from its connection.
It is like the fragrance of *caṇpaka* flowers [infusing] oil. Furthermore, there is no similarity between memory and the prior experience;

on the contrary, they are utterly distinct by virtue of having either erroneous or non-erroneous objects. Where even similarity does not exist, an "inherence" (*āveśa*) is not even to be suspected; for that [inherence] consists in a form such as "as if identity" (*tādātmyam iva*).

Prāṇa: But is this not precisely what it means to be born from a mental impression—that it arises from the knowledge of experience through a succession? In that case, even the cognition of yellow arises from the immediately preceding condition (samanantara-pratyaya) as its material cause (upādāna-kāraṇa), or from the blue cognition as its remote material-cause-of-the-material-cause (upādānopādāna). Therefore, that too—

Why is it not said to be "born of mental impressions" (*saṃskāraja*)? He explains with the word "therefore" (*tataḥ*) that in the commentary, non-contact, dissimilarity, and non-penetration—indicated by the seventh case as the cause—are the things to be proven in the sense of having a different "acquisition and preservation" (*yogakṣema*).

Here, "acquisition" (*yoga*) means the obtaining of what was not previously obtained; however, in this context, it refers to the essential nature characterized by manifestation (*prakāśa*), which is indicated by that term.

Security (*kṣema*) is the preservation of what has been attained; however, the objective portion (*viṣayāṃśa*) is indicated by that [security]. Both of these—[the security and the objective portion]—are distinct from the experience (*anubhava*), because they appear in memory (*smṛti*) as something new (*apūrva*) and because the object (*viṣaya*) is not a real entity (*avastutva*).
Now, as for what was stated in the *Vṛtti* regarding the fact that error (*bhrānti*) arises from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), how can that be? For error is not...

Some maintain that [error] arises from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). However, it cannot be said that everything is merely error and memory, because memory is not admitted in cases such as the cognition of silver in front of one's eyes.
Therefore, one must either state that error arises from latent impressions, or specify that it is of the nature of memory. If error arises from latent impressions...

The phrase "for that very reason" (*tata eva*) dispels the two objections as to what constitutes a "grasping" (*graha*). As for what was stated—that error arises from mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), and that it is merely called "error"—this refers only to the erroneous nature of a cognition intended to be a memory;
there is not even a trace of any distinction [between them]. For this is the essential point established by logic.

Form (*rūpa*); therefore, its essence consists solely in being an error. Why? He says: "other" (*anya*). The word "blue" refers to the cognition of blue, while the word "only" (*mātra*) expresses that it is devoid of an object. This is the meaning:
(page 241)

There is another cognition, which is the immediate antecedent condition (*samanantara-pratyaya*) and the material cause (*upādāna*) of that blue-cognition which is devoid of an object and illusory in nature; for the recollection of blue has that as its essence and is identical to it.
To the question "From what does this identity arise?", he says: "Precisely from that," because it does not touch upon the experience and is thus distinct from the experience.

The meaning is "because of its security" (*kṣematvāt*). Others read "the state of being produced from latent impressions" (*saṃskārajatvam*) as referring to error (*bhrānteḥ*). In that case, the construction is as follows: in this commentary, by the statement "What is the point of [saying it is] produced from latent impressions? it is stated that the state of being produced from latent impressions is the object of grasping (*graha*), dogmatic adherence (*abhiniveśa*), and false cognition (*mithyājñāna*), and thus it is described as having the nature of error. How is that so?

"Memory does not arise from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). This is the answer to the two-fold objection: "One must specify that it is 'an error' arising from 'an error'; why has it been stated merely as such? [The reply is: "Precisely for that reason.
That which was stated—namely, that memory arises from a latent impression—and that which was stated merely as "from an error" without further specification—that is not incorrect.

"From the reason already explained"—this is what is meant: in the view of the opponent, memory has been examined; and no distinction whatsoever can be established for it from other types of error by which it might be distinguished, such that for the sake of establishing its status, its being produced from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) would be accepted on the strength of its utility, because it is established by valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The sequence of this statement is indeed logical, as it implies that [memory] must be of an unerring nature. Consequently, the following [position] is refuted from every side: that memory itself is not erroneous, nor is it produced by a latent impression (*saṃskāra*), nor does it establish the object; rather, memory—being produced by a latent impression—is erroneous and thereby establishes the object. || 4 ||

If the determination were an error, the object could not be established by means of an insentient [cognition]. Therefore, since it is not insentient, it must rest upon its own internal reflection; consequently, the object cannot be established.

Is it not the case that there is similarity merely to this extent—that the previous experience and its object are determined by that [subsequent cognition]—and not in every respect? And it is for the sake of establishing this similarity that [the cognition] is said to be born of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*).
Even though the object of perception is determined by a conceptualization (*vikalpa*) of perception, nevertheless, that...
Since direct perception is not determined [as such], it is not said that this [cognition] arises from a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) by virtue of its similarity to memory.
(Page 242)

This being the case, it is precisely through this determination (*adhyavasāya*) that memory establishes its object. Furthermore, although this determination is illusory in nature, it functions in accordance with the actual state of things; thus, nothing is defective in this determination of memory. In all instances, the determination of an object occurs solely through determination, and that—

Even in the string of words, "it is indeed an error," "an error itself," "the universal is apprehended," "conceived," "ascertained," or "conceptualized," we ask you: is a real entity (vastu) revealed by this [string of words] or not? If it is revealed, then its being an error is untenable.
Indeed, the erroneous nature [of cognition] will be refuted at length by means of the aspect of manifestation (prakāśanāṃśa) through the aspect of that which is manifested (prakāśyamānāṃśa).

Now, if, in order to establish the erroneous nature of the determinative cognition (avasāya), its character as manifestation is abandoned and some other distinct character as determination is asserted, then, regarding that [determination] which is to be established...

That determination through memory (*smṛtyadhyavasāya*) regarding an object previously experienced is inert (*jaḍa*), because it does not manifest that [object]; like the cognition of blue, it is not "blue" or "like blue" with respect to yellow. How, then, could it serve to establish that [object]? For this [determination] is grounded in consciousness (*saṃvinniṣṭhā*). But surely, the nature of manifestation exists in the determination through memory with respect to self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) and its own form; that being so—

How could this [cognition] be insentient? If that were so, then even though there exists non-insentience—which arises from its manifestation as being established in itself and established in its own form—the establishment or determination of an external object through that cognitive determination would not be possible, because that object is distinct from both its own self and its own form; such is the meaning of the aphorism.

The compound *nijollekha* (in the phrase *nijollekha iti svātmollekha iti*) in both the Sūtra and the Vṛtti is a dvandva compound. Since it is impossible for non-conceptual [cognition] to be erroneous anywhere, that which was stated somewhat obscurely in the Sūtra by way of restatement—
that the determination (*adhyavasāya*) alone is the regulator in all cases, and that this [determination] is of the nature of an error— is [here clarified].

Thus, what is this objection: "How is the determination of an object established through error? Both of these points he clarifies in the commentary by way of affirmation: "It is precisely *adhyavasāya* (determinative cognition). That which was described as the determiner of the object, characterized by error—that is, by the nature of delusion—is indeed *adhyavasāya*, and not self-awareness (*svasaṃvit*).
Nor is the consciousness of its own manifesting form non-conceptual in nature.

Thus, this state of being an error is established only in relation to the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*). And that [determinative cognition] alone is [the basis for the cognition] of the object.
"The determiner [functions] through error, by means of the conceit of unifying the perceived and the conceptualized.

To this, the proponent of the established doctrine (siddhāntin) replies: "And that... The word "and" (*ca*) here has the sense of "then" (*tarhi*), indicating the logical impossibility of the opponent's position. That determination (*adhyavasāya*), then, would be insentient with respect to the external object intended to be determined, because it is of a non-luminous nature.

If, however, it were of the nature of manifestation (*prakāśa*) therein, then—just as for a yogi—there would be a clear prior manifestation of that object previously intended to be conceptualized; thus, it would not be a memory, nor would it have the character of a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*), because it would consist solely of the form of direct experience (*anubhava*). Now, if it is not a manifestation with respect to the external [object], by which...

It possesses the nature of experience, nor is it in every respect non-luminous such that it would be insentient; rather, it is of the very nature of light within itself, in its own manifestation, and in its own form. If that is so, then once again it would be insentient with regard to the external object, and thus it could not be the cause for the establishment of external objects. For that [establishment] resides in consciousness, and never otherwise.

Regarding the phrase "resting in the insentient" (*jaḍaniṣṭhā*): as for this unification of the internal and the external through the form of error, nothing at all is touched by that [unification] regarding the external; for if it were touched, error would be impossible. The meaning of the commentary is that, according to its intent, there is no determination whatsoever of either real silver or of mother-of-pearl by means of the cognition of silver. Thus, in the Sūtra...

In the *Vṛtti*, the nature of mere determination (*adhyavasāya*) alone has been refuted, and by extension, that of recollective determination (*smṛty-adhyavasāya*). Furthermore, the mention of "past" in the *Vṛtti* is an illustration for conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), because even the conceptual construction of poetic imagination (*utprekṣā-vikalpa*)—by virtue of its entry through dependence upon prior experience—is in fact past; thus, the *Ṭīkā* also [refers to] determination.

It is established solely on the basis of the mother [text]. As for the statement therein, "for it is a cognition consisting of memory," that should be understood as intended to support the subject at hand by means of the logic of citing a determination (*adhyavasāya*). Even in the Buddhist system, the commentator, demonstrating the nature of error, shows that there is no error in non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), nor indeed in all cases.

He connects [the term] "in conceptual construction" with the phrase "appearing as consciousness. Within one's own consciousness and its corresponding form, no consciousness—whether non-conceptual or conceptual—is established as an error. For it is precisely that [consciousness]...
(page 244)

It is by means of a subverting cognition (*bādhaka-pramāṇa*) that consciousness is made known as having a contrary object; that very [consciousness], because it consists in a lack of stability, ought to be considered an error (*bhrānti*). Now, one might object: "Is that which, according to the actual state of things, is a contrary cognition, an error? What is the use of a subverting cognition, since it merely makes known the fact that [the cognition] has a contrary object?"
By this specific qualification. He says "otherwise," meaning if this specific qualification were not relied upon.

"The experience of pleasure" means that the very cognition which has blue as its object takes the form of an experience of pleasure, which is the opposite of that [blue]. By this specific qualification, "in the Buddhist view," one sets aside the experience of a jar, which is the opposite of a cloth, and so forth.

It has been stated that even the experience of pleasure would be erroneous. Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the opposite [of error] is grasped as real because it is supported by that [specific] location? Furthermore, pleasure and the like are not experienced by being supported by the form of a non-blue location, but rather by being supported by the nature of consciousness itself; for this very reason, these are mental factors (*caitta*)."
Pleasure and so forth are what are being discussed. However, the case of the double moon involves the apprehension of a single moon as occupying two locations;

in reality, this [apprehension] is the opposite of that [actual state], and since it is grasped even by non-conceptual perception (*nirvikalpaka*), why would the non-conceptual perception regarding the double moon not be erroneous? Nevertheless, precisely to exclude such cases, the word "erroneous" (*bhrānta*) was added to the definition of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
[The opponent] objects: Granted that in the case of the error regarding silver, the mother-of-pearl (*śukti*) first appears as supported by another location;

thus, it appears in its non-perverted form in the indeterminate (*nirvikalpaka*) cognition. Therefore, that perception is indeed indeterminate and non-erroneous. However, the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of silver—which occurs while the mother-of-pearl is supported by the location of the mother-of-pearl—is, in reality, [an error].

"It becomes erroneous" means that the error lies precisely in the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) itself; however, this restriction—that the determinative cognition *must* be of the nature of an error—is not logically tenable. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even so... The mention of "form" (*rūpa*) is based on identity (*tādātmya*), and not on a substratum-relationship (*ādhāratā*) through difference (*vyatireka*).

He demonstrates this: "That" (tat) means "even so" (tathāpi). How could there be an identity between the perceived double moon and a single moon? The very nature of that [perception] is the double moon itself.
That alone is indicated as the "place" (deśa) by way of being oriented toward activity and attainment; nothing else is. By the word "apivā,"...

To begin with, spatial location for a substratum that is distinct [from its properties] is not tenable, because all phenomena (dharmas) are devoid of relational connection. Thus, he indicates by way of a bold assertion (*prauḍhavāditā*) that this is a position accepted for the sake of argument (*abhyupagamyavāda*). [This applies] to light.

(Page 245) In the cognition "the jar appears," the manifestation of the jar has a support in another location. Now, it might be argued that its being in another location is not made known by a subverting cognition; for that light is indeed capable of enduring that very form.

Because the relationship of container and contained (*ādhārādheyabhāva*), as it appears, is uncontradicted. [Objection: But surely the double moon cannot occupy the same location as a single moon; for the [single moon] as the container does not appear [in that way]. [Reply: In that case, you must abandon the claim that the error arises from occupying a different location as the substratum (*adhikaraṇadeśa*), and [you must accept] identity (*tādātmya*) instead.
If there is no manifestation, how can there be delusion? But it is not the case that the double moon appears while being non-existent.
Do not say so; for existence is nothing other than the state of appearing. Thus, to say "that which is non-existent appears" is a contradiction.

Furthermore, since things like jars—which are considered real—would also be non-existent insofar as they appear under a different form, the cognition of them would likewise have to be delusion. This is what he says:
And [it is not] the theory of the manifestation of the non-existent (*asatkhyāti*), and so forth. Now, one might object: "Being manifest does not constitute existence;

rather, it is the capacity for causal efficiency (*arthakriyākāritva*). And that is absent in the case of a double moon. Anticipating this view of others, [the author] shows that it is unestablished by stating: "Even the capacity for causal efficiency... The phrase "of the non-existent" means "of that which is intended as such by virtue of its non-existence."

There is delight for the child and the one with cataracts, and agitation for the discerning person. But surely, that which is seen as one by others is embraced by duality by this [discerning person]. And it is not the case that this "one" performs a causal function (*arthakriyā*) by virtue of being embraced by duality. Who says such a thing? For it performs its causal function in exactly that way; for the causal function follows the appearance. Therefore—

If there is manifestation, then there must also be causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) corresponding to it; and since that [efficiency] exists only through manifestation—otherwise there would be an infinite regress—manifestation itself is existence. Having grasped this in his heart, he concludes with the words "in its own self. For if something were non-existent while its form is being manifested...
How could there even be the appearance [of such an object]? He confirms this very point with the words "for thus" (*tathā hi*) and "not of that" (*na tasya*).
On the contrary, for him, that is correct knowledge. Accordingly, a physician wishing to treat his cataract asks:
"Sir, do you truly see two moons? And he replies in the same manner: "I truly see them."
Regarding this, he states an illustration with the words "for not" (*na hi*).

(Page 246) "One who possesses magic" (*indrajālavān*) refers to one who has spells, ritual procedures, medicinal herbs, and so forth. "By way of its unreality" (*asatyatvena*) means by way of its non-externality.
"No. If even that [cognition] were erroneous, it would proceed toward external objects; but it does not do so. For this very reason, he declares:

"I am not deluded, but I cause the world to wander. [Objection: In that case, the talk of error would have ceased everywhere. [Response: No; he says "and therefore," because this is so, therefore this...

The meaning is that another object of cognition (*prameya*) has been obtained. What is that? He says: "of the non-existent" (*asataḥ*). This refers to the perception of a double moon—which, though appearing, lacks an internal or external form—as having existence; or rather, it is the perception of the form of cognition itself as an external object, or as something other than the self (*anātmatvena*). That is *bhrama* (error). Alternatively, the word "ca" has the sense of "but" (*tu*). Therefore:

The cognition following the appearance of two moons is of the nature of a conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*). In this view, through the alternative explanation of the phrase "therefore" (*tataśca*) by means of the words "and not" (*na ca*), it is demonstrated that the very force of that cognition necessitates its being of the nature of a conceptual determination. Thus, the word "and" (*ca*) serves to include another form [of cognition] which follows from the logic of the argument.

The word *ca* [is used]. In the second explanation, the causal passage for the statement that "cognition, being of the nature of a determinative act (*adhyavasāya*), is erroneous" begins with *na ca* and so forth. The particle *ca* has the sense of *hi* (for/indeed). That which is manifesting, that which is appearing, is the real object (*vastu*).
It possesses a determined form; exactly as it appears, so it is—it does not become something other than that.

Therefore, that non-conceptual cognition of his which is of the nature of luminosity cannot in any way tolerate "otherness," that is, the state of being a contrary experience; for this reason, there is no other cognition distinct from the non-conceptual cognition.
And even that [other cognition] is not every kind, but rather only that by which the contrary is determined. Nor does this...

There is a reversal regarding its own object of apprehension. Therefore, in the case of a form that appears as the object of non-conceptual [perception], that very thing which determines the reversal is the nature of determination (*adhyavasāya*); it is logical that this alone is erroneous in every instance of deluded cognition.
[Objection: Let it be that way immediately following the non-conceptual [perception]. [Response: No; he says "and that" (*tac ca*). This refers to the state of being non-conceptual (*avikalpakatva*).

This very thing is the state of having the nature of being first manifested (*prathamānārūpatva*). However, the activity of joining, separating, and so forth, is conceptual construction (*vikalpana*).

Thus he says, "But for that which has the nature of conceptual construction," the connection being that it is logical for it to be an error (*bhrāntitva*). For that [conceptual construction] indeed possesses the quality of falling away from the state of being first manifested.

Regarding this, he says: "the object of perception" (*dṛśya*). Is there error in every case? No; he says: "contrary" (*viparīta*). When, with respect to a mother-of-pearl that is being perceived, one determines its identity with silver—which is contrary to that perceived object—then...

[The opponent argues: "There is error [in conceptualization]. But when the blue object is perceived, what error is there in its identity with the blue conceptualized [object]? Others, however, explain:

"Every conceptualization is erroneous when it determines an identity between the clearly perceived [object] and the unclearly [perceived] conceptualized [object]. Nevertheless, because it is rooted in reality and thus leads to the attainment [of the object], it is not conventionally designated as 'erroneous'."

Because it is the blue itself that is attained, and because there is the conceit [of attainment] due to its performing a causal function (*arthakriyā*), one disregards internal distinctions such as clarity or lack of clarity. However, he who does not determine identity with the perceived object remains entirely non-erroneous, being restricted solely to his own object which consists of the conceptualized form. He concludes this with the words "Therefore" (*ataḥ*).

The appearance of two moons, which is non-conceptual, does not constitute error because the appearance exists insofar as it manifests. For this very reason, the manifestation of blue is logical even when the blue object itself is absent. Indeed, its manifestation is not its own inherent form, such that if the object were absent, the manifestation would likewise not occur like a gesture; rather, [it is so].
Its consciousness is manifesting, and since that [consciousness] exists, its manifestation would occur even in the absence of blue;

thus, the emptiness of external objects is logical. If there were no manifestation of blue, what could exist by whose power the manifestation of blue would manifest? If there were no manifestation of blue, nothing at all would manifest—whatever it may be.

The nature of luminosity does not belong to anything else; in the absence of that [luminosity], it does not shine, just as the light consisting of radiance does not appear in the absence of a lamp or similar source. And so, since the manifestation of the manifestation of blue is not a property of something else, the rule is that when that [blue] is absent, its manifestation—which would otherwise occur everywhere—is not observed.

By means of the reason of being an entity (*vastutva*), its state of being a different property (*anyadharmatva*) has been established as a pervader; thus, this is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).

Therefore, Bhadraśaṅkaranandana maintains that the emptiness of consciousness is indeed outside the scope of logic. Consequently, the non-conceptual [perception] of a double moon, as well as the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) based solely on such a conceptualized object, are not erroneous.

For in this case, a subverting argument is effective against neither of the two positions; indeed, even when the darkness has ceased, one does not have the realization, "A double moon did not appear to me.
(page 248)

For it is precisely from that manifestation (*pratibhāna*) that the treatment for cataracts and so forth proceeds. As for the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) that "this double moon is external and common to all," that alone is erroneous, because it is known as such by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*).
Once the cataract has been removed, the realization occurs: "That which was perceived by me as an external double moon—"

That which was determined as common [to all] does not appear as such; rather, it appears as something non-external and unique, arising from other causes such as ophthalmia (timira), yet one misapprehends it as being external and common to all. And that is not so, as is shown by the subverting cognition (bādhaka).

It is not uprooted by cognition; therefore, it is to be treated as erroneous, like the portion of self-cognition [that perceives itself]. Thus, there is the non-perception of the cause for both the appearance of two moons and the conceptual determination (*adhyavasāya*) of two moons, because the conventional usage of "error" is invariably accompanied by a cause.
And because no other cause is possible, it is not [the case that sublation is the cause]; rather, the very state of being uprooted is the cause, and that is not perceived here. As Bhaṭṭa said:
"The non-existence of the unreal outside [of the real] is sublation; therefore, existence is twofold."

Thus, even for that which is being conceptualized, there is no lack of invalidity because of the absence of error; for nothing is done to it by a subverting cognition (*bādhaka*), but rather, as the context proceeds, only the determination of the non-difference between the perceived and the conceptualized is uprooted. Thus he says:
