"But when there is a difference in appearance, what object could there be? In that case, the non-difference is the nature of the error. [Objection: "If the non-conceptual cognition of two moons is thus designated as an error, then what is the intention of the Master [Dignāga] in his statement regarding 'timira', 'rapid rotation', and so forth? To this he says: "And even the determination of externality... etc.

By means of *timira* (ocular disorder), this uncommon appearance (*ābhāsa*) is produced; because one does not perceive it [as internal], there is the determination (*adhyavasāya*) of its externality. What is meant by this is that an appearance, as it arises, occurs predominantly as something caused by an external object, due to the power of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of firm habitual practice, from the very beginning.

From that point onward, that appearance, manifesting within both consciousness and the act of determination, appears as if its externality has been drawn inward; thus, for one of dull intellect, it is said to be a delusion from the very beginning, like a magical illusion or an optical aberration such as *timira*.
But he who understands that the appearance of the grove and so forth [moving] while walking is caused by [an eye disease such as] *timira* does not determine it to be external.
And thus: "Look, look! The trees on the bank are moving backward for one who has boarded a boat."

To the child who says with astonishment, "They are running very fast, very fast," he replies, "The trees are not like that; it is merely seen thus. By this, it is stated that this is merely a property of appearance (*pratibhāsa-dharma*). Thus, through non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), this [erroneous perception] is sublated by the acceptance of external reality.

The intention of the other [opponent] is this: error regarding one's own self is tolerable, but in the case of the illusion of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell, it is not tolerable because there is no acceptance of the silver by the initial non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*). "For now" (*tāvat*): what is useful here has been shown; however, the rest will be shown later. "Of yours" (*bhavatām*): that which is the nature of error in your own system is what is addressed here.
It has not yet been demonstrated—this is the sense. As it is said in the *Nareśvaraviveka*:

"Even for others, cognition regarding hair and the like is an error directed toward the external. Thus, by way of illustration, [we refer to] that third aspect of determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) which exists within the form of error as it is commonly recognized in the world.

therefore, it is not logical for determination (*adhyavasāya*) to be the establisher of the object, as is the case with the memory-cognition under discussion. For one who has become thus, the utterance of a conventional word— designated as a signifier— for the sake of producing either a determination (*adhyavasāya*) of an object-form similar to that which was previously determined within oneself, or for the sake of generating such a determination of an object-form that had not previously existed in that manner, serves to clarify the narrative.

How could this be? The particle *ca* is used here in the sense of "and" (*anvācaya*). The determination (*vyavasthāpanā*) is what must be ascertained; thus, the narrative (*upākhyāna*), providing support for the manifestation (*prakhyā*), is designated here as its assistant. Now, one might object: let the determination be a property of the object itself, according to the logic of the Bhaṭṭas.
(251) Here he says: "with respect to each cognizer. For the property of an object does not differ with respect to each cognizer;

It is observed that what appears clearly to one person may not appear at all to another; however, this is not possible if [the cognition] were a property of the object (*viṣayadharma*). The state of being distinct from each cognizer is pervaded by non-stability, which is the opposite of that [stability]; thus, there is the perception of what is pervaded by the opposite of the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). "Of the cognizer" (*pramātuḥ*) indicates that this is indeed a property of the cognizer. And he for whom this property—characterized by the manifestation and description of objects—is present, is alone called "non-inert" (*ajaḍa*). The word "api" (also/even) occurs in the *Vṛtti*.

This indicates the irrationality of the opponent's admission: "Even though you have accepted [the self] as being of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), nevertheless it is not free from defects. Regarding the phrase "that very same [self]," it means that by him, both manifestation (*prakhyā*) and description (*upākhyā*) must be performed in relation to that very thing. And since that is indeed external—meaning that which exists there as both manifested and described—it is entirely full (*pūrṇa*).

If it were [merely] manifested, there would be no difference between this determinative cognition (*smṛty-adhyavasāya*) and direct perception (*pratyakṣa*); for this very reason, it is said to be "by way of the nature of consciousness" (*saṃvidātmanā*). For what activity can there be of that which has consciousness as its own nature, other than consciousness itself? Even when designated by such terms as "determinative cognition" (*adhyavasāya*) and so forth—

The Light alone is full. Therefore, whatever does not possess the nature of full Light in a given place cannot even be of the nature of error there, just as self-awareness is in the case of pleasure. And so, in the determination of a memory regarding an object that is not its proper domain, whatever manifestation is not full therein is indeed erroneous, like [the perception of] silver.

The statement "that cognition is something [distinct]" is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*). Although there is no fault even if non-erroneousness is conceded, the commentary (*vṛtti*) states that very point as a fault with the intention that, in the case of equality with direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), there would be a contradiction regarding cognition. And for that very reason, both points are stated in the sub-commentary (*ṭīkā*). "Non-object" (*anartha*) refers to one's own self.
And that which is the mental representation (*svallekha*) is precisely the object manifested to the determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*); the external object, however, is not manifested at all.
If that is so, then this external object must be insentient (*jaḍa*).
(page 252)

For there is no "horn" of insentience (*jāḍya*). The meaning is that whatever does not have the nature of appearing in a certain place is called "insentient" there, just as blue is [called insentient] elsewhere. The phrase "in the objective portion" (*arthāṃśe*) means when one intends to establish [the object] as external. "One's own self" (*svātmā*) is of the nature of consciousness (*saṃvidrūpa*), and "representation" (*ullekha*) is by means of its own activity through imaginative construction (*utprekṣaṇa*).

As if carved out within itself, or as if extracted and being depicted like a painting, it is "blue" in the form of a mere shadow. Let both of these be established by a determinative cognition (*adhyavasāya*) which, through its capacity for manifestation, touches upon that very [internal reality] while possessing both appearance (*prakhyā*) and verbal designation (*upākhyā*), and not as something external.

This is the meaning of the word *mātra* (only). To this extent, in the Buddhist system, the very establishment of an object (*artha*) is not possible in any way; for that [establishment], which is animated by the reflection upon what precedes and follows, cannot be accomplished by non-conceptual cognition (*nirvikalpaka*), and because conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*), being of the nature of a determination (*avasāya*), is insentient (*jaḍa*) with respect to an external object, it cannot effect its establishment.

This has been shown because [such a thing] is untenable. For mere manifestation (*prakhyāna*) is of the nature of non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpaka*), devoid of any descriptive characterization (*upākhyā*). That is not the determination of an object; nor is mere characterization devoid of illumination. And as for that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) which appears as perception, what does it perform therein?

It has already been stated that [an object] may be compared through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Consequently, it has also been indicated how the establishment of external objects (*bāhyārtha*) is possible.

For this very reason, the proponent will demonstrate in his own system the mutual inseparability of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), by which the determination of objects becomes easily attained even as "external. For that [determination] consists of manifestation (*prakhyā*) and designation (*upākhyā*); these two alone...

And since both manifestation (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) belong to the object, how could consciousness—which consists of these two—not be of the nature of the determination of the object?

Thus, there is nothing here that is difficult to establish. Furthermore, the claims that "the ascertainment has become the perception" or "the perception has become the ascertainer" are merely different ways of expressing the same thing based on human intellect; they are not ultimately real.

Let it be that the opponent’s objection—that the cognition "I see" is not a fitting form for a vision that is free from conceptual determination (*niścaya*), since by such [a cognition] the nature of a conceptual determination would result—stands refuted; for this reflective awareness "I see" is indeed the very form of a conceptual determination. Let us leave it at that. || 5 ||
In this way, if cognitions were mutually distinct and incapable of mutual awareness, the stability of human existence—which arises from the synthesis of those cognitions—would perish. (6)

(Page 253) With the words "tadevam" and so forth, he introduces the sūtra in brief. Regarding the word "jñānam" (cognition): it does not "āskandati"—that is, it does not seize or appropriate—the object belonging to another cognition. How so?

Its appropriation is possible. He says: "intrinsic" (*nija*) means that which has its stability and repose (*niṣṭhā-viśrānti*) in its own nature and in its own object alone; [this refers to] that other object which is to be appropriated, by means of the knowledge belonging to it. Now, one might ask: when that object is being appropriated, how does the knowledge of it serve as a medium? It is said in reply:
"Another than that" (*tadapara*) means that other knowledge which is to be apprehended, because it becomes an object of awareness.

Now, one might raise the objection: "If knowledge itself is what is being experienced, then how can its object be accepted? Anticipating this doubt, it is said: "another than that," referring to that other knowledge.

For an object is that which is to be known (*saṃvedya*). The meaning is this: since knowledge has the nature of illuminating its own object, by the very act of making that [object] known, the knowledge necessarily also takes possession of its object. Now, if this—namely, the fact of being known by another cognition—is the means for knowledge to take possession of an external object, then—
"Let it be so. Then that [simultaneity] might be resorted to, if it were possible; but it is not possible, as he says:
"Because things arise sequentially, cognitions are indeed distinct. But what follows from that? He says:

they are of the nature of illumination with respect to their own appearance—that is, their own essential nature—and with respect to the object, which consists of the shadow of its own form; but not with respect to the nature of another.

"In another object" means in a distinct object. "Likewise, the function [of the mind] consists in its own self alone. Here, the reason is the principle established immediately prior. By that principle, what is accomplished? He says: "It is the mere essential nature. With this much, the first half of the verse has been explained; he now explains the second half with the words "And from that. From that...

Furthermore, because there would be no acceptance of the object of another’s cognition, the attainment of purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) preceded by engagement would not occur for those seeking an object, since the very desire for it would not arise. For that [desire] occurs only when there is a certainty regarding a specific object that is sought and constitutes the objective of engagement. And an object becomes something to be sought only if it has previously [been experienced].

The certainty that [the object] is perceived as a means to pleasure; and thus, this certainty, which consists in the union with the object, is the cause of longing. Since that [certainty] is absent, there is an absence of longing due to the non-perception of its cause, and by that very [absence], [there is an absence of subsequent stages].

If there were an absence of effects, the worldly course— consisting of prayer, determination, activity, attainment, loss, acquisition, social interaction, and so forth— would perish. Having rendered the continuous stream of consciousness, which arises in succession, variegated, [it would cease].

Through various modes of diversity, such as the joining together of fetters and so forth, there occurs a convergence regarding some object—namely, the form [of recognition] such as: "The very same object that you see today was previously observed by me in this very way";
by means of that, indeed, there is the performance of what is capable of that [object], namely, the specific purpose of the sphere of activity.
It would be established in certainty; however, that itself is not tenable. By this, it is explained that [memory] is born from synthesis (*anusandhāna*).
Even though the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) is singular, because it is imagined as momentary, it is incapable of uniting objects.
And since the investigation of recollective cognition (*smṛtijñāna*) has begun, the word "entire" (*akhila*) is used. This applies even to the first cognition.

The thought "I know this" culminates in the sense of "I" (*ahantā*); and this "I" manifests as resting upon the reflective awareness of one's own nature as prior and posterior. In the absence of such a resting point, even that [cognition] would be nothing at all. This same path applies even to pleasure, pain, and so forth; and thus, this subject (*pramātā*) is characterized by the single flavor of continuous synthesis (*anusandhi*).
The continuity [of consciousness] must necessarily be established, for in its absence, one would become as if unconscious during worldly activity.

Now, it may be argued: let cognitions not be of the nature of manifesting only their own appearance; rather, let them be of the nature of manifesting external objects. And these external objects exist either as a continuous stream or as stable entities.

Alternatively, by virtue of belonging to the same class (*tajjātīyatvena*), that very object which was perceived by the preceding cognition is perceived by the subsequent cognition; thus, the convergence of objects is established. This would be established if "the state of having been perceived" (*dṛṣṭatā*) were a property (*dharma*) of that object.
However, it is nothing other than the very form of the preceding cognition. Furthermore, there is no [identity] between the intrinsic natures (*svarūpa*) of the two cognitions.

Identity (*tādātmya*). For this would indeed be the case if the difference between cognitions were not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*). He demonstrates this with the words "distinct" (*vyatirikta*) and so forth. Indeed, the conjunction of objects could occur either as a property of the object belonging to the state of being perceived, or through the identity of the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the two cognitions, or through their mutual awareness; it cannot be otherwise.
"This is an extreme position. [The opponent objects: "Well then, let this be the third alternative. [The author] says "no," for he states: "even that" (*tad api*).

That is, even such knowledge—even though it consists in the illumination of an object distinct [from itself]. "Independently" (*svātantryeṇa*) means precisely without touching upon the acquisition or preservation (*yogakṣema*) of the preceding cognition.

(Page 255) Now, if that cognition were to apprehend that object by taking a preceding cognition as its precursor, what contradiction would there be? On the contrary, in this matter, direct experience (*pratīti*) is the witness, [testifying]: "This object is known. This—

Having raised the objection that knowledge is cognizable by another knowledge—a position accepted by the followers of Akṣapāda (the Naiyāyikas)—he begins to refute it with the words "of cognitions," etc.
Here, the reasoning is stated in brief: [otherwise] there would be the consequence of insentience (*jaḍatā*). Thus it was said.

Regarding the passage "The vision is indeed self-manifesting" (1.3.2), here the author, having elaborated at length to reveal his own intention, establishes that [the vision] does not become an object of another cognition even while possessing self-luminosity, by means of the argument beginning with "because its nature is self-awareness," and so forth. It is not the case here that...
The section ending with "some sublation" (*kaścid bādhaḥ*) and the section ending with "they exist" (*bhavanti*) represent the proponent's position as restated by the opponent (*pūrvapakṣavādin*).

By this, the connection of the negative particle (*nañ*) with "cognition" (*saṃvedana*) in the commentary—namely, "not cognizable by another" (*aparasaṃvedyāni*)—is explained. If it were connected with the word "another" (*para*), the reason (*hetu*) would be indistinguishable from the thesis (*sādhya*).

Having thus restated [the opponent's position], he states his own view with the words "from what? (kutaḥ). And this is his underlying intention (*ākūta*): just as when one lamp is lit, another lamp shines without having gone [to it], there is no contradiction; so too in the case of cognition, [another] cognition [is perceived]. For by this much, nothing is impaired in that apprehending cognition, for it— (Note: The provided source text ends mid-sentence. The translation reflects the partial nature of the input.)
Would it grasp what is insentient or what is sentient? If it possesses the nature of a grasper, what loss is there? To this he says: "Just as [it grasps] the insentient," and so forth.

What refutation is there even for the object of cognition (*grāhya*)? If you say, "It would result in its becoming insentient," it is not so. For knowledge, although it is luminous, manifests itself in such a way that its very nature is the illumination of another.

It exists—thus, because its manifestation of another is inseparable from its own self-manifestation, its nature as the manifestation of itself is never absent. And that alone constitutes its non-inertness (*ajaḍatva*). Furthermore, so-called "manifestability" is not its essential nature.

It is exactly like a jar; therefore, even that [non-manifestation] does not bring about insentience in it. This is what he means by the words "of being manifest and not being manifest. Non-manifestness is the linguistic usage "this has not been manifested"; that [usage] does not belong to the object.
(Page 256) Just as there is the linguistic usage, "This [object] has its own nature manifested," he shows that when this cognition is apprehended by a cognizer,
it is only its being manifested by another that is logically established, and not its self-manifestation. For by that [which manifests it],...

If this manifestation of the object, in its form as light, becomes an object of cognition for the subject by that very same [light], then it follows that even a jar would ultimately become an object of cognition. For, in the absence of another cognition [of that cognition], what difference would there be between the substance of the self and the substance of the jar? Therefore, its so-called "cognizability" is merely the cognition itself, just like the jar.

Another cognition [is established], for the reason for its being distinct from the jar is precisely this luminosity of it, which consists in its being of the nature of light with respect to its own object. Indeed, being of the nature of light is not the intrinsic body of the object.
He states this very point with the words "for that very [consciousness] is its light. The opponent concludes his own position with the words "thus, therefore."

The state of being manifest to knowledge is simply another instance of knowledge; however, it has been shown that the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of that which is manifesting consists in its having the form of manifesting another, because it possesses the nature of light (*prakāśātmatva*) and because its intrinsic character is the manifestation of another.
Therefore, whether [the object] is of the nature of knowledge or of the nature of the insentient (*jaḍa*), there is no distinction whatsoever for the apprehending knowledge.

This has been shown by the term "refutation" (*khaṇḍana*). It was stated that even by another cognition, as expressed by the words "in this way," nothing is lost of the cognized cognition. That which does not invalidate its own definition in a given case is not contradictory therein—just as the reflection of another clear mirror occurs in the clarity of a mirror. And so it is.

In the case of cognition, being apprehended by another cognition is not its own defining characteristic (*sva-lakṣaṇa*). For that which exists as manifesting itself, the fact of having the nature of manifesting another does not subvert it; thus, there is a non-perception of the pervader (*vyāpakānupalabdhi*).
Indeed, contradiction occurs only in certain instances, not everywhere. And if [something] were contradictory even when it does not subvert the defining characteristic, [it would lead to absurdity].

It might be argued that everything would be contradictory to everything else; thus, even the properties of being an effect or a cause would not belong to blue, because they would be contradictory. In this way, since the pervader—namely, the possession of a restrictive rule—is subject to the consequence of non-perception, the conventional usage of "contradiction" is excluded from its opponent by virtue of a form that does not subvert its defining characteristic.

It is pervaded by the non-sublation of the definition; and that [sublation] is not perceived here. He refutes this with the words "In this regard, it is said," and so forth. By this, while demonstrating the non-establishment of the non-sublation of the definition, he establishes the very contradiction.

(Page 257) Knowledge indeed consists in the manifestation of the jar. In that regard, the state of being manifested is not some property residing in the jar; rather, it is the very nature of knowledge itself. And if that...

If the state of being manifest, even when residing in a cognition, is itself merely the nature of another cognition, then the cognized cognition would be devoid of any nature whatsoever. Furthermore, the manifestation of the apprehending cognition as well would be nothing but another apprehending cognition; by this sequence, everything [would be reduced to further cognitions].
With the intention that knowledge would be devoid of its own nature (*niḥsvarūpa*), he begins with the words "Just as," and so forth.
The phrase "even while being manifested" means even when there is an acceptance based on mere verbal assertion.

The term "to be cognized as 'I'" (*ahamiti-pratyeya*) uses a gerundive (*kṛtya*) in the sense of fitness (*arhe*). [This refers to] the independence from anything else regarding the state of being manifested.

The characteristic of consciousness (*bodha*) consists in being independent of anything else in its state of being an object of apprehension; otherwise, it would indeed be sublated. By the word "only" (*eva*), he expresses this independence. The connection is: "For that alone is worthy of manifesting in the form 'I'.

The intervening passage, beginning with "of 'I' alone," is stated here as the reason. But [one might object]: [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the portion available.]

Thinking that "I" is not this cognition, but rather the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the knower, and that it is cognition which is being investigated here, he says: "But when... The two occurrences of the word "but" (*tu*) indicate a distinction: although there is no difference in reality, there is a distinction between "cognition-ness" and "knower-ness" based on whether there is a delimitation of the object or not.

This illuminates two points. What is meant is this: there is certainly no such thing as a "self" that is a distinct substance which, like a jar, is manifested by cognition. For if that were the case, nothing at all would be manifested. To explain: the state of being manifested belongs not to the jar's own nature, but rather to the cognition.
Even its state of being manifest is not its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), but rather another cognition;

thus, there would be a non-duality of the unmanifest, and the world would be as if in deep sleep. Therefore, consciousness alone, in the form of the subject (*pramātṛ*), even when it has assumed the contraction of being delimited by the internal body, vital breath, the void (*śūnya*), and so forth, is [the reality] directed toward the external—

Due to limitation (*avaccheda*), *māyā*—which is of the nature of the subject (*pramātṛ*)—is not yet contracted externally; however, when it has attained external contraction, it takes the form of cognition (*jñāna*). Even in that state, its uncontracted form persists as an underlying presence, for otherwise, synthesis (*anusaṃdhāna*) would be impossible; thus, cognition is said to be an attribute of the Self (*ātma-dharma*).

(258) By the words "Even by the followers of the Sugata," and so forth, [the author] states that for everyone, this manifestation is exactly thus: first of all, for everyone, that which is characterized by luminosity is permeated by a form colored by the shadow of objects, whether stable or unstable.

This is established by internal experience and is not subject to denial; yet, those unable to substantiate it resort to the straw of *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass. For instance, the Buddhists accept that its ultimate nature is indeed unstable, while stability is merely a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) based on the continuum (*saṃtāna*) of cognition.

By the Mātravādins and the Sāṃkhyas, form is held to be unstable, produced by the coloring of the reflection of objects, while its nature as light is attributed to the influence of the reflection of the Puruṣa; this is said by the proponents of the principle of *buddhi*. One should understand that "primary" here does not mean primary in a real sense, but rather according to appearance; for this very reason, he says:
Regarding the phrase "while [the intellect] is manifesting": for true subjectivity belongs to the *puruṣa* alone.

Alternatively, because the *puruṣa* consists solely of consciousness (*citimātra*), its designation as a "subject" and so forth is figurative, being produced by its conformity with the fluctuations (*vṛtti*) such as valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and error (*viparyaya*). This is because it is accepted that the discernment (*vyāvṛtti*) is non-distinct from the fluctuation of the intellect (*buddhi*).

However, the primary status of being a cognizer (pramātṛbhāva) belongs precisely to the principle of the intellect (buddhitattva) when it is colored by the reflection of the Person (puruṣa). It is "of both forms," meaning it is both this cognition and this cognizer. As for those such as the Naiyāyikas and others, the manifestation characterized by cognition—since, in their view, the manifestation of an object occurs only upon the arising of cognition—is [the same].

Beyond that, the "knower" (*pramātṛ*) is a specific, eternal, and all-pervading substance denoted by the word *ātman*. Even in that case, it is accepted that the manifestation of the object appears as non-different from that substantial self; however, it is merely stated that *samavāya* (inherence) is the cause for such an appearance. As for how...

Just as a cloth that is "red-and-white" appears as a variegated fabric permeated by both redness and whiteness, so too, even in the cognition "I am the knower," this Self must possess a nature woven together (*otaprotasvabhāva*) by the manifestation consisting of the knowledge of a jar and the manifestation consisting of the knowledge of the knowledge of a cloth; thus, it is of the nature of manifold manifestations.

We have rightly stated that the self is indeed permeated [by consciousness]; it is that very self which is knowledge and the cognizer. Now, one might object: "Inherence is a relation, and like conjunction, it exists only through difference. Anticipating this, he shows that while it is true, because knowledge is inseparable (ayutasiddha), its manifestation as something distinct is never tenable.
"Otherwise" means that, despite being absolutely distinct from individuals— which possess the opposite qualities of pervasiveness and permanence—
in terms of their acquisition (*yoga*) and loss (*kṣema*), the universal (*jāti*) exists and appears as if it were identical with the individual. Such is its nature.

With the intention of asking how the greatness of *samavāya* (inherence) could possibly accept the appearance of a distinction between a quality (*guṇa*) and its possessor (*guṇin*), who are absolutely identical in their acquisition and preservation (*yogakṣema*), he employs the universal (*jāti*) as an example,
beginning with the words "for not," etc. Since an example serves to reinforce the nature of the reason (*hetu*), it is an auxiliary factor for establishing the point at hand.

The word *hi* indicates the reason for this intention: if the universal (*jāti*) were independent, it would either exist or appear; in that case, it would be nothing other than a substance (*dravya*) and would manifest as such. For the very life of a universal consists in its producing a cognition of non-difference among things that are distinct. Now, if the Omniscient One perceives the six categories as distinct, then [he must perceive] the universal...

One might also consider that one could perceive [the universals] as distinct; for even at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), when individual instances (*vyakti*) are absent, one must necessarily perceive the universals (*jāti*), since they exist at that time by virtue of their eternity. Anticipating this objection, he says: "Even for the Omniscient One.
For the Omniscient One does not perceive objects in a manner that is contrary to their true nature (*ayathāsvarūpa*); for if he did so, he would indeed be deluded (*bhrānta*).
It would be so. Furthermore, because of his omniscience, even during the dissolution of the universe (*pralaya*), he perceives past and future things directly as manifest;
thus, he understands that a genus (*jāti*) has its very life dependent upon being colored by those [particulars]. This is what is expressed by the word "deserves" (*arhati*).

Having explained the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), he applies it to the subject of the illustration (*dārṣṭāntika*) with the words "in the same way" (*tadvat*). For [the self] is manifested as the appearance of self-luminosity (*ahaṃprakāśa*).

The cognizer is the Self (*ātman*). It is only through non-difference from that [Self] that cognition possesses appropriate manifestation, just as whiteness [is manifest] through its non-difference from a jar, because it is a quality thereof. For if something manifesting as distinct were to be a quality of that [Self], then the entire universe would likewise be a quality of it; thus, the property of being a quality is excluded from the counter-example by the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of such lack of restriction.

It is pervaded by the probandum, which is the manifestation of non-difference from that [subject]; thus, it is an essential reason (*svabhāvahetu*). And so, knowledge appears appropriately as "I am the knower. However, when there is an appearance as "this," it is knowledge itself that appears—though appearing as something external to the knower, possessing qualities other than those [of the subject], or appearing as an independent entity with different qualities.
Thus, it is taught in all philosophical systems that the manifestation of knowledge occurs precisely through its internal abiding within the cognizer, who is capable of such self-manifestation.
(Page 260)

Regarding "knowledge": it is not logical for knowledge to be cognizable by another instance of knowledge. Now, let us grant that this [object] as "this" may not be manifest, and let it be that [the self] is manifest as "I"; however, just as in cases such as "I am happy," "I desire," "I hate," or "I exert effort," happiness, desire, and so forth—by virtue of being inherent in the self—are [manifested] precisely through that which is inherent in the self.

Anticipating the objection that illumination occurs through a distinct cognition— just as the knower is known by another cognition inherent in the same substrate— the author, holding in his heart that this very example is inappropriate, defines the nature of the self-luminous manifestation itself with the word "svayam" (itself).

This is called "consisting of self-luminosity": it is the sovereignty over being manifested, which does not depend on another. Otherwise, because there would be no cessation of one manifestation after another, nothing at all would ever be manifested;
this has been determined more than once.

"For the repose of light within itself is indeed the state of 'I-ness'... (Aparokṣānubhūti-prakāśa-siddhi, verse 22). For that Naiyāyika for whom the self is always only indirect (*parokṣa*), how could its attribute, which exists in an indirect mode, be manifest? How can this be so? And how can that which is manifest as distinct be inseparable (*ayutasiddha*)?

It might be argued that even though the sky is not manifest, sound is manifest; but how could this be so? Furthermore, how could there be a lack of perception regarding the contact between a tree and the wind? Now, it may be said that the self indeed shines forth in the cognition "I am"; yet in that case as well, the cognition "I am" is not self-luminous. That too must be apprehended by another cognition. And that [cognition]...

It must be considered by what form a subsequent cognition arises. If it were "this," then it would have an existence external to the self. If, on the other hand, it were "I," then this would be a cognition of the self, not a cognition of the cognition of the self; and due to infinite regress, nothing at all would be manifest. The arising of a cognition [is the manifestation] of the object.

For the statement "it is luminous" would either imply an identity between knowledge and its object, or else— like saying that the very act of a jar carrying water is the same as the act of a cloth covering something— it would reveal the speaker’s madness. Therefore, the nature of knowledge is self-luminosity independent of anything else, whereas [the luminosity] dependent on anything else...
Since being manifest is contradictory [with being an object], and that very [manifestness] constitutes being graspable by another cognition, cognition is not cognizable by another cognition.
(Page 261)

"Regarding its object" means the established orders of those objects which belong to cognitions; their "finality" (*niṣṭhā*) means their completion by way of the absence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*). "That very [nature]" refers to the essential nature of this cognition, which consists in its being a self-luminous manifestation of the "I" directed toward the object. "What else?"—for what other quality could it have?

First of all, cognition itself does not appear, because there is the manifestation of nothing other than the illumination of the object. Furthermore, even if that [cognition] were manifesting, since it would be of the nature of a knowledge-form common to other qualities such as color and so forth, it would not manifest as such;
thus, cognition would not be manifested at all. He concludes this with the word "tat" (therefore): for the reason that has been stated.

When knowledge manifests as something differentiated from the state of "I-ness" (*ahambhāva*), which is the nature of the sovereignty of light—manifesting as "this"—then it becomes manifest by resting upon the ultimate realization: "I am the knower, consisting of the manifestation of the object. This is just as [one realizes]: "This is the quality white."

Regarding the conceptual construction that "the cloth exists there [in the threads] as a distinct entity through the relation of inherence," the nature of the quality (white) is apprehended only through the mediation of another conceptual construction, namely "this cloth is white," and not directly.
Likewise, in the case of "this is my knowledge" or "now," that which manifests does so by virtue of the power of another's illumination.

The state of being expressed as "this" (idantā) is insentient (*jaḍa*); that which, by virtue of its self-luminosity, has the form of "I" (*ahantā*), is non-insentient (*ajaḍa*). Thus, if the definition of the insentient is that which is dependent on another for its manifestation and is itself manifested, let it be so; however, in another way, "thisness" consists in being distinct from light, whereas [the sentient] is non-distinct from it.

If one says that what is to be manifested—having abandoned the distinction between the insentient and the sentient based on the notion "I am this"—is insentient, then what is its state of being manifested? If one says it is the arising of cognition, then nothing at all would have been said regarding its own nature.
And thus, since it is incompatible with the definition of the insentient, blue and so forth would have to be non-insentient. This has indeed been stated by you yourself.

Having grasped in his heart that, because such [a definition] is impossible in the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), there is neither over-extension (*ativyāpti*) nor lack of extension (*avyāpti*) here, he demonstrates the lack of fixed distinction between the insentient and the sentient by showing the non-contradiction of their definitions through a different approach, beginning with the words "And therefore" (*ataśca*). This is not only because [the definition] does not touch upon the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or the non-essential nature (*asvarūpa*).
Even if the contact with its own nature were admitted, [the following would occur]:

furthermore, because there would be no contradiction between the characteristics of the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*), even that which is insentient would become sentient. This is due to the absence of contradiction—
He indicates this by means of the two words "eva" and "api. The word "adya" refers to the system we have described.
Regarding "the nature of the object": the object itself is designated as "this" (idantā) when it appears through engagement, attainment, application, and so forth;
however, that which is self-luminous in the form of the knower and the knowledge is designated as "I" (ahaṃtā). And from [this] manifestation...

Difference and non-difference, being mutually contradictory, establish the distinct nature of the two—insentient and sentient—which are pervaded by them, by creating a contradiction between them such that they are incapable of mutual contact.
Thus he says "well-established" (*suvyavasthita*); the meaning is that it is perfectly established or determined. By this much, not...
It has been established that some cognition is cognizable by another cognition. Now, if someone were to say:

"Let there be no mutual relationship of the cognized and the cognizer among other cognitions; however, in the case of memory—which manifests an object as qualified by a prior experience—how can that [relationship] be disregarded?"—to him, on the contrary:

Keeping in mind that if cognition were an object of cognition, there would necessarily be another experience— either having cognition as its object or having an object qualified by cognition— and not a memory, [the author] connects the present topic by stating that this prior experience is not an object of the cognition of memory (*smaraṇajñāna*). Thus, regarding what was previously experienced:

And as for the word "ca" (and): the particle "ca" serves to aggregate further arguments. It is not merely by the previously stated arguments that the fact that cognition is not cognizable by another cognition is established, such that the objectification of a prior experience by a memory-cognition is thereby negated; rather, it is also [negated] by another argument. For instance, [one says], "I remember the jar."

In the cognition [of the object], only the jar appears as the objective content (*viṣayatā*), not the previous experience; that [experience] shines forth merely conjoined with the recollective cognition. Otherwise, if it were to appear separately, the recollection would not have the jar as its object, just as a yogi’s knowledge of another's mind does not have that other person's mind as its object [when it appears separately].
As it has been said: "And it does not have an object, because that [past cognition] has not become its objective domain.
Now, one might object: the nature of memory is indeed "I am experiencing the jar that was previously experienced. In that case—
The quality of having been experienced (*anubhūtatva*) is an attribute of the object; it does not attain identity with the act of recollection. It is said:
(page 263) This is indeed recognition (*pratyabhijñā*), which consists of the synthesis of what is being remembered and what is being perceived, and not a pure [recollection].

Recollection (*smaraṇa*). In that [recollection], what is delineated as "it was experienced" is the pastness of the experience; this alone is the specific, individual form of recollection. Even there, that pastness is constructed by the limitation imposed by the adjunct of the object, because it is no longer in the state of being experienced, even though it exists in itself. This is also expressed in the thought: "I remember what was experienced."

The phrase "experienced during the act of practice" is a clarification of this very point: namely, that it is not a memory of something experienced in the past, but rather that cognition, being ever-present, is called "memory" when it is characterized by a preceding cognition in its intensified state. Thus he says: "having attained identity with the experience. Only...

The Buddhist explains this in some way through experience by means of the depositing of a potentiality in the form of a latent impression (*vāsanā*) within one's own continuum; the Naiyāyika also explains it by means of the depositing of a mental trace (*saṃskāra*) in the self, but not by means of recollection. For their view is that "experience is known. Thus, indeed, [there would be] the cognition of a prior cognition—

Form (rūpa) would be nothing other than a subsequent experience, and not a memory. Furthermore, how could a cognition that has long since passed away and is devoid of intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) possess the character of manifesting an object? Even if a cognition in its state of perishing were indeed known by another cognition due to their inherence in the same substrate (ekārthasamavāya), a yogi, however, [cannot know] that which has long since perished at the present moment.

What possibility is there that it "knows"? If you say that it does not know, but rather remembers, then it follows that it knows the knowledge of knowledge; and in that case too, this very same fault remains—thus it was rightly said. But it is not "intermediate," meaning an experience occurring in the interval or middle between the memory and the object.

It is not tenable to say that memory, while illuminating the object, illuminates it as something appearing through memory and thereby presents that object to the act of remembering; for this is not experienced in such a way. Rather, this alone is logical: that the experience itself, whose nature is the illumination of the object, is already contained within the very structure of the memory. For memory indeed illuminates that experience.

If one accepts the position that "that which illuminates the object" [is consciousness], then the illumination of the object does not reside within the object itself, since the theory of *prakaṭatā* (manifestness) has been refuted; rather, its very illumination is the experience (*anubhava*) of that object. And if that [experience] does not manifest by itself, nothing at all would be manifested.

Now it is said that its manifestation occurs through recollection; for the manifestation of the experience— which is the object to be manifested— is not a property of the object itself, but rather, recollection itself constitutes the manifestation of that experience.

If this experience, having fallen into the level of the object, were insentient in form and distinct from light, how could it be the illumination of the path? [In that case], the expression "I remember the jar" would result in a state of utter blindness.
This is what he says: "That"—namely, the nature of the illumination of the object—would not belong to the prior experience because of its being characterized as "this-ness" (idantā).

Because the insentient (*jaḍa*) is manifest by virtue of being [dependent on] manifestation. In other cases, such as in the cognition of memory, this experience indeed has that [manifestation] as its face and is dependent upon it for its own manifestation. Thus, having established that "this-ness" (*idantā*)—namely, the state of being manifested, which is distinctness from manifestation—is the very nature of the insentient, he says "And so" (*evaṃ ca*), fearing that [his statement] might contradict his own position. By this...

The light of "I" and "this," through the distinction between the characteristics of the insentient (*jaḍa*) and the sentient (*ajaḍa*), is the Self that is the Lord (*īśvara*). In this regard, one might ask: how can there be oneness between the insentient and the sentient? To this it is replied: here, even when "this" (*idam*) appears, its true nature is nothing other than the ultimate reality of Light (*prakāśa*); otherwise, if it were not conjoined with Light, even the state of being "this" would be like blind darkness. It is merely due to *māyā*—

Although [the object] is non-different from the Light by virtue of its power (*śakti*), there is the conceit (*abhimāna*) that it is different from the Light; this is called "insentience" (*jaḍatā*), as it is produced by the manifestation of the subject and the object as appropriate. And in the state of the Lord (*īśvaradaśā*), those objects which are the domain of the conceit of being different from the Light for the bound subjects (*paśupramātṛ*) are, in the ultimate sense, of the nature of the Light.

It consists of the nature of reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*). While those [objects] may indeed be considered insentient from the perspective of the limited subject (*paśu-pramātṛ*), the luminous aspect of the limited subject's own form is in reality non-different from the divine light (*aiśvara-prakāśa*).
Consequently, even though this form of "this-ness" (*idam*) flashes forth according to the analogy of lightning, it lacks any further growth or development.

The grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between "I-ness" (*ahaṃtā*) and "this-ness" (*idantā*) is said to mean that rest (*viśrānti*) occurs in "I-ness" alone. And thus, although this "this-ness" being referred to (*anūdyamānā*) appears first, nevertheless, because it is unfit for its own rest according to experience, it attains the status of a predicate (*vidhīyamāna*) only by following after the "I-ness" that is being enjoined; therefore, [it is subordinated to] "I-ness."

It is precisely a matter of measure. Thus, "then" refers to the state of the Lord (*īśvara*). "There is no excess" means that there, the so-called "this-ness" (*idantā*) is not something additional to the light whose nature is the "I-ness" (*ahantā*); for in reality, this-ness is nothing other than the very majesty of freedom.
(Page 265)

In this context, the author dispels the delusion of the opponent by means of an example well-established for him alone, beginning with "Just as... (*yathā hi*). By way of this stylistic approach, the author has stated this single example through both its similarity and its dissimilarity.
Just as form (*rūpa*) is indeed form itself at the time of the arising and the destruction of a configuration (*saṃniveśa*), because it is accepted that it remains "that very same thing" throughout.

Thus, consciousness is the very arising and dissolution of the universe; it is consciousness alone, and there is no excellence or superiority in it—this is the illustrative example based on similarity. As for form, however, because of its momentariness, some kind of excellence is admitted in various ways; but that [excellence] is not possible in consciousness. Since consciousness is of a single nature, even the slightest trace of distinction is untenable.

For it has been said thus: "The manifestation [of consciousness] is not differentiated by the coloring of blue and so forth, because for all proponents [of such views], it would follow that the nature of manifestation remains undifferentiated. (Nareśvaraviveka)

Thus [it is said]. And he says, "let that be," meaning that this subject matter will be explained at length later; that is to say, the time for indifference toward this object of knowledge has arrived. Just as the configuration (*saṃniveśa*) of a form is not a separate entity from the form itself, so too no excellence whatsoever is possible within the nature of consciousness (*bodharūpa*); such is the application [of the argument] based on similarity. The particle *tu* has the sense of the restrictive particle *eva*.

In this context, however, [the particle] *tu* indicates a distinction in the case of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya*). Just as there might be a specific quality (*viśiṣṭatā*) in the case of form (*rūpa*), so too is a specific excellence (*atiśaya*) consisting of a particular nature suspected in the case of the nature of consciousness (*bodharūpa*); yet that does not exist at all—this is the application regarding dissimilarity. For since it is thus (indicated by *hi*), there is no superiority in the nature of consciousness during the state of the Lord (*īśvara*).

The word "something" (*kiṃcit*) is the connection [to the context]. He concludes the reason for the classification of the characteristics under discussion with the words "it is established, first of all" (*siddhaṃ tāvat*). The fact that cognition is perceivable by another (*parasaṃvedyatā*) is what must be negated;

it is negated by the reason that cognition consists of self-awareness (*svasaṃvidrūpatvena*). For that which pervades the object to be negated is "this-ness" (*idantā*), and [self-awareness] is its opposite.

It is pervaded by "I-ness" (*ahantā*), for "I-ness" alone is the defining characteristic of consciousness. Therefore, by means of that which is pervaded by what is contradictory to the pervader—namely, its own self-manifesting nature (*svasaṃdrūpatva*)—its being cognizable by another (*parasaṃvedyatva*) is negated.
For here, the opponent accepts that cognition has the nature of self-consciousness; however, even while it exists in such a state, he still maintains that it is cognizable by another.
The nature of consciousness as its own inherent self is self-luminosity; however, its being cognizable by another consists in the arising of a subsequent cognition directed toward that object.
(page 266)
"What is the contradiction between these two?"—to this he replied with the words beginning "For what indeed is the contradiction," and so forth.

Now, by demonstrating that contradiction, his delusion has been pacified. For the characteristic of being cognizable by another is its difference from light, its insentience (*jaḍatva*), and its state of "thisness" (*idantā*); whereas for that which is of the nature of consciousness, whose essence is self-manifestation, there is [no such difference from] light.

Identity (*tādātmya*) is non-inertness and I-consciousness (*ahaṃtā*); thus, by way of these definitions, there is indeed a contradiction between the two. Therefore, being perceivable by another is negated by its nature as self-awareness (*svasaṃvidrūpatva*). For that [perceivability by another] is the opposite of "this-ness" (*idam*), which is the differentiation from light; whereas the pervader of the cause—namely, the nature of self-awareness—is the form of "I" (*aham*). By means of that [opposite], [the former is negated].

"Permeated by that characteristic" means as follows: he shows that whatever is a reason based on essential nature (*svabhāvahetu*) in a positive formulation (*vidhi*), that very same thing becomes a reason of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhihetu*) in the form of the apprehension of a contradictory (*viruddhopalabdhi*) when the negation of that [nature] is to be established. For example: when momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*)—that is, impermanence—is to be proven, existence characterized by the capacity for successive causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) is its essential nature.

This is the reason (*hetu*). However, when permanence (*nityatva*) is to be negated, there is the "perception of that which is pervaded by what is incompatible with the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). The defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) that pervades a permanent entity is the property called "having a single nature" (*ekasvabhāvatva*); and its opposite is "having a diverse nature" (*bhinnasvabhāvatva*).
This very [diverse nature] is the pervading characteristic of the performance of causal efficiency (*arthakriyā*) in succession. [The reason is: because of performing causal efficiency successively.

For this is the ultimate meaning of what is said [when one says] "it acts": that it possesses a manifold nature. Thus, even in the case [of the inference] "this is not a non-tree because it is a *śiṃśapā*," the property of being a non-tree (*avṛkṣatva*) has as its pervader (*vyāpaka*) the characteristic of possessing no branches and so forth;
and since the state of being a *śiṃśapā* is pervaded by the possession of branches and so forth—which is the opposite of that [non-pervader]—it is a pervader...

This is precisely the perception of what is pervaded by the contradictory (*viruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). Now, that pervasive property which constitutes the definition is not drawn out separately by way of exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*), because drawing it out separately serves no purpose when the object for the sake of which it is intended to inform another has already been established. In that case, by means of "tree-ness" (*vṛkṣatva*), which is contradictory to "non-tree-ness," "śiṃśapā-ness" [is established].

The statement "it is pervaded" constitutes the perception of the pervasion of a contradictory [property]. However, when even in a *śiṃśapā* tree "treeness" is not treated as distinct because it is well-known, and only that "non-treeness" which has been superimposed through delusion is removed, then it is simply the perception of a contradiction with its own nature (*svabhāvaviruddhopalabdhi*).

If, in the case of the subject as well, the state of being perceivable by another and the state of being "this" (idantā) were one and the same reality, there would be the perception of something pervaded by its opposite.

If, moreover, the state of being "I" (ahantā) and the state of having the nature of self-consciousness were also one and the same reality, that would likewise be simply the perception of what is opposed to its own essential nature.

But here, the state of being cognizable by another and the state of being self-cognizable are established for the other only by way of definition (*lakṣaṇataḥ*), not in reality (*tattvataḥ*). For this very reason, he considers there to be no contradiction between those two; with this intention, [the author states that] that pervasive property [of being self-cognizable] belongs to both of them by way of definition.

Having distinguished [the two], the author of the commentary has shown that this is an "observation of what is pervaded by the contradictory of the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). Even the argument "it is not fireless because there is smoke" is likewise simply an "observation of the effect of the contradictory" (*viruddhakāryopalabdhi*). One should pay attention to this principle in each respective case; enough with these intermediate details. Having thus refuted the notion of being perceived by another in the case of the non-inert (*ajaḍa*), [the author proceeds to] the other...
He shows that even in the case of an object of cognition (*saṃvedya*), there is no nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvidrūpatā*) by saying "even of a jar" (*ghaṭasyāpi*).

Although the nature of self-awareness for a jar is not accepted by anyone, this was stated nonetheless to clarify the contradiction. For one who maintains that the manifestation of an object's properties [occurs through external means], it follows by force of logic; yet, this is not tenable.

By this, he demonstrates the point "due to contradiction. "By this very [means]" means that this is precisely that same class of non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*). "The pervader of the object of negation, which is the nature of self-awareness (*svasaṃvidrūpa*), is 'I'. This [notion of 'I'] is contradictory to that; therefore, being cognizable by another (*parasaṃvedyatva*) is pervaded by it. He concludes this with "Thus, in this way," [referring to] the entire universe without exception.

Whether it be apprehended successively or simultaneously, even so, a single present cognition grasps only its own object; it does not know the fact that some object has been grasped by another cognition. For a cognition is not known by another cognition, as that would entail the consequence of insentience (*jaḍatā*). [Regarding] another cognition—

And even if it were accepted, because there would be no cognition that "this was previously unknown by me as being of the nature of suffering" or "this is determined to be a means for accomplishing a purpose, a means to happiness," one would not, upon seeing it, develop a state of longing characterized by the desire to endure or to acquire it— just like one possessed by a spirit. In the absence of that [longing], one would neither abandon nor grasp it.

If desire and aversion were not preceded by memory, they would not arise in their absence; consequently, there would be no worldly activity— beginning with the effort of intention, consisting of bodily movement, and ending with the acquisition or rejection of objects— since such effort produced by desire would be impossible,
and thus the conjunction with objects resulting from that effort could not occur.
Because of the non-attainment of differentiation and so forth, one would remain like a cognizer dwelling on the island of Sadyojāta-nālikīra; or,
if even they possess some degree of synthesis and so on, then those cognizers would be more pitiable than [ordinary] cognizers, and would not truly be cognizers at all.

(268) By this much, the Sūtra has been explained. If there were a unification of cognitions upon a single object of synthesis, then from that [unification] would arise a state of being born (*janasthiti*), whereby worldly activity such as rejection and acquisition (*tyāgopādāna*) would perish. The commentary (*vṛtti*) also states:

The mutual collision of cognitions regarding their respective objects is as follows: for instance, in the case of conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*), there is the thought "I am conceptualizing this which was perceived" with respect to the object of experience; and in the case of that same conceptual cognition, there is the thought "I am seeing exactly that which was conceptualized by inference," and so forth. In both cases, there is memory (*smṛti*), and of that [memory] as well...

Recognition and so forth occur in many ways; yet, when that very thing which is the primary cause of worldly transaction—the root source—is refuted within this [process] whose nature is conjunction, how could such a transaction exist? For it has already been stated that its accomplishment cannot occur through latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) alone.
In the compound *vṛttau ca*, the genitive case in *jñānānām* is used in the sense of the compound itself;

thus, by referring back to them [the cognitions] in the sūtra, there is a compound because the act of coordination (*anusandhāna*) is necessarily dependent [on its object]. Otherwise, it would not be possible, just as in the case of "Caitra’s brindled cows. Coordination, however, is necessarily dependent because it is transitive.

Regarding this action— the contact with the object— although there is no contradiction in forming a compound even when "of them" (*teṣām*) is expected because of the predominance [of the action], nevertheless, if the meaning of the object is subordinate and yet expects "of them," the absence of a compound would result;
that [is what is meant by] the object's state of being necessarily dependent.

This has been answered by the statement "because of the dependence on an object" (*viṣayāpekṣaṇāt*). Furthermore, here the formation of a secondary derivative (*taddhita-vṛtti*) is also indicated in brief. For one does not say, "the road consists of cakes made of grains" (*dhānyānām apūpamayī yātrā*); however, in this case, the connection with an object is eternally dependent [upon another word] by way of the object, and thus it is indeed valid, as in the expression "at the time of the acquisition of wealth" (*dhanasyārjanasamaye*). Now, [one might object]: [The objection continues: "But..."

This worldly transaction of the deluded is a mere illusion, charming only so long as it is not investigated. What room is there for an examination of reality therein? This [world] is unreal, because a regularity of worldly transactions cannot be established through mere illusion;
for this [person] abandons only certain things and accepts only certain others. In the absence of a fixed cause for that, from where could such regularity arise? Or, let it be granted.

The author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) demonstrates how the conventional practice of those who are not deluded can be validated, whereas the practice of the deluded is a distortion, by stating "the ultimate reality" (*paramārtha*), and so forth.
(Page 269)

He explains this with the words "even by those who have known what is to be known. "Reality" (tattvam) refers to this, and not to worldly convention. "This very sequence" refers to the recollection of what was previously experienced and so forth. If one asks why, he says: "For even they... The word "even" (api) implies that it is not only the deluded who act thus, but "they" as well. "Previously known" refers to the experience.

He demonstrates this: "In this way, 'this'" refers to conceptualization preceded by the recollection and synthesis [of what was previously taught]. "To the disciples as well" means, in other words, to those who are to be initiated. Alternatively, this sequence applies not only to the instruction consisting in the composition of the treatise, but also on the occasion of the instruction involving the transmission to a disciple present nearby.

The word "api" (even/also) is used here. This is what is meant: first of all, it is established that one who is not omniscient, when composing a treatise or explaining to another a reality already established within himself through scripture, inference, yogic perception, and so forth, must explain it by repeatedly recollecting and conceptualizing it. As for even one who is omniscient regarding the entire universe...
He perceives directly; and he, desiring to bring about an awakening in the disciple who has approached him,

or wishing to instruct him, or wishing to compose a treatise, perceives the fitness for verbal expression and the fitness for the mental cultivation of the audience of disciples within the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) that is being directly perceived— from that direct perception itself.

Having emerged from [the state of absorption] through the relish of sovereignty or the relish of compassion, [the Lord], having directly realized "this is it," might teach after connecting it with the conceptualization "it is thus.
And this conceptualization occurs by means of the recollection of words and so forth, which involves the re-presentation of what was previously perceived. At that time, he too—
Without the synthesis of knowledge regarding the preceding and the succeeding, how could he teach? As you yourselves have stated:
"The Buddha, having emerged from suchness, will teach suchness.
This is also found in the Āgamas.
"For the sake of favoring men, even the Supreme has assumed a non-supreme state.
Likewise, Śaṅkara will remain exactly as those disciples shall ask him.
And so forth.
"Of them also" refers to those who are awakened. "Worldly course" refers to such acts as rescuing others. "One's own self" refers to... [text continues].

The meaning is: "by those who exist right now," being settled in the illumination of their own objects and in the illumination of the Self alone. "All indeed" refers to both the awakened and the unawakened.
"Motionless" means those who are as if possessed by a spirit; for even an omniscient one does not remain like one possessed by a spirit.

Since that [consciousness] would also be incapable of conceptualization, it would follow that it lacks autonomy, which entails the consequence of its being insentient (*jaḍatā*). For this very reason, even for the Lord Paramaśiva, the process of manifestation— beginning with His Power (*śakti*) and proceeding through the stages of Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Vidyeśvara, and so forth, down to the level of the subject of Māyā (*māyā-pramātṛ*) by way of dissolution (*laya*), enjoyment (*bhoga*), and authority (*adhikāra*)— is indeed the conceptualization (*vikalpana*).

The "form of the other" (*pārarūpa*) is indeed insentience (*jāḍya*), which is the state of being devoid of vibration (*niḥstimitatva*). For reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)—designated as radiance, pulsation (*sphurattā*), vibration (*spanda*), and so forth—is precisely the specific power (*śakti-viśeṣa*) of the Lord that stands in opposition to this lack of vibration. It is by the gradations of its deficiency that insentience extends down to the level of stationary objects (*sthāvara*), and it is by the gradations of its excellence that [sentience] culminates in the Supreme Lord.
"We shall explain that 'awakened state' extends up to Śiva; that is *sphurattā* (the state of vibration)," as stated in [Tantrāloka] 1.5.14 and elsewhere.
Now, one might object: "Even this instruction, because it is subject to sublation (*viplava*), cannot have an ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) object."

Anticipating the objection that [this] touches upon [the ultimate], he says: "Even of the instruction on the ultimate. Let it be granted for now that worldly conventional practice is deceptive; however, if this [instruction] were also deceptive, then that ultimate which was taught and cultivated would—lacking the nature of the ultimate previously elucidated—not be the ultimate.

"How could that which has been touched be attained? For meditation preceded by an instruction on a false ultimate reality would, once performed upon that very false ultimate reality, clarify it alone—
whatever exactly is intensely meditated upon."

This is according to the [established] principle; now, he clarifies that which is indeed the ultimate reality as it was made an object of prior experience, and therefore there is no error. And thus, the convergence of the objects of cognitions has been achieved—this is the underlying intention.
But what is the use of this convergence of objects here? For instance, from a seed, [the sprout arises] through a sequence beginning with the first excellence (*ādyātiśaya*).
In the world, a diverse relationship between cause and effect is well known, such as a sprout arising from soil that has reached its ultimate excellence, or a jar [arising] from clay, and so forth.
(page 271)
And in that case, no conjunction of objects is either required or possible; likewise, as previously stated:

first there is experience, then conceptualization, then instruction, then application to meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), then the perfection of cultivation, and finally, upon the arising of knowledge, this very [perfection] becomes perfectly clear—this indeed is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

Regarding the term "attainment" (*prāpti*): having raised the doubt, "What is the use here of this effort to justify the union of objects? he says, "And this is not... The word "merely" (*mātra*) is used to indicate that this is a relationship of cause and effect, and not a process similar to that of seeds and sprouts, which are insentient. The underlying intention is as follows: in this case, it is by means of the mere relationship of cause and effect...

Since experiences, conceptualizations, and the like possess a nature similar to insentient matter, they are restricted to their own essential forms and are thus incapable of acting upon anything else; therefore, conventional activities such as the direct perception, conceptualization, and recollection of an object consist essentially in operations whose ultimate reality is the manifestation (*prakāśana*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśana*) residing within the object itself.
How could these [mental constructs] exist? For they are established within [the mind] and cannot be denied.

Moreover, how could these be conceived without having a single object? Indeed, their very life-force consists in the thought, "I conceptualize what was seen," and "I remember. And since that [perception] cannot be refuted, conceptual constructions appear as direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Why is it proclaimed that "experience deposits the seed of memory by determining a non-object—which is its own appearance—to be an object," and so forth? For that [proclamation] merely sets up a snare to achieve the state of having a single object; yet that state is not established by that much alone—this is all that we are saying. He says this: "This is a cognition," namely experience.

Instruction—consisting of conceptualization, the desire to teach, the teaching itself, meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and so forth—is indeed a consciousness established upon the object of cognition; it is not some self-contained form, like a seed or other insentient things. [The opponent asks: "What follows from that? [The author] replies: "And cognition... That which is the actual knowledge of the ultimate reality belonging to the teacher is [not...].
Because one who is to be instructed cannot be an instructor due to the impossibility of that role, and because the future ultimate knowledge—

which is the clear result for the practitioner— is the very object of those two knowledges, if that [object] were not the object of the series consisting of the memory-conceptualization of the desire to instruct and the instruction-conceptualization of the cultivation, then it would be something else.
It might be that one thing is known, another is conceptualized, another is taught, another is cultivated, and yet another is attained;
but this is not tenable.
Whatever is intensely meditated upon,
when that meditation reaches completion, it results in a clear conceptual cognition.

This is because it has been shown that [the cognition] "this" and "that" have a single object (*ekaviṣayatva*). For even from a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), activity, attainment, and so forth, are sustained by the intention of a continuum (*saṃtāna*) precisely through having a single object; otherwise, the distinction between valid and invalid means of knowledge would be untenable. He concludes all of this with the words "therefore. This refers to the awakened and the unawakened...
Conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*) culminates in the Buddha; it is the mutual attainment of objects.

For the attainment of an object residing in one cognition within another cognition—such as in memory and so forth—and the attainment of an object belonging to one cognizer within another cognizer—such as in injunctions, instructions, and so forth—is called conventional discourse with respect to one's own self and the Supreme Self. [The prefix] *vi-* [indicates] "apart from" (*vyeti*).

In the case of exchange (*vyatihāra*), the root *harati* means "to bring about. That exchange is pervaded by having a single object. Its opposite is the state of having multiple objects. And if cognitions were manifold in nature, that [state of multiple objects] would necessarily follow as a pervasive property. For that [exchange] is possible in three ways; however, two of those ways have been refuted. Indeed, visibility is not an object...
This is *dharma*. As Bhaṭṭa said:
"The activity of a cognition toward an object belongs to that [cognition] which does nothing at all toward it.
[Thus, when one says] "it is apprehended," it is the very act of apprehension (*pratipatti*) itself that is somehow described as an "existence" (*bhāva*), but not the existence of the object.

An excellence of form (*rūpātiśaya*) is produced. If that were the case, one would not require the operation of another sense organ for the cognition of that [excellence], just as what has already been made does not need to be made again by another, and so forth. Therefore, it is not logical that this [excellence] should be a property of the object.
Furthermore, the cognisability (*vedyatā*) of cognitions has already been refuted. And if this remaining mode [of manifestation]...

There would not be the unity of cognitions characterized by a single nature; thus, this conventional usage—due to the perception of what is pervaded by that which is contradictory to the pervader—would simply not exist. The commentary on the sūtra "naśyet" (it would perish) is explained as "kathaṃ na syāt eva" (how could it not be so?), using the optative suffix (*liṅ*) to express possibility. Furthermore, by the question "how? (*katham*), its non-deniability is established.

By stating this regarding conventional discourse (*vyavahāra*), he asserts that, by the principle of elimination (*pāriśeṣya*), the fact that cognitions possess a single nature as the inward-turned reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) is indeed established. For this very reason, the meaning of the aphorism—"if not [as such], then immediately following [it]"—flashes forth here. 6.

If the Great Lord were not one whose infinite universal form is contained within himself, he would not possess a single conscious body endowed with the powers of knowledge, memory, and the removal [of ignorance]. (7)
And because its conventional reality is unassailable, its oneness is established;
this is the intended meaning even when proceeding by way of negation. For it is for this very purpose that the word "if" (*yadi*) is used;
indeed, it expresses the firmness of one's own position, as [the opponent's view] necessarily follows, even if it is not something they themselves would accept.

Illuminating the term "possibility" (*saṃbhava*), he states this very intention in the introductory commentary (*avatāraṇikā*) with the words "it would be appropriate" (*yujyeta*), using the optative suffix (*liṅ*) to express the relationship between cause and effect. The reason for the possibility of linguistic usage (*vyavahāra*) is the single nature (*ekātmatā*) of cognitions.
The phrase "of such a kind" (*etādṛśaḥ*) means that which resides in both the awakened and the unawakened, consisting of a single object. [This refers to] pure consciousness (*cinmātra*).

"By way of being the essence" (*sāratvena*) is the explanation for "the body of consciousness" (*cidvapuḥ*). "Of the universal self" (*viśvātmanaḥ*) refers to [the passage] beginning with "contained within.

"Of the Supreme Lord" (*parameśvarasya*) refers to "Maheśvara. "Self" (*ātmā*) means inherent nature (*svabhāva*). "These" (*etāḥ*) refers to those well-known to all people. "Diverse" (*vicitrāḥ*) means they possess various manifestations and withdrawals by the power of that respective sovereignty.

The "powers" (*śaktayaḥ*) are dependent upon that [Lord], but they are neither independent nor distinct from His essential nature, existing merely through the relationship of attribute and substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*). Thus he says: "and characterized by the possession of powers. This alone is His sovereignty (*māheśvarya*). By this, the passage beginning with "knowledge" and so forth has been explained. Having thus explained the intended meaning (*tātparya*), [the author proceeds].

The phrase "if not" (*na cet*) refers to the Sūtra; "otherwise, however" (*anyathā tu*) [refers to the Vṛtti]. To begin with, the principle of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*), whose nature is luminosity, is self-established as the foundation of all means of valid cognition (*pramā*); it is not something to be proven. With the intention that another [entity] must be examined upon the surface of that foundation, the author of the Vṛtti, by way of restating that [self-established consciousness], explains the Sūtra’s statement regarding its "universal form" (*viśvarūpatva*).

The commentator explains [the term] as "of the nature of light" (*prakāśarūpa*). For this reason—since it is so—the author of the *Vṛtti* states this, which consists of both an injunction and a restatement. And therein he provides the logical justification; such is the connection at a distance.
By this much, the meaning of the sūtra established from the beginning has been recalled. [The phrase] "of blue, pleasure, and so forth" refers to that which is external as well as internal.

And "of all" means up to this point. "Of that which is considered insentient" means that although it is in reality of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), it has assumed the state of insentience merely through the conceit (*abhimāna*) of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) which is of the nature of *māyā*.
(Page 274)

"By itself" (svayam) is stated to be the definition of the insentient (jaḍa)—namely, that it does not possess its own light. [Objection: In that case, its light must be something else. [Reply: No, he says: "And because it does not have that nature" (atadrūpatve ca). Whatever is not the nature of something else cannot, in ultimate reality, be designated as being in grammatical coreferentiality (samānādhikaraṇatayā) with it, just as vermilion is not [coreferential] with blue.
