And thus, if an entity were by nature non-luminous, it would not be designated as such by means of luminosity, because such designations are necessarily governed by identity [between the designator and the designated]; this is a non-perception of the cause, since identity is the cause [of the designation].
Yet, that which is considered insentient by the opponent is designated as "it shines" in grammatical coreferentiality with luminosity.

Therefore, the pervasion of the essential reason—that "it is of that very nature"—has just now been established through the non-perception of the cause. But is it not the case that the subject is designated as such by means of a distinct quality, namely whiteness?
Thus, the reason is inconclusive. Not so; for the reason has been drawn away from the dissimilar instance (vipakṣa) by a subverting proof.

Because when pervasion (*vyāpti*) with the probandum is established, there is no room for deviation (*vyabhicāra*). Indeed, it is not logical that whiteness should belong to something through a distinct quality of white; as stated in the *Nareśvaraviveka*: "The palace itself is neither white nor non-white... [and so forth].

This is the statement of one who lacks authoritative means of knowledge (*aprāmāṇika*). For it is not possible for an object to exist that is devoid of either of two real properties (*vastudharma*) which are established through mutual exclusion. This will be demonstrated [in the passage]:
"The luminous self is the object to be illuminated... (1.5.3).
In such passages as these: [one might object], "Now, it was begun here to establish that there is a single self (ātman) of cognitions;

so why is this identity of a single self asserted even for insentient things? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "of those appearing as distinct" (*bhinnāvabhāsinām*). The particle *ca* indicates the aforementioned doubt. The word *api* [implies] the maxim of the staff and the cake (*daṇḍāpūpīya*).

By this reasoning, the establishment of the subject matter under discussion is indicated: wherein even distinct entities, by the power of the reflective awareness of freedom consisting of self-referential ideation (*abhimananātmaka-svātantrya-vimarśa*), appear as such; yet, because they are grasped as "this-ness" (*idantā*), they are in the ultimate sense of the nature of nothing but the manifestation of "I" (*aham-prakāśa-mātra*).
In that regard, since cognitions appear as something exceeding the "I-component" (*ahamaṃśa*), how could they not possess that very nature?
For these [cognitions] indeed have an excess over the "I-component," as well as non-pervasiveness and impermanence.

That which appears as contracted due to its conformity with the nature, place, and time of the object is indeed produced by the limiting condition (*upādhi*) of being directed toward the object. However, since the object itself is of the nature of light (*prakāśātman*), even the possibility of such an excess is uprooted. He says this very thing with the words "nevertheless" (*tathāpi*); by that [statement] also, it is shown in the manner of non-difference from the "I"-portion (*ahaṃ-aṃśa*).
The meaning is "of those that are present. Regarding the object (*viṣaya*), there is a distinction arising from mere conceit (*abhimāna*) produced by the power of *māyā*;
by means of that, a distinction is fashioned through disregard—that is, fashioned so as not to take root—and constructed according to one's own will (*svācchandyena*).
Of these cognitions (*jñāna*) possessing such a distinction, even in this state of *māyā*...

The ultimate nature of the self, which consists of the light of consciousness, remains entirely undivided. For *māyā* is the power (*śakti*) of the Lord; it does not conceal His essential nature (*svarūpa*), because that which possesses power (*śaktimat*) cannot be concealed by its own power.
Thus, although this has already been stated in the context of establishing the subject matter at hand, [it is reiterated] in this section...

According to the direction of the established doctrine (*siddhānta*), another object to be proven is also established through the impossibility of accounting for worldly transaction otherwise (*vyavahārānyathānupapatti*).

By the use of the particle *eva*, it is indicated that transactions are not possible without luminosity, and that this luminosity belongs only to the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*) and nothing else; thus, the non-duality of autonomous consciousness (*svatantracidadvaita*) is also established.

The author of the *Vṛtti* states that the accomplishment of the meaning of all scriptures is achieved without effort by this much alone. Thus, the portion of the Sūtra beginning with "antaḥkṛtānantaviśvarūpaścidvapurjñānādiśaktimān" has been introduced.
[The phrase] "antaḥkṛtam" means that although the external form exists, because it is of the single nature of the self as the subject (*pramātṛ*), it is not even slightly...

The "Infallible" (acyuta) is that which has been made—that is, brought about—by the power of absolute freedom (svācchandyashakti); having existed internally as identical with the single self of the subject, it is then fashioned by the manifestation of external form. It is infinite, exceeding even the enumerated forms such as the four, six, sixteen, twenty-four, thirty-six, and so forth.
By the maxim "then, by that [means] of his," he enters the universal form which is being conceived; it is that by which the entire collection of objects of knowledge is contained within it.

As for the phrase "na cet" (if not), it has already been explained by the author of the *Vṛtti* [on the *Bhāṣya*] in accordance with the Sūtra; how so? By this connection to the meaning of another Sūtra, the author of the *Vṛtti* establishes that the two parts of the Sūtra, "naśyet" and "na cet," form a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatva*).

It has been clearly established that "the accomplishment [of the goal] is said to be characterized by a reason. Now, an objection is raised: "Was it not previously stated that the maintenance of human existence arises from synthesis (*anusandhāna*)?
Therefore, it must be explained here how there could be no synthesis; otherwise, how can it be said that [the self] has consciousness as its essence?
Anticipating this doubt, the author of the commentary (*vṛttikṛt*) says: "[There is] the mutual synthesis of all cognitions of objects without exception..."

"Sandhāna is the nature of consciousness (*cittattva*). By way of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) and continuity, "sandhāna" refers to the unification of even those cognitions that are considered discrete; it is consciousness itself turned inward, and nothing else whatsoever. In this context, the root *dadhāti* (to place/hold) has both an object and an agent. It is the self-unification of the [consciousness]—the "bandage" (*paṭṭa*).

It is like [the expression] "pieces of cotton. Now, if *sandhāna* means "mixing," even so, because that which mixes is not other than the principle of consciousness (*cittattva*), it is logical to employ this metaphorical designation of non-difference between the action and the agent, since they are ultimately one. By this, the following is stated: it is true that the existence of people arises from synthetic awareness (*anusandhāna*).

That synthesis, characterized by having a single object, is not possible through any other means according to the method previously stated; therefore, by the process of elimination, it results in being dependent solely on the nature of a single consciousness (*ekacid-rūpatā*). By beginning with the words "otherwise" (*anyathā*) and so forth, [the author] asserts that [synthesis] consists of the grasping of a fixed [object], such as "mere space" (*kevalapradeśa*) and so on.

By stating that the condition of worldly existence (*janasthiti*), which is the root of all conventional discourse, would be untenable, [the author] shows the syntactic unity between "if not" (*na cet*) and "the condition of worldly existence would perish" (*naśyet janasthitiḥ*). In this regard, let alone the activities, attainments, and instructions shown in the subsequent sūtras, commentaries, and sub-commentaries— namely, those conventional usages— [they too would perish].
In those cases where a clear synthesis (anusandhi) is perceived, even that cognition of a single,

determinate object which appears to be independent of synthesis due to its resting within itself, could not occur for outward-directed cognitions if they lacked the nature of inward-turned self-awareness.

The determination of that [object]: with the intention that even the linguistic convention of apprehension—which is said to have both self and other as its objects through the exclusion of others—would not be sustainable, he examines precisely the Buddhist method for establishing non-existence.
(Page 277)
In this regard, it has been demonstrated more than once that knowledge is of a single nature consisting of self-luminosity. As the venerable [author] said:
"Just as light is not illuminated by another light, so too that which is of the nature of knowledge is not illuminated by anything else."
Thus, [the object] cannot be associated with another cognition within a single cognition such that one could say:

"If there were two cognitions, then the cognition of that [second] cognition would be a third; however, this is the cognition of a single cognition, therefore there are not two cognitions. In this regard, the jar serves as the example by way of dissimilarity (*vaidharmya-dṛṣṭānta*).

He explains that very point with the words "experiencing [it]," meaning by way of self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). And this phrase, "mere knowledge of the location," is an adjective qualifying the subject. Now, if the absence of the jar is thus ascertained and established, what further goal remains for us to prove regarding the ascertainment of the absence of the cognition of the jar?
"No," he says. "It might be so"—that is, this might be the case; however, it is not so, because it functions in this way—this is the meaning.

The intended sense is that without that [prior cognition], that very thing is neither ascertained nor established. "Granted" (*kāmam*) means: let it be for now according to your view, to this extent; such is the sense. "Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means: if it were said that [the object] is not established unless [the prior cognition] exists.

Therefore, it necessarily follows that "the jar exists there. And when that [jar] is present, there is no cognition of two objects in a bare location; rather, there is the apprehension of them through a single causal complex (*ekasāmagrī*). Thus, that would be a cognition of a location *with* a jar, and not a cognition of a location *without* a jar, which is the opposite of this. As for the second [alternative], however...

[It is] distinct. By what means? For the existence of another cognition is not known by the cognition of a location devoid of a jar, such that its non-existence might also be known. But surely, while determining its own self, a cognition—having as its object a bare location—is itself manifest; whereas the cognition of a location containing a jar...

"If something else were present at that time, it too would be manifest; but this is not the case. Therefore, let it be determined that [the other] does not exist"—this objection of the opponent is refuted by the words "and not" (*na ca*). The connection is that it is not proper to say "and so on. For (*hi*), by what means has this very thing been known in the place where the jar is?
"It exists as self-luminous knowledge.
(Page 278) Now,
regarding the statement "the cognition of a place devoid of a jar is manifest," this very principle applies to the case of a place containing a jar as well.

"Knowledge does not manifest"—to this he says "not a jar. For here, by way of *paryudāsa* (exclusion), the manifestation of another entity shines forth; it is not, however, a mere *prasajya-pratiṣedha* (absolute negation) consisting in the absence of the manifestation of the knowledge of the location containing the jar. [Objection: But surely, since existence and non-existence are mutually exclusive, even in the case of *paryudāsa*, [there must be a negation].

The negation of an object contrary to that [perceived one] is indeed accomplished; however, it is the negation of that which is suspected to be identical [to the perceived], and not of that which is distinct and merely possible at this time. For by the manifestation of non-blue—which is itself self-manifesting—the absence of the nature of the manifestation of blue within itself is certainly made known, but not [the absence] of...
[Regarding] that which has become separate: surely, just as the cognition of a location manifests, so too does that which is separate [manifest].
Even the absence of the cognition of a location where there is no jar would manifest, if absence were a cognition;
for how could that which is of the nature of a void (*tuccha*) be a manifestation? [This is said] with the intention that it must be one or the other.
There is no non-deviation—that is, no invariable concomitance (avinābhāva)—of the cognition of a location as "with a jar," because such a cognition is absent when there is no jar;

furthermore, the mere cognition of a location is possible in both ways [whether a jar is present or not]. Now, one might argue that the existence of the jar is the cause of the cognition of a location as "with a jar," and that the existence of the jar is pervaded by [the cognition of the location as with a jar]. However, this is not so.

[The definition is] being cognizable by the cognition of another object that is grasped through a causal complex (*sāmagrī*) of conditions. For even if a jar exists, if that [cognizability] were not present, there would never be a cognition of a location containing a jar. Nor is its pervader perceived;
on the contrary, what is perceived is the opposite of that—namely, the cognition of a bare location. And that...
When the pervader is perceived, the absence of a jar is ascertained through the perception of what is incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*).

Once the absence of the jar is determined, the absence of the cognition of that location as containing a jar is ascertained through the non-perception of its cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*). Alternatively, the perception of something incompatible with the cause of the pervader (*kāraṇavyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi*) alone serves to negate the effect that is pervaded by what is itself incompatible with it.

It will [not] arise. Furthermore, is the pot merely a single location, or is it composed of infinite successive atoms, or does it consist of infinite constituent parts situated together? In that regard, if there were as many distinct cognitions as there are substances, then, because each would be self-luminous individually, there would be no manifestation of them as a single unified aggregate.
There would be no cognition of that specific location at all;

yet, since that cognition of the location does appear, [the opponent argues] out of fear of the undesirable consequence of the non-perception of what is perceptible, [of those things whose nature is form].

Since objects present before one are excluded from the counter-example—defined as being apprehended by multiple cognitions—they are pervaded by being apprehended by a single cognition. Thus, if a jar consisting of form is present, it must be apprehended solely by the cognition of that bare location which apprehends the portion consisting of form; therefore, [it would be] a bare location...
Cognition itself would have to be the cognition of the location together with the jar; however, it is not so, but rather the opposite.

Thus, by the perception of a property incompatible with the pervader (*vyāpaka-viruddha-vyāptopalabdhi*), the jar is negated. Visual cognition of the location does not exist separately from the visual cognition of the jar within its own scope, because it is visual in nature.

The pervader (*vyāpaka*) of distinctness (*pṛthaktva*) is the non-restriction to unity (*ekatvāniyama*). Its opposite is the restriction to unity (*ekatvaniyama*). Since visibility (*cākṣuṣatva*) is pervaded by that [restriction to unity] according to the aforementioned reasoning, this is an "observation of what is pervaded by the opposite of the pervader" (*vyāpakaviruddhavyāptopalabdhi*). If that were the case, then the absence of the cognition of a jar would be cognizable solely through inference and would never be perceptual.

Furthermore, if it were to be known through inference, there would be an infinite regress, and thus it would remain unestablished. To explain: the non-perception of a perceptible object—whether external, consisting of another entity, or internal, consisting of another cognition—is indeed established by perception itself;
it is only through a conceptualization based on perception that it becomes an object of conventional usage, being employed merely in the form of an absence as "it does not exist."

It depends upon another means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), which is why it is said: "Whatever negation there may be, all of it is due to non-apprehension" (anupalabdhi). However, if it were inferential, then even that non-apprehension of the essential nature (svabhāvānupalabdhi) would be established through the non-apprehension of something else—such as a pervader (vyāpaka)—or through the apprehension of its opposite; in that case, that [second] non-apprehension would also...

[The argument that] "it is by the non-perception of one thing or by the perception of something incompatible with it"—this leads to an infinite regress. For even incompatibility (*virodha*) is determined as a definitional characteristic (*lākṣaṇika*) only upon the certain non-perception of that [incompatible thing] when the other is being perceived.

And this non-perception occurs through non-apprehension (*anupalabdhi*), which results in an infinite regress. Furthermore, the incompatibility consisting in non-coexistence (*sahānavasthāna*) is also insufficient...

The absence [of the effect] when the cause is present [but the other factor is absent] is to be determined through the observation of contradiction; and that absence is established by non-perception (*anupalabdhi*). Thus, as the Master Dharmakīrti stated: "Because of the experience of perceiving one thing, one thinks, 'I do not perceive this.'"
The arising of the conceptualizing intellect occurs as "I perceive" or "I do not perceive."
Through the experience of a qualified form, the [possibility of] identity with or difference from others is excluded;
therefore, there is the perception of that qualified [object], and thus its non-perception also [is established].
Therefore, this non-apprehension is established by perception itself;
otherwise, the non-existence of an object is understood through non-apprehension.

"The non-existence of perception [is established] by means of another; thus there is an infinite regress. Furthermore, every synthesis has its life-force in the synthesis of memory, and it is simply not possible without the unification of objects. Now, if it is said "thus" (*evam*) because of that reason being stated, then [it refers to] one's own conceptual construction—

The syntactical connection of the sentence is as follows: because one follows that logic which, not being supported by worldly consensus (*lokapratīti*), leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) such that "this [series] would be so great. However, if, from our perspective, it is accepted that the self-cognition (*svasaṃvedana*) of cognitions is inward-turned and indeed one and the same, then, due to the absence of a cognition qualified by itself, there is non-existence.

Your statement that "conventional usage is meaningful," and that "the establishment of cognition does not occur through another cognition or through a specific existence," and so forth, is tenable, and not otherwise. For instance, if there were two cognitions occurring at the same time— one of a location with a jar and one of a location without a jar— then of these two, one would be its own...

The sensation would appear precisely as that form; and that [sensation], appearing as distinct from those two forms, while establishing the negation of the self-awareness of two forms, effects the negation of simultaneous dual cognition by means of its very self-luminosity. Therefore, there is no contradiction even in the perception of a restricted object.

If self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*) is not admitted, [the existence of cognition] is not established. Furthermore, even for one who immediately follows logic, it appears that at the moment of perceiving a bare location, the cognition of a jar does not exist.
And it has been stated that following such logic leads to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*). Even granting this, it is said: "Let there be no infinite regress here; in this case..."

But what is to be done? He shows that even this cannot be asserted by saying "or rather" (*yadivā*). In total darkness, everyone has the cognition: "I do not see form. And how could that [cognition] exist?
The meaning of the word "even" (*api*) is that this too is both contrary to experience and fruitless. Why is it not possible?
He says: "by a different sense-faculty.
For this [cognition] belongs to those things—such as a jar or a cloth—which are present and graspable by cognitions produced by non-different sense-faculties.

The rule is this: that [two things] must be apprehended by a single cognition. Now, color and touch, or color and taste, are not apprehended by the same sense organ; therefore, it would be impossible for there to be a single cognition having them as its objects that manifests as both color and touch, or as both color and taste. If, on the other hand, it is argued that color-cognition and touch-cognition occur simultaneously—

If those two [the visual organ and the object] had existed simultaneously, the subsequent conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) would have apprehended them both together, and memory would have remembered them;

yet this is not the case. Thus, by the non-perception of the effect (*kāryānupalabdhi*), the absence of the cognition of form (*rūpajñāna*) is established. To this, it must first be said: according to the principle that "causes do not necessarily [produce their effects]," how can the non-perception of the effect [prove the absence of the cause]?
One might think that it causes [the object] to go to non-existence. If you say that when it has reached another state it no longer exists, let it not be so;

but how can it be said that "that [object] does not exist"? Furthermore, at the time of the cognition of touch, one who considers this to be the absence of the cognition of form performs actions such as withdrawing the lamp and other factors based on that absence within oneself.

It is perceived, but it does not wait for the absence of its effect. Furthermore, how could a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) that precedes the cognition of form (*rūpajñāna*) negate it? For when one is constructing either touch (*sparśa*) or the cognition of touch, there is neither the construction of form nor the construction of the cognition of form. That which is now being constructed as touch—[is what would negate it].

But how could the cognition [of touch] manifest that "at a previous time, the cognition of form did not exist for him"? For when the cognition of form exists at that time, there is no loss whatsoever for the conceptualization of the cognition of touch— even as it belongs to another cognizer— by virtue of which that [cognition of touch], being itself present, [could negate] his own previous cognition of form existing at its own time.
One would establish its existence by means of its non-deviation from [the object's] absence. The same should be stated regarding memory as well.
This is what he says with the words "nor even," and so forth. The connection is "it is not even this. Regarding that, he states the reason for another text with the word "since" (*yataḥ*).
Having stated both—either a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) or memory—as appropriate, [he applies] that very logic...

Because of its proximity, [the author], desiring brevity of the text, addresses the objection of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and its resolution solely by means of recollection (*smṛti*). Now, it may be asked: just as a specific location is the object of visual cognition, so too is the cognition itself the object of both recollection and conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*). In that case, just as through the cognition of the location—[which is a single cognition]— [The text continues: ...[it is established that] there is no contradiction between the two cognitions, since they do not occupy different times or locations. Therefore, even if the object of memory is the cognition itself, there is no fault, because the two cognitions are not distinct in terms of time or place. Thus, the objection is refuted. Furthermore, since the cognition is the object of memory, it is not the case that the object of memory is something other than the cognition; rather, the cognition is apprehended by itself through the medium of memory. Consequently, the status of the object is not compromised. This concludes the refutation of the objection. Thus, the point is established. End of section. End of chapter. End of work. Just as the exclusion of a jar that is present and capable of contact is effected,
so too does tactile cognition, while apprehending a pure object through both memory and conceptual cognition—

By these two [reasons], the rejection of a second, co-existent form-cognition capable of being remembered through conceptualization will be effected. Thus, there is indeed an absence of deviation from the prior absence of a second form-cognition in the case of a mere appearance of tactile cognition being a cognition that is a conceptual memory; so how can there be an absence of non-deviation?

Anticipating this objection, he says: "For [it is] based on memory" (*smārtaṃ hi*). Since this is so, the connection is that there is simply no non-deviation (*avyabhicāra*). For, because it is born from a mental impression (*saṃskāra*), the cognition of memory imitates a prior experience;
it does not, however, manifest [the object] as its own objective domain (*viṣaya*), since the fact that cognitions are known by another [cognition] has been explained at length.

Because it has been refuted. "By which" means by the state of directly realizing autonomy. For if memory were to manifest the previous tactile cognition as an object through its own power of manifestation—that is, through autonomy—then, because it would appear as qualified by a previous time due to appearing as "in the past," [it would follow that] from the tactile cognition...

Cognition of form, which is contrary to the characteristic— that is, the mode— of cognition of touch, being unable to maintain its identity with respect to its own object, [is excluded] from a second cognition of form existing at a prior time, which, by virtue of being associated with the same single cognition, has as its object that which is capable of being the object of a memory-cognition of it.

Just as the cognition of a pure location can lead to the establishment of the non-existence of a jar, such is not the case here. For memory merely imitates a previous experience, specifically that which is related to the object to be remembered. And the experience of the tactile cognition of the object to be remembered must be imitated accordingly. Thus, just as that tactile [experience]—

Knowledge within oneself exists as an internal experience through self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*); at its own time, it does not know even the name of the cognition of form in any way, even according to your own view. Likewise, if the memory of the cognition of touch—which is of a nature that imitates that [cognition of form]—were to occur as a memory of the cognition of form, even then, it would be of the nature of the cognition of touch.

One would simply not remember the coexistence of the two cognitions previously grasped. If one were able to remember it in that way, then—in the absence of remembering their coexistence—one might indeed conclude that there was no coexistence of those two even previously;
this is the intended meaning. The connection [of the phrase] "tataḥ" (therefore) is with the fact that [the cognition] is not directly perceptual by its own power.
The general statement "conceptual cognition" (*vikalpajñāna*) also includes memory; it is with this very intention that he says, "it refers to what has been experienced.
(page 283)

Others, however, say: "Even conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is indeed memory (*smṛti*) from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), because it is produced by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of experience; it is only because the experience has ceased not long ago and [the object] is colored by that [experience] in its entirety, such that the aspect of 'this-ness' (*idantā*) does not manifest, that it does not appear as memory due to its appearing as a direct experience (*anubhava*). Thus, it is called a distinct conceptual construction."

He shows that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) by saying, "I experience. Even if both cognitions (*jñāna*) thus appear within the conceptual construction, nevertheless their coexistence is not perceived, because that [coexistence] was not previously grasped by the two cognitions of the reality (*tattva*), and because the conceptual construction grasps an object independently that was not previously grasped.
By implication. And therefore, let that non-conceptual cognition, while being grasped by a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), be designated as it pleases;

and let the absence of a second cognition be non-different from it. However, this [conceptual construction] lacks the capacity to designate that which was the non-existence of a distinct second cognition at a prior time, because of its own prior nature.

Because neither coexistence nor separation is apprehended in relation to cognition that is distinct from sensation, and because conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) has that [sensation] as its cause, such conventional usage occurs; this is the non-apprehension of the cause (*kāraṇānupalabdhi*). By means of this—namely, by the reason consisting in the non-apprehension of simultaneity with that [sensation] at the time of grasping the pair—one would refute [the existence of the object] at the preceding time.

The connection is as follows: "the conceptual cognition (*vikalpajñāna*) which reflects upon the cognition of touch, which is mounted upon its own manifestation (*svābhāsa*) that is distinct from the cognition of form, [and] which has form as its condition. However, this is not tenable; thus he says, "insofar as...
and "not by itself," because both [cognitions] are restricted to being merely self-cognized (*svasaṃvedana*). "[By that which is born from the impression (*saṃskāra*) of that... means:

Independently, like the cognition of a yogin, there is the grasping of the coexistence or non-coexistence residing in the two preceding cognitions; the meaning is that this occurs by implication because [the subsequent cognition] depends upon the two faces of those two self-awarenesses. And he says "nor even" (*na cāpi*) to indicate that this was stated while merely granting the opponent's position. For it has been said:

"And if the determination were an error, the object would not be established by means of something insentient" (1.3.5). When, however, there is a single reality of consciousness (*cittattva*) that is inward-turned and self-aware,
rather than separate acts of self-awareness, then if two cognitions were to exist simultaneously, [there would be] a single self-awareness—
That [object] would appear when it is at rest; however, since it does not do so during the time of darkness, one determines that there is no cognition of form within oneself,
and thus [one concludes] regarding the entire class of subjects who belong to the same category as oneself.

In the same way, because of the certainty of its absence, one acts without hesitation in worldly affairs—such as covering or shielding the body for the purpose of avoiding the distress produced by extreme heat; thus, what was desired is established. As for the one who says that the existence of the mind is the regulator for the production of a single cognition, for him too, there is no simultaneity of cognitions.

Once the restriction to the object of cognition (*padyaniyama*) is established, the perfection of the mind (*manaḥsiddhi*) follows; however, one must consider why that very [restriction] is so. Furthermore, because they exist at the same time as another cognition, two cognitions would necessarily have to be apprehended by that other cognition. Why? Because even though they exist at the same time, mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) and the like are not apprehended by another cognition. Moreover, the self (*ātman*) is one and is the locus of inherence (*samavāyin*) for those cognitions.
Even while existing as the cause, how could one know: "Two cognitions have not arisen in me"? [Objection:
But surely, upon their arising, two objects would be manifested. [Reply: Ah! What is this deluded prattle?
For the statement "two objects are manifested" refers to nothing other than the two cognitions themselves, and that is precisely what has been questioned. As for manifestation...
Furthermore, even regarding the nature of objects (*arthadharmatā*), how is it known that the manifestation (*prakāśa*) has not arisen as residing in both form and taste?

Moreover, if cognition were produced without manifestation, there would be no awareness of the distinction between self and other. For instance, who are you whose cognition of a jar exists? The cognition of a jar belongs to another as well; the inherence (*samavāya*) is also the same. [It must be] the Self (*ātman*).

"It does not manifest," or "it manifests through another cognition"—all such claims are equally problematic. Therefore, one must accept a single, inward-turned reality of consciousness (*saṃvittattva*) characterized by self-luminosity that is independent of anything else. When this exists, there is no room for any kind of error or delusion. For instance, if there were two cognitions:

One of these must be self-awareness (*svasaṃvedana*). Yet, it cannot be one [of the two], because it appears merely as the self-awareness of the cognition of touch, as has already been stated. That which shines forth by its own luminosity, independent of anything else, is "I"; that which does not do so is "the other. Thus, everything is settled.

This is what he expresses with the words "tadevam" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "even of those [cognitions] produced by the senses": the meaning is that if even for those [senses] upon whose existence the entire world relies—feeling secure that "this has been grasped" and "this has not been grasped"—such is the state of affairs, then what confidence can there be in other forms of knowledge? Regarding the phrase "even of objects": [knowledge...]

For the restriction of the existence of an object is indeed established by a restrictive rule; if that were not restricted, how could there be even the conventional usage of "separation from a particular location"?
(page 285)

We have stated that because it is inferential, it is undermined by the fallacy of infinite regress; thus, there can be no certain determination of the rule regarding existence or non-existence with respect to objects perceivable by a single sense organ. The word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even the word 'one'" (*ekaśabdo'pi*) implies that not only has the scriptural term *cidvapuḥ* been explained by this [word], but the word "one" as well—this is the force of the particle *api*. Now, [one might object]: what of the many cognitions?

Apprehension is not the grasping [of an object] through another conceptualization (*vikalpa*), nor is it the case that another conceptualization itself is the true nature of consciousness (*cittattva*).
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And in memory, etc. For it has been stated that one cognition is not cognizable by another cognition.
Therefore, that single inward-turned form which these [cognitions] possess is, by virtue of its own will, [the source of their manifestation].

As long as one desires to grasp [an object], so long does it appear; thus, there is no consequence of simultaneous synthesis of all [objects]. Regarding the consequence stated in the sūtra "it would perish" (*naśyet*), that has been explained in the preceding commentary (*vṛtti*).
How so? By that very same [explanation], the portion of the sūtra beginning with "if not" (*na cet*) is also explained.

Disregarding that very point, one must not rest right here; for since the manifestation of the state of being a person (*janasthiti*) cannot be denied by a mere curse such as "let it perish," that reversal of the context which occurs by force alone is explained here in the *Vṛtti*. However, the commentator has also explained [the reading] as "let it be known" (*naśyet* = *jñāyet*).

It was stated at the very beginning that [the author] demonstrates the impossibility of such a restriction. Now, one might object: "If this single conscious essence (*cidvapuḥ*) is indeed filled by the entire circle of objective entities, then those entities would necessarily appear either always manifest or always submerged;
how then can their diversity be occasional? Anticipating this doubt:

With the intention that the very freedom of luminosity (*prakāśasvācchandyam*) is the nature of consciousness (*cittattvam*), that which was stated in the *Sūtra* beginning with "in knowledge" (*jñāne*) and described in the *Vṛtti* beginning with "of this very [consciousness]" (*asyaiva*),
he now explains by saying "and of that, thus" (*tasya caivam*). By the aforementioned arguments,
[he establishes] the oneness of that [consciousness].
"The luminous self is the object to be illuminated" (1.5.3),
and so on,
according to the Master.
The power called knowledge belongs to that which is full of all states of being, as will be explained in the following passages beginning with "iti". What follows from this?
(page 286)

He said: Having assumed the various forms of each respective entity—whether manifest or unmanifest—that which exists as the manifestation of the independent [subject], yet because it is non-different from consciousness, appears as "this" by prioritizing an insentient nature consisting of a separation from that [consciousness] and whose very life is dependence; this [is what resides] within the limited subject (*paśupramātṛ*). In that regard, that which...

The connection is as follows: that power called "knowledge" (jñāna) is that whose essential nature consists in the exercise of capacity, which is itself characterized by autonomy. This is what is meant:
[it is] that of which [the power] of will alone... [is the source].

According to this principle, the Blessed One—who is filled with all things beyond enumeration—by virtue of His absolute freedom (*svātantrya*), separates a certain entity from the midst of the mass of entities as being distinct from the nature of light (*prakāśa-svarūpa*), and then manifests that which has been separated; for it would not be logical to manifest something that has not been separated [from the light]. Thus, it is not [the case that He manifests an external object].

He does not separate [the limited subject] from the Great Light; rather, He fashions the illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*) as a form of non-ultimate light that is superimposed. Furthermore, this manifestation through contraction is itself called the Lord’s own creation within His own self. And thus, the illusory subject [is distinct] from the body—

As long as it exists with a nature of light that is fragmented and contracted, it manifests an object as distinct from itself; that outward-turned form of its, colored by ever-new shadows of that [object], is called ever-new knowledge (*jñāna*). And therein, that which is the divine sovereignty (*svātantrya*) is—

The two functions are "the power of knowledge" (*jñānaśakti*) and "manifestation" (*avabhāsana*). Nevertheless, since the nine manifestations are seized by arising and dissolution at every moment, how can they be of use for worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)?
[The answer is: that which was previously an outward-turned consciousness regarding a manifested object, its inward-turned [aspect]...

Form (*rūpa*), while persisting for a period of time, reflects upon that very same extroversion directed toward a specific object residing within its own self; this is said to be "remembering" by the subject of *māyā*. In that regard, the capacity to manifest such a subject and so forth is the Lord’s power of memory (*smṛti-śakti*). That which...

He will say, "of the object previously illuminated. By this, he will explain the utility of the prior cognition by way of its having been previously illuminated. The "prior" [cognition] refers to that consisting of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) directed toward externality and so forth, not the present one; in that context, there is a "new" manifestation (*prakāśa*). Thus, even in the word *prakhyāpana*, there are two causative suffixes (*ṇic*).

(Page 287) Now, one might ask: "Why is this power (*śakti*) of the Blessed One, consisting of knowledge and so forth, so designated? Anticipating this objection, he says: "Because of the difference in results. This refers to the object of instruction within the undivided sphere of reality (*akhaṇḍamaṇḍala*), which performs infinite purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*).
Since linguistic usage, such as instruction and so forth, would not be established [otherwise], for the sake of establishing that, by means of various diverse causal efficacies (*arthakriyā*),

each [entity] is delimited and that single object is designated in many ways— as "fire is a burner," "a cooker," or "an illuminator. In that regard, when there is a predominance of the reflective awareness of multiplicity, it is called a "power" (*śakti*).

Regarding linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*): when there is a predominance of a single reflective awareness of that [object], there arises a corresponding conventional usage. Furthermore, even this is not unreal, because it has been created by the Supreme Lord himself in that manner. As it is said in the *Āgama*:
"The burning power of fire is not perceived as something separate [from the fire itself]."
"This is merely the beginning of the existence of pure knowledge upon entering [it]" (Vi.bhai. 19), and likewise:
"The power of Śiva is here called the mouth" (Vi.bhai. 20).

And so forth. Let this matter rest for now. Now, one might ask: "For what purpose is the word 'great' (mahat) included in the Sūtra? For its sovereignty is indeed obtained simply through the possession of that power. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And that... Although such knowledge belongs to the bound soul (paśu-pramātṛ), and therefore he too is not *not* the Lord by virtue of that power, [he is nonetheless distinct].

Nevertheless, his own will does not prevail there, because he lacks the quality of having unimpeded resolve. Therefore, he alone whose will is unobstructed in that regard—namely Maheśvara—is endowed with such power. For it has been taught by the Blessed One in the Āgama:
"The power of the Lord, the self, and the vital breath—these three together," and so forth.
Therefore, in reality, it is logical that the Blessed Lord alone knows, remembers, and excludes [objects] through those respective forms.
As it has been said:
Although it has been stated [in the *Āgamaprāmāṇyasiddhi*] that "the status of an object...

(APSi 20), etc., it is logical here [to say] "he possesses knowledge, etc. with that intention. However, for the subjects under the influence of *māyā*, the very non-manifestation of their non-separateness from the Supreme Lord constitutes their state as subjects under *māyā*; this is the intention of the Blessed One.
In the *Gītā*,

the phrase "from me" (*mattaḥ*) indicates that this [result] arises from my power (*matsāmarthyāt*), and not that it belongs to me; furthermore, this very point is expressed here in the aphorism by the word "power" (*śakti*).

By showing that knowledge and the rest do not belong to me merely by being touched, but rather that which exists through its power is my sovereignty (*svātantrya*), [the author] indicates that the term "power of knowledge" (*jñānaśakti*) is to be analyzed in both ways in various places: either as "knowledge itself is the power" (*jñānam eva śaktiḥ*) or as "the power belonging to that [knowledge]" (*tasya ca śaktiḥ*). For this very reason, the power of will (*icchāśakti*) is not separately mentioned here.

Even though it is mentioned in the Āgamas, she is accepted by the very terms *amaheśvara* and *śakti*, which express the unimpeded nature of knowledge and the other [powers]. Furthermore, for one who maintains that the ultimate reality consists of the essence of manifestation (*ābhāsa*), based on the appearance of uncontradicted cognition such as "Fire is power" and "It burns," power (*śakti*) and action (*kriyā*) are one and the same.

Both [theories] must be accepted. However, although that [power] is distinct from the object, it is the very nature of an entity—which, being pervasive, performs multiple causal functions—and because it is not perceived as separate, it must be understood through inference and presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), as it is determined by the force of the distinction between different causal functions; what contradiction is there? This is *śakti* (power).

As for the objection that "if the power acts, it must be created by the possessor of the power (the potent), and if the power is joined with another power, there is an infinite regress," this is of no consequence; for since it does not exceed the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of the entity, whether it be eternal or non-eternal according to what is observed, what loss is there? For this very reason, the challenge—"What is the use of auxiliary causes (sahakārin) for the arising of the effect?"—is likewise [invalid].

Since there is no contradiction in the appearance [of the cause] being the same even when other auxiliary factors are present—due to its being uncontradicted—how can those auxiliaries be denied? This same principle applies to potencies as well. Thus, this potency is said to be "residing" by being brought forward as the very nature of the entity; it does not appear as something separate from that nature. Therefore, it is a potency co-inherent with the essential nature (*svarūpa-sahakārin*).

The dual status of categories as both efficient cause (*kāraṇa*) and essential nature (*lakṣaṇa*), as well as the claim that this is "power" (*śakti*), does not bring any harm whatsoever to our position; indeed, all of this is already accepted in the scriptures (*āgama*). As it has been said:
"That power which is described as inherent (*samavāyinī*) in the Creator of the world..."
"O Goddess, that [power] becomes his Will when he desires to create. (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 3.5) [page 289]
"Yoga is his own inherent powers... (Mālinīvijayottara Tantra 4.5).
Thus, all this world is his powers, while Maheśvara is the possessor of power.
Thus, the power (śakti) beginning with Vidyā and the rest belongs to Śambhu as his consort.
And thus: "it bears fruit" means it reaches its culmination as a result; it is not, however, obstructed for him. Other [powers]...

Those causes which consist of the auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), the material cause (*upādāna*), and so forth— their capacity, or indeed that very capacity itself, brings about the power of those [beings] from Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śakra down to the subject who is a mere worm, by means of their cooperation and association, because they depend upon the face of the Lord’s determined power.

Due to their complete exhaustion, although they possess their own powers and are thus *īśvaras*, they are not *maheśvaras*—that is to say, they do not possess supreme lordship. Likewise, "thus" means that even though [the Lord] is of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*) by virtue of having the universal form (*viśvarūpatā*), He is so because He brings about knowledge and other faculties, and because He effects the maintenance of all living beings. Now, let it be granted that the Blessed Maheśvara possesses such a nature; however, by that much alone—

But what is the point of accepting a single Self? Furthermore, there are two doubts: how could the universal form of Maheśvara and His possession of powers such as knowledge—which exceed the nature of mere consciousness—be the form of the luminous self-awareness, given that they are insentient and thus non-luminous?

"It obstructs the *cittattva* (the nature of consciousness). This resolves the first objection: that the *cittattva* itself is the form of Maheśvara, and that there is no self (*ātman*) whatsoever other than the *cittattva*. Furthermore, the *cittattva* is said to be nothing other than the sovereignty of light (*prakāśa-svātantrya*). And its manifestation as the self-nature of the universe is precisely what is called "newly appearing."

Now, the reflective awareness (*parāmarśana*) of the objects of knowledge and the knowing subject as being merely an appearance of a human being is, in brief, fourfold through their mutual differentiation; furthermore, from the perspective of its full expansion (*prastāra*), it consists of tens of millions of billions of varieties. Thus, the manifestation of exclusion (*apohana*) should be understood as having also dispelled other potential doubts.
"At the beginning" means for this very reason, as [stated] in the passage beginning with "yathābhīṣṛ... (1.6.11).
(Page 290)

In such passages as "by way of having been previously manifested," [the author] excludes a new manifestation—just as in the case of recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) and the like—by means of the distinction between subjects (*pramātṛ*) regarding the previous manifestation and that which follows upon the previous manifestation. And since manifestation is invariably concomitant with it, the previous reflective awareness (*pūrvavimarśa*) remains present as well. Furthermore, the employment of the instrumental case (*tṛtīyā*) likewise refers to such reflective awareness.

He said: "As they have stated, 'even that which is momentary is grasped. However, although reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) pertains to the present, it does not bestow upon the object either its temporality or its manifestation at that specific time; rather, it rests solely in the non-removal of the previous manifestation and awareness. Having thus explained cognition and memory, [he continues:]

He explains *apohana* with the words beginning "place" (*deśa*), and so forth. That sovereign power of the Lord by which the conceptual cognition—residing in the illusory subject (*māyīya-pramātṛ*) and consisting of mental construction—is brought about or accomplished, is what is denoted by the term *apohana*. How is it brought about? He says: by means of the differentiation of manifestations (*avabhāsa-bheda*) [of] the non-conceptual...

The latent impression (*vāsanā*) in the form of a mental trace (*saṃskāra*) which has been produced by an object that appeared [to consciousness],—by that alone, when it is awakened even without the appearance of a further object and so forth, and having gained its functional activity in performing its own effect characterized as conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). How is its awakening? It is said: by the appearance of space (*deśa*) and by the appearance of time (*kāla*).

Previously, the particular (svalakṣaṇa), consisting of the fusion of appearances, manifested as delimited; [now it manifests] by the removal of that very delimitation by space and time. For this very reason, when the spatial delimitation of that appearance is removed, there is omnipresence (vibhutva), and when the temporal delimitation is removed, there is eternity (nityatva). And that...
Appearance, which is the object of conceptual construction, is called the universal;
therefore, whatever particularity is perceived by means of a certain property [is the universal].
It cannot be established by anything other than that; therefore, its distinct status is determined by it alone.

And according to this principle, since conceptualization arises with respect to every manifestation, even when conceptualization occurs regarding the manifestations of space and time, it occurs as having a universal nature because it is not delimited by [specific] space and time. Even the conceptualization "this" is delimited; it is a reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of a form common to all present objects situated in front.
It is indeed the self. As it has been stated by the venerable Teacher himself (p.
"This reflective awareness that 'this [object] is determined' occurs with respect to that which stands before one."
It arises solely through the commonality of the "this-ness" (idantā) inherent in all existing things.

Thus it is said. What need is there for more? Even that specific distinction which predominates in the meaning of a sentence—which flashes forth even in conceptual thought during the assembly of differentiated objects, such as "Now this cow is seen by me"—and which involves the ascertainment of each individual word-meaning accepted therein, must necessarily be common to other such sentence-meanings existing in different places, times, and subjects.

It arises by taking form as its object. Therefore, every conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) manifests a universal (*sāmānya*) that is devoid of the delimitation of spatial, temporal, and other such appearances. [Objection: But when something has been experienced as delimited by space and so forth, how can it be awakened by a latent impression (*vāsanā*) produced by that [experience] to have an object delimited by those same factors? [Reply: It is said: they are diverse and not to be questioned.

From the very will of the Blessed Lord Śiva, whose form is Great Light, the universe—which is characterized primarily by mutual differentiation—is brought forth; and from that same source, she manifests the subjects of *māyā*, who serve as the foundational ground for the manifestation of that differentiation.
This occurs through such a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) consisting of a general manifestation. Now, [one might ask], what is this conceptual construction?

Anticipating the objection— "Why is that power of the Blessed One which produces [cognition] not called simply 'the power of knowledge' (*jñānaśakti*), and why is it instead called 'the power of exclusion' (*apohanaśakti*) in its specific form when that [knowledge] is seen?"— he says "the suspected" (*śaṅkita*). Those opponents who have been suspected— that is, superimposed by virtue of doubt— are those whose bodies are the intended blue [object].

The exclusion of those properties— such as the incapacity to perform the specific causal function— that are conceptually constructed as distinct from the properties of entering [the cognition] which do perform various causal functions; this exclusion consists in the removal of those [properties], like pulling them by the neck with one's hand, even though they are present before one.

The state (*tattva*) of those for whom that very thing—the supreme, primary duty consisting of an uncommon operation—is their essence: for that reason, that power which generates conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is called "the power of exclusion" (*apohanaśakti*), because it generates a form in which exclusion is predominant; such is the connection [of the words]. This is what is meant: although conceptual construction...

Although it appears at first glance that cognition has various forms, nevertheless, because it imitates, enters into, or depends upon that [object], it follows for this reason that it is itself [determined] by the object, the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). (Page 292)

Because it has not attained the status of being an object of knowledge—whether by means of a generality consisting of the fusion of appearances, or merely through the appearance of identity—it is possible even in the absence of an external object. Thus, this [process] which operates in various ways is an undertaking once the goal is already established; "twice-bound" refers to firmness (*dārḍhya*), and that is as follows:

According to the principle that "doubts are [resolved] by the exclusion of others," it is precisely the operation of *apoha* (exclusion) that is described as having the nature of excluding others. And here, [the categories of] action, relation, generality, and so forth... (2.2.1).
Thus, although a universal may arise through the process of future possibility, it is accepted either by direct perception or through the nature of experience;

therefore, even that acceptance is not the operation of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Now, one might object: when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) is manifest, how can there be any suspicion of what is not of that nature (*atadrūpa*) which could then be excluded (*apohyate*)?
Because there exists a relationship of sublated and sublator between the mind of ascertainment and the mind of superimposition,
[the latter] would not [arise] if another quality were not joined [to the object] by means of a cause of error.
Or the form of silver [appears] in a mother-of-pearl shell.

If it is argued that there is apprehension due to superimposition (*samāropa*) by means of such a view, [we reply: since superimposition has a conceptualized object as its domain, and since every other conceptualization is likewise preceded by superimposition, there would be an infinite regress (*anavasthā*) of a succession of conceptualizations and superimpositions; thus, even in millions of aeons (*yugakoṭi*), there would be no certain determination of blue. Furthermore, there are many branches of fallacies, such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). If...
In the *Apohasiddhi*, Bhaṭṭa stated that the exclusion of other cognitions occurs through implication alone: "With regard to blue, [the cognition] 'this is not non-blue' [arises]."
"It must be performed by means of the counter-positive of exclusion;
it does not depend upon the presence of a superimposition."
And so forth. Even in that case, one must state: when a specific object has appeared, what occasion is there for the possibility of it being otherwise?

[One might say: "The possibility or superimposition is produced by ignorance (*avidyā*); it is beginningless. [If you say: "Habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) consists in the capacity to generate such things as the possibility or superimposition," [we reply:]...
That very same infinite regress results from the conceptualization and the superimposition [of one upon the other], because both of these are themselves of the nature of conceptual construction.
For blue is superimposed by conceptualizing it as non-blue, and when non-blue is being conceptually constructed, blue is superimposed.

The Naiyāyikas have also demonstrated many branches of refutation, such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*). Furthermore, regarding the claim that "the internal and external forms are apprehended by conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as superimposed," even in that case, if they lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāvatva*), it follows that there would be no distinction between the conceptual constructions of blue and yellow. If you argue, "Blue is apprehended by conceptual construction as if it were [external], but not as blue itself," then what [is the basis for this]?

By that [conceptualization], it is grasped as "as if blue," such that it is compared to or superposed upon [the blue]; for through the determination (*adhyavasāya*), it appears as if in the blue, but not as the manifestation itself. Furthermore, what is the nature of that [manifestation] by which it could be designated in this way? Therefore, there is no distinction of the object of conceptualization from another conceptualization, whether by way of the apprehended aspect (*grāhyāṃśa*) or the determined aspect (*adhyavaseyāṃśa*).
This is appropriate. For what distinction can there be for that which is insubstantial? Indeed, how could there be two real entities within a single reality? As Bhaṭṭa [said]:
"And absence is not distinguished [as a separate entity]."

If it is argued that there is a distinction [between the object and its cognition] by way of the external form superimposed [upon the cognition] as the object of determination (*adhyavaseya*), then since even this superimposition is of the nature of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), the same infinite regress (*aniṣṭhā*) follows. Even when it is said that "blue is the object" merely by way of conceit (*abhimāna*), one must ask whether that object is manifested or unmanifested within that conceit; no third alternative is possible.

As for what was said regarding those who consider themselves experts in the delivery of variegated blows and the like, there, the term "conceit" (abhimāna) denotes merely the perception of similarity. For the form of the weapon as it falls is exactly the same as that of the painted weapon situated within the hand-configuration of the painted assailant.

And just as a wise man bears a certain appearance—due to his wisdom being accompanied by delusion, or due to his supreme wisdom regarding the ultimate truth—he carries himself with a neck held high and is intent upon performing deeds such as teaching for the benefit of all people;
in exactly the same way does even one who is unwise. Furthermore, wherever he hears from the world, "This man is wise," there...

Seeing some particular form and desiring for oneself such gains, honors, and so forth, one deliberately assumes that form; this is called the conceit of scholarship (*pāṇḍityābhimāna*). Thus, by means of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), nothing at all of the blue [object] is heard or seen.

Or rather, one might form such a conceit (*abhimāna*). Even though conceits such as superimposition (*āropa*) are mental factors (*cittadharma*) like shame and so forth, they lack the power to touch the actual object; therefore, an object constructed by conceit is not [a real] object. [This has been] refuted.

And regarding the fact that determination (*adhyavasāya*) rests solely upon its own internal appearance, and concerning the error of such determination— as stated in [Dignāga’s *Pramāṇasamuccaya*] 1.3.5:
"Therefore, when the particular characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) has appeared, how could a form contrary to it be suspected, by which..."
He dispels the student's apprehension that "the removal of that [superimposition] would be fruitful" by stating "as a distinct entity.

Here, it might be suspected that a thing could lack that nature either because it is mixed with another object—like milk and water—or because its very essence is that of a different object. However, neither of these two possibilities is tenable.

This has been stated by means of two qualifiers: even though an entity— which is unconnected with other objects, unmixed with others, restricted to its own context, and of a single nature— appears through its very own nature as performing various purposeful actions,
and even though it appears as if turned away (avāṅmukhībhūta) due to the power of illusion (māyāśakti), nevertheless, precisely because it is manifest, there [exists] a single...

One who desires a specific purposeful action suspects various and numerous opposing factors that are devoid of performing that particular action; for example, when a jar performs hundreds of purposeful actions such as carrying water, removing thirst, or obstructing the expanse of the sky, one who requires it for carrying water suspects those things that do not perform that function.
One might suspect that a jar is not red or not elevated by means of its captivating nature and so forth. If one asks why, he says:

"Because of their mutual identity. For even though a single entity is in reality identical with others, even if it is rendered separate by the power of *māyā*, nevertheless, precisely because it appears as such, it manifests their mutual identity.

To the question "How so?", he says: "The Lord (Īśvara). The Lord is the nature of the self-awareness "I am all this. His state of being a limb (*aṅgabhāva*) means his inseparability (*tadavinirbhaktatām*). For it has been stated that if one does not reach the limit of that [inseparability], there would be no manifestation at all. And although manifestation extends up to the realization of identity with Supreme Śiva, [the process continues further].
Nevertheless, because the nature of an entity does not manifest there in any way whatsoever, there is no mutual identity at all;
however, where that [nature] has manifested, that very thing is shown to be the Lord (Īśvara). And that [identity] is not established there through contact with Māyā.
(Page 295) By the word "as if" (*iva*), it is stated that [the individual soul] would become a limb of the Lord, such that there would be a state of mutual identity. Thus,
without the refutation of each respective counter-argument as it is being raised, that [objection] remains by itself.

A cognizer who seeks purposeful action (*arthakriyā*) is unable, by means of that [cognition], to engage in worldly transaction (*vyavahāra*)—that is, to make himself capable of rejecting, accepting, buying, or selling—and likewise cannot cause another to engage in such transaction. The same applies to the second [party]. Consequently, how can there be a mutual worldly transaction? This is likewise the case regarding the body, speech, and so forth.

Even when an object exists in the form of an illusory subject (*māyā-pramātṛ*), other subjects and objects of knowledge that stand as its opposites must be negated. To this extent, even within a single entity, because there are many factors opposed to its various specific causal functions due to its capacity for multiple effects, [this process] is performed by establishing numerous conceptual alternatives (*vikalpa*) through the removal of such doubts.
By this very [principle], it is explained that even though there are many individuals— such as "the pot is high" or "red," or "I am thin, fair-complexioned, and have weak digestion"—

there is a unity of conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Thus, although an object such as a herd of cows performs various purposeful actions (*arthakriyā*) according to the differences among its individuals,
it remains unmixed with other categories of objects, such as the class of buffaloes and the like.

In that regard, suppose someone desires a specific, singular [entity]—the object of a single conceptual reflection—which possesses a restricted nature capable of performing a specific purposeful action (*arthakriyā*), such as carrying or milking, and which occurs only within those very individuals [that possess that nature].
For that person, there are counter-entities (*pratipakṣa*) that do not perform that action and which might be suspected; and regarding that suspicion:

The reason is as stated before: it is one. And thus, through the exclusion (*apohana*) of a single counter-correlate consisting of the class of entities such as buffaloes and the like, there arises a single conceptual cognition (*vikalpa*)—namely, "cow, cow"—even with respect to many individuals. As it was said by the venerable Teacher himself: "There are as many groups of non-performers of that [specific] causal function as there are types of causal functions."
There are as many superimpositions upon that [reality] as there are negations of it; they are equal in number.
Thus: "Likewise,

that single reflective judgment which occurs even with respect to many things that perform a certain action— this too must have a basis, since it arises from the commonality of their exclusion from those that do not perform that action."

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "If fullness consists in being another self while being a limb of the Lord, then it is more logical that this is rather the ultimate form, the very nature [of the soul]. To this, he replies: "Of those belonging to Māyā" (p.

For this state of māyā belonging to the subjects (pramātṛ) and the objects of knowledge (prameya) is now being investigated. In that regard, if [the world] were of an ultimately real nature, its very status as māyā would be sublated. That which is infinitely branched, [arising] from subjects with respect to subjects, from subjects with respect to objects, and from objects with respect to both—

Enumeration (*saṃkhyā*) means division or differentiation; for this very [differentiation] is the primary form inherent in the state of being composed of *māyā*. This is the intended meaning: here, because their essential nature is pure luminosity, there is indeed an immersion into a single form through identity with all subjects and objects whatsoever.
It is real; and even within the realm of *māyā*, it remains unceasing, for otherwise there would be the consequence of its non-manifestation. It is simply this:

by the power of the sovereign capacity (*svātantrya-śakti*) whose nature consists of the reflective awareness "not as other than one another," while remaining unreflected upon, it initially remains, as it were, indifferent within its full essential nature—like the poison or fire of a serpent whose fangs have been paralyzed by a powerful person. Of which [it is said]:

Whatever form is real, even if it is obstructed by the power of one who knows that [reality], its capacity to destroy the object—like a poison—is not denied. And thus, the universe possesses the nature of the Universal Self (*viśvātmatva*). For the cause of non-suspicion is either the impossibility of that [destructive] nature existing in it, or, even if that nature were present, its non-perception. Indeed, not...

The fact that hunger is pacified by food is suspected [to be false] by a child, or the lethality of a venomous serpent whose power has been paralyzed; this is the "perception of what is incompatible with the cause" (*kāraṇaviruddhopalabdhi*). Furthermore, for every cognizer, such a state of being the Self of Īśvara indeed shines forth; thus, the nature of being the Self of the universe is not unmanifested. As it was said in the *Ādi*—:

In the *Siddhasūtra*, [it is said]: "For without this, there would be emptiness of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and so forth. Furthermore, even in the state of *māyā*, the doubt that the Lord (*īśvara*), who is the latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that light, has not transcended [the state] arises precisely from the majesty of the subject (*pramātṛ*); as will be stated:
"Because it consists merely in the exclusion of what is not that, by means of the manifestation of that [object] and the non-manifestation of the other,
this conceptual construction 'this is a jar' is said to be a determination of that [object]" (1.6.3),
and so forth; by which there is no consequence of faults such as infinite regress caused by separate conceptualization, superimposition, and the like.
As for that which was stated by the Noble One: "For a person established in a single cognition called 'unified reflection' (ekapratyavamarśa),
the cognizer himself distinguishes between entities that are causes of that [reflection] and those that are not."
(Page 297) Thus, it will be explained later that even an object that has flashed forth [in consciousness] is difficult to establish. Now, one might ask:

"But *apohana* is the very body of cognition (*jñāna*)—specifically of that which takes the form of conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and of memory (*smṛti*), which is a particular kind of conceptualization. What, then, is its [nature]?"

By way of separate enumeration: how could these beginningless [impurities] residing in an illusory subject (māyīya-pramātṛ) exist in Arjuna’s Guru, who is of the nature of a non-illusory subject (amāyīya-pramātṛ), since one does not observe the functioning of attributes belonging to one thing in another?
He dispels these two doubts with the word "tat" (that). For all those worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) which are characterized by duality...

They have been enlivened, being impelled by this power of removal (*apohana-śakti*); therefore, although it is internal, it is mentioned separately because of its predominance. Nor is he a guru who is a subject under *māyā*; rather, he is one by whom the state of the Great Lord (*maheśvarabhāva*), that is, sovereignty (*māheśvarya*), has been pervaded and accepted on all sides (*ā-samantāt*). Thus he is.
"Assuming the form of the teacher, Śiva cuts the bonds.
Thus, it is stated in the Āgama that the true status of being a teacher belongs to the Supreme Lord alone, who presides over the teacher through non-difference. For instance:
"I give you divine vision; behold my sovereign yoga" (11.8);
thus, "behold today the entire universe, with its moving and unmoving beings, situated here in one place."
"In my body... (11.7).
With these words, he bestowed upon Arjuna the realization that the entire universe resides within his own body as the Supreme Self.
This was done solely for the sake of the present context, as it will be of further utility through its integration with the future narrative.

"These are all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra"—(11.26)—he displayed such things as they actually existed at that time; otherwise, it would have been a mere illusion (*indrajāla*), since at that moment they were situated outside exactly as they were. And thus, its utility was indeed demonstrated.
"And whatever else you wish to see" (11.7).
Thus, in all instances, the term "I" refers exclusively to the ultimate nature consisting of light (*prakāśa*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).
(Page 298)

But this is not a matter of illusory four-armed forms and the like, because that would contradict perception and other means of knowledge such as [the statement] "I am the Himalaya" regarding stationary objects; for it is I who am praised everywhere, expanding through the multitude of all states of being.

I spontaneously bow down to that Goddess, the abiding state of one's own Self, whose nature is the manifestation of "I" in its full activity— the wondrous realization of the ultimate truth that is devoid of interruption.

Thus [it is said]. Now, one might object: "Even so, since the Lord's being composed of *māyā* is untenable, how can there be a connection with conceptual construction (*vikalpa*)? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "The operation of conceptual construction. For the Lord does not possess such attributes as the manifestation of what was never before known, recollection, or conceptualization; rather, these arise for subjects under the influence of *māyā* through His sovereignty—thus [the state] of the Lord [is established].
In each respective case, autonomy is called the powers of knowledge (*jñāna*) and so forth; it is for this very purpose that the term "power" (*śakti*) is employed.
Conceptualization (*vikalpana*) is the activity belonging to the limited subject (*paśu-pramātṛ*), which must be performed by the power of the Lord.

For it is the Lord alone who assumes the reflective awareness of "not-this" (*neti-vimarśa*) in the state of Īśvara. [This occurs] through the non-exclusion of the reflective awareness of "not-this"...

For in the act of unification (*mīlana*), since the state of "this-ness" (*idambhāva*)—which consists of the reflective awareness of all aspects other than the nature of consciousness—is entirely absent, how could there be a cognition consisting of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of "I am this" (*idamahamiti*)?
Therefore, even in that case, that power of exclusion (*apohana*) certainly exists. As it has been said:
The period (daśā) has Rudra as its presiding deity; it is of the nature of negation, and in the northeast quarter, I am indeed everything.

Thus, it is in the *Gītā* that the very nature of the Lord (*īśvaratā*) is shown to be his universal form (*viśvarūpatā*). Here too, for this very reason, it is said that "he has internalized the infinite universal form. And precisely because of this non-distinction from the universal form, even the subjects under the influence of *māyā* appear there as non-different from the ultimate reality; this applies to conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) and so forth as well.

O Blessed One, [these states] are not ultimately far removed. For that very reason, the qualification by the meaning of all words—such as "knowing," "acting," "illuminating," and so forth—would not be restricted; otherwise, if conceptualization and the like were possible within one's own self, then whatever "taste" might arise therein, one would simply be "unaware" of it regarding one's own object.
Omniscience and all such qualities would necessarily belong to him in common with everyone else, because they are restricted solely to that [one source];

however, due to their limitation, they do not belong to him as something illusory (*māyīya*). Therefore, the phrase "from me" (*mattaḥ*) establishes both the causality and the substratum-nature of one's own self.

It is accepted [as a separate category] by the fifth [author]. It occurs [in the locative case] when the cause (*hetu*) is intended, and also when the suffix *lyap* is elided, as in the phrase "from which" (*yataḥ*). Now, one might object: "Previously, it was stated that 'the agent' and 'the knower' are indeed the powers of knowledge and action in the Lord; but now, memory and the power of exclusion (*apohana*) are mentioned as additional—what does this mean?
Anticipating this doubt, he says: "And" (*ca*). [This means that] cognitions, memory, and direct perception [are all included].
And conceptualization is what is expressed by the word "exclusion" (apohana). In that regard, it is power (śakti), and those very [powers] are power. || 7 ||

Thus ends the third chapter, the Investigation into the Inconsistency of Other Philosophical Systems, within the *Jñānādhikāra* (Chapter on Knowledge) of the *Īśvarapratyabhijñāvivṛtivimarśinī*, composed by the illustrious Mahāmāheśvara, the venerable Ācārya Abhinavagupta. || 3 ||
